seven-symbol source on which top-down splitting is exactly balanced at the
first two levels and still overpays:

p(a), \dots, p(g) \;=\; .01,\; .24,\; .05,\; .20,\; .47,\; .01,\; .02 .

The split \{a, b, c, d\} against \{e, f, g\} carries mass .50 against
.50, and the next split of the left half is .25 against .25. The
resulting code spends 2 bits on e and 3 bits on every other symbol:
L = 2 \cdot .47 + 3 \cdot .53 = 2.53 bits. The optimal symbol code for
the same source, built by the merge rule in exercise 8, has lengths
(6, 2, 4, 3, 1, 6, 5) and L = 1.97 bits. Perfect balance overpaid by
0.56 bits per symbol, 28%, on a source of entropy H \approx 1.93.

The failure is structural. A top-down splitter commits the short
codewords first, while it sees only coarse halves of the mass: here it
locks e, nearly half of all draws, into 2 bits before ever examining the
rare symbols. The fix reverses the direction of construction.

A perfectly balanced top-down split can overpay by half a bit per symbol.
Optimality requires deciding the tree bottom-up: the deepest level first,
rarest symbols first.

documents.title: The algorithm: merge the two least probable, repeat
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Source coding › Huffman coding › The algorithm: merge the two least probable, repeat
documents.text:
The algorithm: merge the two least probable, repeat

Required: for a known distribution p, a prefix code minimizing the
expected length L = \sum_x p(x)\,\ell(x) of
Prefix codes and code trees. Method, from
Huffman's 1952 paper: build
the code tree from its leaves, maintaining a pool of weighted subtrees.

Initialize. One node per symbol, weighted by its probability.

Merge. Remove the two nodes of smallest weight; make them the two
children of a new node whose weight is their sum; return the new node
to the pool.

Repeat until a single node of weight 1 remains: the root. An
m-symbol source takes exactly m - 1 merges.

Read off. Each symbol's codeword is the branch string from the root
to its leaf, one bit per branch, under any fixed 0/1 labeling.

The merge step encodes one commitment: the two least probable symbols in
the pool will end as siblings, sharing a parent and differing only in
their last bit. Seen from the parent, the pair is a single symbol of the
summed probability, so each merge shrinks the alphabet by one and the same
rule applies again. The optimality section proves this commitment safe;
first, the run.

One merge per frame, always the two smallest weights in the pool. Final frame: 0/1 per branch, codewords at the leaves.

Step through the merges. Before advancing each frame, name the two
smallest weights in the pool and predict the new node's weight:
.15 + .1 = .25, then .25 + .25 = .50, then .5 + .5 = 1.0. In the
final frame verify the tally L = 1.75 bits.

The run as a table

Each row lists the pool before the merge, sorted for inspection:

step

pool

merged pair

new weight

1

.5,\ .25,\ .15,\ .1

C + D

.25

2

.5,\ .25,\ .25

B + (CD)

.50

3

.5,\ .50

A + (BCD)

1.00

Reading the tree with the figure's labeling gives A \mapsto \texttt{1},
B \mapsto \texttt{01}, C \mapsto \texttt{001},
D \mapsto \texttt{000}: lengths (1, 2, 3, 3) and

L = .5 \cdot 1 + .25 \cdot 2 + .15 \cdot 3 + .1 \cdot 3 = 1.75

Bounds check: the merge weights sum to the same number,
.25 + .50 + 1.00 = 1.75. This is an identity, not a coincidence: a
draw's codeword length counts the internal nodes above its leaf, and an
internal node's weight is exactly the probability that a draw passes
through it, so summing the internal weights computes
\sum_x p(x) \cdot \mathrm{depth}(x) = L. The identity is a fast check on
any hand-built Huffman tree.

The output is the matched code of Prefix codes and code trees, produced
this time by an algorithm rather than by inspection. Its cost sits 0.007
bits above the source entropy H \approx 1.743, and the optimality proof
below shows that no prefix code sits lower.

The finished code: lengths (1, 2, 3, 3), expected length 1.75 bits, 0.007 bits above the entropy floor.

Huffman coding is a single move applied to exhaustion: merge the two
lightest nodes into one of their summed weight. An m-symbol source needs
m - 1 merges, and the internal weights sum to the expected length L.

documents.title: Ties: different trees, identical cost
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Source coding › Huffman coding › Ties: different trees, identical cost
documents.text:
Ties: different trees, identical cost

When several pool weights tie for smallest, the merge rule does not say
which pair to take. The choice is genuinely free:
MacKay (§5.5) states that
when there is more than one way of selecting the two least probable
symbols, the choice may be made in any manner and the expected length of
the code does not depend on it. The trees, however, can differ, down to
their length multisets.

Symbols a, b, c, d with p = (\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac14,
\tfrac1{12}). The first merge is forced:
\tfrac14 + \tfrac1{12} = \tfrac13. The pool is now three nodes of weight
\tfrac13 each — the tie — and any two of them may be merged.

Choice 1: merge the two original symbols. a + b \to \tfrac23; the
root joins \tfrac23 with the (cd) node. Depths: a, b at 2, and c,
d at 2 below the (cd) node. Lengths (2, 2, 2, 2):
L = 2 \cdot (\tfrac13 + \tfrac13 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac1{12}) = 2 bits.

Choice 2: merge an original with the made node. b + (cd) \to
\tfrac23; the root joins it with a. Depths: a at 1, b at 2, c, d
at 3. Lengths (1, 2, 3, 3):
L = \tfrac13 \cdot 1 + \tfrac13 \cdot 2 + \tfrac14 \cdot 3 + \tfrac1{12}
\cdot 3 = \tfrac13 + \tfrac23 + \tfrac34 + \tfrac14 = 2 bits.

Different shapes, different length multisets, the same L = 2 bits
exactly. Both length sets spend the Kraft budget of
The Kraft inequality completely: 4 \cdot \tfrac14 = 1 and
\tfrac12 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac18 + \tfrac18 = 1.

One tie, two trees: lengths (2, 2, 2, 2) and (1, 2, 3, 3) both cost exactly 2.00 bits on this source.

Two further freedoms change nothing: the 0/1 labels on branches
(Prefix codes and code trees established that cost lives in the lengths
alone) and which merged node becomes the left child. A drawing that
differs from someone else's is not evidence of an error; the number to
compare is L.

Huffman trees are not unique: tie-breaking and bit labeling are free, and
even the length multiset can vary. Every Huffman tree for a source has
the same expected length.

documents.title: Optimality: the exchange argument
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Source coding › Huffman coding › Optimality: the exchange argument
documents.text:
Optimality: the exchange argument

One swap repairs a bad assignment

The engine of the proof is a swap computation. Take the tree shape with
lengths (1, 2, 3, 3) and assign the running source's symbols against
their probabilities: D \mapsto \texttt{1}, B \mapsto \texttt{01},
C \mapsto \texttt{001}, A \mapsto \texttt{000}, putting the rarest
symbol on the shortest codeword. The cost is

L = .1 \cdot 1 + .25 \cdot 2 + .15 \cdot 3 + .5 \cdot 3 = 2.55

Swapping the codewords of A and D leaves all four lengths in place and
moves .4 of probability mass from depth 3 to depth 1:

\Delta L = -(p_A - p_D)(3 - 1) = -(.4)(2) = -0.8 \text{ bits,}

and L drops to 1.75. In general, swapping the leaves of symbols i
and j changes L by (p_i - p_j)(\ell_j - \ell_i): whenever the more
probable symbol sits deeper, the swap helps or is neutral.

The exchange argument: swapping a deep frequent leaf with a shallow rare one never raises L.

Step through the three frames. In frame 2, recompute the tally
.5 \cdot 1 + .25 \cdot 2 + .15 \cdot 3 + .1 \cdot 3 = 1.75 and check it
against 2.55 - 0.8 from the swap formula.

The lemma: the two rarest can sit as bottom siblings

For every source there is an optimal prefix code in which the two least
probable symbols have codewords of maximal length that differ only in
their last bit — deepest siblings in the code tree.

Fix an optimal prefix code and sort the symbols so that
p_1 \ge p_2 \ge \dots \ge p_m. Three repairs, none increasing L:

Order lengths against probabilities. If p_i > p_j but
\ell_i > \ell_j, swapping the two codewords changes L by
(p_i - p_j)(\ell_j - \ell_i) < 0, contradicting optimality. Swaps
between symbols of equal probability change nothing, so after neutral
swaps \ell_1 \le \ell_2 \le \dots \le \ell_m.

Deepest codewords come in sibling pairs. Let w be a codeword of
maximal length and consider its sibling node. No codeword lies strictly
below the sibling — it would be longer than the maximum — so the sibling
either carries a codeword or is unclaimed. If unclaimed, replace w by
its parent: the parent's only codeword descendant was w, so the code
stays prefix-free while L drops by p_w > 0, contradicting optimality.
Hence the sibling carries a codeword, itself of maximal length.

Move the two least probable to one such pair. With lengths sorted,
\ell_m is maximal, and by the previous step the sibling of symbol m's
codeword carries some symbol k \le m - 1 with p_k \ge p_{m-1} and
\ell_k maximal. Swapping symbols k and m - 1 changes L by
(p_k - p_{m-1})(\ell_{m-1} - \ell_k) \le 0; optimality forces the change
to be exactly 0, so the swap is free. After it, symbols m and m - 1
are siblings at maximal depth.

The theorem: greedy merging is optimal

The lemma converts one merge into an exact accounting identity. Commit C
and D of the running source to being deepest siblings and view their
parent as a single symbol (CD) of weight .25. A code for the reduced
source (.5, .25, .25) — say A \mapsto \texttt{1},
B \mapsto \texttt{01}, (CD) \mapsto \texttt{00} with
L' = .5 + .5 + .5 = 1.5 — expands to a code for the original source by
appending one bit to the pair's codeword, and that extra bit is paid
exactly when the draw is C or D:

L = L' + p_C + p_D = 1.5 + .25 = 1.75 .

The added constant p_C + p_D does not depend on which codes are chosen,
so minimizing L over the original source and minimizing L' over the
reduced source are the same problem.

For every finite source distribution the Huffman procedure produces a
prefix code of minimum expected length. By McMillan's theorem
(The Kraft inequality), no uniquely decodable code of any kind
does better.

Induction on the alphabet size m. For m = 2, Huffman assigns
\texttt{0} and \texttt{1}; no nonempty codewords are shorter.

Assume the claim for m - 1 symbols and sort
p_1 \ge \dots \ge p_m. Any prefix code C' for the reduced source
p' = (p_1, \dots, p_{m-2},\, p_{m-1} + p_m) expands, by appending
\texttt{0} and \texttt{1} to the merged symbol's codeword, into a
prefix code C for p with

L(C) = L(C') + p_{m-1} + p_m .

Conversely, the exchange lemma provides an optimal code C^{*} for p
with symbols m - 1 and m as deepest siblings; collapsing the pair
into its parent gives a prefix code for p' with expected length
L(C^{*}) - (p_{m-1} + p_m). The two directions together give

L^{*}(p) = L^{*}(p') + p_{m-1} + p_m ,

where L^{*} denotes the optimal expected length. Huffman's first merge
realizes exactly this reduction, and by induction its recursive output is
optimal for p'; adding the constant, its output is optimal for p.
Finally, McMillan's theorem bounds every uniquely decodable code by the
same Kraft budget that prefix codes obey, so the prefix optimum is the
global optimum among uniquely decodable codes.

Each merge is provably safe: some optimal tree has the two least probable
symbols as bottom siblings, and collapsing them shrinks the problem by one
symbol at the fixed cost p_{m-1} + p_m. Induction over merges makes the
greedy tree optimal.

documents.title: The one-bit guarantee: H(X) ≤ L < H(X) + 1
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Source coding › Huffman coding › The one-bit guarantee: H(X) ≤ L < H(X) + 1
documents.text:
The one-bit guarantee: H(X) ≤ L < H(X) + 1

A certificate code from ceiling lengths

The entropy floor of Prefix codes and code trees bounds the Huffman code
from below: H(X) \le L. An upper bound needs a witness: any explicit
prefix code will do, since Huffman can only improve on it. The witness assigns
each symbol the ceiling of its surprisal, \ell(x) = \lceil -\log_2
p(x) \rceil: the integer-rounded version of the target lengths
\ell(x) \approx -\log_2 p(x) identified in
Prefix codes and code trees.

On the running source the surprisals are (1,\ 2,\ 2.737,\ 3.322), so the
ceiling lengths are (1, 2, 3, 4). Their Kraft sum is
2^{-1} + 2^{-2} + 2^{-3} + 2^{-4} = \tfrac{15}{16} \le 1, so the
shortest-first construction of The Kraft inequality realizes
them, at cost

L_{\lceil \cdot \rceil} = .5 \cdot 1 + .25 \cdot 2 + .15 \cdot 3 +

The ceiling code is not optimal — Huffman's 1.75 beats it — but each of
its lengths overshoots the surprisal by less than one bit, which is all
the bound requires.

For every source X, the expected length L of a Huffman code satisfies

H(X) \le L < H(X) + 1 .

Lower bound. H(X) \le L holds for every prefix code; the statement
is in Prefix codes and code trees and the proof, via the Kraft
inequality, in The source coding theorem.

Upper bound. Set \ell(x) = \lceil -\log_2 p(x) \rceil. Then
2^{-\ell(x)} \le 2^{\log_2 p(x)} = p(x), so
\sum_x 2^{-\ell(x)} \le \sum_x p(x) = 1: the lengths satisfy the Kraft
inequality, and a prefix code with them exists by the sufficiency
construction. Since \ell(x) < -\log_2 p(x) + 1,

L_{\lceil \cdot \rceil} = \sum_x p(x)\,\ell(x)

Huffman's code is optimal, so L \le L_{\lceil \cdot \rceil} < H(X) + 1.

Equality is the dyadic case

L = H(X) forces every codeword length to equal its symbol's surprisal
(the equality condition of the entropy floor), so it requires every
probability to be a power of \tfrac12 — a dyadic distribution. On
(\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18) the surprisals (1, 2, 3, 3)
are integers and Huffman achieves L = H = 1.75 bits exactly
(exercise 3). On the running source the surprisals 2.737 and 3.322
are not integers, and the 0.007-bit gap is the rounding cost. Huffman
does not "achieve entropy"; it achieves the best that integer lengths
allow.

Huffman lands in [H, H+1): a 0.007-bit gap for the running source, a 0.531-bit gap for the 90/10 coin.

The optimal symbol code is trapped in [H, H+1): integer codeword lengths
must round surprisals up, the rounding is the entire gap, and the gap
vanishes exactly when every probability is a power of \tfrac12.

documents.title: The flaw that remains: up to one bit per symbol
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Source coding › Huffman coding › The flaw that remains: up to one bit per symbol
documents.text:
The flaw that remains: up to one bit per symbol

A half-bit source forced to pay a full bit

The guarantee's weak spot is the additive 1: it is one bit per symbol.
Take the biased coin p = (.9, .1). Its entropy is
H = .9 \cdot 0.152 + .1 \cdot 3.322 \approx 0.469 bits, yet any symbol
code must give both outcomes nonempty codewords; the best lengths are
(1, 1) and L = 1 bit. The overhead 0.531 bits is 113% of the
information actually delivered, and no cleverness within symbol coding
removes it.

MacKay's §5.6 sharpens the
point with English text: in the context strings_of_ch, the next nine
characters are nearly determined, carrying about 0.13 bits in total, yet
a Huffman coder must spend at least one full bit on each — nine bits for
an eighth of a bit of information. The same section names a second
practical defect: Huffman needs the distribution before coding starts, and
a source whose statistics drift forces rebuilding and retransmitting the
table. Adaptive variants exist and are out of scope here.

Blocks shrink the overhead

Code the (.9, .1) coin two flips at a time. The pair distribution is
p(\text{HH}) = .81, p(\text{HT}) = p(\text{TH}) = .09,
p(\text{TT}) = .01. Merges: .01 + .09 = .10, then .09 + .10 = .19,
then .81 + .19 = 1.00. Lengths: \text{HH} \mapsto 1,
\text{HT} \mapsto 2, \text{TH} \mapsto 3, \text{TT} \mapsto 3.

L = .81 \cdot 1 + .09 \cdot 2 + .09 \cdot 3 + .01 \cdot 3 = 1.29

Bounds check: the merge weights give .10 + .19 + 1.00 = 1.29. The
per-flip overhead falls from 0.531 to 0.645 - 0.469 = 0.176 bits, and
the pair entropy obeys the guarantee: 0.938 \le 1.29 < 1.938.

The mechanism generalizes: coding blocks of n symbols pays the up-to-one
bit overhead once per block, so at most 1/n bits per symbol. The
price is an alphabet of size 2^n and a code table to match.
The source coding theorem turns this limit into the
source coding theorem; Compression as prediction removes
the symbol boundary altogether with stream codes, which need no table at
all.

History. Huffman devised the algorithm in 1951 as a term paper in Robert
Fano's MIT information-theory course; the assignment was the optimal-code
problem that Shannon's and Fano's own top-down constructions had left
open. The paper appeared in 1952. The top-down method of the first
section, splitting mass as evenly as possible, is the Shannon–Fano
construction his algorithm displaced.

Practice. DEFLATE (gzip, zlib, PNG) and baseline JPEG store data with
Huffman tables, in canonical form: only the length of each codeword is
transmitted, and the codewords are reconstructed by the shortest-first
convention of The Kraft inequality. Formats for which the
sub-bit gap matters — arithmetic coders in video standards,
asymmetric-numeral-system coders in zstd — implement the stream-code fix
of Compression as prediction.

Huffman is optimal among symbol codes, and symbol codes are the wrong tool
for low-entropy sources: the up-to-one-bit overhead is paid per symbol.
Spreading it over blocks or streams is the subject of the next lessons.

documents.title: Exercises
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Source coding › Huffman coding › Exercises
documents.text:
Exercises

Run the Huffman algorithm on the source p(E) = .4, p(F) = .3,
p(G) = .2, p(H) = .1. List every merge with the pool before it, give
the codeword lengths, compute L two ways (probability-weighted lengths
and summed merge weights), and compare with the chain-question tree built
for this source in exercise 1 of Prefix codes and code trees. Check the
one-bit guarantee against H \approx 1.846 bits.

Merges: pool .4, .3, .2, .1, merge G + H \to .3; pool .4, .3, .3,
merge F + (GH) \to .6; pool .4, .6, merge to the root 1.0.

Depths: E at 1, F at 2, G and H at 3 — lengths (1, 2, 3, 3).

L = .4 \cdot 1 + .3 \cdot 2 + .2 \cdot 3 + .1 \cdot 3 = 1.9

and the merge weights agree: .3 + .6 + 1.0 = 1.9.

The chain tree of the earlier exercise (E at depth 1, F at 2, G and
H at 3) has the same lengths and the same L = 1.9: that hand-built
code is now certified optimal. Guarantee:
1.846 \le 1.9 < 2.846 holds, with a gap of 0.054 bits.

Run the Huffman algorithm on the five-symbol source
p = (.3, .25, .2, .15, .1). A tie appears after the first merge; resolve
it both ways and show the resulting codes have the same lengths per
symbol. Give L, verify it against the summed merge weights, and check
the guarantee against H \approx 2.228 bits.

First merge: .15 + .1 = .25 (symbols d + e). Pool:
.3, .25, .2, .25 — the two smallest are .2 and one of the two .25s,
a tie between symbol b and the made node (de).

Resolution 1: merge c + (de) \to .45; pool .3, .25, .45; merge
a + b \to .55; root. Depths: a, b at 2; c at 2, d, e at 3.

Resolution 2: merge c + b \to .45; pool .3, .25, .45; merge
a + (de) \to .55; root. Depths: b, c at 2; a at 2; d, e at 3.

Both give the same lengths per symbol: (2, 2, 2, 3, 3) for
(a, b, c, d, e).

L = 2(.3 + .25 + .2) + 3(.15 + .1) = 1.5 + .75 = 2.25 \text{ bits;}

merge weights (resolution 1): .25 + .45 + .55 + 1.00 = 2.25. Guarantee:
2.228 \le 2.25 < 3.228, gap 0.022 bits.

Run the Huffman algorithm on the dyadic source
(\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18). Compute L, then compute
H by the surprisal-weighted method of
Entropy, and explain why the two are
equal here. State the exact class of distributions on which Huffman meets
the entropy.

Merges: \tfrac18 + \tfrac18 = \tfrac14; \tfrac14 + \tfrac14 =
\tfrac12; \tfrac12 + \tfrac12 = 1. Lengths (1, 2, 3, 3) and

L = \tfrac12 \cdot 1 + \tfrac14 \cdot 2 + \tfrac18 \cdot 3 + \tfrac18

Surprisals: -\log_2 \tfrac12 = 1, -\log_2 \tfrac14 = 2,
-\log_2 \tfrac18 = 3 (twice). Weighted:
H = \tfrac12 \cdot 1 + \tfrac14 \cdot 2 + \tfrac18 \cdot 3 + \tfrac18
\cdot 3 = 1.75 bits = L.

The sums agree term by term because every codeword length equals its
symbol's surprisal, which is possible only when every surprisal is an
integer. That holds exactly when every probability is a power of
\tfrac12: the dyadic distributions, and only they, give L = H.

For the source (\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac14, \tfrac1{12}), run Huffman
twice, resolving the three-way tie of the second merge in both ways shown
in the lesson. Give both length sets, verify that both are complete
(Kraft sum exactly 1), show both have L = 2 bits, and check the
guarantee against H \approx 1.855 bits.

Forced first merge: \tfrac14 + \tfrac1{12} = \tfrac13.

Resolution (a), merge the two original thirds: lengths (2, 2, 2, 2).
Kraft sum 4 \cdot 2^{-2} = 1. L = 2 \cdot 1 = 2 bits.

Resolution (b), merge one original third with the made node: lengths
(1, 2, 3, 3). Kraft sum \tfrac12 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac18 + \tfrac18 =
1. L = \tfrac13 + \tfrac23 + \tfrac34 + \tfrac14 = 2 bits.

Both codes cost exactly 2 bits, and 1.855 \le 2 < 2.855: the
guarantee holds with a gap of 0.145 bits.

The code A \mapsto \texttt{000}, B \mapsto \texttt{01},
C \mapsto \texttt{001}, D \mapsto \texttt{1} is proposed for the
running source (.5, .25, .15, .1). Compute its expected length, list
every pair of symbols violating the ordering
p_i > p_j \Rightarrow \ell_i \le \ell_j, apply the single most valuable
codeword swap, compute \Delta L from the swap formula, and identify the
resulting code.

Lengths: A: 3, B: 2, C: 3, D: 1.
L = .5 \cdot 3 + .25 \cdot 2 + .15 \cdot 3 + .1 \cdot 1 = 2.55 bits.

Ordering violations (more probable but strictly longer): (A, B),
(A, D), (B, D), (C, D).

Most valuable swap: A \leftrightarrow D, the largest probability gap
across the largest length gap.
\Delta L = (p_A - p_D)(\ell_D - \ell_A) = (.4)(1 - 3) = -0.8 bits, so
L falls to 1.75.

The result is A \mapsto \texttt{1}, B \mapsto \texttt{01},
C \mapsto \texttt{001}, D \mapsto \texttt{000}: the matched code, the
Huffman output for this source, and (by the optimality theorem) the
minimum. No violating pairs remain.

Show that the lengths of every Huffman code satisfy the Kraft inequality
of The Kraft inequality with equality — every Huffman code is
complete. Verify the equality on the length sets of exercises 1 and 2,
and state what completeness rules out, using the slack result of that
lesson.

Run the merges backwards: the finished tree is produced from the single
root by repeatedly expanding a leaf at some depth \ell into an internal
node with exactly two children at depth \ell + 1 (every internal node
has two children, because every merge joins exactly two nodes). The root
alone has leaf sum 2^{-0} = 1, and each expansion changes the sum by
-2^{-\ell} + 2 \cdot 2^{-(\ell+1)} = 0. So the final leaves — the
codewords — always satisfy \sum_i 2^{-\ell_i} = 1.

Checks: (1, 2, 3, 3): \tfrac12 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac18 + \tfrac18 = 1.
(2, 2, 2, 3, 3): 3 \cdot \tfrac14 + 2 \cdot \tfrac18 = 1.

Completeness rules out free improvements: by the slack result, any code
with \sum_i 2^{-\ell_i} < 1 admits a strictly shorter length set at no
cost. A Huffman code leaves no such slack — consistent with its
optimality, since an incomplete optimal code would be a contradiction.

For the coin p(\mathrm{H}) = .9, p(\mathrm{T}) = .1: (a) compute
H(X) by the surprisal-weighted method of
Entropy; (b) explain why every symbol
code for a two-outcome source has L = 1 bit and give the per-flip
overhead; (c) rebuild the pair-block code of the worked example from
scratch and give the new per-flip cost and overhead.

(a) Surprisals: -\log_2 .9 \approx 0.152 and -\log_2 .1 \approx
3.322. H = .9 \cdot 0.152 + .1 \cdot 3.322 \approx 0.137 + 0.332 =
0.469 bits.

(b) Codewords are nonempty, so both lengths are at least 1; lengths
(1, 1) are achievable (\texttt{0} and \texttt{1}) and give L = 1
bit exactly. Overhead: 1 - 0.469 = 0.531 bits per flip, 113% of the
information.

(c) Pairs: (.81, .09, .09, .01). Merges: .01 + .09 = .10;
.09 + .10 = .19; .81 + .19 = 1.00. Lengths (1, 2, 3, 3) for
(\text{HH}, \text{HT}, \text{TH}, \text{TT}).
L = .81 + .18 + .27 + .03 = 1.29 bits per pair, 0.645 per flip.
Overhead: 0.645 - 0.469 = 0.176 bits per flip — the same source, the
same theorem, one third of the waste.

Run the Huffman algorithm on the seven-symbol source of the first
section, p(a), \dots, p(g) = .01, .24, .05, .20, .47, .01, .02. List
the merges, give each symbol's codeword length, compute L both ways,
and compare with the balanced top-down code's 2.53 bits.

Merges, smallest pair each time:

a + f \to .02; pool .47, .24, .20, .05, .02, .02.

(af) + g \to .04 (a tie between the two .02s — either order gives
the same weights); pool .47, .24, .20, .05, .04.

(afg) + c \to .09; pool .47, .24, .20, .09.

(afgc) + d \to .29; pool .47, .24, .29.

(afgcd) + b \to .53; pool .47, .53.

root \to 1.00.

Depths: e at 1; b at 2; d at 3; c at 4; g at 5; a, f at 6 —
lengths (6, 2, 4, 3, 1, 6, 5) for (a, b, c, d, e, f, g).

L = .01 \cdot 6 + .24 \cdot 2 + .05 \cdot 4 + .20 \cdot 3 + .47 \cdot 1

merge weights: .02 + .04 + .09 + .29 + .53 + 1.00 = 1.97. Against the
perfectly balanced top-down code's 2.53 bits, the greedy bottom-up tree
saves 0.56 bits per symbol, and with H \approx 1.93 it sits only
0.04 bits above the entropy floor.

D. A. Huffman, "A Method for the Construction of Minimum-Redundancy Codes," Proceedings of the IRE, 40(9), 1952 — the original algorithm and optimality argument. https://doi.org/10.1109/JRPROC.1952.273898

T. M. Cover, J. A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006 — §5.4 proves H \le L^* < H + 1 via ceiling lengths; §5.6–5.7 the Huffman procedure, worked examples, and non-uniqueness; §5.8 the exchange lemma and the induction proof of optimality (Lemma 5.8.1, Theorem 5.8.1).

D. J. C. MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms, Cambridge University Press, 2003 — ch. 5 "Symbol Codes": §5.5 the Huffman algorithm, the suboptimality of balanced top-down splitting, and the tie invariance; §5.6 "Disadvantages of the Huffman code": the extra bit and the changing-ensemble problem, motivating the stream codes of ch. 6. Free online: https://www.inference.org.uk/mackay/itila/

documents.title: The source coding theorem
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Source coding › The source coding theorem
documents.text:
No lossless code achieves fewer expected bits per symbol than the source
entropy. This lesson gives the argument. The route: every prefix code
implicitly bets on a distribution q(x) = 2^{-\ell(x)}; the expected length
decomposes as L = H(p) + D(p\,\|\,q) + \text{slack} with every term
non-negative, which proves the floor; the Shannon code
\ell(x) = \lceil -\log_2 p(x) \rceil lands within one bit of the floor;
block coding shrinks the remaining per-symbol overhead to at most 1/n; and
the typical set explains why nH bits is the right total for n symbols.

documents.title: A code is a bet: lengths are probabilities
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Source coding › The source coding theorem › A code is a bet: lengths are probabilities
documents.text:
A code is a bet: lengths are probabilities

The Kraft inequality priced a codeword of length \ell at
2^{-\ell} of a budget of one, and its closing remark observed that for a
complete code the claims 2^{-\ell_i} are positive and sum to exactly 1:
formally a probability distribution. That observation now carries weight.

The claims of the matched code, read as a distribution

The matched code for the running source, A \mapsto \texttt{1},
B \mapsto \texttt{01}, C \mapsto \texttt{001}, D \mapsto \texttt{000},
has lengths (1, 2, 3, 3) and claims

q = \bigl(\tfrac12,\ \tfrac14,\ \tfrac18,\ \tfrac18\bigr).

On the dyadic source with exactly these probabilities, every codeword length
equals its symbol's surprisal and L = H = 1.75 bits (exercise 6 of
The Kraft inequality): the code is exact for q. Used on the
actual running source p = (.5, .25, .15, .1), the same code acts as if C
occurred with probability \tfrac18 when it occurs with .15, and as if D
occurred with probability \tfrac18 when it occurs with .1. The code bets
on q; the source draws from p.

Lengths (1, 2, 3, 3) are the bet q = (½, ¼, ⅛, ⅛); the true source is p = (.5, .25, .15, .1). The mismatch sits at C and D.

The implied distribution of an arbitrary prefix code

For a code that is not complete, the claims sum to less than 1 and
normalizing them yields a distribution.

Let a prefix code have lengths \ell(x) and Kraft sum
c = \sum_x 2^{-\ell(x)} \le 1. Its implied distribution is

q(x) = \frac{2^{-\ell(x)}}{c},

and every codeword length is a surprisal under q plus a constant:
\ell(x) = -\log_2 q(x) + \log_2 \tfrac{1}{c}, with
\log_2 \tfrac{1}{c} \ge 0 by the Kraft inequality.

Short codewords are exactly high implied probabilities: assigning C a
3-bit codeword and assigning C implied probability \tfrac18 are the same
act. The Kraft budget of The Kraft inequality is the statement
that the bets of a prefix code cannot sum past 1.

Choosing codeword lengths is choosing a probability distribution:
length \ell(x) is the bet q(x) \propto 2^{-\ell(x)}, and shortness
spent on one symbol is probability withdrawn from the others.

documents.title: The floor: expected length is entropy plus mismatch
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Source coding › The source coding theorem › The floor: expected length is entropy plus mismatch
documents.text:
The floor: expected length is entropy plus mismatch

The bet reading turns the gap L - H into a computable quantity. The
concrete cases first.

Two codes priced against the entropy

The running source has H(p) \approx 1.743 bits
(Prefix codes and code trees). The balanced code (all lengths 2) costs
L = 2.00 bits, a gap of 0.257; the matched code costs 1.75, a gap of
0.007. Both gaps are exactly the mismatch between p and each code's bet.

For each code, compute \sum_x p(x) \log_2 \tfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}, the
probability-weighted log-ratio of truth to bet.

Balanced code: lengths (2,2,2,2), complete, so
q = (\tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14). The terms:

.5 \log_2 \tfrac{.5}{.25} = .5, \quad

Sum: .5 - .111 - .132 + 0 \approx 0.257 bits: the gap 2.00 - 1.743.

Matched code: q = (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18). The A
and B terms vanish (p = q there); the rest:

.15 \log_2 \tfrac{.15}{.125} \approx .0395, \qquad

Sum: \approx 0.007 bits: the gap 1.75 - 1.743.

Bounds check: individual terms go negative (the code over-bets on D),
but each total is positive and equals its code's gap exactly.

The decomposition: L = H + D + slack

The agreement is an identity. Take any prefix code with lengths \ell(x),
Kraft sum c, and implied distribution q(x) = 2^{-\ell(x)}/c. Substituting
\ell(x) = -\log_2 q(x) + \log_2 \tfrac1c into the expected length:

L = \sum_x p(x)\,\ell(x)

The middle term is the Kullback–Leibler divergence D(p\,\|\,q), the
expected extra bits from betting q when the truth is p; it gets a lesson
of its own (KL divergence). The slack term prices an
incomplete tree: unclaimed budget is length wasted on no symbol
(The Kraft inequality showed any slack buys a shorter code).
What remains to prove is that the mismatch term is never negative.

For probability distributions p and q on a finite set,

D(p \,\|\, q) = \sum_x p(x) \log_2 \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} \;\ge\; 0,

with equality if and only if p = q.

If q(x) = 0 for some x with p(x) > 0, the sum is +\infty and the
inequality holds. Otherwise use \ln t \le t - 1, an inequality valid for
all t > 0 with equality only at t = 1 (the graph of \ln lies below its
tangent at 1). Applied to t = q(x)/p(x) inside the sum:

-D(p\,\|\,q) \cdot \ln 2

Hence D(p\,\|\,q) \ge 0. Equality forces q(x)/p(x) = 1 wherever
p(x) > 0 and \sum_{x:\,p(x)>0} q(x) = 1, i.e. q = p.

The theorem: no code beats the entropy

Every uniquely decodable code for a source X with distribution p
satisfies

L \;\ge\; H(X),

with equality if and only if \ell(x) = -\log_2 p(x) for every outcome:
a complete code on a dyadic distribution.

By McMillan's theorem (The Kraft inequality), the lengths of any
uniquely decodable code satisfy c = \sum_x 2^{-\ell(x)} \le 1, so the
implied distribution q and the decomposition above apply:

L = H(p) + D(p \,\|\, q) + \log_2 \tfrac{1}{c} .

Gibbs' inequality gives D(p\,\|\,q) \ge 0, and c \le 1 gives
\log_2 \tfrac1c \ge 0; hence L \ge H(p). Equality requires both
q = p and c = 1, which together say 2^{-\ell(x)} = p(x), i.e.
\ell(x) = -\log_2 p(x): every probability a power of \tfrac12, every
length its symbol's surprisal.

This settles the bound that Prefix codes and code trees stated without
proof and Huffman coding used as the lower half of its
guarantee. The proof also says exactly where a code's cost goes: the
entropy is the part no code avoids, the mismatch D is the price of
betting on the wrong distribution, and the slack is the price of wasting
tree.

Both codes pay the same H(p) = 1.743-bit floor; the difference is the amber mismatch D(p‖q): 0.257 bits for the balanced bet, 0.007 for the matched one.

L = H(p) + D(p\,\|\,q) + \text{slack}: entropy is the unavoidable part,
mismatch and slack are non-negative, so no lossless code averages below
H(p), and every excess bit is attributable to a wrong bet or a wasted
node.

documents.title: Achievability: rounding surprisals up costs less than a bit
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Source coding › The source coding theorem › Achievability: rounding surprisals up costs less than a bit
documents.text:
Achievability: rounding surprisals up costs less than a bit

The floor is approachable from above. The equality condition says lengths
should be \ell(x) = -\log_2 p(x); when the surprisals are not integers,
round them up:

\ell(x) = \lceil -\log_2 p(x) \rceil .

This is the Shannon code: the ceiling-length witness that
Huffman coding built to prove its one-bit guarantee, now
under its proper name. Since 2^{-\lceil -\log_2 p(x) \rceil} \le p(x), the
Kraft sum is at most \sum_x p(x) = 1 and the lengths are achievable; since
each length overshoots its surprisal by less than one bit, L < H(p) + 1.
On the running source the Shannon lengths are (1, 2, 3, 4), costing
L = 1.85 bits: the rounding gaps (0, 0, 0.263, 0.678), weighted by p,
add the 0.107 bits above H \approx 1.743.

The Shannon code rounds each surprisal up to an integer length. Every gap is below 1 bit, so L = 1.85 < H + 1.

Huffman coding can only improve on this witness, which yields the two-sided
guarantee proved in Huffman coding: the optimal symbol code
satisfies H(X) \le L^* < H(X) + 1.

The floor is approachable: betting q as close to p as integer lengths
allow costs less than one extra bit per symbol, so the optimal symbol code
is trapped in [H, H+1).

documents.title: Blocks: the overhead is per block, not per symbol
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Source coding › The source coding theorem › Blocks: the overhead is per block, not per symbol
documents.text:
Blocks: the overhead is per block, not per symbol

The remaining defect is the one Huffman coding ended on:
the +1 is paid per symbol. The 90/10 coin has H \approx 0.469 bits,
yet any symbol code spends L = 1 bit per flip, an overhead of 113%. The
fix is to enlarge the symbol.

A block of n symbols is one symbol with entropy nH

Treat n consecutive independent draws X_1, \dots, X_n as a single
super-symbol X^n over the 2^n (in general |\mathcal{X}|^n) possible
blocks. Its entropy needs no new machinery: probabilities of independent
draws multiply, so surprisals add
(Surprisal),

-\log_2 p(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} -\log_2 p(x_i),

and taking expectations term by term gives H(X^n) = n\,H(X).

For an i.i.d. source X and any block length n, the optimal prefix code
for blocks of n symbols has expected length L_n satisfying

H(X) \;\le\; \frac{L_n}{n} \;<\; H(X) + \frac{1}{n} .

Apply the entropy floor and the Shannon-code bound to the super-symbol
source X^n: H(X^n) \le L_n < H(X^n) + 1. Substitute
H(X^n) = nH(X) and divide by n.

The up-to-one-bit rounding cost is now paid once per block: at most
1/n bits per symbol, squeezed toward zero by growing n.

The 90/10 coin, coded in blocks

Running the Huffman algorithm of Huffman coding on the
2^n block probabilities gives the exact optimal cost per symbol:
