The n = 2 row is the pair code built by hand in
Huffman coding. By n = 6 the gap is a thousandth of a
bit. The price is the alphabet: 2^n codewords must be built, stored, and
transmitted.

One block size per frame. Watch the amber points fall onto the blue entropy line while staying below the dashed H + 1/n guarantee.

Step through the five frames and check each gap against the guarantee: at
every n the point sits below H + 1/n. Then reproduce the plot in the
demo below: load the 90/10 preset and drag n from 1 to 8; the per-symbol
cost should fall from 1.000 to within 0.01 of the entropy line. Switch
to the fair-coin preset and note the gap is 0 at every n: surprisals
are already integers.

The exact per-symbol cost is not monotone in n: the table shows n = 6
beating both n = 7 (0.474) and n = 8 (0.476) on this coin, because
how well 2^n block probabilities happen to fit integer lengths varies
with n. The theorem never promised monotonicity; it promises the
squeezing band [H,\, H + \tfrac1n), and every value in the table obeys
it.

Block coding pays the rounding bit once per block: H \le L_n/n < H + 1/n,
so the achievable cost per symbol converges to the entropy as the block
length grows.

documents.title: The typical set: where the probability concentrates
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Source coding › The source coding theorem › The typical set: where the probability concentrates
documents.text:
The typical set: where the probability concentrates

The block bound proves that nH bits per block suffice; the typical set
shows what those bits index. It is the structural reason block coding
works, and it returns for channel coding in
The noisy-channel coding theorem.

One hundred flips of the 90/10 coin

A block of n = 100 flips has 2^{100} possible outcomes. They are far
from equally likely:

The single most probable sequence, all heads, has surprisal
100 \cdot 0.152 = 15.2 bits: probability 2^{-15.2}, about
3 \cdot 10^{-5}.

A sequence with the expected composition, 90 heads and 10 tails, has
surprisal 90 \cdot 0.152 + 10 \cdot 3.322 = 46.9 bits, exactly
nH. There are \binom{100}{10} \approx 2^{44} such sequences.

The all-tails sequence has surprisal 100 \cdot 3.322 = 332 bits:
probability \approx 10^{-100}, an event that never occurs in practice.

The draws that actually occur crowd around the expected composition:
sequences with 5 to 15 tails number about 2^{58} (a 2^{-42} fraction
of the 2^{100}), yet carry 93.6\% of the probability. Almost every draw
is one of relatively few, roughly equiprobable sequences.

Near-average surprisal defines the set

The engine is the
law of large numbers
applied to surprisals: the per-symbol surprisal of a block,
-\tfrac1n \log_2 p(X^n) = \tfrac1n \sum_i \bigl(-\log_2 p(X_i)\bigr), is
an average of n independent draws of a quantity whose mean is H(X), so
it concentrates near H(X) as n grows.

For an i.i.d. source X and tolerance \varepsilon > 0, the typical
set T_\varepsilon^{(n)} is the set of length-n sequences whose
per-symbol surprisal is within \varepsilon of the entropy:

T_\varepsilon^{(n)} = \Bigl\{ x^n :

Each member has probability between 2^{-n(H+\varepsilon)} and
2^{-n(H-\varepsilon)}.

For every \varepsilon > 0, as n \to \infty:

\Pr\bigl(X^n \in T_\varepsilon^{(n)}\bigr) \to 1: almost all draws are
typical.

\bigl|T_\varepsilon^{(n)}\bigr| \le 2^{\,n(H+\varepsilon)}: there are
only about 2^{nH} typical sequences.

\bigl|T_\varepsilon^{(n)}\bigr| \ge (1-\varepsilon)\,
2^{\,n(H-\varepsilon)} for n large: and not substantially fewer.

Sketch only; the full statement and proof are Chapter 3 of
Cover & Thomas. (1) is the law of large numbers applied to the i.i.d.
surprisals -\log_2 p(X_i), which have mean H(X) and finite variance on
a finite alphabet. (2) is counting: each typical sequence has probability
at least 2^{-n(H+\varepsilon)}, and the total probability is at most 1,
so at most 2^{n(H+\varepsilon)} of them fit. (3) follows the same way
from (1): the set eventually holds mass at least 1 - \varepsilon, and
each member's probability is at most 2^{-n(H-\varepsilon)}.

The typical set: a vanishing fraction of sequence space (≈2⁴⁷ of 2¹⁰⁰ for 100 flips of the 90/10 coin) that carries almost all the probability.

Why nH bits is the right count, in both directions

The typical set explains the block bound's number. Sufficiency: a block
coder can spend \lceil n(H+\varepsilon) \rceil + 1 bits to index the
typical sequences and fall back on n + O(1) raw bits for the rare
atypical remainder; the expected cost per symbol approaches H.
Necessity: the \approx 2^{nH} typical sequences are nearly
equiprobable, and no lossless scheme can give short names to more than a
vanishing share of 2^{nH} nearly equal claimants: fewer than
n(H - \varepsilon) bits provide 2^{n(H-\varepsilon)} names, a
2^{-n\varepsilon} fraction of what is needed.

This section asserts the typical set's properties with a sketch rather than
a full proof: the "lite" of this lesson. The floor proved
earlier needed none of it: the decomposition argument is complete on its
own. MacKay's chapter 4
builds the source coding theorem entirely on the typical set instead.

A long block concentrates on \approx 2^{nH} roughly equiprobable typical
sequences: naming one of them takes nH bits, and almost every draw is one
of them: compression is possible exactly because so few sequences
actually occur.

MacKay's accounting makes the same point with two numbers. The raw bit
content of n flips is \log_2 2^n = n bits: the cost of naming any
outcome whatsoever. The essential bit content H_\delta is the cost of
naming any outcome outside a set of probability at most \delta that the
coder agrees to ignore. His Theorem 4.1: for any fixed tolerance
\delta > 0, the essential bit content per symbol tends to H as
n \to \infty: the plateau of nearly all the probability sits at
\approx 2^{nH} outcomes regardless of how strict \delta is. Allowing
any fixed failure probability, however small, buys the full compression to
H; allowing none still costs n bits for the last atypical stragglers,
which is why practical schemes attach a cheap escape code instead of
ignoring them.

documents.title: The source coding theorem
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Source coding › The source coding theorem › The source coding theorem
documents.text:
The source coding theorem

The pieces assemble into the module's headline result, first stated as
Theorem 9 of Shannon's 1948 paper
(the "fundamental theorem for a noiseless channel").

Let X be an i.i.d. source with entropy H(X). Then:

Converse. Every uniquely decodable code for blocks of n symbols
has expected length per symbol at least H(X).

Achievability. For every n there is a prefix code for blocks of
n symbols with expected length per symbol below H(X) + \tfrac1n.

The infimum of achievable expected bits per symbol over all lossless codes
and all block lengths is exactly H(X).

Both halves were proved above. The converse is the entropy floor applied to
the super-symbol source X^n: L_n \ge H(X^n) = nH(X), using McMillan to
cover every uniquely decodable code. Achievability is the Shannon code on
blocks: L_n < H(X^n) + 1 = nH(X) + 1. Dividing both by n gives the two
statements, and letting n \to \infty closes the infimum onto H(X).

Entropy thereby acquires its operational meaning: H(X) is not merely
a formula from Entropy but the measured
price, in bits per symbol, of transmitting the source losslessly: the
number that the best possible engineering converges to and cannot cross.

What the theorem does and does not say

Three boundaries, each load-bearing:

The bound is on the expectation. Individual messages compress below
H routinely: the all-heads block of 100 flips gets a short codeword in
any good block code. The average over the source cannot.

Lossless is essential. Codes that tolerate reconstruction error can
go below H; how far, as a function of the tolerated distortion, is the
subject of Rate-distortion theory.

Independence is assumed. For sources with memory (English text is
the standing example), the floor is the entropy rate, the per-symbol
entropy given unbounded context, which is lower than the single-symbol
H. Entropy of English text measures it.

The source coding theorem on the 90/10 coin: lossless codes approach the entropy wall from the right and never cross it.

The module in one line: the Kraft inequality decides which length sets
exist, Gibbs' inequality proves none of them averages below H(X), the
Shannon code comes within one bit, and block coding closes the gap:
entropy is exactly the cost of lossless description.

The bet reading of this theorem is the bridge to the machine-learning
module. A code's cost decomposes as H(p) + D(p\,\|\,q); a probabilistic
model assigned the role of q pays the same two terms, and
\sum_x p(x) \log_2 \tfrac{1}{q(x)} = H(p) + D(p\,\|\,q) is exactly the
cross-entropy loss minimized when training a classifier or a language
model (Cross-entropy). Training a model to predict
and designing a code to compress are the same optimization; the exact
correspondence is Compression as prediction.

documents.title: Exercises
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Source coding › The source coding theorem › Exercises
documents.text:
Exercises

For the running source p = (.5, .25, .15, .1) and the balanced code with
lengths (2, 2, 2, 2): compute the Kraft sum c, the implied distribution
q, and D(p\,\|\,q) term by term, and verify the decomposition
L = H(p) + D(p\,\|\,q) + \log_2 \tfrac1c numerically
(use H(p) \approx 1.743).

Kraft sum: c = 4 \cdot 2^{-2} = 1: complete, slack \log_2 \tfrac11 = 0.
Implied distribution: q = (\tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14).

Terms of D(p\,\|\,q):
.5 \log_2 \tfrac{.5}{.25} = .5 \cdot 1 = .5;
.25 \log_2 \tfrac{.25}{.25} = 0;
.15 \log_2 \tfrac{.15}{.25} = .15 \cdot (-0.737) \approx -.111;
.1 \log_2 \tfrac{.1}{.25} = .1 \cdot (-1.322) \approx -.132.

D(p\,\|\,q) \approx .5 + 0 - .111 - .132 = 0.257 bits.

Decomposition: H + D + \text{slack} \approx 1.743 + 0.257 + 0 = 2.000
bits, matching L = \sum_x p(x) \cdot 2 = 2 exactly.

The matched code's lengths (1, 2, 3, 3) are assigned to a source with the
probabilities reversed: p = (.1, .15, .25, .5) against lengths
(1, 2, 3, 3) in that order — the shortest codeword on the rarest symbol.
Compute L, then compute D(p\,\|\,q) against the code's implied
distribution q = (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18), and verify
L = H(p) + D(p\,\|\,q). (H(p) \approx 1.743: entropy is invariant
under relabeling, per Entropy.)

Expected length:
L = .1 \cdot 1 + .15 \cdot 2 + .25 \cdot 3 + .5 \cdot 3 = 2.65 bits.

Mismatch, term by term:
.1 \log_2 \tfrac{.1}{.5} = .1 \cdot (-2.322) \approx -.232;
.15 \log_2 \tfrac{.15}{.25} = .15 \cdot (-0.737) \approx -.111;
.25 \log_2 \tfrac{.25}{.125} = .25 \cdot 1 = .25;
.5 \log_2 \tfrac{.5}{.125} = .5 \cdot 2 = 1.

D(p\,\|\,q) \approx -.232 - .111 + .25 + 1 = 0.907 bits.

Verification: the code is complete (c = 1, no slack), and
H + D \approx 1.743 + 0.907 = 2.650 = L. Betting exactly backwards costs
0.907 extra bits per symbol, more than half the entropy itself.

Build the Shannon code for the source p = (.4, .3, .2, .1): compute the
four surprisals, the ceiling lengths, and the Kraft sum; verify the lengths
are achievable; compute L and check H \le L < H + 1 with
H \approx 1.846 (computed in Entropy).
Compare with the Huffman cost 1.9 bits found in exercise 1 of
Huffman coding.

Surprisals: -\log_2 .4 \approx 1.322, -\log_2 .3 \approx 1.737,
-\log_2 .2 \approx 2.322, -\log_2 .1 \approx 3.322.

Ceiling lengths: (2, 2, 3, 4). Kraft sum:
\tfrac14 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac18 + \tfrac1{16} = \tfrac{11}{16} \le 1:
achievable by the shortest-first construction of
The Kraft inequality.

Expected length:
L = .4 \cdot 2 + .3 \cdot 2 + .2 \cdot 3 + .1 \cdot 4 = 2.4 bits.

Bounds: 1.846 \le 2.4 < 2.846: the guarantee holds. Huffman achieves
1.9 bits on the same source: the Shannon code proves the H + 1 bound
but is not optimal — its large slack (\log_2 \tfrac{16}{11} \approx 0.54
bits) is exactly the sort of waste Huffman eliminates.

For the uniform three-symbol source p = (\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13),
H = \log_2 3 \approx 1.585 bits: (a) give the Shannon-code lengths and
cost; (b) run the Huffman algorithm and give its cost; (c) explain via the
equality condition of the entropy floor why no code reaches 1.585;
(d) code pairs of symbols (9 equiprobable outcomes) with Huffman lengths
and give the new per-symbol cost.

(a) Every surprisal is \log_2 3 \approx 1.585, so every Shannon length is
\lceil 1.585 \rceil = 2: L = 2 bits.

(b) Merges: \tfrac13 + \tfrac13 = \tfrac23, then the root. Lengths
(1, 2, 2): L = \tfrac13 (1 + 2 + 2) = \tfrac53 \approx 1.667 bits.

(c) Equality requires \ell(x) = -\log_2 p(x) for every symbol; 1.585 is
not an integer, so no integer length set attains the floor. The Huffman
gap 1.667 - 1.585 = 0.082 bits is irreducible at block length 1.

(d) Pairs: 9 outcomes of probability \tfrac19 each. Huffman on 9
equiprobable symbols gives 7 codewords of length 3 and 2 of length 4
(Kraft sum 7 \cdot \tfrac18 + 2 \cdot \tfrac1{16} = 1):
L_2 = \tfrac{7 \cdot 3 + 2 \cdot 4}{9} = \tfrac{29}{9} \approx 3.222 bits
per pair, i.e. 1.611 per symbol. The gap falls from 0.082 to 0.026
bits, consistent with the block bound \tfrac{L_2}{2} < H + \tfrac12.

Using the block coding bound, find a block length n that guarantees an
overhead below 0.01 bits per symbol for every i.i.d. source. Then explain
what the 90/10 table's n = 6 row (gap 0.001) shows about the difference
between the guarantee and actual performance.

The bound gives overhead \tfrac{L_n}{n} - H < \tfrac1n, so
\tfrac1n \le 0.01, i.e. n \ge 100, guarantees the target for any
source.

The guarantee is a worst case over sources. For the 90/10 coin the exact
optimal block code already has a gap of 0.001 < \tfrac16 at n = 6: the
2^6 = 64 block probabilities happen to fit integer lengths well. The
bound certifies 1/n without inspecting the source; particular sources
reach the floor much faster (and non-monotonically: the n = 8 gap is
larger than the n = 6 gap).

For n = 100 flips of the 90/10 coin, using the surprisal arithmetic of
Surprisal: (a) compute the surprisal of a sequence
with 90 heads and 10 tails and compare it to nH; (b) compute the
surprisal and per-symbol surprisal of the all-heads sequence, and state
whether the single most probable sequence is typical; (c) estimate the
fraction of the 2^{100} sequences that the \approx 2^{nH} typical
sequences occupy.

(a) Surprisals add over independent flips:
90 \cdot 0.152 + 10 \cdot 3.322 = 13.68 + 33.22 = 46.9 bits, exactly
nH = 100 \cdot 0.469. Any sequence with the 90/10 composition lands
exactly on nH; that is what makes it typical.

(b) All heads: 100 \cdot 0.152 = 15.2 bits, per-symbol surprisal
0.152. This is the most probable single sequence, but 0.152 is far
from H \approx 0.469, so it lies outside every small-\varepsilon
typical set: typicality means average-looking composition, not high
probability of the individual sequence.

(c) 2^{nH} / 2^n = 2^{46.9 - 100} = 2^{-53.1} \approx 10^{-16}: the
typical set is a vanishing sliver of sequence space, which is why indexing
it with \approx 47 bits instead of 100 is possible.

The theorem claims no lossless code beats H, not merely no prefix code.
Reconstruct the chain of results that closes this gap, naming the theorem
from The Kraft inequality that does the work and stating where
the entropy-floor proof uses it.

A lossless code here is a uniquely decodable code: every concatenated
message has exactly one parse. McMillan's theorem states that the codeword
lengths of any uniquely decodable code satisfy the same Kraft budget
\sum_i 2^{-\ell_i} \le 1 that prefix codes obey.

The entropy-floor proof uses only that budget: it needs c \le 1 to make
q(x) = 2^{-\ell(x)}/c a distribution and to make the slack
\log_2 \tfrac1c non-negative. Nothing in the decomposition
L = H + D + \text{slack} refers to the prefix property itself. So the
floor binds every uniquely decodable code; and conversely, by Kraft
sufficiency, any lengths such a code achieves are achievable by a prefix
code — the optimum over both classes coincides, and restricting attention
to prefix codes loses nothing.

The best symbol code for the 90/10 coin has lengths (1, 1) and L = 1
bit, an overhead of 0.531 bits (Huffman coding).
Compute the implied distribution of that code and show that the overhead
is exactly D(p\,\|\,q): identify the wrong bet the code is forced to
make.

Lengths (1, 1) give claims (\tfrac12, \tfrac12) with Kraft sum 1:
q is the fair coin. The code is forced to bet that heads and tails are
equally likely, because integer lengths on a binary alphabet leave no
other complete choice.

D(p\,\|\,q) = .9 \log_2 \tfrac{.9}{.5} + .1 \log_2 \tfrac{.1}{.5}

which equals L - H = 1 - 0.469 exactly (slack is 0). The entire symbol-
code overhead is the KL cost of modeling a 90/10 coin as fair — and block
coding removes it by letting the code bet on compositions of many flips
instead.

C. E. Shannon, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication," Bell System Technical Journal, 27, 1948 — Part I, Theorem 9: the fundamental theorem for a noiseless channel, stating H as the achievable limit of bits per symbol.

T. M. Cover, J. A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006 — §5.3–5.4: the bounds H \le L^* < H + 1 (Theorem 5.4.1), the D(p\|q) wrong-code decomposition, and block coding (Theorem 5.4.2); ch. 3: the asymptotic equipartition property and the typical set in full.

D. J. C. MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms, Cambridge University Press, 2003 — ch. 4 "The Source Coding Theorem": raw and essential bit content, the typical set, and the block-coding proof (Theorem 4.1); §4.4–4.6 for the typical-set figures this lesson's schematic follows. Free online: https://www.inference.org.uk/mackay/itila/

documents.title: Joint and conditional entropy
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Joint and conditional entropy
documents.text:
Conditional entropy H(Y|X) is the uncertainty remaining in Y once X is
observed; the chain rule decomposes joint uncertainty into sequential
parts. This lesson extends entropy from one variable to a pair: the joint
distribution table and its marginals, the joint entropy H(X,Y), the
conditional entropy H(Y \mid X) computed two equivalent ways, the chain
rule H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y \mid X), and the inequality
H(Y \mid X) \le H(Y) with its equality case.

documents.title: The joint table: one probability per pair
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Joint and conditional entropy › The joint table: one probability per pair

documents.title: Joint entropy: plain entropy on the flattened table
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Joint and conditional entropy › Joint entropy: plain entropy on the flattened table
documents.text:
Joint entropy: plain entropy on the flattened table

The uncertainty of the whole day is the entropy of the pair. A pair-valued
variable is still a discrete variable; its outcomes are the four cells.
Reading the table as one flat distribution
\{\tfrac{1}{2}, 0, \tfrac{1}{4}, \tfrac{1}{4}\} over pair-outcomes
reduces the problem to the three-step computation of
Entropy.

Compute H(X,Y) for the table above.

Step 1: surprisal of each nonzero cell.
(\text{clear}, \text{dry}): -\log_2 \tfrac{1}{2} = 1 bit;
(\text{overcast}, \text{dry}) and (\text{overcast}, \text{wet}):
-\log_2 \tfrac{1}{4} = 2 bits each. The zero cell is skipped.

Step 2: weight each surprisal by its cell probability.
\tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 1 = 0.5; \;\tfrac{1}{4} \cdot 2 = 0.5;
\;\tfrac{1}{4} \cdot 2 = 0.5.

Step 3: sum. H(X,Y) = 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.5 bits.

Bounds check. The value lies below \log_2 3 \approx 1.585 bits, the
maximum for a distribution supported on three cells.

The joint entropy of a pair of discrete random variables (X, Y) with
joint probability mass function p(x,y) is

H(X,Y) = -\sum_{x,y} p(x,y) \log_2 p(x,y)

measured in bits. Cells with p(x,y) = 0 contribute nothing.

No new machinery enters: joint entropy is the entropy formula applied to
pairs. It is symmetric, H(X,Y) = H(Y,X), because transposing the
table permutes the same multiset of cell values. One observation to hold:
the marginal entropies are H(X) = 1 bit (a fair coin) and
H(Y) = H(\tfrac{1}{4}) \approx 0.811 bits, so
H(X) + H(Y) \approx 1.811 > 1.5 = H(X,Y). The coupled pair is 0.311
bits cheaper than its parts priced separately; the last two sections
account for the gap.

Joint entropy is not a new primitive: flatten the table into one
distribution over pairs and apply the entropy formula.

documents.title: Conditional entropy: the average leftover uncertainty
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Joint and conditional entropy › Conditional entropy: the average leftover uncertainty
documents.text:
Conditional entropy: the average leftover uncertainty

A forecaster who sees the sky needs a number for the uncertainty that
remains about the ground. That number must average over what the sky can
show.

Each row, renormalized, is a conditional distribution

Dividing a row of the joint table by its row sum p(x) gives the
conditional distribution p(y \mid x). Here:

Given clear, the row (\tfrac{1}{2}, 0) renormalizes to (1, 0):
certainty. Leftover uncertainty H(Y \mid X{=}\text{clear}) = 0 bits.

Given overcast, the row (\tfrac{1}{4}, \tfrac{1}{4}) renormalizes to
(\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}): a fair coin.
H(Y \mid X{=}\text{overcast}) = 1 bit.

Each is an ordinary entropy of a two-outcome distribution, the binary
entropy function of Entropy. Two
numbers result, one per value of X.

One number: weight the rows by how often they occur

The single summary weights each row's entropy by the probability of that
row:

H(Y \mid X) = \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 0 + \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 1 = 0.5

Half of all days the sky settles the question completely; the other half
it leaves a fair coin.

Conditional entropy in three steps: row entropies, row weights, weighted sum H(Y|X) = 0.5 bits.

Step through the three frames. In frame 3, check the sum: the certain row
contributes \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 0 = 0 and the fair-coin row contributes
\tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 1 = 0.5, so H(Y \mid X) = 0.5 bits.

The conditional entropy of Y given X is

H(Y \mid X) = \sum_{x} p(x)\, H(Y \mid X{=}x)

measured in bits. Values x with p(x) = 0 are skipped: p(y \mid x) is
undefined there, and such rows carry weight zero.

The two forms are the same sum

Expanding the first form shows the equality: substitute
H(Y \mid X{=}x) = -\sum_y p(y \mid x) \log_2 p(y \mid x) and use
p(x)\, p(y \mid x) = p(x,y) to merge the weights into the joint
probabilities. The second form needs no renormalization step, which makes
it the faster route on a given table.

Recompute H(Y \mid X) for the weather table from
-\sum_{x,y} p(x,y) \log_2 p(y \mid x), one nonzero cell at a time.

(\text{clear}, \text{dry}): p(y \mid x) = 1, term
-\tfrac{1}{2} \log_2 1 = 0.
(\text{overcast}, \text{dry}): p(y \mid x) = \tfrac{1}{2}, term
-\tfrac{1}{4} \log_2 \tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{1}{4}.
(\text{overcast}, \text{wet}): likewise \tfrac{1}{4}.

Sum: 0 + 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5 bits, matching the weighted-average form.

H(Y \mid X) is one number, averaged over x; it is not
H(Y \mid X{=}x) for any particular x. The distinction matters because
a single observation can raise uncertainty: here
H(Y) \approx 0.811 bits, yet seeing an overcast sky leaves
H(Y \mid X{=}\text{overcast}) = 1 bit — more uncertainty than before
looking. The inequality proved two sections below bounds only the
average.

H(Y \mid X) is the p(x)-weighted average of the row entropies: one
number, 0.5 bits here, summarizing every possible observation of X.

documents.title: The chain rule: one total, two splits
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Joint and conditional entropy › The chain rule: one total, two splits
documents.text:
The chain rule: one total, two splits

The three computed numbers satisfy an exact identity:

H(X) + H(Y \mid X) = 1 + 0.5 = 1.5 = H(X,Y).

Total uncertainty about the day equals uncertainty about the sky plus the
average uncertainty about the ground once the sky is known: learn X,
then learn Y given X.

The other order: learn Y first

The split works equally in the other order, with the columns playing the
rows' part. Given dry (probability \tfrac{3}{4}), the column
renormalizes to p(x \mid \text{dry}) = (\tfrac{2}{3}, \tfrac{1}{3}),
with entropy \log_2 3 - \tfrac{2}{3} \approx 0.918 bits; given wet, the
column is (0, 1), entropy 0. So

H(X \mid Y) = \tfrac{3}{4} \cdot 0.918 + \tfrac{1}{4} \cdot 0

The chain rule: the same 1.5-bit total splits as H(X) + H(Y|X) or as H(Y) + H(X|Y).

For discrete random variables X and Y,

H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y \mid X) = H(Y) + H(X \mid Y).

For every cell with p(x,y) > 0, the product rule
p(x,y) = p(x)\, p(y \mid x) gives, after taking -\log_2,

-\log_2 p(x,y) = -\log_2 p(x) - \log_2 p(y \mid x).

Average both sides with weights p(x,y). The left side is H(X,Y). The
first term on the right is
\sum_{x,y} p(x,y) \bigl(-\log_2 p(x)\bigr)
= \sum_x p(x) \bigl(-\log_2 p(x)\bigr) = H(X), since
\sum_y p(x,y) = p(x). The second term is the joint form of
H(Y \mid X). Exchanging the roles of X and Y gives the second
equality. This is Cover & Thomas,
Theorem 2.2.1.

H(Y \mid X) = 0.5 while H(X \mid Y) \approx 0.689: the two
conditional entropies differ, and only the total H(X,Y) is symmetric.
Subtracting the two forms of the chain rule fixes the difference exactly:
H(X \mid Y) - H(Y \mid X) = H(X) - H(Y), here
1 - 0.811 = 0.189 bits.

The area picture: uncertainties tile an interval

The chain rule makes the five quantities fit one additive diagram, the
bar form of MacKay's
figure 8.1. H(X) and H(Y) overlap inside the total H(X,Y); the
crescent of H(X) outside the overlap is H(X \mid Y), the crescent of
H(Y) outside it is H(Y \mid X).

The additive diagram: H(X) and H(Y) tile H(X,Y) with a 0.311-bit overlap; the crescents are the conditional entropies.

The overlap has width
H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y) \approx 0.311 bits: uncertainty counted in both
marginals but only once in the total. It is the same 0.311-bit gap
observed after the joint-entropy definition, still unnamed here.

One total, two splits: H(X,Y) decomposes as H(X) + H(Y \mid X) and as
H(Y) + H(X \mid Y), and the conditionals differ by exactly
H(X) - H(Y).

documents.title: Conditioning reduces entropy on average
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Joint and conditional entropy › Conditioning reduces entropy on average
documents.text:
Conditioning reduces entropy on average

In the weather table, H(Y \mid X) = 0.5 < 0.811 \approx H(Y): on
average, seeing the sky removed uncertainty about the ground. This is a
theorem, not a feature of the example.

For discrete random variables X and Y,

H(Y \mid X) \le H(Y),

with equality if and only if X and Y are independent.

Sketch; Jensen's inequality
for the concave \log_2 is used without proof, as in the range theorem of
Entropy. Sum over cells with
p(x,y) > 0:

H(Y \mid X) - H(Y)

using p(x,y) = p(x) p(y \mid x) in the middle step and, in the last,
that \sum p(x) p(y) over a subset of pairs is at most 1. Strict
concavity makes the Jensen step an equality only when the ratio
p(y)/p(y \mid x) is constant on the support; combined with the last
inequality being tight, the constant is 1, i.e.
p(y \mid x) = p(y) wherever p(x) > 0: independence. This is
Cover & Thomas,
Theorem 2.6.5.

The two endpoints: independence and determinism

Independence is the equality case. The product table with the same
marginals as the weather table has cells
p(x,y) = p(x)\,p(y): rows (\tfrac{3}{8}, \tfrac{1}{8}) and
(\tfrac{3}{8}, \tfrac{1}{8}). Every row renormalizes to
(\tfrac{3}{4}, \tfrac{1}{4}), each row entropy is 0.811 bits, and the
average is H(Y \mid X) = H(Y). The chain rule then reads
H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y): joint entropy is additive exactly for independent
variables, the distribution-level echo of the additivity of surprisal in
Surprisal.

Determinism is the other endpoint. If Y is a function of X, every
row of the table is certain, each row entropy is 0, and
H(Y \mid X) = 0; the chain rule collapses to H(X,Y) = H(X). The
reverse conditional need not vanish: in the weather table the wet column
already determines the sky, yet H(X \mid Y) \approx 0.689 > 0, and
Exercise 6 builds a deterministic Y = f(X) with
H(X \mid Y) = \tfrac{5}{3} \approx 1.667 bits.

Same marginal H(Y) = 0.811 bits in all three tables; coupling alone shrinks the average leftover H(Y|X) from 0.811 to 0.5 to 0.

Step through the three frames. The column sums, and with them
H(Y) = 0.811 bits, never change; check that the amber H(Y \mid X) bar
alone shrinks: 0.811, then 0.5, then 0.

Observation never hurts on average: H(Y \mid X) \le H(Y), with equality
exactly under independence. A particular observation can still raise
uncertainty; only the average cannot.

documents.title: The drop H(Y) − H(Y|X): what conditioning bought
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Joint and conditional entropy › The drop H(Y) − H(Y|X): what conditioning bought
documents.text:
The drop H(Y) − H(Y|X): what conditioning bought

Across the three tables of the sequence, the drop H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) is
0, 0.311, and 0.811 bits: the uncertainty about rain that seeing
the sky removes. By the chain rule the drop equals
H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y), the overlap width in the area diagram, so both
routes measure one quantity. Mutual information defines
mutual information as exactly this drop and develops its properties.

Load the three presets in order and watch the difference readout:
independent gives 0, realistic a partial drop, perfectly linked
drives H(\text{rain} \mid \text{sky}) to 0 so the difference equals
H(\text{rain}). Then drag mass into the clear–wet cell of the realistic
preset and check that the difference shrinks toward 0 as the rows grow
proportional.

documents.title: Exercises
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Joint and conditional entropy › Exercises
documents.text:
Exercises

For the joint table p(a,c) = \tfrac{1}{2}, p(a,d) = \tfrac{1}{4},
p(b,c) = \tfrac{1}{8}, p(b,d) = \tfrac{1}{8} (rows X \in \{a,b\},
columns Y \in \{c,d\}): compute the marginals, H(X,Y), H(X), and
H(Y \mid X) by the weighted-average form, and verify the chain rule.
Use \log_2 3 \approx 1.585.

Marginals. Row sums: p(a) = \tfrac{3}{4}, p(b) = \tfrac{1}{4}.
Column sums: p(c) = \tfrac{5}{8}, p(d) = \tfrac{3}{8}.

Joint entropy. The flattened table is
\{\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{4}, \tfrac{1}{8}, \tfrac{1}{8}\} — the
four-symbol source of Entropy, so
H(X,Y) = \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot 1 + \tfrac{1}{4}\cdot 2 +
\tfrac{1}{8}\cdot 3 + \tfrac{1}{8}\cdot 3 = 1.75 bits.

Marginal entropy. H(X) = H(\tfrac{1}{4}) =
-\tfrac{3}{4}\log_2\tfrac{3}{4} - \tfrac{1}{4}\log_2\tfrac{1}{4}
= \tfrac{3}{4}(2 - 1.585) + \tfrac{1}{4}\cdot 2 \approx 0.811 bits.

Conditional entropy. Row a renormalizes to
(\tfrac{2}{3}, \tfrac{1}{3}):
H(Y \mid X{=}a) = \log_2 3 - \tfrac{2}{3} \approx 0.918 bits. Row b
renormalizes to (\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}):
H(Y \mid X{=}b) = 1 bit. Average:
H(Y \mid X) = \tfrac{3}{4}\cdot 0.918 + \tfrac{1}{4}\cdot 1
\approx 0.689 + 0.25 = 0.939 bits.

Chain rule. H(X) + H(Y \mid X) \approx 0.811 + 0.939 = 1.75
= H(X,Y).

Recompute H(Y \mid X) for the table of Exercise 1 using the joint form
-\sum_{x,y} p(x,y)\log_2 p(y \mid x), and confirm agreement with the
weighted-average value. Use \log_2 3 \approx 1.585, so
-\log_2 \tfrac{2}{3} \approx 0.585.

The conditionals are p(c \mid a) = \tfrac{2}{3},
p(d \mid a) = \tfrac{1}{3}, p(c \mid b) = p(d \mid b) = \tfrac{1}{2}.
Cell terms:

(a,c): -\tfrac{1}{2}\log_2\tfrac{2}{3} \approx \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot 0.585
= 0.293.
(a,d): -\tfrac{1}{4}\log_2\tfrac{1}{3} \approx \tfrac{1}{4}\cdot 1.585
= 0.396.
(b,c): -\tfrac{1}{8}\log_2\tfrac{1}{2} = 0.125.
(b,d): likewise 0.125.

Sum: 0.293 + 0.396 + 0.125 + 0.125 = 0.939 bits, matching Exercise 1.
The two forms are the same sum with the weights either kept separate
(p(x) times a row entropy) or merged into the joint probabilities.

For the weather table of the lesson, compute H(X \mid Y) directly from
the column conditionals, verify the second form of the chain rule,
H(Y) + H(X \mid Y) = H(X,Y), and check the difference identity
H(X \mid Y) - H(Y \mid X) = H(X) - H(Y).

Columns. Given dry (p = \tfrac{3}{4}):
p(x \mid \text{dry}) = (\tfrac{2}{3}, \tfrac{1}{3}), entropy
\log_2 3 - \tfrac{2}{3} \approx 0.918 bits. Given wet
(p = \tfrac{1}{4}): p(x \mid \text{wet}) = (0, 1), entropy 0.

Average. H(X \mid Y) = \tfrac{3}{4}\cdot 0.918 +
\tfrac{1}{4}\cdot 0 \approx 0.689 bits.

Chain rule. H(Y) + H(X \mid Y) \approx 0.811 + 0.689 = 1.5
= H(X,Y), matching H(X) + H(Y \mid X) = 1 + 0.5.

Difference. H(X \mid Y) - H(Y \mid X) \approx 0.689 - 0.5 = 0.189
and H(X) - H(Y) \approx 1 - 0.811 = 0.189: equal, as subtracting the
two chain-rule forms requires.

In the weather table, identify a value x with
H(Y \mid X{=}x) > H(Y), and state why this does not contradict the
theorem H(Y \mid X) \le H(Y).

x = \text{overcast}: the conditional distribution is
(\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}), so H(Y \mid X{=}\text{overcast}) = 1
bit, exceeding H(Y) \approx 0.811 bits. Seeing an overcast sky moves
the rain distribution from (\tfrac{3}{4}, \tfrac{1}{4}) to a fair coin
— closer to uniform, hence more uncertain. No contradiction: the theorem
bounds the average over x, and the average
\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot 0 + \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot 1 = 0.5 bits stays below
0.811, because the overcast row's excess is outweighed by the clear
row's certainty.

Build the independent table with marginals
p(\text{clear}) = \tfrac{1}{2} and p(\text{dry}) = \tfrac{3}{4}, then
verify H(Y \mid X) = H(Y) and H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y), the latter by
computing H(X,Y) directly from the cells. Use
\log_2 3 \approx 1.585, so \log_2 \tfrac{8}{3} \approx 1.415.

Cells. p(x,y) = p(x)p(y):
p(\text{clear},\text{dry}) = p(\text{overcast},\text{dry}) =
\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{3}{4} = \tfrac{3}{8};
p(\text{clear},\text{wet}) = p(\text{overcast},\text{wet}) =
\tfrac{1}{8}.

Conditional entropy. Both rows renormalize to
(\tfrac{3}{4}, \tfrac{1}{4}), each with entropy
H(\tfrac{1}{4}) \approx 0.811 bits; the weighted average of two equal
values is that value, so H(Y \mid X) = 0.811 = H(Y) bits.

Joint entropy directly.
$H(X,Y) = -2\cdot\tfrac\log_2\tfrac

2\cdot\tfrac\log_2\tfrac
\approx 2\cdot\tfrac\cdot 1.415 + 2\cdot\tfrac\cdot 3
= 1.061 + 0.75 = 1.811$ bits.

Additivity. H(X) + H(Y) \approx 1 + 0.811 = 1.811 = H(X,Y): the
chain rule with H(Y \mid X) = H(Y).

Roll a fair die X and set Y = 1 if X \ge 5, else Y = 0. Compute
H(X), H(Y), H(Y \mid X), H(X,Y), and H(X \mid Y), the last both
by the chain rule and directly from the conditional distributions. Use
\log_2 3 \approx 1.585.

H(X) = \log_2 6 \approx 2.585 bits: a uniform six-outcome draw, per the
range theorem of Entropy.

Y takes value 1 with probability \tfrac{2}{6} = \tfrac{1}{3}, so
H(Y) = H(\tfrac{1}{3}) = \log_2 3 - \tfrac{2}{3} \approx 0.918 bits.

Y is a function of X: every row of the joint table is certain, so
H(Y \mid X) = 0, and the chain rule gives
H(X,Y) = H(X) + 0 \approx 2.585 bits.

By the other order, H(X \mid Y) = H(X,Y) - H(Y) \approx 2.585 - 0.918
= 1.667 bits. Directly: given Y = 1 (probability \tfrac{1}{3}), X
is uniform on \{5, 6\}, entropy 1 bit; given Y = 0, uniform on
\{1,2,3,4\}, entropy 2 bits; average
\tfrac{1}{3}\cdot 1 + \tfrac{2}{3}\cdot 2 = \tfrac{5}{3} \approx 1.667
bits. Determinism is one-sided: H(Y \mid X) = 0 while
H(X \mid Y) \approx 1.667 > 0.

Surprisal established the per-event decomposition
I(A \cap B) = I(A) + I(B \mid A) for surprisal. Derive the chain rule
H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y \mid X) from it by averaging.

Apply the decomposition to the events A = \{X{=}x\} and
B = \{Y{=}y\} for a cell with p(x,y) > 0:

-\log_2 p(x,y) = -\log_2 p(x) - \log_2 p(y \mid x).

Take the expectation of both sides under the joint distribution, i.e.
multiply each cell's equation by p(x,y) and sum. The left side becomes
H(X,Y) by the definition of joint entropy. The first right-hand term
becomes \sum_{x,y} p(x,y)(-\log_2 p(x)) = \sum_x p(x)(-\log_2 p(x))
= H(X), since the inner sum over y collapses to the marginal. The
second becomes -\sum_{x,y} p(x,y)\log_2 p(y \mid x) = H(Y \mid X), the
joint form of the definition. Hence H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y \mid X): the
chain rule is the surprisal decomposition, holding cell by cell, taken in
expectation.

T. M. Cover, J. A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006 — §2.2 defines joint and conditional entropy and proves the chain rule (Theorem 2.2.1); Theorem 2.6.5 is conditioning reduces entropy.

D. J. C. MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms, Cambridge University Press, 2003 — ch. 8 "Dependent Random Variables", §8.1: joint ensembles, marginal and conditional entropy, the chain rule, and the additive diagram (fig. 8.1) recreated in this lesson. Free online: https://www.inference.org.uk/mackay/itila/

C. E. Shannon, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication," Bell System Technical Journal, 27, 1948 — §6 lists H(x,y) = H(x) + H_x(y) and H(x,y) \le H(x) + H(y) among the properties of entropy.

documents.title: Mutual information
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Mutual information
documents.text:
Mutual information I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y) quantifies, in bits, how much
observing one variable reduces uncertainty about the other. This lesson
computes that drop on the weather table of the previous lesson, defines
mutual information, proves it symmetric with range 0 to
\min(H(X), H(Y)), rewrites it as a divergence from independence, and
closes with a dependent pair that correlation cannot detect.

documents.title: Naming the drop: I(X;Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Mutual information › Naming the drop: I(X;Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y)
documents.text:
Naming the drop: I(X;Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y)

Joint and conditional entropy ended with an unnamed
0.311-bit gap. Its weather table, sky
X \in \{\text{clear}, \text{overcast}\} and ground
Y \in \{\text{dry}, \text{wet}\}, produced five entropies: H(X) = 1,
H(Y) \approx 0.811, H(X,Y) = 1.5, H(Y \mid X) = 0.5, and
H(X \mid Y) \approx 0.689 bits.

Before the ground is observed, uncertainty about the sky is H(X) = 1
bit. After, an average of H(X \mid Y) \approx 0.689 bits remains. The
observation removed

H(X) - H(X \mid Y) \approx 1 - 0.689 = 0.311 \text{ bits}.

The same drop appears in the other direction. Observing the sky removes
H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) \approx 0.811 - 0.5 = 0.311 bits of uncertainty
about the ground. One number measures the coupling from either end.

The mutual information between discrete random variables X and Y
is

I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y),

measured in bits: the average reduction in the uncertainty of X
produced by observing Y.

Observing Y splits H(X) into the part it removes, I(X;Y), and the part it leaves, H(X|Y).

No new primitive enters: every term comes from the joint table by the
previous lesson's recipes, marginals from row and column sums,
conditional entropy as the weighted average of row entropies. The units
follow the log base of the entropies: bits under \log_2, nats under
\ln.

I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) is the average number of bits that
observing one variable removes from the uncertainty of the other:
0.311 bits in the weather table, from either direction.

documents.title: Symmetry: Y says as much about X as X says about Y
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Mutual information › Symmetry: Y says as much about X as X says about Y
documents.text:
Symmetry: Y says as much about X as X says about Y

The two drops agreeing at 0.311 bits is not a feature of the weather
table. The chain rule of
Joint and conditional entropy forces it for every joint
distribution.

For discrete random variables X and Y,

I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)

and in particular I(X;Y) = I(Y;X).

The chain rule gives H(X,Y) = H(Y) + H(X \mid Y), so
H(X \mid Y) = H(X,Y) - H(Y). Substituting into the definition:

I(X;Y) = H(X) - \bigl(H(X,Y) - H(Y)\bigr) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y).

The right side is symmetric in X and Y: it is unchanged by swapping
them, since H(X,Y) = H(Y,X). Applying the same substitution with the
roles exchanged, using H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y \mid X), yields
H(Y) - H(Y \mid X). This is
Cover & Thomas,
Theorem 2.4.1.

Check on the weather table:
H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y) \approx 1 + 0.811 - 1.5 = 0.311 bits, matching
both drops.

The third form completes the area diagram left open in the previous
lesson: H(X) and H(Y) overlap inside H(X,Y), and the overlap,
counted in both marginals but once in the total, is exactly I(X;Y).
The picture is the bar form of
MacKay's figure 8.1.

Mutual information is the overlap of H(X) and H(Y) inside H(X,Y): one region, three ways to read its width.

Setting Y = X gives I(X;X) = H(X) - H(X \mid X) = H(X), since
knowing X leaves no uncertainty about X: H(X \mid X) = 0. A
variable shares its entire entropy with itself, which is why entropy is
also called self-information.

The overlap picture is an aid, not a theory. Mutual information is not a
distance: I(X;X) = H(X) \ne 0, so "zero iff identical" fails in the
metric direction, and I satisfies no triangle inequality. The picture
also stops at two variables: the natural three-variable analogue of the
overlap, the interaction information I(X;Y;Z), can be negative, so no
Venn diagram with nonnegative areas represents three general variables.
Both points are beyond this course's scope; Cover & Thomas §2.5 treats
the multivariate extensions that do work (chain rules for mutual
information).

Mutual information is symmetric: Y reveals exactly as many bits about
X as X reveals about Y, whatever the joint distribution.

documents.title: The range: zero at independence, min(H(X), H(Y)) at determinism
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Mutual information › The range: zero at independence, min(H(X), H(Y)) at determinism
documents.text:
The range: zero at independence, min(H(X), H(Y)) at determinism

Two theorems pin down the possible values of I(X;Y). Both are one-line
consequences of results already proved.

I(X;Y) \ge 0, with equality if and only if X and Y are
independent.

Conditioning reduces entropy on average
(Joint and conditional entropy, after Cover & Thomas
Theorem 2.6.5): H(X \mid Y) \le H(X), with equality exactly under
independence. Subtracting, I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) \ge 0, with
equality in the same case.

I(X;Y) \le \min\bigl(H(X), H(Y)\bigr). Equality I(X;Y) = H(X) holds
if and only if X is determined by Y (that is, H(X \mid Y) = 0),
and symmetrically for H(Y).

Conditional entropy is an average of entropies, hence nonnegative:
H(X \mid Y) \ge 0. So I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) \le H(X), with
equality exactly when H(X \mid Y) = 0: every value of Y pins down
X. The bound I(X;Y) \le H(Y) follows by symmetry.

The bound has an operational reading: observing Y cannot teach more
about X than the total uncertainty H(X) that exists to remove. In
the weather table, I \approx 0.311 \le \min(1, 0.811), and the bound
is slack: neither variable determines the other.

0 \le I(X;Y) \le \min(H(X), H(Y)): zero exactly at independence, the
full marginal entropy exactly when one variable determines the other.

documents.title: The dependence dial: independent to lockstep
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Mutual information › The dependence dial: independent to lockstep
documents.text:
The dependence dial: independent to lockstep

The two endpoints, and everything between, fit in one family of tables.
Let X and Y be binary with uniform marginals, coupled only through
the agreement probability q = P(Y = X): each diagonal cell holds
q/2, each off-diagonal cell (1-q)/2.

One q per frame. Watch the amber I(X;Y) segment grow from 0 to the full bit of H(X) as probability mass concentrates on the diagonal.

One table worked: q = 0.75

The table has diagonal cells \tfrac{3}{8} and off-diagonal cells
\tfrac{1}{8}; row and column sums are all \tfrac{1}{2}, so
H(X) = H(Y) = 1 bit.

Step 1: condition on each value of Y. Given Y = 0 (probability
\tfrac{1}{2}), the column (\tfrac{3}{8}, \tfrac{1}{8}) renormalizes
to p(x \mid y{=}0) = (\tfrac{3}{4}, \tfrac{1}{4}), with entropy
H(\tfrac{1}{4}) \approx 0.811 bits. Given Y = 1, the column
renormalizes to (\tfrac{1}{4}, \tfrac{3}{4}): the same entropy.

Step 2: average.
H(X \mid Y) = \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 0.811 + \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 0.811
= 0.811 bits.

Step 3: subtract.
I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) \approx 1 - 0.811 = 0.189 bits.

Cross-check via the joint form. The flattened table
\{\tfrac{3}{8}, \tfrac{3}{8}, \tfrac{1}{8}, \tfrac{1}{8}\} has
H(X,Y) = 2 \cdot \tfrac{3}{8} \cdot 1.415 + 2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{8}
\cdot 3 \approx 1.811 bits, and
H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y) \approx 1 + 1 - 1.811 = 0.189 bits.

The whole dial in one formula

The computation generalizes: every column conditions X to the
distribution (q, 1-q), so H(X \mid Y) = H_2(q), the binary entropy
function, and

I(X;Y) = 1 - H_2(q).

At q = \tfrac{1}{2} every cell equals \tfrac{1}{4}, the product of
the marginals: independence, I = 0. At q = 1 the variables are in
lockstep and I = 1 bit, the full H(X), hitting the upper bound. The
formula is symmetric under q \leftrightarrow 1-q: perfect
disagreement is as informative as perfect agreement, since swapping
the labels of Y changes no conditional distribution's entropy.

Load the three presets in order and read the split: independent gives
I = 0 with the full bar left as H(X \mid Y); noisy channel gives a
partial split; lockstep drives H(X \mid Y) to 0 so
I(X;Y) = H(X) = 1 bit. Then drag the dependence slider slowly and
check that the two segments always sum to the same H(X): coupling
moves bits between the segments, never creates them.

documents.title: Divergence from independence
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Mutual information › Divergence from independence
documents.text:
Divergence from independence

Since I = 0 characterizes independence, mutual information should
measure how far the joint distribution sits from the independent one
with the same marginals. Rewriting the definition makes this exact.

I(X;Y) = \sum_{x,y} p(x,y) \log_2 \frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)\,p(y)}.

Write both terms of the definition as sums over the joint table, using
\sum_y p(x,y) = p(x) for the first:

I(X;Y) = -\sum_{x,y} p(x,y) \log_2 p(x)

Multiplying numerator and denominator by p(y) and using
p(x \mid y)\, p(y) = p(x,y) gives the stated ratio. Cells with
p(x,y) = 0 contribute nothing, by the usual convention. This is the
definition Cover & Thomas §2.3 takes as primary.

The right side compares the true joint p(x,y) against the product
p(x)\,p(y), the table the variables would have if independent with
the same marginals. A later lesson,
KL divergence, names this comparison for arbitrary
distribution pairs: the KL divergence D(p \Vert q), the expected
extra bits paid for coding p with a code built for q. Mutual
information is the special case
I(X;Y) = D\bigl(p(x,y) \,\Vert\, p(x)\,p(y)\bigr): the coding price
of pretending the variables are independent.

Same marginals, different tables: mutual information is the divergence of the true joint from the independent product.

The per-cell quantity
\operatorname{pmi}(x,y) = \log_2 \tfrac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)}, the
pointwise mutual information, carries a sign: positive where the pair
occurs more often than independence predicts, negative where it occurs
less. In the weather table the cell (overcast, dry) has
\operatorname{pmi} = \log_2 \tfrac{2}{3} \approx -0.585 bits.
I(X;Y) is the p(x,y)-weighted average of these terms and is never
negative; Exercise 7 runs the full tally. Do not read the nonnegativity
of I as a statement about individual cells.

I(X;Y) = D\bigl(p(x,y) \Vert p(x)p(y)\bigr): mutual information is
the divergence of the joint from the independent product, which is why
it vanishes exactly at independence and never below zero.

documents.title: What correlation misses
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Mutual information › What correlation misses
documents.text:
What correlation misses

Zero mutual information means statistical independence. The familiar
weaker diagnostic, the correlation coefficient, certifies much less:
zero correlation rules out only linear dependence. A pair can be
deterministically coupled and still uncorrelated.

Let X be uniform on \{-1, 0, 1\} and Y = X^2.

Correlation. \mathbb{E}[X] = 0 and
\mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[X^3]
= \tfrac{1}{3}(-1 + 0 + 1) = 0, so
\operatorname{cov}(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X]\,
\mathbb{E}[Y] = 0: the correlation is exactly zero.

Mutual information. Y is a function of X, so
H(Y \mid X) = 0 and I(X;Y) = H(Y). Since Y = 1 with probability
\tfrac{2}{3} and Y = 0 with probability \tfrac{1}{3},

I(X;Y) = H(Y) = H\bigl(\tfrac{1}{3}\bigr)

Cross-check from the other side. H(X) = \log_2 3 \approx 1.585
bits. Given Y = 1, X is uniform on \{-1, 1\}: 1 bit. Given
Y = 0, X = 0: 0 bits. So
H(X \mid Y) = \tfrac{2}{3} \cdot 1 + \tfrac{1}{3} \cdot 0 =
\tfrac{2}{3}, and
I = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) \approx 1.585 - 0.667 = 0.918 bits: the same
value, as symmetry requires.

Correlation projects the dependence onto a straight line, and this
dependence is a parabola: the projection vanishes. Mutual information
works on the joint table itself, so no functional shape hides from it.

Y = X² on a symmetric X: the correlation is exactly zero while the variables share 0.918 bits.

Zero correlation rules out only linear dependence; zero mutual
information rules out all dependence. Independence is the stronger,
cleaner condition, and mutual information is its exact witness.

This exactness is why mutual information, not correlation, is the
working currency of what follows: the next lesson,
The data-processing inequality, proves that no processing of
data can increase it, and later lessons build on it as an objective —
Channel capacity maximizes it over channel inputs,
The information bottleneck trades it between compression and
relevance, and The InfoNCE bound bounds it from raw samples.

documents.title: Exercises
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Mutual information › Exercises
documents.text:
Exercises

For the weather table (p(\text{clear},\text{dry}) = \tfrac{1}{2},
p(\text{clear},\text{wet}) = 0,
p(\text{overcast},\text{dry}) = p(\text{overcast},\text{wet}) =
\tfrac{1}{4}), compute I(X;Y) three ways: as H(X) - H(X \mid Y),
as H(Y) - H(Y \mid X), and as H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y). Use the
entropies quoted in the lesson.

From the previous lesson: H(X) = 1, H(Y) \approx 0.811,
H(X,Y) = 1.5, H(Y \mid X) = 0.5, H(X \mid Y) \approx 0.689 bits.

Route 1: I = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) \approx 1 - 0.689 = 0.311 bits.
Route 2: I = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) \approx 0.811 - 0.5 = 0.311 bits.
Route 3: I = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y) \approx 1 + 0.811 - 1.5 = 0.311
bits.

All three agree, as the three-forms theorem requires: they are the same
overlap read off different pairs of bars.

For the joint table p(a,c) = \tfrac{1}{2}, p(a,d) = \tfrac{1}{4},
p(b,c) = \tfrac{1}{8}, p(b,d) = \tfrac{1}{8} (the table of the
previous lesson's Exercise 1, with H(X) \approx 0.8113,
H(X,Y) = 1.75, H(Y \mid X) \approx 0.9387 bits), compute H(Y) and
then I(X;Y) by two routes. Use \log_2 5 \approx 2.3219 and
\log_2 3 \approx 1.5850.

Marginal of Y. Column sums: p(c) = \tfrac{5}{8},
p(d) = \tfrac{3}{8}. Then
-\log_2 \tfrac{5}{8} = 3 - \log_2 5 \approx 0.6781 and
-\log_2 \tfrac{3}{8} = 3 - \log_2 3 \approx 1.4150, so

H(Y) = \tfrac{5}{8} \cdot 0.6781 + \tfrac{3}{8} \cdot 1.4150

Route 1. I = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) \approx 0.9544 - 0.9387 = 0.0157
bits.

Route 2. I = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y) \approx 0.8113 + 0.9544 - 1.75
= 0.0157 bits.

The table is nearly independent: the variables share only about
0.016 bits, two orders of magnitude below \min(H(X), H(Y))
\approx 0.81.

Write out the dependence-dial table at q = 0.9 and compute I(X;Y).
Use H_2(0.9) \approx 0.469 bits, the entropy of the 90{:}10 coin
from The source coding theorem. Compare with the
lockstep value at q = 1.

Diagonal cells q/2 = 0.45, off-diagonal cells (1-q)/2 = 0.05;
marginals uniform, H(X) = 1 bit.

Each column of the table renormalizes X to (0.9, 0.1) (or its
mirror), so every conditional entropy is H_2(0.9) \approx 0.469 bits
and H(X \mid Y) = 0.469 bits. Therefore

I(X;Y) = 1 - H_2(0.9) \approx 1 - 0.469 = 0.531 \text{ bits}.

At q = 1 the off-diagonal cells vanish, H(X \mid Y) = 0, and
I = 1 bit: lockstep attains the upper bound I = H(X). The last ten
percentage points of agreement are worth 0.469 bits, nearly as much
as the first forty (0.531 bits): mutual information rises steeply
near determinism.

Let X be uniform on \{-2, -1, 1, 2\} and Y = X^2. Show that X
and Y are uncorrelated, then compute I(X;Y) by two routes.

Correlation. \mathbb{E}[X] = \tfrac{1}{4}(-2 - 1 + 1 + 2) = 0 and
\mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[X^3] = \tfrac{1}{4}(-8 - 1 + 1 + 8) = 0,
so \operatorname{cov}(X,Y) = 0 - 0 = 0.

Route 1. Y is a function of X, so H(Y \mid X) = 0 and
I = H(Y). Y takes values 1 and 4 with probability \tfrac{1}{2}
each: H(Y) = 1 bit, so I(X;Y) = 1 bit.

Route 2. H(X) = \log_2 4 = 2 bits. Given Y = 1, X is uniform
on \{-1, 1\}: 1 bit; given Y = 4, uniform on \{-2, 2\}: 1
bit. So H(X \mid Y) = 1 and I = 2 - 1 = 1 bit.

The pair shares a full bit, the identity of |X|, while the
correlation sees nothing: the dependence is symmetric about zero, so
its linear shadow vanishes.

Prove I(X;X) = H(X) from the definition, and evaluate it for one
fair die roll. State why the result names entropy "self-information".

I(X;X) = H(X) - H(X \mid X). Given X = x, the value of X is
certain: each conditional distribution is a point mass with entropy
0, so the average H(X \mid X) = 0 and I(X;X) = H(X).

For a fair die, I(X;X) = H(X) = \log_2 6 \approx 2.585 bits.

Reading: mutual information measures the bits one variable carries
about another, and a variable carries about itself exactly its entire
uncertainty. Entropy is the information a variable shares with itself,
hence self-information. This also shows the upper bound
I \le \min(H(X), H(Y)) is tight.

Roll a fair die X and set Y = 1 if X \ge 5, else Y = 0 (the
construction of the previous lesson's Exercise 6, where
H(X) = \log_2 6 \approx 2.585, H(Y) \approx 0.918, and
H(X \mid Y) = \tfrac{5}{3} bits were computed). Compute I(X;Y) by
two routes and verify that it attains the upper bound
\min(H(X), H(Y)).

Route 1. Y is a function of X, so H(Y \mid X) = 0 and
I = H(Y) - 0 = H(\tfrac{1}{3}) = \log_2 3 - \tfrac{2}{3}
\approx 0.918 bits.

Route 2. I = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) \approx 2.585 - 1.667 = 0.918
bits: agreement.

Bound. \min(H(X), H(Y)) = \min(2.585, 0.918) = 0.918 = I. The
bound is attained on the H(Y) side because Y is determined by X:
all of Y's uncertainty is shared. It is far from attained on the
H(X) side: knowing Y still leaves \tfrac{5}{3} bits of X
unresolved.

Compute the pointwise mutual information
\operatorname{pmi}(x,y) = \log_2 \tfrac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)} for each
nonzero cell of the weather table, identify the negative cell, and
verify that the p(x,y)-weighted average equals I(X;Y) \approx 0.311
bits. Use \log_2 3 \approx 1.585.

Marginals: p(\text{clear}) = p(\text{overcast}) = \tfrac{1}{2};
p(\text{dry}) = \tfrac{3}{4}, p(\text{wet}) = \tfrac{1}{4}.

(\text{clear}, \text{dry}): product \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot \tfrac{3}{4}
= \tfrac{3}{8}; ratio \tfrac{1/2}{3/8} = \tfrac{4}{3};
\operatorname{pmi} = \log_2 \tfrac{4}{3} = 2 - \log_2 3 \approx
0.415 bits.

(\text{overcast}, \text{dry}): product \tfrac{3}{8}; ratio
\tfrac{1/4}{3/8} = \tfrac{2}{3};
\operatorname{pmi} = 1 - \log_2 3 \approx -0.585 bits — the
negative cell: overcast-and-dry occurs less often than independence
predicts.

(\text{overcast}, \text{wet}): product \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot
\tfrac{1}{4} = \tfrac{1}{8}; ratio 2; \operatorname{pmi} = 1 bit.

(\text{clear}, \text{wet}) has p = 0: weight zero, skipped.

Weighted average:

\tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 0.415 + \tfrac{1}{4} \cdot (-0.585)

Individual cells go negative; the average, mutual information, does
not.

T. M. Cover, J. A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006 — §2.3 defines mutual information as the divergence D(p(x,y) \Vert p(x)p(y)); §2.4 proves the entropy identities (Theorem 2.4.1) and I(X;X) = H(X); §2.6 gives nonnegativity via the information inequality.

D. J. C. MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms, Cambridge University Press, 2003 — ch. 8 "Dependent Random Variables", §8.1: mutual information among the entropies of a joint ensemble, with the area diagram (fig. 8.1); §§8.2–8.3 drill it in exercises. Free online: https://www.inference.org.uk/mackay/itila/

C. E. Shannon, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication," Bell System Technical Journal, 27, 1948 — §12 introduces R = H(x) - H_y(x), the "actual rate of transmission": mutual information before its modern name, as the quantity a noisy channel transmits.

documents.title: The data-processing inequality
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › The data-processing inequality
documents.text:
For any variable T computed from X, no processing can increase information
about a third variable Y: if Y, X, T form a Markov chain, then
I(T;Y) <= I(X;Y). This lesson watches the loss happen on a four-symbol
table, states the Markov condition that makes "computed from X" precise,
proves the inequality by expanding one quantity two ways with the chain
rule, characterizes the equality case as sufficiency, and reads the result
as a ceiling over every learned representation: no feature of X knows more
about a target than X does.

documents.title: A merge that loses bits: I drops from 0.811 to 0.467
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › The data-processing inequality › A merge that loses bits: I drops from 0.811 to 0.467
documents.text:
A merge that loses bits: I drops from 0.811 to 0.467

The setup: a four-symbol source with a binary label

Take the four-symbol source used since
Entropy: X \in \{a,b,c,d\} with
probabilities \tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{4}, \tfrac{1}{8}, \tfrac{1}{8}, so
H(X) = 1.75 bits. Attach a binary label Y: Y = 1 if
X \in \{c, d\}, else Y = 0. The joint table has one nonzero cell per
column:

p(x,y)

x = a

x = b

x = c

x = d

p(y)

y = 0
