Y is a function of X: every column is certain, so
H(Y \mid X) = 0, the determinism endpoint of
Joint and conditional entropy. The marginal is
p(Y{=}1) = \tfrac{1}{8} + \tfrac{1}{8} = \tfrac{1}{4}, so
H(Y) = H_2(\tfrac{1}{4}) \approx 0.811 bits, and by the definition of
mutual information,

I(X;Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) \approx 0.811 - 0 = 0.811 \text{ bits}.

X resolves the label completely; 0.811 bits is the entire budget in
play.

The processing step: collapse b and c into one symbol

Process the data: define T = f(X) with f(a) = a,
f(b) = f(c) = m, f(d) = d, a quantizer that merges the two middle
symbols. T is computed from X alone; it never sees Y.

Compute I(T;Y) for the merged variable.

Step 1: distribution of T. Merging adds probabilities:
p(a) = \tfrac{1}{2}, p(m) = \tfrac{1}{4} + \tfrac{1}{8} =
\tfrac{3}{8}, p(d) = \tfrac{1}{8}.

Step 2: label given T. Given a: Y = 0, certain. Given d:
Y = 1, certain. Given m: the merged column holds b's mass
\tfrac{1}{4} with Y = 0 and c's mass \tfrac{1}{8} with Y = 1,
so p(Y{=}1 \mid m) = \tfrac{1/8}{3/8} = \tfrac{1}{3}.

Step 3: conditional entropy. Only the m slice is uncertain, with
H_2(\tfrac{1}{3}) = \log_2 3 - \tfrac{2}{3} \approx 0.918 bits:

H(Y \mid T) = \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 0 + \tfrac{3}{8} \cdot 0.918

Step 4: subtract.

I(T;Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid T) \approx 0.811 - 0.344 = 0.467

Merging b (pure Y = 0) with c (pure Y = 1) hides the one distinction that carried 0.344 of the 0.811 bits about Y.

The merge cost 0.344 bits because it fused a pure-Y{=}0 column with a
pure-Y{=}1 column: inside m the label is uncertain. The theorem of
this lesson states that the direction of this comparison is universal:
for every T computed from X, whatever the map,
I(T;Y) \le I(X;Y).

Processing dropped the information about Y from 0.811 to 0.467
bits: the merged symbol m hides the b/c distinction, and that
distinction is where 0.344 of the bits about Y lived.

documents.title: The Markov condition: what "computed from X" means
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › The data-processing inequality › The Markov condition: what "computed from X" means
documents.text:
The Markov condition: what "computed from X" means

The merge is one instance of a general shape: T is produced from X
by a fixed rule, possibly with added randomness, and without access to
Y. The probabilistic statement of "without access to Y" is
conditional independence.

Random variables Y, X, T form a Markov chain, written
Y \to X \to T, if

p(t \mid x, y) = p(t \mid x) \quad \text{whenever } p(x,y) > 0;

equivalently, if Y and T are conditionally independent given X:
p(y, t \mid x) = p(y \mid x)\, p(t \mid x).

The Markov chain Y → X → T: all of T's dependence on Y routes through X, so the T span cannot exceed the X span.

Three consequences fix the scope of the hypothesis:

Deterministic maps qualify. T = f(X) gives
p(t \mid x, y) = \mathbf{1}\{t = f(x)\}, which does not involve
y: every function of the data, including the merge above, forms a
Markov chain.

Randomized processing qualifies. If T is computed from X and
fresh noise independent of (X,Y), e.g. T = X \oplus N, the
condition still holds. The proof below uses the Markov property only,
never determinism.

The chain reverses. Factoring
p(y,x,t) = p(x)\, p(y \mid x)\, p(t \mid x) is symmetric in y and
t, so Y \to X \to T holds exactly when T \to X \to Y does. One
hypothesis serves both reading directions.

If T is built with access to Y itself, the condition
p(t \mid x,y) = p(t \mid x) fails and the conclusion can fail with it:
Exercise 3 constructs a T with I(T;Y) = 1 bit while I(X;Y) = 0.
Checking the Markov property is not a formality; it is the entire
content of "T was computed from X".

Y \to X \to T states exactly that all of T's dependence on Y
routes through X: determinism is not required, fresh randomness is
allowed, access to Y is not.

documents.title: The proof: expand I(Y; X,T) two ways
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › The data-processing inequality › The proof: expand I(Y; X,T) two ways
documents.text:
The proof: expand I(Y; X,T) two ways

The proof needs one new quantity and one identity, both assembled from
entropies the course already owns.

Conditional mutual information: the missing primitive

The conditional mutual information of Y and T given X is

I(Y;T \mid X) = H(Y \mid X) - H(Y \mid X, T)

where I(Y;T \mid X{=}x) is the mutual information of the conditional
joint distribution p(y,t \mid x).

Each slice I(Y;T \mid X{=}x) is an ordinary mutual information, hence
nonnegative by the nonnegativity theorem of
Mutual information; the weighted average inherits the
bound: I(Y;T \mid X) \ge 0, with equality exactly when Y and T
are independent inside every slice. That equality condition is the
Markov property, restated.

On the running table both conditional informations are computable
directly. Given X = b, the value T = m is certain, and a constant
is independent of everything: every slice of I(Y;T \mid X) is zero,
so I(Y;T \mid X) = 0. The mirror quantity I(Y;X \mid T): the
slices T = a and T = d determine Y, contributing zero; the slice
T = m holds X \in \{b, c\} with probabilities
(\tfrac{2}{3}, \tfrac{1}{3}) and Y follows X inside it, so its
mutual information is H_2(\tfrac{1}{3}) \approx 0.918 bits. Averaging:

I(Y;X \mid T) = \tfrac{3}{8} \cdot 0.918 \approx 0.344 \text{ bits},

which is numerically the loss I(X;Y) - I(T;Y) observed in the first
section. The chain rule turns this coincidence into an identity.

The chain rule for mutual information

For any discrete random variables Y, X, T,

I(Y;\, X, T) = I(Y;X) + I(Y;T \mid X) = I(Y;T) + I(Y;X \mid T).

The pair (X,T) is one discrete variable, so
I(Y;\, X,T) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X, T). Insert H(Y \mid X):

I(Y;\, X,T)

The first bracket is the definition of I(Y;X); the second is the
definition of I(Y;T \mid X). The pair enters only as a pair, so the
same insertion with H(Y \mid T) in place of H(Y \mid X) gives the
second equality. This is the chain rule for information,
Cover & Thomas
Theorem 2.5.2, in the two-variable case.

The identity reads: the information the pair (X,T) carries about Y
can be tallied X-first or T-first, and both tallies equal the same
total.

The theorem

If Y \to X \to T, then

I(T;Y) \le I(X;Y),

with equality if and only if I(Y;X \mid T) = 0.

Expand I(Y;\, X,T) both ways with the chain rule:

I(Y;X) + I(Y;T \mid X) = I(Y;\, X,T) = I(Y;T) + I(Y;X \mid T).

The Markov property makes Y and T conditionally independent given
X, so I(Y;T \mid X) = 0 and the left side collapses to I(Y;X):

I(Y;X) = I(Y;T) + I(Y;X \mid T).

Since I(Y;X \mid T) \ge 0, the right side is at least I(Y;T), which
is the inequality; equality holds exactly when the residual term
I(Y;X \mid T) vanishes. This is
Cover & Thomas
Theorem 2.8.1, with the chain relabeled Y \to X \to T.

One quantity, two expansions: the Markov property zeroes one conditional term, nonnegativity of the other yields the inequality.

Step through the three frames, then check the conclusion on the table
of the first section: I(Y;X) = 0.811, I(Y;T) = 0.467, and the
destroyed information I(Y;X \mid T) = 0.344 satisfy
0.811 = 0.467 + 0.344 exactly.

The theorem compares averages over the joint tables. It does not order
individual events: for a particular outcome, observing T = t may
shift the conditional distribution of Y more than observing some
uninformative value X = x would. As with the pointwise mutual
information of Mutual information, only the
expectation obeys the inequality.

For a Markov chain, I(X;Y) = I(T;Y) + I(Y;X \mid T): the information
about Y splits exactly into the part that survives in T plus the
part the processing destroyed, and the destroyed part cannot be
negative.

documents.title: No function of the data beats the data
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › The data-processing inequality › No function of the data beats the data
documents.text:
No function of the data beats the data

For any function f and any Y,

I(f(X);\,Y) \le I(X;Y).

More generally, if each stage of a pipeline
X \to T_1 \to T_2 \to \cdots is computed from the previous stage
(deterministically or with independent randomness), then
I(T_k;Y) is non-increasing in k.

T = f(X) satisfies p(t \mid x,y) = \mathbf{1}\{t = f(x)\}
= p(t \mid x), so Y \to X \to T and the theorem applies. For the
pipeline, each stage T_{k+1} depends on Y only through T_k, so
Y \to T_k \to T_{k+1} is a Markov chain and
I(T_{k+1};Y) \le I(T_k;Y); chaining the inequalities gives the
monotone sequence.

The corollary covers every post-processing step in an engineer's
toolbox: a hash, a quantizer, a cropped or downsampled image, a summary
statistic, a neural network layer. Each is a T computed from its
input, so each can only shed information about any fixed target.

A pipeline under the DPI ceiling: each stage is processed from the one below, so I(stage; Y) can only shrink going up.

What representation learning does under the ceiling

I(X;Y) counts bits, not the ease of extracting them. Reading the
label from raw pixels may require exactly the computation a trained
network performs; reading it from the last-layer feature needs one
linear map. Training a representation rearranges a fixed information
budget into usable form; it never grows the budget.

The contrapositive is a working debugging rule: a learned feature that
appears to know more about Y than the raw input did is evidence of
leakage: somewhere, the pipeline touched Y or a proxy for it
directly, and the Markov chain assumed in evaluation does not hold.

The same machinery prices what a learning algorithm memorizes. For a
training set S and learned weights W,
Xu & Raginsky (2017) bound the
expected generalization gap of any algorithm with a \sigma-sub-Gaussian
loss by

\left|\, \mathbb{E}[\text{gen}(S,W)] \,\right|

where n is the number of training examples: an algorithm whose output
shares few bits with its training set cannot overfit it. The mutual
information between data and hypothesis plays the same gating role that
I(X;Y) plays across a Markov chain.

Every stage of a pipeline lives under one ceiling:
I(\text{stage};\, Y) \le I(X;Y). A representation can concentrate the
bits about Y into accessible form; only measuring new data raises the
ceiling.

documents.title: Equality: sufficient statistics
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › The data-processing inequality › Equality: sufficient statistics
documents.text:
Equality: sufficient statistics

The proof localizes the entire loss into one term:
I(T;Y) = I(X;Y) exactly when I(Y;X \mid T) = 0, that is, when,
given T, the original X carries no further information about Y.
In that case Y \to T \to X is also a Markov chain: T stands fully
between the data and the target.

A variable T with Y \to X \to T is a sufficient statistic for
Y if

I(T;Y) = I(X;Y),

equivalently, if X and Y are conditionally independent given T.

On the same table, merge the other pair: T' = g(X) with g(a) = a,
g(b) = b, g(c) = g(d) = e.

Step 1: distribution of T'. p(a) = \tfrac{1}{2},
p(b) = \tfrac{1}{4}, p(e) = \tfrac{1}{8} + \tfrac{1}{8} =
\tfrac{1}{4}.

Step 2: label given T'. Given a or b: Y = 0, certain.
Given e: both merged columns carry Y = 1, so Y = 1, certain.
Hence H(Y \mid T') = 0.

Step 3: subtract.
I(T';Y) = H(Y) - 0 \approx 0.811 bits = I(X;Y): equality. T' is
a sufficient statistic for Y.

Compression check. T' is strictly coarser than X:
H(T') = \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 1 + \tfrac{1}{4} \cdot 2 + \tfrac{1}{4}
\cdot 2 = 1.5 bits, against H(X) = 1.75. The merge discarded a
quarter bit of X, all of it irrelevant to Y.

Two merges of the same X: one destroys 0.344 bits about Y, the other loses nothing — equality in the DPI is sufficiency.

T' is sufficient for this Y. For the target X itself the same
merge is lossy: I(T';X) = H(T') = 1.5 bits, below
I(X;X) = H(X) = 1.75 bits (self-information,
Mutual information). A statistic sufficient for one
target can destroy information about another; sufficiency is a property
of the pair (statistic, target). Exercise 5 works the comparison.

Classical statistics states the same notion with the target a model
parameter: T(X) is sufficient for a family p(x;\theta) when
\theta \to T(X) \to X, i.e. the conditional law of X given T does
not involve \theta, and
Cover & Thomas
§2.9 shows this coincides with the information-preservation condition
I(\theta; T) = I(\theta; X): a sufficient statistic is one at the
DPI's equality case for every prior on \theta.

Equality in the data-processing inequality is exactly sufficiency: T
may be far smaller than X, provided the discarded bits are ones Y
never touched.

documents.title: Where the inequality operates next
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › The data-processing inequality › Where the inequality operates next
documents.text:
Where the inequality operates next

Three later results are applications of this theorem, each in one
sentence:

The converse of the
noisy-channel coding theorem
runs the same machinery through Fano's inequality (Cover & Thomas
§2.10), turning "information was lost across the chain
message \to channel \to decoder" into an explicit lower bound on
decoding error.

In Rate-distortion theory, the reconstruction \hat{X} is
processed from the compressed description of X, so the DPI pins the
information any reconstruction can retain to what the bit budget let
through.

The The information bottleneck objective trades I(X;T)
against I(T;Y) over encoders X \to T; its entire feasible region
sits under the ceiling I(T;Y) \le I(X;Y) established here.

documents.title: Exercises
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › The data-processing inequality › Exercises
documents.text:
Exercises

Let X be uniform on \{1, 2, 3, 4\} and Y = 1 if X \ge 3, else
Y = 0. Consider two merges: T_1 maps \{1,2\} \to s and
\{3,4\} \to t; T_2 maps \{1,3\} \to u and \{2,4\} \to v.
Compute I(X;Y), I(T_1;Y), and I(T_2;Y), verify the
data-processing inequality for both merges, and identify which merge is
a sufficient statistic for Y.

I(X;Y). Y is a function of X, so H(Y \mid X) = 0;
p(Y{=}1) = \tfrac{1}{2}, so H(Y) = 1 bit and I(X;Y) = 1 bit.

T_1. Given s, X \in \{1,2\}, so Y = 0 certain; given t,
Y = 1 certain. H(Y \mid T_1) = 0 and
I(T_1;Y) = H(Y) = 1 bit = I(X;Y): equality, so T_1 is a
sufficient statistic. The merge respects the Y-boundary.

T_2. Given u, X is 1 or 3 with probability \tfrac{1}{2}
each, so p(Y{=}1 \mid u) = \tfrac{1}{2}; likewise given v. Every
slice of Y is a fair coin: H(Y \mid T_2) = 1 bit, so
I(T_2;Y) = 1 - 1 = 0 bits.

DPI check. 1 \le 1 and 0 \le 1: both merges obey the bound.
T_2 crosses the Y-boundary in both merged pairs and destroys all
information about the label while keeping a full bit of X
(H(T_2) = 1): how many bits survive and which bits survive are
different questions.

On the lesson's table with the lossy merge T (b, c \to m), compute
I(Y;\, X, T) directly, then verify both chain-rule expansions
numerically: I(Y;X) + I(Y;T \mid X) and I(Y;T) + I(Y;X \mid T).

Direct. T = f(X), so the pair (X,T) takes the same values as
X with the same probabilities: H(Y \mid X, T) = H(Y \mid X) = 0,
and I(Y;\, X,T) = H(Y) - 0 = H_2(\tfrac{1}{4}) \approx 0.811 bits.

X-first. I(Y;X) \approx 0.811 bits (lesson, first section).
Given any X = x, the value T = f(x) is certain, so every slice of
I(Y;T \mid X) is zero: I(Y;T \mid X) = 0. Sum:
0.811 + 0 = 0.811 bits.

T-first. I(Y;T) \approx 0.467 bits (worked example). For
I(Y;X \mid T): slices T = a and T = d determine Y, contributing
0; the slice T = m (probability \tfrac{3}{8}) holds
X \in \{b,c\} with conditional probabilities
(\tfrac{2}{3}, \tfrac{1}{3}), and within the slice Y is determined
by X, so the slice's mutual information is
H_2(\tfrac{1}{3}) \approx 0.918 bits. Average:
\tfrac{3}{8} \cdot 0.918 \approx 0.344 bits. Sum:
0.467 + 0.344 = 0.811 bits.

Both expansions match the direct value, and the T-first expansion
exhibits the loss as the residual term I(Y;X \mid T) = 0.344 bits.

Construct random variables Y, X, T for which
I(T;Y) > I(X;Y), and state which hypothesis of the data-processing
inequality your construction violates.

Let X and Y be independent fair bits and set T = Y.

Then I(X;Y) = 0 (independence, the nonnegativity equality case of
Mutual information), while
I(T;Y) = I(Y;Y) = H(Y) = 1 bit: the "processed" variable carries one
full bit more than X.

The violated hypothesis is the Markov condition: here
p(t \mid x, y) = \mathbf{1}\{t = y\} depends on y, so
p(t \mid x, y) \ne p(t \mid x) and Y \to X \to T fails. T was
not computed from X; it was computed from Y directly. The
inequality bounds processing of the data, not arbitrary side
information.

Let Y be a fair bit, X = Y \oplus N_1, and T = X \oplus N_2,
where N_1, N_2 are independent \mathrm{Bernoulli}(0.1) flips, also
independent of Y. Verify that Y \to X \to T is a Markov chain, then
compute I(X;Y) and I(T;Y) and check the data-processing inequality.
Use H_2(0.1) \approx 0.469 and H_2(0.18) \approx 0.680.

Markov. T is computed from X and the noise N_2, which is
independent of (Y, X): p(t \mid x, y) = p(t \mid x), so
Y \to X \to T holds. Randomized processing qualifies.

I(X;Y). Given Y, X differs from it with probability 0.1:
H(X \mid Y) = H_2(0.1) \approx 0.469 bits. By symmetry X is a fair
bit, H(X) = 1. So
I(X;Y) = 1 - 0.469 = 0.531 bits (the q = 0.9 dial value of
Mutual information, Exercise 3).

I(T;Y). T = Y \oplus N_1 \oplus N_2 differs from Y when
exactly one flip fires:
0.1 \cdot 0.9 + 0.9 \cdot 0.1 = 0.18. So
H(T \mid Y) = H_2(0.18) \approx 0.680, H(T) = 1, and
I(T;Y) = 1 - 0.680 = 0.320 bits.

Check. 0.320 \le 0.531: the second noisy stage destroyed a
further 0.211 bits. Cascading channels degrades information at every
stage, exactly as the pipeline corollary requires.

The lesson showed that T' (the merge c, d \to e) is a sufficient
statistic for Y. Show that the same T' is not sufficient when
the target is X itself: compute I(T';X) and I(X;X) and compare.

T' is a function of X, so H(T' \mid X) = 0 and
I(T';X) = H(T') - H(T' \mid X) = H(T'). From the worked example,
H(T') = \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 1 + \tfrac{1}{4} \cdot 2 + \tfrac{1}{4}
\cdot 2 = 1.5 bits.

The benchmark is I(X;X) = H(X) = 1.75 bits: a variable shares its
whole entropy with itself (self-information,
Mutual information).

Comparison: I(T';X) = 1.5 < 1.75 = I(X;X). Taking the target to be
X, the chain X \to X \to T' gives I(T';X) \le I(X;X) with a
strict 0.25-bit gap: the merge cannot distinguish c from d, and
that distinction is worth
\tfrac{1}{4} \cdot 1 = 0.25 bits of X. Sufficient for Y, lossy
for X: sufficiency is relative to the target.

Encode the lesson's source with the prefix code
a \to 0, b \to 10, c \to 110, d \to 111 (the optimal code for
\{\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{4}, \tfrac{1}{8}, \tfrac{1}{8}\} from
Huffman coding), and let T be the codeword. Compute
the expected codeword length, and prove that I(T;Y) = I(X;Y) for
every random variable Y, using the data-processing inequality
twice.

Expected length.
\tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 1 + \tfrac{1}{4} \cdot 2 + \tfrac{1}{8} \cdot 3 +
\tfrac{1}{8} \cdot 3 = 1.75 bits per symbol, equal to H(X): the
code is complete and the source probabilities are powers of two, so the
code meets the entropy floor of
The source coding theorem exactly.

Equality of information. T is a function of X, so
Y \to X \to T holds for any Y and the DPI gives
I(T;Y) \le I(X;Y). The code is prefix-free, hence uniquely decodable
(Prefix codes and code trees): there is a decoding function g with
X = g(T). Then X is a function of T, so Y \to T \to X also
holds and the DPI gives the reverse bound I(X;Y) = I(g(T);Y) \le
I(T;Y). Both directions together force I(T;Y) = I(X;Y).

An invertible map is a sufficient statistic for every target: lossless
compression changes the representation of the data, never its
information content about anything.

For a Markov chain Y \to X \to T, show that conditioning on the
processed output can only reduce the dependence between the endpoints:

I(Y;X \mid T) \le I(Y;X).

Then evaluate both sides on the lesson's table with the lossy merge
T.

Expand I(Y;\, X,T) both ways, using the Markov property
I(Y;T \mid X) = 0 as in the theorem's proof:

I(Y;X) = I(Y;T) + I(Y;X \mid T)

Since I(Y;T) \ge 0 (nonnegativity of mutual information), the right
side is at most I(Y;X), which is the claim.

On the table: I(Y;X \mid T) \approx 0.344 bits and
I(Y;X) \approx 0.811 bits, and indeed
0.344 = 0.811 - 0.467 \le 0.811. Observing T "explains away"
0.467 of the 0.811 bits of dependence between X and Y; only
the part T failed to capture remains.

T. M. Cover, J. A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006 — §2.5 defines conditional mutual information and proves the chain rule for information (Theorem 2.5.2); §2.8 states and proves the data-processing inequality (Theorem 2.8.1) with its corollaries; §2.9 connects the equality case to sufficient statistics; §2.10 develops Fano's inequality, the error-bound form used in the channel-coding converse.

D. J. C. MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms, Cambridge University Press, 2003 — ch. 8 "Dependent Random Variables": the joint-ensemble entropy and mutual-information identities this lesson's proof reuses, with the data-processing theorem among the chapter's exercises. Free online: https://www.inference.org.uk/mackay/itila/

A. Xu, M. Raginsky, "Information-theoretic analysis of generalization capability of learning algorithms," Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30, 2017 — the generalization bound \sqrt{2\sigma^2 I(S;W)/n} quoted in the aside. https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.07809

documents.title: Entropy of English text
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Entropy of English text
documents.text:
English text carries roughly one bit of information per letter while ASCII
spends eight; the gap is redundancy, and Shannon's guessing game measures
it. This lesson establishes that number in four steps: the ladder of
conditional entropies F_N, which drops as context grows; the entropy
rate, defined as its limit; the guessing game of
Shannon's 1951 paper,
which turns a reader's next-letter guesses into upper and lower bounds on
the rate; and the resulting redundancy of roughly 75%. Throughout, the
alphabet is the 27 symbols a–z plus space, with case and punctuation
dropped; every number below is tied to that choice.

documents.title: Context buys bits: the ladder of conditional entropies
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Entropy of English text › Context buys bits: the ladder of conditional entropies
documents.text:
Context buys bits: the ladder of conditional entropies

The single-letter frequencies of English give an entropy of about 4.1
bits per character, computed in
Entropy. That number treats each letter
as an independent draw. English letters are not independent: after the
letter q, the next letter is almost always u, and the conditional
distribution of the next letter collapses nearly to a point. Its entropy,
H(X_{n+1} \mid X_n = q), is close to zero bits, against 4.1 without
the context.

Averaging over all contexts is exactly the conditional entropy of
Joint and conditional entropy. Shannon organized these
averages into a sequence: the N-gram entropy F_N is the conditional
entropy of the next letter given N-1 preceding letters,

F_N = H(X_N \mid X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{N-1}),

with F_1 = H(X_1), the monogram entropy, and F_0 = \log_2 27 \approx
4.76 bits by convention: the cost of a letter with no statistics at all.

Measured rungs: Shannon's 1951 table

From letter, digram, and trigram frequency tables, and from word
frequencies via Zipf's law,
Shannon computed the first rungs for the 27-letter alphabet:

F_N

conditions on

bits per letter

F_0

nothing: 27 equiprobable symbols

4.76

F_1

letter frequencies

4.03

F_2

one preceding letter (digrams)

3.32

F_3

two preceding letters (trigrams)

3.1

F_{\text{word}}

word frequencies (Zipf fit)

2.14

Each added letter of context buys bits: 0.73 from F_1 to F_2,
another 0.2 to F_3. The word-level figure comes from an entropy of
11.82 bits per word divided by 5.5 symbols per word (average word
length 4.5 letters plus one space). The ladder stops at N = 3 for a
mechanical reason: an N-gram table has 27^N entries, and no corpus of
1951 (or a printed table) supported reliable frequencies past trigrams.

Shannon's ladder for the 27-symbol alphabet: every added rung of statistical structure lowers the per-letter entropy.

The monogram values differ across sources: Shannon's counts give
F_1 = 4.03 bits, while the table in
MacKay §2.1, used in
Entropy, gives 4.11. Letter
frequencies are corpus estimates, and every rung inherits their
uncertainty; the shape of the ladder, not the second decimal, is the
result.

The 4.1-bit monogram figure is not the entropy of English: it prices
letters as independent draws and ignores all structure between them. Each
letter of conditioning context strictly lowers the per-letter cost.

Shannon's 1948 paper, §3,
runs the same ladder in the generative direction: sample text from each
approximation and watch it approach English. A trigram-level sample reads
"IN NO IST LAT WHEY CRATICT FROURE BIRS GROCID…", and a second-order word
approximation produces "THE HEAD AND IN FRONTAL ATTACK ON AN ENGLISH
WRITER THAT THE CHARACTER OF THIS POINT IS THEREFORE ANOTHER METHOD…":
locally plausible, globally empty. The better a model's sample text looks,
the fewer bits per letter the model needs; the ladder read in either
direction is the same fact.

Shannon's own samples, one rung per frame: each added order of structure moves the text closer to English.

documents.title: The entropy rate: the limit of the ladder
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Entropy of English text › The entropy rate: the limit of the ladder
documents.text:
The entropy rate: the limit of the ladder

The measured rungs decrease: 4.76, 4.03, 3.32, 3.1, \ldots The sequence
cannot decrease forever, since every conditional entropy is at least 0.
A decreasing sequence bounded below converges; the limit is the number the
opening paragraph promised.

For a stationary source X_1, X_2, \ldots over a finite alphabet, the
entropy rate is

H_{\text{rate}} = \lim_{N \to \infty} H(X_N \mid X_1, \ldots, X_{N-1})

in bits per symbol: the per-letter uncertainty given unlimited preceding
context. For stationary sources this limit exists and equals
\lim_{N \to \infty} \tfrac{1}{N} H(X_1, \ldots, X_N)
(Cover & Thomas,
Theorem 4.2.1); Exercise 3 connects the two forms.

Stationary means the statistics do not depend on position: the
distribution of (X_{k+1}, \ldots, X_{k+n}) is the same for every shift
k. English prose is treated as approximately stationary: letter
statistics in chapter 12 match those in chapter 1.

For a stationary source, F_{N+1} \le F_N for every N \ge 1, and the
limit H_{\text{rate}} exists.

Fix the shorter context (X_2, \ldots, X_N). For each of its values,
adding the observation X_1 cannot raise the average uncertainty about
X_{N+1}: this is conditioning-reduces-entropy from
Joint and conditional entropy, applied under each context
value and then averaged over contexts. Hence

F_{N+1} = H(X_{N+1} \mid X_1, \ldots, X_N)

By stationarity, shifting all indices down by one leaves the right side
unchanged: H(X_{N+1} \mid X_2, \ldots, X_N) = H(X_N \mid X_1, \ldots,
X_{N-1}) = F_N. The sequence (F_N) is non-increasing and bounded below
by 0, so it converges.

F_N against context length: the curve falls toward its limit, the entropy rate — on the order of one bit per letter.

The entropy of English means the entropy rate: per-letter uncertainty with
unlimited context. For English it is on the order of 1 bit per letter,
a quarter of the monogram figure.

documents.title: Shannon's guessing game: the speaker is the model
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Entropy of English text › Shannon's guessing game: the speaker is the model
documents.text:
Shannon's guessing game: the speaker is the model

Extending the table method to F_{100} requires the joint statistics of
27^{100} contexts. No corpus fills that table. What is needed is the
conditional distribution of the next letter given a long context; where it
lives is in the head of every fluent reader, who has absorbed the words,
grammar, and idioms of the language. Shannon's method queries that
implicit model directly.

The protocol: show a subject N-1 letters of an unfamiliar text. The
subject guesses the next letter; if wrong, guesses again, until correct.
Record the number of guesses, reveal the letter, advance one position, and
repeat. The output is one guess rank per position: a 1 means the
first guess was right, a 17 means sixteen wrong guesses came first.

The guessing game on a five-symbol text. Each position yields one number: how many guesses the correct letter took.

Step through the five frames. Check that context is doing the work: the
first position, guessed blind, costs 4 tries, while every position with a
word underway costs 1 or 2. The output of the whole game is only the tally
row: ranks 4, 2, 1, 2, 1.

Shannon's demonstration runs show how strong human prediction is. On a
129-letter passage, his subject guessed 89 of the letters (69%) right on
the first try. In the guess-until-correct variant on a 102-symbol text, 79
positions took one guess, 8 took two, 3 took three, 2 each took four and
five, and only 8 needed more. For the systematic experiment he drew 100
passages from a novel and had the subject play at every context length
N-1 = 0, 1, \ldots, 14, and 99.

The reduced text: ranks carry the same information

The rank sequence looks like a loss of information; it is not. Suppose a
second subject exists with exactly the same prediction model:
Shannon's "identical twin", in practice the same person following a fixed
guessing rule. Given the ranks alone, the twin replays the game: at each
position the twin generates guesses in the same order, and the rank says
which guess is the true letter. The text reconstructs perfectly; Exercise
6 runs this decoding on a toy predictor.

The predictor is therefore an invertible transducer: original text in,
reduced text (the rank sequence) out, and back again with the same
predictor. Both directions look only at the current symbol and the N-1
preceding text letters, so the transformation preserves N-gram
statistics, and the reduced text has the same entropy per symbol as
English itself. What the translation changes is the shape of the
frequencies: complicated constraints among letters become a single wildly
skewed distribution over ranks, mass piled on rank 1.

Text and rank sequence are two encodings of the same information: given
the predictor, each reconstructs the other. Measuring the ranks measures
English.

documents.title: Bounds from the guess-rank frequencies
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Entropy of English text › Bounds from the guess-rank frequencies
documents.text:
Bounds from the guess-rank frequencies

Let q_i denote the fraction of positions resolved on guess i when the
subject knows N-1 preceding letters, with q_1 \ge q_2 \ge \cdots \ge
q_{27} and q_{28} = 0. For an ideal predictor — one that always guesses
in order of decreasing conditional probability — the rank frequencies pin
F_N between two computable numbers.

For the ideal predictor with N-1 known letters,

\sum_{i=1}^{27} i\,(q_i - q_{i+1}) \log_2 i

The upper bound holds for any predictor whose guessing order is a fixed
function of the known context, a human included; the lower bound is proved
only for the ideal predictor.

Sketch of the upper bound. The rank sequence has the same N-gram entropy
as the text (previous section). By the ladder theorem, its per-symbol
conditional entropy F_N is at most its F_1, and F_1 of the rank
sequence is exactly the entropy of the rank distribution,
-\sum_i q_i \log_2 q_i: ignoring inter-rank structure can only
overestimate. Any deterministic guesser yields a valid rank encoding, so
the bound needs no ideal predictor.

The lower bound is Shannon's rectangular-decomposition argument
(1951, §5):
among all sources whose ideal-prediction rank frequencies equal q, the
least uncertain one splits into blocks of equally probable guesses, and
its entropy is the left-hand sum. Equality requires every context to offer
a set of equally probable next letters; real English does not, which is
one reason the two bounds stay apart.

The coding reading of the upper bound: build a prefix code for the rank
alphabet matched to q, per Prefix codes and code trees. The rank stream
then costs about -\sum_i q_i \log_2 q_i bits per symbol
(The source coding theorem), and the rank stream
reconstructs the text. A concentrated guess distribution is a cheap code
for English; the peaked histogram is the low entropy.

Guess-rank frequencies from the worked 40-position game below. The mass piled on rank 1 is what drives both bounds down.

Shannon's measured bounds

Applying the bounds to the guess tallies at each context length (100
samples per column, smoothed) gave:

known letters

upper bound

4.03

lower bound

3.19

The same measurement as the table, as Shannon plotted it: the gap between the bounds never closes.

The zero-context column reproduces the monogram F_1 = 4.03 exactly: with
no context the ideal guesser works from letter frequencies alone. At 99
letters of context the estimate lands between 0.6 and 1.3 bits per
letter. The bumps along the way (the lower bound rising from 1.0 to
1.2) are sampling error from 100-sample columns, flagged by Shannon
himself.

Three qualifications. The bounds coincide only in idealized limits; a
finite game gives a range, not a value. The upper bound measures the
predictor's model of English, which can only overestimate the true rate:
a better predictor produces a more concentrated rank distribution and a
lower bound on the same text.
Cover and King (1978)
sharpened the protocol by having subjects bet on their guesses, estimating
approximately 1.3 bits per symbol. And every figure is relative to the
declared 27-symbol alphabet: restoring case and punctuation changes each
number. Compression as prediction replaces the human with
a trained language model and reads its loss as exactly this game's score.

documents.title: A worked estimate from one short game
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Entropy of English text › A worked estimate from one short game
documents.text:
A worked estimate from one short game

Suppose a 40-position game on an unfamiliar passage produces the tally

guess rank i

1

2

6

positions

26

6

1

q_i

.65

.15

.025

Upper bound: the entropy of the rank distribution. Surprisals:
-\log_2 .65 = 0.621, -\log_2 .15 = 2.737, -\log_2 .10 = 3.322,
-\log_2 .05 = 4.322, -\log_2 .025 = 5.322. Weighted:

.65 \times 0.621 + .15 \times 2.737 + .10 \times 3.322

= 0.404 + 0.411 + 0.332 + 0.216 + 0.266 = 1.63 \text{ bits.}

Lower bound: \sum_i i\,(q_i - q_{i+1}) \log_2 i, with q_7 = 0.
The i = 1 term vanishes (\log_2 1 = 0), and i = 5 vanishes
(q_5 = q_6):

2(.15 - .10)(1) + 3(.10 - .05)(1.585) + 4(.05 - .025)(2)

= 0.100 + 0.238 + 0.200 + 0.388 = 0.93 \text{ bits.}

Estimate. The game places the per-letter entropy between 0.93 and
1.63 bits, consistent with Shannon's 0.6–1.3 from a hundred times
the data. Forty positions is a small sample; the bounds carry error bars
of the same order as the interval itself.

A non-estimate, for contrast. The average number of guesses is
(26 \cdot 1 + 6 \cdot 2 + 4 \cdot 3 + 2 \cdot 4 + 1 \cdot 5 + 1 \cdot 6)/40
= 69/40 \approx 1.7 guesses per letter. That number is not an entropy;
only the distribution of ranks, pushed through the bounds, is.

Run the game yourself, with a partner and a paragraph the guesser has not
read. Use the 27-symbol alphabet: lowercase everything, drop punctuation,
keep spaces. Play 40 positions, tally the ranks into counts, convert to
frequencies q_i, and compute both bounds as in the example. Expect an
upper bound between roughly 1 and 2.5 bits depending on the text and
the guesser.

documents.title: Redundancy: what the gap is worth
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Entropy of English text › Redundancy: what the gap is worth
documents.text:
Redundancy: what the gap is worth

A raw fixed-width encoding of the 27-symbol alphabet spends \log_2 27
\approx 4.76 bits per letter; ASCII spends 8. If the entropy rate is
about 1.2 bits per letter, the fraction of the raw encoding that carries
no information is

\text{redundancy} = 1 - \frac{H_{\text{rate}}}{\log_2 27}

Shannon's statement: long-range statistics reduce the entropy of ordinary
literary English to about one bit per letter, "with a corresponding
redundancy of roughly 75%". His 1948 estimate, using only statistics out
to about eight letters, was 2.3 bits per letter and roughly 50%
redundancy; the extra 25 points came from the long-range structure only
the guessing game could reach.

Per letter stored: 4.76 bits (fixed-width) or 8 (ASCII). Per letter carried: about 1.2. The rest is redundancy.

By the source coding theorem of
The source coding theorem, the entropy rate is the floor
for lossless compression of English, and the redundancy is exactly the
compressible fraction: a perfect compressor would shrink ASCII text by a
factor near 8/1.2 \approx 7. Reaching the floor requires a coder driven
by a model as good as the human predictor: the subject of
Compression as prediction, and the reason
MacKay (ch. 6) builds stream
codes around a predictive model.

Redundancy = 1 - H_{\text{rate}} / \log_2 27 \approx 75\%: roughly
three quarters of printed English is determined by structure rather than
free choice, and that fraction is what lossless compression can remove.

Redundancy is why damaged English survives. Shannon's 1948 discussion
notes that a language of zero redundancy would make any letter string
valid text: errors would be undetectable, and (his example) any
two-dimensional letter array would be a valid crossword. English's
redundancy is what lets a reader repair "th_ r__m w_s n_t v_ry l_ght",
and what crossword constructors fight against: too much redundancy and
few grids fill; none, and every grid does. The same margin is what
error-correcting codes will spend deliberately in the channel-coding
module.

documents.title: Exercises
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Shared information › Entropy of English text › Exercises
documents.text:
Exercises

A toy language over the alphabet \{t, h, e\} has adjacent-pair joint
distribution

p(x_1, x_2)

x_2 = t

x_2 = h

x_2 = e

x_1 = t

0

3/8

1/8

x_1 = h

0

0

1/4

x_1 = e

1/8

1/8

0

Compute the marginal entropy H(X_2) and the conditional entropy
H(X_2 \mid X_1) by the weighted-average form, and state the toy
language's first ladder step F_1 \to F_2. Use
\log_2 3 \approx 1.585.

Marginals. Rows: p(t) = \tfrac12, p(h) = \tfrac14,
p(e) = \tfrac14. Columns: p(t) = \tfrac18,
p(h) = \tfrac38 + \tfrac18 = \tfrac12,
p(e) = \tfrac18 + \tfrac14 = \tfrac38.

Marginal entropy.
H(X_2) = \tfrac18 \cdot 3 + \tfrac12 \cdot 1 + \tfrac38 \log_2
\tfrac83 = 0.375 + 0.5 + 0.375 \times 1.415 \approx 1.41 bits.

Row entropies. Given t: (0, \tfrac34, \tfrac14), entropy
H(\tfrac14) \approx 0.811 bits. Given h: (0, 0, 1), entropy 0.
Given e: (\tfrac12, \tfrac12, 0), entropy 1 bit.

Weighted average.
H(X_2 \mid X_1) = \tfrac12 \times 0.811 + \tfrac14 \times 0 +
\tfrac14 \times 1 \approx 0.656 bits.

Ladder step. F_1 \approx 1.41 bits, F_2 \approx 0.66 bits: one
letter of context removes 0.75 bits, more than half the per-letter
uncertainty: the toy version of English's 4.03 \to 3.32.

A 20-position guessing game yields the tally: rank 1 fourteen times,
rank 2 three times, rank 3 twice, rank 4 once. Compute Shannon's upper
and lower bounds on the per-letter entropy. Use \log_2 .7 \approx
-0.515, \log_2 .15 \approx -2.737, \log_2 .10 \approx -3.322,
\log_2 .05 \approx -4.322, \log_2 3 \approx 1.585.

Frequencies: q_1 = .7, q_2 = .15, q_3 = .10, q_4 = .05,
q_5 = 0.

Upper bound.
-\sum q_i \log_2 q_i = .7 \times 0.515 + .15 \times 2.737 + .10 \times
3.322 + .05 \times 4.322 = 0.360 + 0.411 + 0.332 + 0.216 \approx 1.32
bits.

Lower bound. \sum i (q_i - q_{i+1}) \log_2 i: the i = 1 term is
0; i = 2: 2(.15 - .10)(1) = 0.100; i = 3:
3(.10 - .05)(1.585) = 0.238; i = 4: 4(.05 - 0)(2) = 0.400. Sum
\approx 0.74 bits.

The 20-position game brackets the entropy between 0.74 and 1.32
bits per letter, with error bars the size of the interval: the tally is
ten times smaller than one column of Shannon's experiment.

Using the two-variable chain rule of
Joint and conditional entropy repeatedly, show that

H(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_N) = \sum_{k=1}^{N} F_k ,

and conclude that \tfrac{1}{N} H(X_1, \ldots, X_N) — the per-letter
cost of describing a block of N letters — is the running average of
the ladder, and therefore also converges to H_{\text{rate}} for a
stationary source.

Chain. The two-variable rule H(A, B) = H(A) + H(B \mid A) with
A = (X_1, \ldots, X_{N-1}) and B = X_N gives

H(X_1, \ldots, X_N) = H(X_1, \ldots, X_{N-1})

The last term is F_N. Applying the same step to
H(X_1, \ldots, X_{N-1}), and so on down to H(X_1) = F_1, unrolls the
joint entropy into \sum_{k=1}^N F_k.

Average. Dividing by N,
\tfrac1N H(X_1, \ldots, X_N) = \tfrac1N \sum_{k=1}^N F_k: the mean of
the first N rungs. If F_k \to H_{\text{rate}}, then for any
\varepsilon all but finitely many terms lie within \varepsilon of
the limit; the finitely many exceptional terms contribute at most a
constant divided by N, which vanishes. Hence the running mean
converges to the same limit (the Cesàro-mean argument), which is
Theorem 4.2.1 of Cover & Thomas: block description cost per letter and
conditional-entropy limit agree.

A novel contains 500{,}000 characters. Compute its size in ASCII
(8 bits per character), its information content at an entropy rate of
1.2 bits per character, the ideal compression factor, and the
redundancy relative to a fixed-width 27-symbol encoding
(\log_2 27 \approx 4.755).

ASCII: 500{,}000 \times 8 = 4{,}000{,}000 bits = 500{,}000 bytes,
about 0.5 MB. Information content: 500{,}000 \times 1.2 = 600{,}000
bits = 75{,}000 bytes. Ideal compression factor:
8 / 1.2 \approx 6.7. Redundancy:
1 - 1.2/4.755 \approx 1 - 0.252 = 0.748 \approx 75\%.

The entropy rate is a floor, not an achieved figure: reaching 75 kB
requires a coder whose predictive model matches a fluent reader's;
dictionary compressors with short memories stop well short of it.

Suppose a "language" produces 27 symbols independently and uniformly at
random. Determine the ideal predictor's guess-rank frequencies q_i,
and evaluate both of Shannon's bounds. State what the result says about
flat versus peaked rank histograms.

Every conditional distribution is uniform, so every guessing order is
ideal, and each guess is correct with probability \tfrac{1}{27}
regardless of rank: q_i = \tfrac{1}{27} for i = 1, \ldots, 27.

Upper bound. -\sum_{i=1}^{27} \tfrac{1}{27} \log_2 \tfrac{1}{27}
= \log_2 27 \approx 4.75 bits.

Lower bound. For i < 27, q_i - q_{i+1} = 0; only i = 27
survives: 27 \times \tfrac{1}{27} \times \log_2 27 = \log_2 27.

The bounds coincide at \log_2 27: for a memoryless uniform source the
game measures the entropy exactly, and prediction buys nothing. A
perfectly flat rank histogram certifies incompressibility; the entire
entropy saving of English is visible as the peak of its histogram at
rank 1.

A toy predictor over \{A, B, C\} guesses in a fixed order determined
by the previous letter: after A it guesses B, A, C; after B:
A, C, B; after C: A, B, C; at the start of the text: A, B, C.
Decode the rank sequence 2, 1, 1, 3, 1 into text, then re-encode your
text into ranks to verify the round trip. State what this shows about
the information content of the reduced text.

Decode. Position 1: start order (A, B, C), rank 2 \to B.
Position 2: after B, order (A, C, B), rank 1 \to A. Position 3:
after A, order (B, A, C), rank 1 \to B. Position 4: after B,
order (A, C, B), rank 3 \to B. Position 5: after B, order
(A, C, B), rank 1 \to A. Text: B\,A\,B\,B\,A.

Re-encode. B at the start is guess 2; A after B is guess 1;
B after A is guess 1; B after B is guess 3; A after B is
guess 1. Ranks: 2, 1, 1, 3, 1. The round trip closes.

Given the predictor, text and ranks determine each other, position by
position; the maps are mutually inverse. Two sequences related by an
invertible, context-respecting recoding carry the same information and
have the same entropy rate. This is why measuring the rank distribution
in the guessing game measures English itself.

C. E. Shannon, "Prediction and Entropy of Printed English," Bell System Technical Journal, 30, 1951, pp. 50–64 — the lesson's primary source: §2 the F_N ladder from letter, digram, trigram, and word statistics; §3 the prediction experiments and the reduced text; §5 the entropy bounds from prediction frequencies; §6 the experimental bounds, 0.6–1.3 bits per letter at 100 letters of context.

C. E. Shannon, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication," Bell System Technical Journal, 27, 1948 — §3 the series of approximations to English with generated samples; §7 the ≈50% redundancy estimate from statistics out to about eight letters.

T. M. Cover, J. A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006 — §4.2 entropy rate and Theorem 4.2.1 (the two limits agree); §6.4 the entropy of English; §6.6 the gambling estimate of the entropy of English.

T. M. Cover, R. C. King, "A Convergent Gambling Estimate of the Entropy of English," IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 24(4), 1978, pp. 413–421 — sequential betting at 27-for-1 odds; estimates approximately 1.3 bits per symbol.

D. J. C. MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms, Cambridge University Press, 2003 — §2.1 the English monogram distribution behind the 4.11-bit figure; ch. 6 "Stream Codes": compression driven by a predictive model. Free online: https://www.inference.org.uk/mackay/itila/

documents.title: Channel capacity
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels and capacity › Channel capacity
documents.text:
A noisy channel is a conditional distribution p(y|x), and its capacity is
the largest mutual information any input distribution can push through it:
C = max over p(x) of I(X;Y). This lesson defines the discrete memoryless
channel as a transition table, shows that the information crossing it
depends on the input distribution as well as on the noise, defines capacity
as the maximum of I(X;Y) over inputs, and computes it in full for the two
canonical binary channels: C = 1 - H(p) for the symmetric channel and
C = 1 - e for the erasure channel.

documents.title: A channel is a transition table
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels and capacity › Channel capacity › A channel is a transition table
documents.text:
A channel is a transition table

A bit is sent down a wire. Noise flips it with probability 0.1 and leaves
it intact with probability 0.9, each transmission independently of every
other. The complete physics of the wire, as far as information is
concerned, fits in a 2 \times 2 table of conditional probabilities:

p(y \mid x):\qquad

Each row is a conditional distribution: fix the input x, and the row
gives the probabilities of every possible output. Nothing else about the
medium enters the theory: copper, fiber, or radio with the same table are
the same channel.

A discrete memoryless channel consists of a finite input alphabet
\mathcal{X}, a finite output alphabet \mathcal{Y}, and for each input
x \in \mathcal{X} a conditional distribution p(y \mid x) over
\mathcal{Y}. Memoryless means uses are independent: over n uses,
p(y_1 \ldots y_n \mid x_1 \ldots x_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n p(y_i \mid x_i),
whatever the inputs.

The binary symmetric channel \mathrm{BSC}(p) has
\mathcal{X} = \mathcal{Y} = \{0, 1\} and flips its input with the
crossover probability p:
p(1 \mid 0) = p(0 \mid 1) = p and
p(0 \mid 0) = p(1 \mid 1) = 1 - p.

BSC(p) twice: as a transition diagram and as the matrix p(y|x). Same object.

The general channel is the same picture with more rows and columns: one
row per input symbol, one conditional distribution per row. The rows need
not be permutations of each other, and \mathcal{X} and \mathcal{Y}
need not match; the erasure channel below has three outputs for two
inputs.

A discrete memoryless channel is fully specified by its transition table
p(y \mid x): one conditional distribution per input symbol, independent
across uses.

documents.title: Information through the channel depends on the input
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels and capacity › Channel capacity › Information through the channel depends on the input
documents.text:
Information through the channel depends on the input

The receiver sees Y and wants X. The quantity that measures what the
output tells about the input is the mutual information of
Mutual information,

I(X;Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X),

and both terms have channel readings. H(Y \mid X) is the noise: the
uncertainty the channel adds to a known input, computed row by row from
the transition table. H(Y) is the total variety of the output. What gets
through is the difference.

One term is missing from the table: I(X;Y) is a functional of the
joint distribution p(x)\,p(y \mid x), and the channel supplies only
the second factor. The input distribution p(x) is chosen by the sender.
Different choices push different amounts of information through the same
wire.

Two inputs on the same wire: 0.531 against 0.211 bits

Fix the channel \mathrm{BSC}(0.1) and write \pi = P(X = 1).

Noise term, any input. Given X = 0 the output is distributed
(0.9, 0.1); given X = 1, (0.1, 0.9). Both rows have the binary
entropy H(0.1) \approx 0.469 bits
(Entropy), so the weighted average is
H(Y \mid X) = 0.469 bits regardless of \pi.

Uniform input, \pi = 0.5. Then
P(Y = 1) = 0.5 \cdot 0.9 + 0.5 \cdot 0.1 = 0.5: the output is uniform,
H(Y) = 1 bit, and

I(X;Y) = 1 - 0.469 = 0.531 \text{ bits per use}.

Biased input, \pi = 0.9. Then
P(Y = 1) = 0.9 \cdot 0.9 + 0.1 \cdot 0.1 = 0.82, so
H(Y) = H(0.82) \approx 0.680 bits and

I(X;Y) \approx 0.680 - 0.469 = 0.211 \text{ bits per use}.

Same channel, same noise term, less than half the information: a sender
who almost always transmits 1 gives the receiver little uncertainty
worth removing.

The uniform case has been computed before: the joint table of
\mathrm{BSC}(p) under a uniform input is exactly the dependence-dial
family of Mutual information with agreement probability
q = 1 - p, and its mutual information 1 - H(q) = 1 - H(p) matches the
0.531 bits computed there at q = 0.9.

I(X;Y) over the input bias for BSC(0.1): the peak, at the uniform input, is the capacity.

I(X;Y) through a channel depends on the channel and on the input
distribution: the noise H(Y \mid X) is set by the transition table, but
how much information crosses is partly the sender's choice.

documents.title: Capacity: the maximum over input distributions
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels and capacity › Channel capacity › Capacity: the maximum over input distributions
documents.text:
Capacity: the maximum over input distributions

The curve above has a well-defined peak, and the peak deserves the name.

The capacity of a discrete memoryless channel p(y \mid x) is

C = \max_{p(x)} I(X;Y),

the maximum over all input distributions on \mathcal{X}, measured in
bits per channel use.

The maximum exists: I(X;Y) is continuous in p(x), and the input
distributions form a closed and bounded set. Two bounds pin down the
possible values.

For every discrete memoryless channel,

0 \le C \le \min\bigl(\log_2 |\mathcal{X}|,\ \log_2 |\mathcal{Y}|\bigr).

Nonnegativity: I(X;Y) \ge 0 for every input distribution
(Mutual information, nonnegativity theorem), so the
maximum is \ge 0. Upper bound: for every input,
I(X;Y) \le \min(H(X), H(Y)) (the upper-bound theorem of the same
lesson), and entropy is at most the log of the alphabet size
(Entropy, range theorem):
H(X) \le \log_2 |\mathcal{X}| and H(Y) \le \log_2 |\mathcal{Y}|.
Every value entering the maximization obeys the bound, hence so does the
maximum. This is Cover & Thomas
§7.3.

For a binary-input channel, C \le 1 bit per use: no input distribution
carries more than one bit into a two-symbol alphabet.

A channel where the maximum is visible: the noisy typewriter

Inputs and outputs are \{A, B, C, D\}, arranged in a cycle. Each key
prints itself with probability \tfrac{1}{2} and the next letter with
probability \tfrac{1}{2} (D wraps to A).

Noise term. Every row of the table is a fifty-fifty split over two
outputs: H(Y \mid X) = 1 bit for any input distribution.

Output term. H(Y) \le \log_2 4 = 2 bits, attained when Y is
uniform; a uniform input achieves that. So

C = 2 - 1 = 1 \text{ bit per use}.

The maximizer read as a strategy. A uniform input over \{A, C\}
alone also attains the maximum: A produces an output in \{A, B\}, C
an output in \{C, D\}, the two output sets are disjoint, and the
receiver recovers the input exactly. One error-free bit per use, matching
C. Choosing an input distribution includes choosing which symbols to
use at all.

The typewriter is the exceptional case where capacity is reached with
zero error by symbol-by-symbol signaling. On the BSC no such disjoint
output sets exist; what the number C promises there is the subject of
the next lesson, and this lesson
only computes it.

Load the presets in order and read the capacity: noiseless gives
C = 1; BSC p=0.1 gives C \approx 0.531; BSC p=0.5 flattens the
whole input-bias curve to zero, C = 0; BEC e=0.5 gives C = 0.5.
Then set the BSC slider to p = 0.2 and check the peak lands near
0.278 bits.

Shannon's 1948 paper
(Part II, §12) defines the rate of transmission as
R = H(x) - H_y(x): source entropy minus the equivocation, his name
for H(X \mid Y), the receiver's leftover uncertainty about what was
sent. By the three-forms theorem of
Mutual information, H(X) - H(X \mid Y) = I(X;Y), so his
C = \max R and the modern C = \max I are the same number.

Computing C in general. For a fixed channel, I(X;Y) is a concave
function of the input distribution, so the maximization is a convex
program in |\mathcal{X}| - 1 variables with no spurious local maxima;
the Blahut–Arimoto algorithm
(1972) solves it by alternating maximization and is the standard tool
when no symmetry helps. When symmetry does help, it helps completely:
for a symmetric channel, where every row of the transition table is a
permutation of every other row and likewise every column, the uniform
input is optimal and
C = \log_2 |\mathcal{Y}| - H(\text{row}), the entropy of any single
row (Cover & Thomas §7.2). The BSC and the noisy typewriter are both
instances: 1 - H(p) and 2 - 1.

Capacity is not a property of the noise alone: C = \max_{p(x)} I(X;Y)
optimizes over the input distribution, which the sender designs. The
channel fixes the constraint; the sender picks the point on it.

documents.title: The binary symmetric channel: C = 1 − H(p)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels and capacity › Channel capacity › The binary symmetric channel: C = 1 − H(p)
documents.text:
The binary symmetric channel: C = 1 − H(p)

The worked example above did the case p = 0.1 at two inputs; the full
maximization takes three lines, one per frame below.

The BSC capacity in three moves: fix the noise term, cap the output term, subtract.

Step through the three frames and check each line at p = 0.1: the noise
term is H(0.1) \approx 0.469 whatever the input, the output ceiling is
1 bit, and the difference 1 - 0.469 = 0.531 matches the peak of the
input-bias curve above.

The binary symmetric channel with crossover probability p has

C = 1 - H(p) \text{ bits per use},

attained by the uniform input, where
H(p) = -p \log_2 p - (1-p) \log_2(1-p) is the binary entropy function.

For any input distribution, each row of the transition matrix is a
permutation of (1-p,\ p), so every conditional output entropy is
H(p) and H(Y \mid X) = H(p): the noise term does not depend on the
input. Hence I(X;Y) = H(Y) - H(p) \le 1 - H(p), since Y is binary
and H(Y) \le 1. Equality requires Y uniform; with \pi = P(X = 1),

P(Y = 1) = \pi(1 - p) + (1 - \pi)p = p + \pi(1 - 2p),

which equals \tfrac{1}{2} at \pi = \tfrac{1}{2} (for p \ne
\tfrac{1}{2}, only there). The bound is attained, so
C = 1 - H(p).

Three points on the curve: p = 0, 0.1, 0.5

p = 0: C = 1 - H(0) = 1 bit. A noiseless binary channel carries
exactly one bit per use.

p = 0.1: C = 1 - 0.469 = 0.531 bits. Ten percent noise costs
nearly half the channel.

p = 0.5: C = 1 - H(0.5) = 1 - 1 = 0. Then
P(Y = 1) = 0.5 + \pi \cdot 0 = 0.5 for every \pi: the output is a
fair coin regardless of the input, Y is independent of X, and no
input distribution shares a single bit with the output.

C = 1 − H(p): the capacity curve is the binary entropy curve flipped. Zero sits at p = ½, not at p = 1.

C = 1 - H(p) is symmetric under p \leftrightarrow 1 - p, since
H(p) = H(1-p): a channel that flips with probability 0.9 has the
same 0.531-bit capacity as one that flips with probability 0.1. The
receiver inverts every received bit and faces a \mathrm{BSC}(0.1). At
p = 1 the channel is a deterministic inverter and C = 1: perfectly
wrong is perfectly informative.

A noisy channel and a useless channel are different things, and the
boundary is C = 0: the BSC has positive capacity at every
p \ne \tfrac{1}{2}, and exactly at p = \tfrac{1}{2} the arriving
bits are independent of the sent ones — noise maximal not when errors
are certain, but when they are as likely as not.

documents.title: The binary erasure channel: C = 1 − e
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels and capacity › Channel capacity › The binary erasure channel: C = 1 − e
documents.text:
The binary erasure channel: C = 1 − e

The second canonical channel loses symbols instead of flipping them: with
probability e the receiver gets an erasure mark ?, and with
probability 1 - e the input arrives exactly. Unlike a flipped bit, an
erased bit is a failure the receiver can see.

BEC(e): with probability e the symbol is replaced by a visible erasure mark, never by the wrong symbol.

The receiver's ledger at e = 0.2

Take e = 0.2 and a uniform input, and count leftover uncertainty
through I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y), the decomposition from the input
side. Before transmission, H(X) = 1 bit. After: if the output is 0 or
1 (probability 0.8), it equals the input and zero uncertainty
remains; if it is ? (probability 0.2), the erasure says nothing about
which bit was sent, and the full 1 bit remains. So

H(X \mid Y) = 0.8 \cdot 0 + 0.2 \cdot 1 = 0.2, \qquad

The channel delivers exactly the fraction of symbols that survive.

The binary erasure channel with erasure probability e has

C = 1 - e \text{ bits per use},

attained by the uniform input.

Let \pi = P(X = 1), so H(X) = H(\pi). Condition on the output. If
Y \ne \ ?, then X = Y exactly and the conditional entropy is 0. If
Y = \ ?, an event of probability e for either input, the posterior is
P(X = 1 \mid Y = ?) = \pi e / e = \pi: the erasure leaves the prior
untouched, with entropy H(\pi). Averaging,
H(X \mid Y) = e\,H(\pi), hence

I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) = (1 - e)\,H(\pi) \le 1 - e,

with equality iff \pi = \tfrac{1}{2}. So C = 1 - e.

The derivation ran through H(X) - H(X \mid Y) rather than
H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) because conditioning on the output is trivial here:
either the input is known exactly or nothing was learned. Exercise 7
reruns it from the output side and lands on the same (1-e)H(\pi).

Flipping against erasing: the same 0.2, nowhere near the same cost

Set the two noise parameters equal, p = e = 0.2. The erasure channel
keeps C = 0.8 bits per use. The symmetric channel keeps
C = 1 - H(0.2) = 1 - 0.722 = 0.278 bits per use: not 1 - 0.2,
because a flip costs H(0.2) = 0.722 bits of output entropy, not 0.2.

The gap has one cause. The erasure channel tells the receiver which
symbols failed; the twenty percent that arrive as ? are known losses,
and the rest are certainties. The symmetric channel corrupts silently:
every received bit, correct or not, looks the same, and the doubt spread
over all of them is what H(0.2) prices.

Matched noise, unmatched capacity: at p = e = 0.2 the erasure channel carries nearly three times the bits.

At the same noise level, erasure is far cheaper than flipping:
C_{\mathrm{BEC}} = 1 - e against C_{\mathrm{BSC}} = 1 - H(p), and at
0.2 that is 0.8 against 0.28 bits per use. A channel that flags
its own failures loses only the failed symbols.

documents.title: The second of Shannon's two limits
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels and capacity › Channel capacity › The second of Shannon's two limits
documents.text:
The second of Shannon's two limits

Both canonical channels happened to be maximized by the uniform input,
because both are symmetric. That is a property of the examples, not of
the definition: for an asymmetric channel the optimal input is generally
non-uniform (Exercise 6 shows a channel whose maximizer puts probability
0.4 on one symbol), and in general C is found numerically as the
concave maximization in the Aside above. The lesson on
Mutual information of a neural code applies exactly this quantity to a
biological channel, as the denominator of coding efficiency.

Capacity closes a symmetry that the course opened with entropy. Both
limits are extreme values of the same functional, mutual information:

Shannon's two limits as the two extremes of mutual information: minimize it and you are compressing; maximize it and you are communicating.

On the compression side, The source coding theorem
established H(X) as the fewest bits per symbol a lossless code can
average; the lesson on Rate-distortion theory will exhibit that
side literally as a minimization of I(X;\hat X) over representations.
On the transmission side, this lesson produced the number
C = \max I(X;Y) — and so far only the number. That every rate below
C is actually achievable with vanishing error, and every rate above it
is not, is the noisy-channel coding theorem, the
next lesson; nothing in this
one assumes it. For continuous-valued channels the same maximization
gives the Gaussian-channel formula
C = \tfrac{1}{2}\log_2(1 + P/N), stated and used, not derived, in
Mutual information of a neural code.

Entropy and capacity are the two extreme points of mutual information:
H(X) is the floor reached by minimizing over representations, C the
ceiling reached by maximizing over channel inputs. Units for both sides
of this lesson: bits per channel use, under \log_2.

documents.title: Exercises
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels and capacity › Channel capacity › Exercises
documents.text:
Exercises

Compute the capacity of \mathrm{BSC}(0.2). Show the noise term, the
output ceiling, and the subtraction, as in the derivation frames. Use
\log_2 5 \approx 2.3219.

Noise term. Each row of the transition matrix is a permutation of
(0.8, 0.2), so for any input
H(Y \mid X) = H(0.2) = -0.2 \log_2 0.2 - 0.8 \log_2 0.8. With
\log_2 0.2 = -\log_2 5 \approx -2.3219 and
\log_2 0.8 = \log_2 4 - \log_2 5 \approx -0.3219:

H(0.2) \approx 0.2 \cdot 2.3219 + 0.8 \cdot 0.3219

Output ceiling. Y is binary, so H(Y) \le 1 bit, with equality at
the uniform input (P(Y=1) = 0.2 + 0.5 \cdot 0.6 = 0.5).

Subtract. C = 1 - H(0.2) \approx 1 - 0.7219 = 0.278 bits per use.
A twenty-percent flip rate destroys nearly three quarters of the
channel.

Compute the capacity of \mathrm{BSC}(0.9) and of \mathrm{BSC}(1).
For each, state the decoding move that makes the capacity usable.

C = 1 - H(0.9) = 1 - H(0.1) \approx 1 - 0.469 = 0.531 bits per use,
by the symmetry H(p) = H(1-p): the same capacity as
\mathrm{BSC}(0.1). The receiver inverts every received bit; the
composite channel from input to inverted output flips with probability
0.1.

\mathrm{BSC}(1): C = 1 - H(1) = 1 - 0 = 1 bit per use. The channel
inverts deterministically; inverting again recovers the input exactly.
A channel is useless not when it is usually wrong but when it is
uninformative: capacity falls to zero only at p = \tfrac{1}{2}.

Compute the capacity of \mathrm{BEC}(0.4) and of \mathrm{BSC}(0.4),
and take the ratio. Use \log_2 3 \approx 1.585 and
\log_2 5 \approx 2.3219.

Erasure channel: C = 1 - e = 0.6 bits per use.

Symmetric channel: H(0.4) = -0.4 \log_2 0.4 - 0.6 \log_2 0.6. With
\log_2 0.4 = 1 - \log_2 5 \approx -1.3219 and
\log_2 0.6 = \log_2 3 - \log_2 5 \approx -0.7370:

H(0.4) \approx 0.4 \cdot 1.3219 + 0.6 \cdot 0.7370

so C = 1 - 0.9710 = 0.029 bits per use.

Ratio: 0.6 / 0.029 \approx 21. At forty percent noise the erasure
channel still delivers most of a bit per use, while the symmetric
channel is within three hundredths of a bit of useless: silent
corruption at p = 0.4 leaves the output nearly independent of the
input.

A six-key noisy typewriter has inputs and outputs \{A, \ldots, F\} in
a cycle; each key prints itself or the next letter with probability
\tfrac{1}{2} each. Compute its capacity and give an explicit zero-error
signaling scheme that attains it.

Every row of the transition table is a fifty-fifty split over two
outputs, so H(Y \mid X) = 1 bit for any input. The output alphabet has
six symbols, so H(Y) \le \log_2 6, attained at the uniform input
(each output is reached from two inputs with total probability
\tfrac{1}{6}). Hence

C = \log_2 6 - 1 = \log_2 3 \approx 1.585 \text{ bits per use}.

Zero-error scheme: use only \{A, C, E\}, uniformly. Their output sets
are \{A, B\}, \{C, D\}, \{E, F\}: pairwise disjoint, so the
receiver identifies the input exactly and one of three symbols arrives
error-free, worth \log_2 3 bits per use, which equals C.

An input with P(X = 1) = 0.2 feeds \mathrm{BSC}(0.25). Build the
joint table p(x, y), compute both marginals, then compute I(X;Y) as
H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) using the recipes of
Joint and conditional entropy. Compare with the
capacity of the channel. Use H(0.25) \approx 0.8113 and
H(0.35) \approx 0.9341.

Joint table. p(x, y) = p(x)\,p(y \mid x):

\begin{array}{c|cc}

Marginals. Rows: P(X = 0) = 0.8, P(X = 1) = 0.2 (as designed).
Columns: P(Y = 0) = 0.60 + 0.05 = 0.65, P(Y = 1) = 0.20 + 0.15
= 0.35.

Conditional entropy. Each row of p(y \mid x) is a permutation of
(0.75, 0.25), so
H(Y \mid X) = 0.8 \cdot H(0.25) + 0.2 \cdot H(0.25) = H(0.25)
\approx 0.8113 bits.

Mutual information.
H(Y) = H(0.35) \approx 0.9341 bits, so

I(X;Y) \approx 0.9341 - 0.8113 = 0.123 \text{ bits per use}.

Against capacity. C = 1 - H(0.25) \approx 1 - 0.8113 = 0.189 bits
per use. The biased input realizes 0.123 of the possible 0.189
bits; the remaining 0.066 is lost to the sender's choice, not to the
channel.

The Z-channel transmits 0 faithfully but flips 1 to 0 with
probability \tfrac{1}{2}: p(0 \mid 0) = 1,
p(0 \mid 1) = p(1 \mid 1) = \tfrac{1}{2}. Write \pi = P(X = 1).
(a) Compute I(X;Y) at the uniform input. (b) Show
I(\pi) = H(\pi/2) - \pi and find the maximizing \pi. (c) Compute
C and compare with (a). Use H(0.25) \approx 0.8113 and
H(0.2) \approx 0.7219.

(a) At \pi = 0.5: P(Y = 1) = 0.5 \cdot 0.5 = 0.25, so
H(Y) = H(0.25) \approx 0.8113. The rows have entropies H(0) = 0
(input 0, deterministic) and H(\tfrac{1}{2}) = 1 (input 1), so
H(Y \mid X) = 0.5 \cdot 0 + 0.5 \cdot 1 = 0.5. Hence
I \approx 0.8113 - 0.5 = 0.311 bits.

(b) In general P(Y = 1) = \pi/2, so H(Y) = H(\pi/2), and
H(Y \mid X) = (1 - \pi) \cdot 0 + \pi \cdot 1 = \pi. Thus
I(\pi) = H(\pi/2) - \pi. Setting the derivative to zero, with
H'(q) = \log_2 \tfrac{1-q}{q} and the chain rule factor
\tfrac{1}{2}:

\tfrac{1}{2} \log_2 \frac{1 - \pi/2}{\pi/2} - 1 = 0

(c) C = I(0.4) = H(0.2) - 0.4 \approx 0.7219 - 0.4 = 0.322 bits
per use, against 0.311 at the uniform input. The asymmetric noise
wants an asymmetric input: the symbol 1 is unreliable, so the
maximizer uses it less. Uniform inputs are optimal for symmetric
channels, not in general.

Rerun the BEC capacity derivation from the output side: for
\mathrm{BEC}(e) with \pi = P(X = 1), compute H(Y \mid X) and
H(Y) directly, and verify I(X;Y) = (1 - e)\,H(\pi).

Noise term. Given X = x, the output is x with probability
1 - e and ? with probability e: a two-outcome distribution with
entropy H(e), the same for both inputs. So H(Y \mid X) = H(e).

Output term. Y takes the values 0, ?, 1 with probabilities
(1-e)(1-\pi), e, (1-e)\pi. Expanding the entropy sum and
splitting each \log of a product:

H(Y) = -(1-e)\bigl[(1-\pi)\log_2(1-\pi) + \pi \log_2 \pi\bigr]

which is H(Y) = (1-e)\,H(\pi) + H(e).

Subtract.

I(X;Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) = (1-e)\,H(\pi) + H(e) - H(e)

matching the input-side derivation, and \le 1 - e with equality at
\pi = \tfrac{1}{2}. The erasure entropy H(e) appears in both terms
and cancels: the visible fact that an erasure happened carries no
information about what was sent. Picking the decomposition whose
conditional term is easy — here either works; on the BSC only the
output side is clean — is most of the labor.

C. E. Shannon, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication," Bell System Technical Journal, 27, 1948 — Part II: §11 sets up the noisy discrete channel, §12 defines the equivocation H_y(x), the transmission rate R = H(x) - H_y(x), and the capacity C = \max R; §§15–16 compute capacities of symmetric-noise examples.

T. M. Cover, J. A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006 — §7.1 catalogs the example channels (noiseless binary, noisy typewriter, BSC in §7.1.4, BEC in §7.1.5), §7.2 solves symmetric channels via the uniform input, §7.3 proves the properties of capacity used here; fig. 1.2 is the two-extremes map recreated above.

D. J. C. MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms, Cambridge University Press, 2003 — ch. 9, §§9.5–9.6: mutual information of a channel and capacity, with worked BSC, BEC, and Z-channel calculations including the non-uniform maximizer of the Z-channel. Free online: https://www.inference.org.uk/mackay/itila/

Y. Polyanskiy, Y. Wu, Lecture Notes on Information Theory (MIT 6.441 / UIUC ECE 563), 2016 — ch. 4 treats capacity as a saddle point / information radius; §16.4 works the BSC and BEC capacities.

documents.title: The noisy-channel coding theorem
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels and capacity › The noisy-channel coding theorem
documents.text:
Reliable communication is possible at every rate below the channel capacity
and impossible above it: capacity is a sharp threshold, not a soft
trade-off. This lesson defines block codes and their rates, states the
noisy-channel coding theorem, sketches both halves of the argument
(achievability by random codebooks with joint-typicality decoding, the
converse by Fano's inequality combined with the data-processing
inequality), and works one finite code, the Hamming (7,4), by hand.

documents.title: Brute redundancy: reliability at a vanishing rate
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels and capacity › The noisy-channel coding theorem › Brute redundancy: reliability at a vanishing rate
documents.text:
Brute redundancy: reliability at a vanishing rate

Fix the channel of Channel capacity: \mathrm{BSC}(0.1),
each transmitted bit flipped independently with probability f = 0.1,
capacity C = 1 - H(0.1) \approx 0.531 bits per use. Sending data bits raw
corrupts one in ten. The oldest countermeasure is repetition: transmit
every data bit three times and decode by majority vote.

Each data bit becomes three channel bits; the decoder outputs the majority
of the three received copies. The vote errs exactly when at least two of
the three copies flip:

p_b = 3f^2(1 - f) + f^3 = 3 \cdot 0.01 \cdot 0.9 + 0.001 = 0.028.

Per-bit error falls from 0.1 to 0.028. The price is paid in rate: three
channel uses now carry one data bit, R = \tfrac{1}{3} against the raw
code's R = 1.

Repeating N times continues the pattern: the majority vote fails only
when half the copies flip, an event whose probability falls exponentially
in N, while the rate falls as 1/N.
MacKay (ch. 1) runs the
numbers for a target of p_b \le 10^{-15}, the reliability a disk drive
needs: N = 61 copies, rate \tfrac{1}{61} \approx 0.016. The pattern
suggests a general law: error tends to zero only if rate does. The theorem
of this lesson says the suggestion is false, and that the true boundary
sits at R = 0.531, not at R = 0.

Repetition buys reliability only by spending the entire rate: driving its
error to zero drives R \to 0. That trade is a defect of the code, not a
law of the channel.

documents.title: Codes and rates: the objects the theorem quantifies
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels and capacity › The noisy-channel coding theorem › Codes and rates: the objects the theorem quantifies
documents.text:
Codes and rates: the objects the theorem quantifies

R3 is one instance of a general shape. It assigns M = 2 messages the
codewords 000 and 111 of length n = 3, and maps each received triple
back to a message. The general object replaces 2 and 3 by parameters.

An (M, n) block code for a channel p(y \mid x) consists of an
encoder assigning each message w \in \{1, \ldots, M\} a codeword
x^n(w) \in \mathcal{X}^n, and a decoder
g : \mathcal{Y}^n \to \{1, \ldots, M\}. Its rate is

R = \frac{\log_2 M}{n} \text{ bits per channel use},

so a rate-R code carries M = 2^{nR} distinct messages on n uses.

The maximal block error probability of a code is
\lambda^{(n)} = \max_w \Pr\{g(Y^n) \ne w \mid W = w\}: the worst case
over messages of decoding to anything but the sent message. A rate R is
achievable if a sequence of (2^{nR}, n) codes exists with
\lambda^{(n)} \to 0 as n \to \infty.

One message, n channel uses: the rate R counts message bits per use, and the decoder must undo the flips.

The question the theorem answers: for a given discrete memoryless channel,
which rates are achievable. The limit n \to \infty is part of the
question. At any fixed n some error probability remains; achievability
asks whether a sequence of codes drives it to zero at fixed rate.

documents.title: The theorem: the achievable rates are exactly the rates below C
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels and capacity › The noisy-channel coding theorem › The theorem: the achievable rates are exactly the rates below C
documents.text:
The theorem: the achievable rates are exactly the rates below C

Let a discrete memoryless channel have capacity
C = \max_{p(x)} I(X;Y).

Achievability. Every rate R < C is achievable: there exist
(2^{nR}, n) codes with \lambda^{(n)} \to 0.

Converse. No rate above C is achievable: every (2^{nR}, n) code
with R > C has average block error

P_e \;\ge\; 1 - \frac{C}{R} - \frac{1}{nR},

which is bounded away from 0 as n \to \infty.

This is Theorem 11 of
Shannon's 1948 paper
(Part II, §13). The two directions are separate arguments with separate
tools, sketched in the next two sections: a probabilistic existence proof
for achievability, an information-counting bound for the converse. Neither
direction implies the other.

The n → ∞ picture: error vanishes at every rate left of C and is floored at 1 − C/R right of it.

Capacity is a sharp threshold, not a trade-off: below C the error can be
made arbitrarily small at full fixed rate, above C it cannot be made
small at all. Nothing about the boundary is gradual.

Load the below capacity preset and raise n: the block error falls
toward 0. Load above capacity and raise n again: the error climbs
instead. Then fix the largest n and sweep R across 0.531 to trace
the cliff in one pass.

documents.title: Finite blocklength: the cliff is the n → ∞ limit
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels and capacity › The noisy-channel coding theorem › Finite blocklength: the cliff is the n → ∞ limit
documents.text:
Finite blocklength: the cliff is the n → ∞ limit

At any finite n there is no discontinuity. The error-versus-rate curve
of the best length-n codes is an S-shaped slope through the
neighborhood of C; the theorem describes the limit of these slopes, and
the wall at C is what they steepen into.

n = 10, 100, 1000: each frame steepens the transition around C toward the limiting step.

Step through the three frames and read the transition width at each n:
it shrinks roughly like 1/\sqrt{n}, so sharpening the cliff by another
factor of ten costs a hundredfold longer blocks.

The 1/\sqrt{n} width has an exact form. For error tolerance
\varepsilon, the largest number of messages M^*(n, \varepsilon)
carried by length-n codes satisfies

\log_2 M^*(n, \varepsilon) \;\approx\; nC - \sqrt{nV}\, Q^{-1}(\varepsilon),

where V is the channel dispersion, a variance-like constant of the
channel, and Q^{-1} is the inverse Gaussian tail function. The
best usable rate at finite n sits below C by a deficit shrinking as
\sqrt{V/n}: the normal approximation of
Polyanskiy & Wu
(ch. 20, §20.3), sharpening a line of analysis going back to Strassen
(1962). For \mathrm{BSC}(0.1) at n = 1000 and
\varepsilon = 10^{-3}, the deficit is on the order of 0.03 bits per
use: the theorem's promise is honest, but blocklength is the currency
that pays for it.

documents.title: Achievability: random codebooks, typicality decoding
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels and capacity › The noisy-channel coding theorem › Achievability: random codebooks, typicality decoding
documents.text:
Achievability: random codebooks, typicality decoding

The task: show that for every R < C codes with vanishing error exist.
The obstacle is scale. At n = 1000 and R = 0.4 a codebook assigns
2^{400} \approx 10^{120} messages their thousand-bit codewords; no
explicit construction of that size was known in 1948, and analyzing any
particular one is hopeless. Shannon's argument sidesteps both problems
with two moves: a decoder whose analysis needs only typicality counts,
and an average over all codebooks in place of any particular one.

The decoder: joint typicality

The source coding theorem established the typical set:
for large n, the sequences a source actually produces concentrate on
\approx 2^{nH} roughly equiprobable typical sequences. Apply this to
the pair (X^n, Y^n) under the capacity-achieving input distribution
(uniform, for the BSC): a pair is jointly typical when the input is
typical, the output is typical, and the pair looks like n draws from
the joint distribution p(x)\,p(y \mid x).

The counts for \mathrm{BSC}(0.1) with uniform input: H(X) = 1,
H(Y) = 1, H(X,Y) = 1 + H(0.1) = 1.469, so
H(X \mid Y) = 0.469. Given a received y^n, the inputs jointly typical
with it number \approx 2^{0.469\,n}, out of \approx 2^{n} typical
inputs: a fraction

\frac{2^{nH(X \mid Y)}}{2^{nH(X)}} = 2^{-n I(X;Y)} = 2^{-0.531\,n}.

The decoder: output \hat w if x^n(\hat w) is the unique codeword
jointly typical with the received y^n; declare an error otherwise.

Two failure modes, one union bound

The decoder fails in exactly two ways. First, the true pair
(x^n(w), y^n) falls outside the jointly typical set; the law of large
numbers sends this probability to 0. Second, some wrong codeword is
jointly typical with y^n. A wrong codeword, drawn independently of the
transmission, hits the jointly typical shell of y^n with probability
\approx 2^{-nI(X;Y)}; there are 2^{nR} - 1 wrong codewords, and the
union bound charges them all:

2^{nR} \cdot 2^{-n I(X;Y)} = 2^{-n\,(I(X;Y) - R)} \;\longrightarrow\; 0

Choosing the input distribution that attains the maximum makes
I(X;Y) = C, so every R < C is covered. At n = 1000, R = 0.4:
