2^{400} competitors against an exponent of 2^{-531} leaves total wrong-codeword
probability \approx 2^{-131} \approx 10^{-39}.

Joint-typicality decoding: the true codeword lands in the shell of the received output; each of the 2^nR wrong codewords hits it with probability ≈ 2^−nI.

Step through the four frames and recompute the exponents at R = 0.5 on
the same channel: wrong-codeword mass 2^{-n(0.531 - 0.5)} = 2^{-0.031\,n},
which at n = 1000 is 2^{-31} \approx 5 \times 10^{-10}. Closing in on
capacity thins the safety exponent; only larger n restores it.

The random-codebook trick

The union bound computed an average: codewords were treated as drawn
independently and uniformly at random, so the quantity bounded is the
error probability averaged over all codebooks. The final step is the
oldest argument in the probabilistic method: if the average over
codebooks of the error tends to 0, then for each n at least one
specific codebook does at least as well as the average. Existence
follows; no codebook is named. (The average controls the average-over-messages
error; discarding the worse half of each codebook's messages converts
the guarantee to the maximal error \lambda^{(n)} at a rate cost of
\tfrac{1}{n}, which vanishes —
Cover & Thomas
§7.7.)

The proof is non-constructive twice over. It exhibits no codebook, only
the goodness of an average; and the objects it averages over are
unusable, since a random codebook has no structure to exploit: storing
it takes n \cdot 2^{nR} bits and typicality decoding means searching
all 2^{nR} codewords per received block. The gap between this
existence proof and codes that run on hardware stayed open for
decades; the closing section returns to it.

Random codes beat the noise for every R < C: a wrong codeword is
jointly typical with the output with probability \approx 2^{-nC}, and
even 2^{nR} competitors lose that race whenever R < C. If the
average codebook succeeds, some codebook does.

documents.title: The converse: Fano's inequality and the data-processing bound
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels and capacity › The noisy-channel coding theorem › The converse: Fano's inequality and the data-processing bound
documents.text:
The converse: Fano's inequality and the data-processing bound

The converse must rule out every conceivable code at rates above C,
including codes no one has imagined. The argument therefore cannot
examine decoders; it counts information along the pipeline
W \to X^n \to Y^n \to \hat W and shows the count fails when R > C.
Two bounds do all the work.

Fano: low error forces low conditional entropy

If the decoder is usually right, then given its output \hat W little
uncertainty about W can remain. Fano's inequality makes the
quantifier exact.

Let W take values in a set of size M and let \hat W be any estimate
of W (any function of any data), with error probability
P_e = \Pr\{\hat W \ne W\}. Then

H(W \mid \hat W) \;\le\; H_2(P_e) + P_e \log_2 (M - 1)

Let E = \mathbf{1}\{\hat W \ne W\}, the error indicator. Expand
H(E, W \mid \hat W) both ways with the chain rule of
Joint and conditional entropy:

H(W \mid \hat W) + H(E \mid W, \hat W)

The second term on the left is 0: E is a function of (W, \hat W).
On the right, H(E \mid \hat W) \le H(E) = H_2(P_e), since conditioning
does not increase entropy. For the last term, split on E: given
E = 0, W = \hat W exactly, contributing 0; given E = 1, W is
one of the M - 1 values other than \hat W, so its conditional
entropy is at most \log_2(M-1) (the range bound of
Entropy). Hence

H(W \mid \hat W) \le H_2(P_e) + P_e \log_2 (M - 1),

and the weaker form follows from H_2(P_e) \le 1 and
\log_2(M-1) \le \log_2 M. This is
Cover & Thomas
Theorem 2.10.1.

The reading direction matters: Fano converts an assumed error rate into
an upper bound on leftover uncertainty, so, contraposed, a large
leftover uncertainty forces a large error. The converse manufactures
exactly that large leftover.

The code is a Markov chain, and n uses carry at most nC

Encoder, channel, and decoder form the chain
W \to X^n \to Y^n \to \hat W: each stage is computed from the one
before it. The The data-processing inequality applies twice
and gives I(W; \hat W) \le I(X^n; Y^n). Memorylessness then caps the
middle link:

I(X^n;Y^n) = H(Y^n) - \sum_{i=1}^n H(Y_i \mid X_i)

The equality uses independence of the noise across uses
(H(Y^n \mid X^n) = \sum_i H(Y_i \mid X_i)); the first inequality is
subadditivity of entropy, from the chain rule plus conditioning
(Joint and conditional entropy); the last holds because
each I(X_i;Y_i) enters the maximization defining C. Whatever
dependence the encoder builds across the block, n uses of the channel
pass at most n capacities of information.

The converse in one picture: nR bits must cross a link that passes at most nC, and Fano converts the deficit into an error floor.

The arithmetic of impossibility

Take W uniform over the M = 2^{nR} messages, so H(W) = nR; the
average error P_e under uniform messages lower-bounds the maximal
error, so a floor here floors both. Split H(W) with the
three-forms identity of Mutual information and apply the
two bounds:

nR = H(W) = I(W;\hat W) + H(W \mid \hat W)

Solving for P_e:

P_e \;\ge\; 1 - \frac{C}{R} - \frac{1}{nR}.

For R \le C the bound is vacuous. For any R > C it converges to
1 - C/R > 0: at R = 0.6 on \mathrm{BSC}(0.1), at least 11.5\% of
blocks decode wrongly whatever the code; at R = 1 (uncoded
transmission of a full bit per use), at least 46.9\%. No decoder
design enters the computation. The floor binds every code because it is
an accounting identity about entropy, not an analysis of a mechanism.

Two refinements, both out of scope. Strong converse: above capacity
the situation is worse than the Fano floor: for a DMC, the block error
of any code sequence at fixed R > C tends to 1, not merely to
1 - C/R (Wolfowitz, 1957). The cliff is two-sided: error \to 0
below, error \to 1 above. Feedback: the bound
I(X^n;Y^n) \le nC as derived assumes the encoder does not see the
channel outputs. Shannon proved in 1956 that even a perfect feedback
link changes nothing for a DMC: C_{\text{feedback}} = C. Feedback
shortens delays and simplifies codes; it adds no capacity.

The converse is bookkeeping, not engineering: nR message bits must
pass a link that carries at most nC, and Fano's inequality converts
the shortfall into a hard error floor P_e \ge 1 - C/R - \tfrac{1}{nR}.
Above capacity, no code, present or future, escapes it.

documents.title: Hamming (7,4): three parity checks localize one error
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels and capacity › The noisy-channel coding theorem › Hamming (7,4): three parity checks localize one error
documents.text:
Hamming (7,4): three parity checks localize one error

The theorem names no code; this section builds the classic small one.
The Hamming (7,4) code
(Hamming 1950, already exhibited in §17 of Shannon's 1948 paper)
protects 4 data bits s_1 s_2 s_3 s_4 with 3 parity bits computed
as

t_5 = s_1 \oplus s_2 \oplus s_3, \qquad

and transmits the 7-bit block s_1 s_2 s_3 s_4 t_5 t_6 t_7: rate
R = \tfrac{4}{7} \approx 0.571. Each parity bit makes the total number
of ones in its group even, and the three groups overlap in the pattern
of a three-circle Venn diagram.

Three parity circles over 7 bits: the pattern of failing checks intersects in exactly one bit, the error.

Encode s = 1000. The parities:
t_5 = 1 \oplus 0 \oplus 0 = 1, t_6 = 0 \oplus 0 \oplus 0 = 0,
t_7 = 1 \oplus 0 \oplus 0 = 1. Transmitted block: 1000101.

Corrupt. The channel flips s_2: received 1100101.

Recompute the three checks on the received block (each sums its
circle, and should be even):

check 1 (s_1, s_2, s_3, t_5): 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 = 3, odd — fails;

check 2 (s_2, s_3, s_4, t_6): 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 1, odd — fails;

check 3 (s_1, s_3, s_4, t_7): 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 = 2, even — holds.

Localize. The error lies in every failing circle and in no holding
circle: inside checks 1 and 2, outside check 3. One bit occupies that
region of the Venn diagram: s_2. Flip it back; the data 1000 is
recovered exactly.

The pattern of check results is the syndrome, and the count works out
exactly: 3 binary checks give 2^3 = 8 syndromes, which is one for
"no error" plus one for each of the 7 possible single-bit flips. Every
single error in a block, in data or parity bits alike, is corrected;
blocks with two or more flips decode to the wrong codeword.

The payoff against repetition: structure beats brute redundancy

At f = 0.01, a block fails when at least two of its 7 bits flip:

1 - (1-f)^7 - 7f(1-f)^6 \approx 0.0020,

against 0.039 for 4 unprotected bits. Repetition R3 protecting the
same 4 data bits spends 12 channel uses (rate \tfrac{1}{3}) for a
block failure probability of \approx 0.0012. The Hamming code reaches
a comparable failure rate, within a factor of two, while carrying
71\% more data per channel use. Both codes correct any single error
per block; Hamming simply pays 3 parity bits for 4 data bits where
repetition pays 8 for 4.

Matched protection, unmatched rate: Hamming's three structured parity bits do nearly the work of repetition's eight copies.

Hamming (7,4) is a single (16, 7) code at one fixed rate: its block
error on \mathrm{BSC}(f) is a fixed number, not a sequence tending to
0, and at f = 0.01 its rate 0.571 sits far below the capacity
C = 1 - H(0.01) \approx 0.919 that the theorem makes achievable with
vanishing error. Shannon's §17 shows the code attains the capacity of a
different, specially constrained channel, one guaranteed to corrupt at
most one symbol per block of seven; on the BSC no capacity claim
attaches to it. The code demonstrates that structured redundancy works;
the theorem says how far such structure can be pushed.

Three parity checks pinpoint any single error in seven bits because the
counting is exact: 2^3 = 8 syndromes cover 7 error positions plus
"no error". Redundancy arranged to intersect beats redundancy merely
piled up.

documents.title: From existence to constructions: LDPC, turbo, polar
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels and capacity › The noisy-channel coding theorem › From existence to constructions: LDPC, turbo, polar
documents.text:
From existence to constructions: LDPC, turbo, polar

What the theorem delivers is the exact frontier, in both directions, for
every discrete memoryless channel. What it withholds is a code:
the achievability proof averages over codebooks that cannot be stored or
searched, and for decades no explicit family provably approached C
with practical decoding.

The gap closed in stages.
Gallager's low-density parity-check codes
(1963) generalize Hamming's idea to large sparse random check
matrices; they were computationally ahead of their time, forgotten, and
rediscovered in the 1990s (MacKay & Neal, 1996), whereupon iterative
decoding carried them to within fractions of a decibel of capacity.
Turbo codes (Berrou, Glavieux & Thitimajshima, 1993) reached similar
performance empirically and made near-capacity coding an engineering
commodity. The proof came last:
Arıkan's polar codes (2009) are the
first explicit family with a theorem: they achieve the capacity of every
symmetric binary-input DMC with encoding and decoding complexity
O(n \log n). Later standardization work built on that result: the 5G
cellular standard (3GPP, 2016–2018) adopted polar codes for its control
channels, with LDPC codes carrying the data channels.

One boundary of scope: capacity is a statement per channel use, and
matching a source of entropy rate H to a channel of capacity C is
a further theorem, source-channel separation, which states that
compressing first (The source coding theorem) and
channel-coding second loses nothing for a DMC. Shannon's §14 already
notes the mechanism behind it: natural sources arrive with redundancy of
their own, and coding redistributes it.

The pair of coding theorems gives each course quantity its operational
meaning: entropy is the fewest bits per symbol a source can be
compressed to, and capacity, the maximum of mutual information, is the
most message bits per use a channel can carry reliably. Mutual
information is not a descriptive statistic; it is a rate.

documents.title: Exercises
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Channels and capacity › The noisy-channel coding theorem › Exercises
documents.text:
Exercises

Compute the per-bit error probability of the five-fold repetition code
R5 on \mathrm{BSC}(0.1) under majority decoding, and its rate. Compare
both numbers with R3's (p_b = 0.028 at R = \tfrac{1}{3}), and state
what the comparison illustrates about repetition.

Majority-of-five errs when at least 3 of the 5 copies flip:

p_b = \binom{5}{3} f^3 (1-f)^2 + \binom{5}{4} f^4 (1-f) + f^5

so p_b = 0.0081 + 0.00045 + 0.00001 \approx 0.0086, at rate
R = \tfrac{1}{5} = 0.2.

Against R3: error improves by a factor of \approx 3.3
(0.028 \to 0.0086) while the rate drops from 0.333 to 0.2. Each
step of improvement costs a constant fraction of the remaining rate:
error \to 0 along the repetition family forces R \to 0. The coding
theorem asserts this trade is avoidable at every rate below
C = 0.531.

A system must deliver 300 message bits over n = 1000 uses of
\mathrm{BSC}(0.1); a second design calls for 600 message bits over
the same 1000 uses. For each design, give the rate, state what the
coding theorem says about it, and where applicable compute the error
floor from the converse.

First design: R = 300/1000 = 0.3 < C = 0.531. Achievable: by the
theorem there exist (2^{300}, 1000)-style code sequences whose block
error tends to 0 (and at this margin below capacity, good codes of
blocklength 1000 already exist in practice).

Second design: R = 600/1000 = 0.6 > C. Not achievable. The converse
floor:

P_e \ge 1 - \frac{C}{R} - \frac{1}{nR}

At least 11\% of blocks decode wrongly under every conceivable code;
the specification cannot be met on this channel. The remedy is more
channel uses per message bit, not a cleverer code.

The achievability sketch bounds the wrong-codeword error by
2^{-n(I(X;Y) - R)}. On \mathrm{BSC}(0.1) (so I = C = 0.531 at the
uniform input), evaluate the bound at n = 1000 for R = 0.4 and for
R = 0.53. Then find the blocklength n at which the R = 0.53 bound
matches the R = 0.4, n = 1000 bound. What does the comparison say
about operating near capacity?

At R = 0.4: exponent n(C - R) = 1000 \cdot 0.131 = 131, bound
2^{-131} \approx 10^{-39}.

At R = 0.53: exponent 1000 \cdot 0.001 = 1, bound
2^{-1} = 0.5 — useless at this blocklength.

Matching: the bound is 2^{-n(C-R)}, so n \cdot 0.001 = 131 requires
n = 131{,}000.

The safety margin is the exponent n(C - R): the product of blocklength
and distance from capacity. Halving the distance to capacity doubles the
blocklength needed for the same guarantee; operating within 0.001 bits
of C costs two orders of magnitude more blocklength than operating
0.131 bits below it. The threshold is sharp only in the limit; near
it, n is the price.

A decoder for M = 2^{500} messages (n = 1000, R = 0.5) achieves
P_e = 10^{-3}. Use Fano's inequality to bound H(W \mid \hat W), and
interpret the two terms of the bound. Use
\log_2 10^{-3} \approx -9.97.

The exact form:

H(W \mid \hat W) \le H_2(P_e) + P_e \log_2 (M - 1).

First term: H_2(10^{-3}) = -10^{-3} \log_2 10^{-3} - 0.999 \log_2
0.999 \approx 0.00997 + 0.00144 \approx 0.011 bits. Second term:
10^{-3} \cdot \log_2(2^{500} - 1) \approx 10^{-3} \cdot 500 = 0.5
bits. Total: H(W \mid \hat W) \le 0.511 bits.

Interpretation: out of H(W) = 500 bits of message uncertainty, the
decoder's output leaves at most half a bit unresolved. The first term
prices the uncertainty about whether an error occurred (the indicator
E); the second prices which of the M - 1 wrong messages was sent
when one did, weighted by how rarely that case arises. Small error
probability forces small residual entropy: exactly the lever the
converse pulls in reverse.

Encode s = 0110 with the Hamming (7,4) code. The channel then flips
the parity bit t_6. Compute the received block, run the three checks,
localize the error from the syndrome, and state what the receiver
outputs.

Encode. s_1 s_2 s_3 s_4 = 0110:
t_5 = 0 \oplus 1 \oplus 1 = 0, t_6 = 1 \oplus 1 \oplus 0 = 0,
t_7 = 0 \oplus 1 \oplus 0 = 1. Transmitted: 0110001.

Corrupt. Flipping t_6 gives received block 0110011.

Checks (each sums its circle; even = holds):

check 1 (s_1, s_2, s_3, t_5): 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 2, even — holds;

check 2 (s_2, s_3, s_4, t_6): 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 = 3, odd — fails;

check 3 (s_1, s_3, s_4, t_7): 0 + 1 + 0 + 1 = 2, even — holds.

Localize. The error lies inside check 2 and outside checks 1 and 3.
The only bit in circle 2 alone is t_6 itself. Flip it back to get
0110001; the receiver outputs the data bits 0110, which were in fact
never corrupted. Errors in parity bits are detected and corrected by
the same mechanism as errors in data bits: the syndrome does not care
which kind of bit failed.

Show that Hamming (7,4) is a perfect code: the radius-1 Hamming
balls around its 16 codewords exactly partition the space of 2^7
binary words. Conclude that every pattern of two or more bit errors is
decoded to a wrong codeword.

Ball size. The radius-1 ball around a 7-bit word contains the
word itself plus its 7 single-bit neighbors: 1 + 7 = 8 words.

Disjointness. Single-error correction means every word at distance
\le 1 from a codeword is decoded to that codeword; a word inside two
different codewords' balls would have to decode to both, which is
impossible. So the 16 balls are pairwise disjoint.

Counting. Disjoint balls cover 16 \cdot 8 = 128 = 2^7 words: the
whole space, with nothing left over. The balls partition
\{0,1\}^7 exactly, which is the definition of a perfect code.

Consequence. A received word carrying \ge 2 errors lies at
distance \ge 2 from the true codeword, hence outside its ball. Being
in the partition, it lies inside exactly one other codeword's ball and
is decoded there: a wrong codeword, with certainty. Perfection means
zero slack — every syndrome is spent on single errors, so nothing is
left to even detect double ones.

The binary erasure channel \mathrm{BEC}(e) of
Channel capacity has capacity C = 1 - e. (a) For
\mathrm{BEC}(0.4) and rate R = 0.75, compute the asymptotic converse
floor. (b) Give a direct counting argument, without Fano, for why no
code at rate R > 1 - e can have vanishing error: compare the number of
messages with the number a genie-aided receiver could distinguish if
the erasure locations were announced in advance.

(a) C = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6, and

P_e \ge 1 - \frac{C}{R} = 1 - \frac{0.6}{0.75} = 0.2

asymptotically: at least one block in five fails, under every code.

(b) Over n uses, the law of large numbers puts the number of
unerased positions near (1 - e)n. Hand the receiver a genie that
announces the erasure pattern in advance: the transmission is then
determined entirely by the \approx (1-e)n surviving bits, so the
receiver can distinguish at most 2^{(1-e)n} transmission outcomes.
The code carries 2^{nR} messages, and for R > 1 - e,

\frac{2^{nR}}{2^{(1-e)n}} = 2^{n(R - (1-e))} \longrightarrow \infty:

exponentially many messages per distinguishable outcome, so most
messages share their receivable evidence with exponentially many others
and cannot be decoded reliably. The genie only strengthens the
receiver, so the true channel does no better. This is the converse made
concrete: the channel simply does not deliver enough distinguishable
outputs to separate 2^{nR} messages.

C. E. Shannon, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication," Bell System Technical Journal, 27, 1948 — Part II: §13 states and proves the fundamental theorem for a discrete channel with noise (Theorem 11) by the random-coding argument, with the converse; §14 discusses redundancy already present in the source; §17 exhibits the (7,4) single-error-correcting code and the constrained channel whose capacity it attains.

T. M. Cover, J. A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006 — §7.5 definitions of codes, rates, and achievability; §7.6 jointly typical sequences; §7.7 the channel coding theorem (Theorem 7.7.1) via random coding and joint typicality; §2.10 and §7.9 Fano's inequality and the converse; §7.11 Hamming codes; §7.12 feedback capacity.

D. J. C. MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms, Cambridge University Press, 2003 — ch. 1 repetition codes and the (7,4) Hamming code with the parity-circle picture; §§9.6–9.7 statement of the theorem with the typical-set preview; ch. 10 the full random-coding and joint-typicality proof and the converse. Free online: https://www.inference.org.uk/mackay/itila/

Y. Polyanskiy, Y. Wu, Lecture Notes on Information Theory (MIT 6.441 / UIUC ECE 563), 2016 — chs. 14–16 achievability bounds and the Fano-based converse; ch. 20, §20.3 channel dispersion and the finite-blocklength normal approximation behind the sharpening cliff.

E. Arıkan, "Channel Polarization: A Method for Constructing Capacity-Achieving Codes for Symmetric Binary-Input Memoryless Channels," IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 55(7), 2009 — polar codes, the first explicit capacity-achieving family with O(n \log n) coding complexity. https://arxiv.org/abs/0807.3917

documents.title: KL divergence
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › KL divergence
documents.text:
KL divergence D(p||q) is the expected extra code length paid when data
distributed as p is encoded with a code optimized for q. This lesson computes
that overhead on a concrete pair of sources, defines D(p\,\|\,q) as the
expected log-ratio of truth to model, proves the overhead is never negative,
computes both directions of an asymmetric pair, and establishes the boundary
case that dominates practice: a model assigning probability zero to a real
outcome diverges infinitely.

documents.title: The wrong code: 0.875 extra bits per symbol
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › KL divergence › The wrong code: 0.875 extra bits per symbol
documents.text:
The wrong code: 0.875 extra bits per symbol

The source coding theorem established that a prefix code
with lengths \ell(x) bets on the distribution q(x) = 2^{-\ell(x)}, and
that on a dyadic source (every probability a power of \tfrac12) the
matched code is exact: each length equals its symbol's surprisal and the
expected length equals the entropy. This section runs that machinery on a
mismatched pair and measures the damage.

One code, two sources

A transmitter models its source as q = (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18,
\tfrac18) over \{A, B, C, D\} and builds the exact code for q: lengths
\ell_q = (1, 2, 3, 3), the matched code of Prefix codes and code trees.
The data, however, comes from p = (\tfrac18, \tfrac18, \tfrac14,
\tfrac12): the same alphabet with the probabilities reversed.

The code still decodes perfectly; only the price changes. Expected length
under the true frequencies:

L = \sum_x p(x)\,\ell_q(x)

The exact code for p has lengths (3, 3, 2, 1) and costs H(p) = 1.75
bits. The wrong bet therefore costs 2.625 - 1.75 = 0.875 extra bits per
symbol, paid on every symbol for as long as the code is in use. Nothing is
broken in the tree: it is an optimal code for a source that is not the one
transmitting.

The overhead, symbol by symbol

Per symbol the wrong code is sometimes shorter than the right one: it
spends 1 bit on A where the ideal is 3, a 2-bit saving. The account
balances only after weighting each gap by how often p produces the symbol:

\sum_x p(x)\bigl[\ell_q(x) - \ell_p(x)\bigr]

The savings sit on symbols the source rarely emits; the penalties sit on the
symbols it emits constantly.

One code, two sources: the q-code's lengths (amber), the ideal lengths for p (blue), and the p-weighted gaps, summing to 0.875 extra bits per symbol.

Step through the three frames. In frame 2, check that each blue bar is the
symbol's surprisal under p (for D: -\log_2 \tfrac12 = 1). In frame 3,
recompute the tally by hand; the two savings and two penalties must combine
to +0.875, not 0.

Substituting \ell_q(x) = -\log_2 q(x) and \ell_p(x) = -\log_2 p(x) turns
each bracketed gap into a log-ratio:

\ell_q(x) - \ell_p(x) = \log_2 p(x) - \log_2 q(x) = \log_2 \frac{p(x)}{q(x)},

so the overhead is \sum_x p(x) \log_2 \tfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}: a quantity
computed from the two distributions alone, with no reference to any
particular tree.

The expected overhead of coding source p with the exact code for q is
\sum_x p(x) \log_2 \tfrac{p(x)}{q(x)} bits per symbol — determined by the
two distributions themselves, independent of the code that realizes the bet.

documents.title: The definition: an expectation of the log-ratio
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › KL divergence › The definition: an expectation of the log-ratio
documents.text:
The definition: an expectation of the log-ratio

The number just computed gets a name and a notation.

For probability distributions p and q on a finite set \mathcal{X}, the
KL divergence (relative entropy) of q from p is

D(p \,\|\, q) = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} p(x) \log_2 \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}

with the conventions 0 \log_2 \tfrac{0}{q} = 0 and, for p(x) > 0,
p(x) \log_2 \tfrac{p(x)}{0} = +\infty.

The quantity was introduced by
Kullback and Leibler (1951);
Cover & Thomas (§2.3) call it relative entropy. Term by term it is a
difference of surprisals (Surprisal): \log_2
\tfrac{p(x)}{q(x)} = \bigl(-\log_2 q(x)\bigr) - \bigl(-\log_2 p(x)\bigr),
the model's surprise at x minus the truth's, averaged under the truth.

The identity: cost = entropy + divergence

Splitting the definition's logarithm gives the accounting identity behind
the coding story:

\underbrace{\sum_x p(x) \log_2 \frac{1}{q(x)}}_{\text{cost of } q\text{'s code on } p}

The left side, the expected bits spent when events from p are coded with
q's code, is the cross-entropy H(p, q): the loss function of modern
classifiers, developed in Cross-entropy. Every coding
cost splits into the entropy floor, which no code avoids, plus the
divergence, which measures the bet's error.

The balanced-code example of The source coding theorem is
an instance: on the running source p = (.5, .25, .15, .1), the all-2-bit
code bets on the uniform q = (\tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14) and
pays H(p, q) = 2.000 bits against H(p) \approx 1.743: divergence
D(p\,\|\,q) \approx 0.257 bits.

The uniform model on the running source: cross-entropy 2.000 bits = entropy floor 1.743 + divergence 0.257.

Direction convention. In D(p \,\|\, q) the first argument is the
truth: it supplies the expectation weights, because reality decides how
often each symbol occurs. The second argument is the model: it supplies
the code. This lesson and the whole ML module keep that order — data first,
model second.

With \log_2 the divergence is in bits, matching the coding story. Machine
learning libraries compute with natural logarithms and report nats:
D_{\text{nats}} = D_{\text{bits}} \cdot \ln 2 \approx 0.693 \cdot
D_{\text{bits}}. The conversion is the same unit change as for surprisal
in Surprisal; only the constant differs from 1.

documents.title: Gibbs' inequality: the overhead is never negative
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › KL divergence › Gibbs' inequality: the overhead is never negative
documents.text:
Gibbs' inequality: the overhead is never negative

Individual terms of D(p\,\|\,q) go negative — the wrong code of the first
section saved 2 bits on every A. The sum cannot.
The source coding theorem proved this with the tangent
bound \ln t \le t - 1; the standard proof runs through
Jensen's inequality
and delivers the equality condition in one stroke.

For probability distributions p and q on a finite set,

D(p \,\|\, q) \ge 0,

with equality if and only if p = q.

If some x has p(x) > 0 = q(x), then D = +\infty and the inequality
holds strictly. Otherwise let S = \{x : p(x) > 0\} and consider the ratio
T = q(X)/p(X) for X \sim p. The function \log_2 is strictly concave,
so Jensen's inequality gives \mathbb{E}[\log_2 T] \le \log_2 \mathbb{E}[T]:

-D(p\,\|\,q)

Hence D(p\,\|\,q) \ge 0. Equality in Jensen for a strictly concave
function forces T constant on S: q(x) = c\,p(x) there. Equality in
the last step forces \sum_{x \in S} q(x) = 1, so c = 1 and q has no
mass outside S: q = p.

Gibbs via Jensen: the average of log₂(q/p) sits below the curve, and the curve value at the mean ratio is at most log₂ 1 = 0.

One inequality, many corollaries

Gibbs' inequality is the workhorse result of the course so far, in three
disguises:

The entropy floor. L = H(p) + D(p\,\|\,q) + \text{slack} \ge H(p):
the source coding theorem's converse used exactly this term
(The source coding theorem).

The uniform bound on entropy. Against the uniform u on n symbols,
D(p \,\|\, u) = \sum_x p(x)\log_2\bigl(n\,p(x)\bigr) = \log_2 n - H(p)
\ge 0: the bound H(p) \le \log_2 n of
Entropy, re-proved in one line. The
0.257 bits in the figure above is precisely \log_2 4 - 1.743.

Non-negative mutual information. I(X;Y) = D\bigl(p(x,y) \,\|\,
p(x)\,p(y)\bigr) \ge 0, the divergence form of
Mutual information: dependence is a coding overhead
relative to assuming independence.

The same one-line pattern powers the maximum entropy principle later in the
course (The maximum entropy principle).

D(p\,\|\,q) \ge 0 with equality only at q = p: coding with any wrong
distribution costs, every entropy bound in this course so far is this
statement in disguise, and a model's expected loss can never dip below the
data's entropy.

documents.title: Asymmetry: it matters which distribution is real
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › KL divergence › Asymmetry: it matters which distribution is real
documents.text:
Asymmetry: it matters which distribution is real

D(p\,\|\,q) and D(q\,\|\,p) answer different questions: which
distribution generates the data, and which one built the code. The two
numbers differ, in general substantially.

Let p = (0.99, 0.01) over \{\text{heads}, \text{tails}\} and let
q = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12) be the fair coin.

Forward, D(p\,\|\,q) — fair-coin code on 99/1 data. The terms:

0.99 \log_2 \frac{0.99}{0.5} = 0.99 \cdot 0.985 \approx 0.976, \qquad

so D(p\,\|\,q) \approx 0.976 - 0.056 = 0.919 bits. Coding check: the fair
code spends exactly 1 bit per flip, and
H(p) = 0.99 \cdot 0.0145 + 0.01 \cdot 6.644 \approx 0.081 bits, so the
overhead is 1 - 0.081 = 0.919 bits.

Reverse, D(q\,\|\,p) — 99/1 code on fair data. The terms:

0.5 \log_2 \frac{0.5}{0.99} = 0.5 \cdot (-0.985) \approx -0.493, \qquad

so D(q\,\|\,p) \approx 2.329 bits. Coding check: the ideal code for p
assigns -\log_2 0.99 \approx 0.0145 bits to heads and -\log_2 0.01
\approx 6.644 bits to tails (idealized fractional lengths, approachable by
block coding per The source coding theorem). Fair data hits
the 6.6-bit codeword half the time: cost
0.5 \cdot 0.0145 + 0.5 \cdot 6.644 \approx 3.329 bits per flip, against
H(q) = 1 bit: overhead 2.329 bits.

The directions differ by a factor of 2.5.

The asymmetry is structural, not a numerical accident. The expectation is
taken under the first argument: in D(p\,\|\,q) the badly-modeled
outcome (tails, log-ratio -5.6) occurs 1% of the time; in D(q\,\|\,p)
the badly-modeled outcome (tails again, now with log-ratio +5.6) occurs
50% of the time. Reality decides how often the model's errors are billed.

The same pair of distributions, both directions: 0.919 bits forward, 2.329 bits reverse. The expectation is taken under whichever distribution is real.

Not a metric: a divergence

D fails the symmetry axiom of a metric, and it fails the triangle
inequality too (exercise 5 constructs a counterexample). What survives is
D \ge 0 with D = 0 exactly at p = q: enough to serve as a penalty for
"how far the model is from the data", and the reason the standard term is
divergence rather than distance. Averaging the two directions does not
repair this; the symmetrized quantity (the Jensen–Shannon divergence) is a
different object, outside this course's scope.

Forward and reverse KL play distinct roles in machine learning. Fitting a
model by minimizing the forward direction D(p\,\|\,q) over q — which is
what maximum-likelihood training does, per
Cross-entropy — is mass-covering: wherever the data
puts mass, q must too, or the ratio p/q blows up. Minimizing the reverse
direction D(q\,\|\,p) over q, the choice of variational inference, is
mode-seeking: the expectation under q lets the model simply avoid
regions where p is small, so a unimodal q tends to lock onto one mode of
a multimodal p rather than spread across all of them. Bishop's
Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (§10.1.2) works out both
behaviors on a two-mode Gaussian. The coding story of this lesson is always
the forward direction: D(\text{data} \,\|\, \text{model}).

documents.title: Zeros in the model: the infinite penalty
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › KL divergence › Zeros in the model: the infinite penalty
documents.text:
Zeros in the model: the infinite penalty

The convention p \log_2 \tfrac{p}{0} = +\infty is not a technicality; it
is the definition working as intended. Take the running source
p = (.5, .25, .15, .1) and a model that rules out D entirely:
q = (.5, .3, .2, 0). The four terms of D(p\,\|\,q):

.5 \log_2 \tfrac{.5}{.5} = 0, \quad

Three terms are finite and even sum negative; the single zero swamps them
all: D(p\,\|\,q) = \infty.

The coding reading makes the infinity concrete. The ideal length for D
under the model is -\log_2 0 = \infty: the code for q reserves no
codeword for D, and the first D the source emits cannot be transmitted
at any finite length. No accuracy on the other three symbols compensates,
because no finite number of saved bits offsets an unencodable event.

One zero in the model: three finite terms (summing to −0.128 bits) and one infinite one. D(p‖q) = ∞.

The support condition. D(p\,\|\,q) is finite exactly when
q(x) = 0 implies p(x) = 0: the model's support must cover the data's.
The condition is directional, like the divergence itself: for the same pair
above, the reverse D(q\,\|\,p) \approx 0.162 bits is finite, because p
rules out nothing that q produces.

In practice this is why a language model's softmax never outputs an exact
zero, and why count-based models are smoothed: one occurring token with
model probability zero makes the log-loss, which
Cross-entropy identifies as a coding cost, infinite.

Load the perfect-model preset and verify D(p\,\|\,q) = 0 with
H(p,q) = H(p): Gibbs' equality case. Then drag one bar of q toward zero
while p keeps mass there and watch D grow without bound, and confirm
that H(p) never moves: the entropy is the data's property, the divergence
is the model's fault. Finish on the missing-outcome preset, the static
figure's disaster live.

p(x) > 0 with q(x) = 0 makes D(p\,\|\,q) = \infty: a model that
declares a real outcome impossible pays an unbounded coding penalty, and
finite divergence requires the model's support to cover the data's.

documents.title: Exercises
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › KL divergence › Exercises
documents.text:
Exercises

Let p = (\tfrac34, \tfrac14) and q = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12). Compute
D(p\,\|\,q) and D(q\,\|\,p) in bits, and convert D(p\,\|\,q) to nats.

Forward:
D(p\,\|\,q) = \tfrac34 \log_2 \tfrac{3/4}{1/2} + \tfrac14 \log_2
\tfrac{1/4}{1/2} = 0.75 \log_2 1.5 - 0.25 = 0.75 \cdot 0.585 - 0.25
\approx 0.189 bits.

Reverse:
D(q\,\|\,p) = \tfrac12 \log_2 \tfrac{1/2}{3/4} + \tfrac12 \log_2
\tfrac{1/2}{1/4} = 0.5 \cdot (-0.585) + 0.5 \cdot 1 \approx 0.208 bits.

The two directions differ, as expected. In nats:
0.189 \times \ln 2 \approx 0.189 \times 0.693 \approx 0.131 nats.

The exact code for q = (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18), lengths
(1, 2, 3, 3), is used on uniform data p = (\tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14,
\tfrac14). Compute the expected length L, the entropy H(p), and
D(p\,\|\,q) term by term, and verify L = H(p) + D(p\,\|\,q).

Expected length: L = \tfrac14 (1 + 2 + 3 + 3) = 2.25 bits. Entropy of the
uniform source: H(p) = \log_2 4 = 2 bits.

Divergence terms:
\tfrac14 \log_2 \tfrac{1/4}{1/2} = -0.25;
\tfrac14 \log_2 \tfrac{1/4}{1/4} = 0;
\tfrac14 \log_2 \tfrac{1/4}{1/8} = 0.25;
\tfrac14 \log_2 \tfrac{1/4}{1/8} = 0.25.
Sum: D(p\,\|\,q) = 0.25 bits.

Verification: H(p) + D(p\,\|\,q) = 2 + 0.25 = 2.25 = L. The code is
complete (Kraft sum 1), so there is no slack term.

For the first section's pair, p = (\tfrac18, \tfrac18, \tfrac14, \tfrac12)
and q = (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18), compute the reverse
direction D(q\,\|\,p) and compare it with D(p\,\|\,q) = 0.875. Explain
the result using the relabeling A \leftrightarrow D, B \leftrightarrow C.

Terms of D(q\,\|\,p):
\tfrac12 \log_2 \tfrac{1/2}{1/8} = \tfrac12 \cdot 2 = 1;
\tfrac14 \log_2 \tfrac{1/4}{1/8} = \tfrac14 \cdot 1 = 0.25;
\tfrac18 \log_2 \tfrac{1/8}{1/4} = -0.125;
\tfrac18 \log_2 \tfrac{1/8}{1/2} = -0.25.
Sum: D(q\,\|\,p) = 0.875 bits — equal to the forward direction.

This is a coincidence of the pair's symmetry, not a general law. The
permutation \sigma swapping A \leftrightarrow D and B \leftrightarrow
C maps p to q and q to p (q(x) = p(\sigma(x)) for every x),
and KL divergence is invariant under relabeling both arguments by the same
permutation, since the defining sum is merely reindexed. Hence
D(q\,\|\,p) = D(q \circ \sigma \,\|\, p \circ \sigma) = D(p\,\|\,q). The
99/1-versus-fair example admits no such relabeling, and its two directions
differ by a factor of 2.5.

Let p = (0.4, 0.4, 0.2) and q = (0.5, 0.5, 0). Compute D(p\,\|\,q)
and D(q\,\|\,p), and state the general condition for D(p\,\|\,q) to be
finite.

Forward: the third term is 0.2 \log_2 \tfrac{0.2}{0} = +\infty, so
D(p\,\|\,q) = \infty: the model rules out an outcome the data produces
with probability 0.2.

Reverse, using the convention 0 \log_2 \tfrac{0}{p} = 0:

D(q\,\|\,p) = 0.5 \log_2 \tfrac{0.5}{0.4} + 0.5 \log_2 \tfrac{0.5}{0.4}

D(p\,\|\,q) is finite exactly when q(x) = 0 implies p(x) = 0: the
model's support must cover the data's. The condition is directional, which
is why one direction is infinite and the other finite here.

Show that KL divergence violates the triangle inequality: for
p = (0.1, 0.9), q = (0.5, 0.5), r = (0.9, 0.1), compute
D(p\,\|\,q), D(q\,\|\,r), and D(p\,\|\,r), and compare
D(p\,\|\,r) with D(p\,\|\,q) + D(q\,\|\,r).

D(p\,\|\,q) = 0.1 \log_2 \tfrac{0.1}{0.5} + 0.9 \log_2 \tfrac{0.9}{0.5}
= 0.1 \cdot (-2.322) + 0.9 \cdot 0.848 \approx -0.232 + 0.763 = 0.531
bits.

D(q\,\|\,r) = 0.5 \log_2 \tfrac{0.5}{0.9} + 0.5 \log_2 \tfrac{0.5}{0.1}
= 0.5 \cdot (-0.848) + 0.5 \cdot 2.322 \approx 0.737 bits.

D(p\,\|\,r) = 0.1 \log_2 \tfrac{0.1}{0.9} + 0.9 \log_2 \tfrac{0.9}{0.1}
= 0.1 \cdot (-3.170) + 0.9 \cdot 3.170 = 0.8 \cdot 3.170 \approx 2.536
bits.

Triangle test: D(p\,\|\,q) + D(q\,\|\,r) \approx 0.531 + 0.737 = 1.268 <
2.536 \approx D(p\,\|\,r). Going "through" q would have to be at least
as expensive as going directly for a metric; here the direct divergence
exceeds the two-leg sum by a factor of two. With the symmetry failure of
the worked example, both metric axioms beyond non-negativity fail: D is a
divergence, not a distance.

Exercise 1 of Huffman coding built the Huffman code for
q = (0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1): lengths (1, 2, 3, 3), cost 1.9 bits. That
code is now used on data from p = (0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4) (same symbol
order, probabilities reversed). Compute the expected length L, the
implied distribution of the code, and D(p\,\|\,\hat q) against it, and
verify the decomposition L = H(p) + D(p\,\|\,\hat q) from
The source coding theorem. Use H(p) \approx 1.846
(entropy is invariant under relabeling).

Expected length:
L = 0.1 \cdot 1 + 0.2 \cdot 2 + 0.3 \cdot 3 + 0.4 \cdot 3
= 0.1 + 0.4 + 0.9 + 1.2 = 2.6 bits.

Implied distribution: lengths (1, 2, 3, 3) give
\hat q = (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18), Kraft sum 1
(complete, no slack).

Divergence terms:
0.1 \log_2 \tfrac{0.1}{0.5} = 0.1 \cdot (-2.322) \approx -0.232;
0.2 \log_2 \tfrac{0.2}{0.25} = 0.2 \cdot (-0.322) \approx -0.064;
0.3 \log_2 \tfrac{0.3}{0.125} = 0.3 \cdot 1.263 \approx 0.379;
0.4 \log_2 \tfrac{0.4}{0.125} = 0.4 \cdot 1.678 \approx 0.671.
Sum: D(p\,\|\,\hat q) \approx 0.754 bits.

Verification: H(p) + D \approx 1.846 + 0.754 = 2.600 = L. A Huffman code
is optimal only for the distribution it was built from; on the reversed
source it pays 0.754 bits per symbol of pure mismatch.

Fix a data distribution p. Using Gibbs' inequality, prove that over all
model distributions q, the expected coding cost
\sum_x p(x) \bigl(-\log_2 q(x)\bigr) is minimized uniquely at q = p.

By the cost identity,
\sum_x p(x)\bigl(-\log_2 q(x)\bigr) = H(p) + D(p\,\|\,q). The first term
does not depend on q; the second satisfies D(p\,\|\,q) \ge 0 with
equality if and only if q = p, by the information inequality. Hence the
cost is at least H(p) for every q, and equals H(p) only at q = p:
the truth is the unique optimal bet. This is the fact that makes
cross-entropy a sensible training loss: the minimizer over models is the
data distribution itself (Cross-entropy).

Let p_\varepsilon = (1 - \varepsilon, \varepsilon) and let
q = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12). Find the behavior of
D(p_\varepsilon\,\|\,q) and D(q\,\|\,p_\varepsilon) as
\varepsilon \to 0, evaluating both for \varepsilon = 10^{-6}, and
connect the answer to the support condition.

Forward: the fair code always spends exactly 1 bit, so
D(p_\varepsilon\,\|\,q) = 1 - H(p_\varepsilon). As \varepsilon \to 0,
H(p_\varepsilon) \to 0, so the divergence increases to 1 bit. At
\varepsilon = 10^{-6}: H \approx 10^{-6} \log_2 10^6 + 1.44 \times
10^{-6} \approx 2.1 \times 10^{-5}, giving D \approx 0.99998 bits.

Reverse:
D(q\,\|\,p_\varepsilon) = \tfrac12 \log_2 \tfrac{1/2}{1-\varepsilon} +
\tfrac12 \log_2 \tfrac{1/2}{\varepsilon} \approx -1 + \tfrac12 \log_2
\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}, which diverges to +\infty. At
\varepsilon = 10^{-6}: -1 + \tfrac12 \cdot 19.93 \approx 8.97 bits.

Interpretation: q has no zeros, so D(p_\varepsilon\,\|\,q) stays
bounded no matter how extreme p_\varepsilon becomes. In the reverse
direction the model p_\varepsilon sends its tails-probability toward
zero while the data q produces tails half the time: the missing-outcome
disaster approached continuously, with the divergence growing like
\tfrac12 \log_2 \tfrac{1}{\varepsilon} on the way to \infty.

S. Kullback, R. A. Leibler, "On Information and Sufficiency," Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 22(1), 1951 — the original paper defining the divergence. https://projecteuclid.org/journals/annals-of-mathematical-statistics/volume-22/issue-1/On-Information-and-Sufficiency/10.1214/aoms/1177729694.full

T. M. Cover, J. A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006 — §2.3 defines relative entropy with the 0 and \infty conventions; §2.6 proves the information inequality (Theorem 2.6.3) via Jensen; §5.4 gives the wrong-code cost H(p) + D(p\|q).

D. J. C. MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms, Cambridge University Press, 2003 — §2.6 defines relative entropy and states Gibbs' inequality; §2.7 covers Jensen's inequality, from which exercise 2.26 derives it. Free online: https://www.inference.org.uk/mackay/itila/

C. M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, Springer, 2006 — §1.6.1 introduces KL divergence in the ML setting; §10.1.2 contrasts the mode-seeking and mass-covering behavior of reverse and forward KL.

documents.title: Cross-entropy
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Cross-entropy
documents.text:
Cross-entropy decomposes as H(p,q) = H(p) + KL(p||q); minimizing
cross-entropy loss minimizes the divergence of the model from the data
distribution. This lesson identifies the training loss of probabilistic
classifiers and language models with the coding cost of
KL divergence and works out the consequences: the loss has a
floor the model cannot lower, the part the model controls is exactly
D(p\,\|\,q), and the unique minimizer is q = p. The route: the
single-example loss as the model's surprisal at the truth, cross-entropy as
its average, the decomposition into entropy plus divergence, the collapse to
negative log-likelihood under one-hot labels, and the unbounded penalty for
confident wrong predictions.

documents.title: The loss on one example: the model's surprisal at the truth
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Cross-entropy › The loss on one example: the model's surprisal at the truth
documents.text:
The loss on one example: the model's surprisal at the truth

A three-class image classifier ends its forward pass in a probability
distribution over labels. On one input it outputs q = (0.70,\ 0.20,\ 0.10)
over \{\text{cat}, \text{dog}, \text{fox}\}. The true label is then
revealed, and training charges the model for that one outcome: the log-loss
on the example is -\log_2 q(\text{truth}). Nothing else in q is billed.

The output is q = (0.70,\ 0.20,\ 0.10); the loss depends on which label is
true.

Truth = cat: -\log_2 0.70 \approx 0.51 bits. Confident and right: near
zero.

Truth = dog: -\log_2 0.20 \approx 2.32 bits.

Truth = fox: -\log_2 0.10 \approx 3.32 bits. The model rated the true
label least likely and pays the most.

The loss is small exactly when the model put high probability on what
happened; the probabilities assigned to the labels that did not occur enter
only through normalization.

The formula is not new. Surprisal defined the
surprisal of an event with probability p(x) as I(x) = -\log_2 p(x); the
log-loss is the same curve evaluated at the model's probability of the
observed outcome. The loss on one example is the model's surprisal at the
truth: how surprised q is that this label occurred.

One curve, two readings: surprisal −log₂ p(x) from lesson 1, and the log-loss −log₂ q(x_true) — the model's surprisal at the truth.

The log-loss on one example is -\log_2 q(x_{\text{true}}): the surprisal
the model assigns to the outcome that occurred. The model is billed by its
own probability for what actually happened.

documents.title: Cross-entropy: the expected log-loss under the truth
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Cross-entropy › Cross-entropy: the expected log-loss under the truth
documents.text:
Cross-entropy: the expected log-loss under the truth

One example gives one bill. Averaging the bill over the data distribution
gives the quantity that training actually minimizes.

The average appeared already in KL divergence: the expected
bits spent when events from p are coded with the exact code for q is
\sum_x p(x)(-\log_2 q(x)), and on the running source
p = (.5, .25, .15, .1) the uniform model q = (\tfrac14, \tfrac14,
\tfrac14, \tfrac14) pays 2.000 bits per symbol against the entropy
H(p) \approx 1.743. That expected cost gets the name.

For probability distributions p and q on a finite set \mathcal{X}, the
cross-entropy of q relative to p is

H(p, q) = -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} p(x) \log_2 q(x) \quad \text{bits,}

the expected surprisal under the model q when outcomes are drawn from p.

Three immediate readings of the same sum:

Coding: the expected codeword length when p-data is coded with q's
code (KL divergence).

Learning: the expected log-loss of model q on examples drawn from
the data distribution p.

Sanity check: H(p, p) = -\sum_x p(x)\log_2 p(x) = H(p): a model that
matches the truth pays exactly the entropy.

Direction convention. Cross-entropy is not symmetric:
H(p, q) \ne H(q, p) in general, because the first argument supplies the
expectation weights and the second supplies the surprisals. The loss is
always H(\text{data}, \text{model}) — data first, model second, the same
order as D(p\,\|\,q) in KL divergence. Exercise 6
computes both directions on a concrete pair.

documents.title: The decomposition: entropy floor plus divergence
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Cross-entropy › The decomposition: entropy floor plus divergence
documents.text:
The decomposition: entropy floor plus divergence

The gap between the uniform model's 2.000 bits and the floor 1.743 was
computed in KL divergence to be D(p\,\|\,q) = 0.257 bits.
That accounting is fully general, and it is the lesson's headline identity.

For probability distributions p and q on a finite set,

H(p, q) = H(p) + D(p \,\|\, q).

Split the logarithm inside the definition:
\log_2 \tfrac{1}{q(x)} = \log_2 \tfrac{1}{p(x)} + \log_2
\tfrac{p(x)}{q(x)} for every x with p(x) > 0. Multiplying by p(x) and
summing,

-\sum_x p(x) \log_2 q(x)

with the conventions of KL divergence covering p(x) = 0
terms (they contribute 0 to every sum) and q(x) = 0 terms (both sides
are +\infty).

The decomposition dissected: cross-entropy = entropy floor + divergence. Only the divergence term depends on the model.

The minimizer: training targets the divergence

The two terms have different owners. H(p) is a property of the data
distribution alone; no choice of q moves it. D(p\,\|\,q) is the model's
mismatch, and Gibbs' inequality (KL divergence) states
D(p\,\|\,q) \ge 0 with equality if and only if q = p. Therefore

\argmin_q H(p, q) = \argmin_q D(p \,\|\, q) = p :

minimizing cross-entropy over models and minimizing model–data divergence
are the same optimization, and its unique solution is the data
distribution itself. A model trained to convergence on cross-entropy loss is
being pushed, in bits, toward q = p.

H(p) does not depend on the model, so minimizing cross-entropy minimizes
D(p\,\|\,q), and the unique minimizer is q = p: cross-entropy training
is divergence minimization under another name.

Training drives q toward p: each step shrinks D(p‖q) while the entropy floor H(p) stays fixed. At q = p the loss equals the entropy.

Step through the four frames and check one number per frame: subtract the
fixed floor 1.743 from the H(p,q) readout and confirm the amber segment
is exactly the difference — 0.257, 0.095, 0.011, then 0. The floor
never moves; only the model's excess shrinks.

The floor is not zero: reading a loss value

A common misreading: "the loss is 0.9, so the model is still wrong."
Whether 0.9 is bad depends entirely on H(p), and H(p) > 0 whenever the
labels carry genuine randomness.

Concrete case: a binary task where annotators genuinely disagree, with
soft label p = (0.7, 0.3) on some input. The hedging model
q = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12) pays H(p,q) = 1.000 bit. The perfect model
q = p still pays H(p) = 0.7 \log_2 \tfrac{1}{0.7} + 0.3 \log_2
\tfrac{1}{0.3} \approx 0.881 bits. Only 0.119 of the hedger's bill was
its own fault; the remaining 0.881 bits are the label noise, and no model
recovers them. A loss above zero is not evidence of a bad model — the
model's true score is the distance above the floor, D(p\,\|\,q), not the
loss itself.

Sometimes the floor is raised on purpose. Label smoothing (Szegedy et al.,
"Rethinking the Inception Architecture",
2016) replaces the one-hot target (1, 0, \ldots, 0) with the softened
(1-\varepsilon, \tfrac{\varepsilon}{k-1}, \ldots), deliberately making
H(p) > 0. The decomposition explains both effects at once: the achievable
loss floor rises from 0 to H(p_{\text{smooth}}), and the minimizer moves
from the point mass to the smoothed target, so the model is no longer pushed
toward infinite logits on the true class. The identity, not the training
loop, is what changed.

documents.title: One-hot labels: cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Cross-entropy › One-hot labels: cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood
documents.text:
One-hot labels: cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood

Classification datasets rarely ship soft labels. The recorded target is a
single class c, encoded as the point mass p = (0, \ldots, 1, \ldots, 0)
with the 1 at position c. The general sum then collapses: every term with
p(x) = 0 vanishes, leaving

H(p, q) = -\log_2 q(c),

the plain log-loss of the first section. The decomposition sharpens
accordingly: a point mass is the certain distribution, so H(p) = 0
(Entropy), and

H(p, q) = D(p \,\|\, q) :

for hard labels the cross-entropy is the divergence. There is no floor,
the minimum loss is 0, and it is reached only at q(c) = 1.

Hardening the label to one-hot sets H(p) = 0: the loss loses its floor and equals D(p‖q) = −log₂ q(true class).

Over a dataset: minimizing the loss is maximizing likelihood

Training averages the per-example loss over a dataset x_1, \ldots, x_N:

\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \bigl(-\log_2 q(x_i)\bigr)

where \hat{p}(x) is the empirical distribution, the fraction of the
dataset equal to x. The training objective is literally a cross-entropy,
with the empirical distribution in the data slot. The same sum is
-\tfrac{1}{N}\log_2 \prod_i q(x_i): minimizing the average log-loss is
maximizing the likelihood \prod_i q(x_i) of the dataset. Cross-entropy
minimization, KL minimization, and maximum-likelihood estimation are one
procedure in three vocabularies.

Two implementation facts. Libraries compute the loss with natural
logarithms, so reported values are in nats: multiply by
1/\ln 2 \approx 1.443 to get bits, the same unit change as in
Surprisal. And when q is produced by a softmax
layer with logits z, the gradient of the (natural-log) loss on a one-hot
target p is \partial \mathcal{L} / \partial z_j = q_j - p_j — prediction
minus target, derived in Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning,
§4.3.4. The clean form is one reason softmax and cross-entropy are paired.

For one-hot labels, H(p) = 0 and the cross-entropy equals both
D(p\,\|\,q) and the negative log-likelihood -\log_2 q(\text{true
class}): the three standard descriptions of the classification loss are
the same number.

documents.title: Confident and wrong: the blowup
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Cross-entropy › Confident and wrong: the blowup
documents.text:
Confident and wrong: the blowup

The log in the loss is gentle near q(\text{true}) = 1 and violent near
0. The same table that priced rare events in
Surprisal now prices predictions.

Per-example loss -\log_2 q(\text{true}) as the model's probability on the
truth falls:

q(\text{true})

loss (bits)

0.9

0.152

0.5

1

0.1

3.32

0.01

6.64

10^{-6}

19.9

The scale is logarithmic in both directions. Being right confidently is
cheap: 131 predictions at q(\text{true}) = 0.9 cost about as much as
one prediction at q(\text{true}) = 10^{-6}
(131 \times 0.152 \approx 19.9). A model that is nearly always confidently
right and once confidently wrong can lose, on average, to a model that
merely hedges — exercise 5 runs the numbers.

The loss −log₂ q(true): flat where the model is confidently right, unbounded where it is confidently wrong. At q(true) = 0 the loss is infinite.

Read one point off the curve: find where the loss crosses 10 bits and
verify it sits at q(\text{true}) = 2^{-10} \approx 0.001. Each further
halving of the model's probability on the truth adds exactly one bit of
loss.

The endpoint q(\text{true}) = 0 is the missing-outcome disaster of
KL divergence arriving in training: a model that assigns an
occurring outcome probability zero takes an infinite loss on that single
example, and no accuracy elsewhere compensates. This is why a softmax never
emits an exact zero and why count-based language models are smoothed — the
support condition of the previous lesson, enforced by the loss itself on
every gradient step.

The loss on one example is unbounded as q(\text{true}) \to 0:
overconfidence on a wrong prediction is punished by the same logarithm that
makes rare events highly surprising, and an exact zero on a real outcome
costs \infty.

documents.title: Exercises
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Cross-entropy › Exercises
documents.text:
Exercises

Let p = (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18) and let q be uniform on
the four symbols. Compute H(p, q), H(p), and D(p\,\|\,q) term by term,
and verify the decomposition H(p,q) = H(p) + D(p\,\|\,q).

Cross-entropy: every symbol has -\log_2 q(x) = \log_2 4 = 2 bits, so
H(p, q) = 2 \sum_x p(x) = 2.000 bits regardless of p.

Entropy: H(p) = \tfrac12 \cdot 1 + \tfrac14 \cdot 2 + \tfrac18 \cdot 3 +
\tfrac18 \cdot 3 = 1.75 bits.

Divergence terms:
\tfrac12 \log_2 \tfrac{1/2}{1/4} = 0.5;
\tfrac14 \log_2 \tfrac{1/4}{1/4} = 0;
\tfrac18 \log_2 \tfrac{1/8}{1/4} = -0.125, twice.
Sum: D(p\,\|\,q) = 0.5 + 0 - 0.25 = 0.25 bits.

Verification: H(p) + D(p\,\|\,q) = 1.75 + 0.25 = 2.000 = H(p,q).

A classifier outputs q = (0.7, 0.2, 0.1) over three classes. Compute the
log-loss in bits for each possible true class, then convert the three values
to nats.

Bits: -\log_2 0.7 \approx 0.515; -\log_2 0.2 \approx 2.322;
-\log_2 0.1 \approx 3.322.

Nats (multiply by \ln 2 \approx 0.693, or compute -\ln q directly):
-\ln 0.7 \approx 0.357; -\ln 0.2 \approx 1.609;
-\ln 0.1 \approx 2.303.

Check on the first value: 0.515 \times 0.693 \approx 0.357 nats.

A dataset x_1, \ldots, x_N has empirical distribution
\hat{p}(x) = \tfrac{1}{N}\,\#\{i : x_i = x\}. Show that the average
log-loss \tfrac{1}{N} \sum_i (-\log_2 q(x_i)) equals H(\hat{p}, q), and
conclude that minimizing it over q is equivalent to maximizing the
likelihood \prod_i q(x_i).

Group the sum by distinct values: each x appears N \hat{p}(x) times, so

\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \bigl(-\log_2 q(x_i)\bigr)

For the likelihood: -\log_2 \prod_i q(x_i) = \sum_i (-\log_2 q(x_i)) =
N \cdot H(\hat{p}, q). Since -\log_2 is strictly decreasing and N is a
positive constant, minimizing H(\hat{p}, q) over q and maximizing
\prod_i q(x_i) over q have identical solutions: cross-entropy
minimization is maximum-likelihood estimation.

On a binary task, human annotators genuinely disagree on some input: the
soft label is p = (0.8, 0.2). State the smallest cross-entropy loss any
model can achieve on this input, name the model that achieves it, and
explain why a reported loss of 0.75 bits here would signal a nearly
optimal model rather than a poor one.

By the decomposition, H(p, q) = H(p) + D(p\,\|\,q) \ge H(p) with equality
iff q = p. The floor is

H(p) = 0.8 \log_2 \tfrac{1}{0.8} + 0.2 \log_2 \tfrac{1}{0.2}

achieved by the model q = (0.8, 0.2) that reports the annotator
distribution exactly. A loss of 0.75 bits is only
0.75 - 0.722 = 0.028 bits of divergence above the irreducible label
noise: the model is nearly perfect. Loss values are meaningful only
relative to H(p), which is zero exclusively for deterministic (one-hot)
labels.

Two models process the same 10 test examples with one-hot labels. Model A
assigns probability 0.9 to the true class on 9 examples and 10^{-6} on
the remaining one. Model B assigns 0.6 to the true class on all 10.
Compute each model's average loss in bits and compare.

Model A: nine examples cost -\log_2 0.9 \approx 0.152 bits each, the
tenth costs -\log_2 10^{-6} = 6 \log_2 10 \approx 19.93 bits. Average:
(9 \times 0.152 + 19.93)/10 \approx (1.37 + 19.93)/10 \approx 2.13 bits.

Model B: every example costs -\log_2 0.6 \approx 0.737 bits. Average:
0.737 bits.

Model B wins by a factor of almost three, although Model A is confidently
correct 90\% of the time: the single confident miss contributes 19.93
bits, more than 14 times the total cost of Model A's nine successes. The
log-loss average is dominated by the worst confident error, which is exactly
the incentive it is designed to create.

Let p = (0.9, 0.1) and q = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12). Compute both
directions H(p, q) and H(q, p), and state which one is the training
loss when the data is 90/10 and the model hedges fair.

Forward: H(p, q) = 0.9 \cdot (-\log_2 0.5) + 0.1 \cdot (-\log_2 0.5) = 1
bit: the fair-coin code spends exactly one bit whatever happens.

Reverse: H(q, p) = 0.5 \cdot (-\log_2 0.9) + 0.5 \cdot (-\log_2 0.1)
= 0.5 \cdot 0.152 + 0.5 \cdot 3.322 \approx 1.737 bits.

The two differ: cross-entropy is not symmetric. The training loss is
H(\text{data}, \text{model}) = H(p, q) = 1 bit: the data distribution
supplies the expectation weights (reality decides how often each label
occurs), the model supplies the surprisals.

A character-level language model achieves a cross-entropy of 1.2 bits per
character on a 10^6-character test text. Using the code-length reading of
cross-entropy from The source coding theorem, compute the
size in bytes to which the model could losslessly compress the text, and
compare with the 8 bits per character of raw ASCII. Given the estimate
from Entropy of English text that English carries roughly 1 bit
per letter, bound the part of the model's rate that is mismatch rather than
irreducible content.

Coding at the model's cross-entropy costs 1.2 \times 10^6 bits total,
i.e. 1.2 \times 10^6 / 8 = 150{,}000 bytes, against 10^6 bytes for
ASCII: a 6.7{:}1 compression ratio.

With the entropy rate of English near 1 bit per character, the floor for
this text is about 10^6 bits = 125{,}000 bytes. The model's excess is
about 1.2 - 1.0 = 0.2 bits per character: its divergence from the true
text distribution, roughly 17\% of its rate. The next lesson
(Compression as prediction) makes the model-to-compressor
construction explicit.

A forecaster privately believes the outcome distribution is p but reports
a distribution r, and is penalized -\log_2 r(x) when outcome x occurs.
Using Gibbs' inequality from KL divergence, prove that the
expected penalty is uniquely minimized by reporting r = p.

The expected penalty under the forecaster's belief is

\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p}\bigl[-\log_2 r(x)\bigr] = H(p, r) = H(p) +

H(p) is fixed by the belief, and Gibbs' inequality gives
D(p\,\|\,r) \ge 0 with equality if and only if r = p. The expected
penalty is therefore at least H(p), with the minimum attained exactly at
the honest report r = p. The log penalty is a strictly proper scoring
rule: it makes truthful reporting of probabilities the unique optimal
strategy, which is the decision-theoretic face of using cross-entropy as a
training loss.

T. M. Cover, J. A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006 — §5.4 derives the wrong-code cost H(p) + D(p\|q) (the decomposition, Theorem 5.4.3); §2.6 proves the information inequality D \ge 0 used for the minimizer.

D. J. C. MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms, Cambridge University Press, 2003 — §2.6 relates entropy and relative entropy; ch. 6 (stream codes) turns a predictive distribution into an actual code, the operational reading of the log-loss. Free online: https://www.inference.org.uk/mackay/itila/

C. M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, Springer, 2006 — §4.3.4 derives the softmax cross-entropy gradient q - p for multiclass logistic regression.

G. Delétang, A. Ruoss, et al., "Language Modeling Is Compression," ICLR 2024 — §2 states the identity between a model's expected log-loss on data and its coding cost, framing log-loss training as compression. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.10668

I. J. Good, "Rational Decisions," Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B, 14(1), 1952 — the logarithmic scoring rule and its properness, background for exercise 8.

documents.title: Compression as prediction
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Compression as prediction
documents.text:
A predictive model defines a compressor and a compressor defines a
predictive model; cross-entropy on a stream equals achievable compressed
size in bits. This lesson establishes both directions of that equivalence
and its accounting. The route: arithmetic coding turns next-symbol
probabilities into a code whose total length is the model's log-loss plus
two bits; the Kraft budget read backwards turns any lossless coder into a
probability model; the expected cost per symbol decomposes as entropy rate
plus divergence; one string coded under three models makes the sizes
concrete; and the measurements of
Delétang et al. (2023) show a language
model outcompressing PNG and FLAC on data it was never trained on.

documents.title: From model to code: arithmetic coding spends the surprisal
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Compression as prediction › From model to code: arithmetic coding spends the surprisal
documents.text:
From model to code: arithmetic coding spends the surprisal

The flaw to fix: symbol codes pay their rounding per symbol

Huffman coding builds the optimal symbol code, and its
guarantee H \le L^* < H + 1 leaves up to one wasted bit on every
symbol: the 90/10 coin of The source coding theorem has
H \approx 0.469 bits but no symbol code beats 1 bit per flip. Block
coding shrinks the waste to 1/n, at the price of building 2^n
codewords per block.

Both fixes share a second, worse limitation: a code table serves one
fixed distribution. The models that matter here are conditional. A
predictor of English emits a fresh distribution q(x_t \mid x_{<t}) at
every position, one per context; a Huffman table per context is a table
per prefix of the text. What is needed: a coder that accepts an arbitrary
distribution at each step and charges the symbol its surprisal under that
step's distribution. How: arithmetic coding, the stream code of
MacKay's chapter 6.

One stream, coded by intervals

The coder maintains an interval [\ell, r) \subseteq [0, 1), initially
[0,1). At each step the model supplies a distribution over the next
symbol; the coder partitions the current interval into subintervals with
widths proportional to those probabilities (in a fixed symbol order)
and keeps the subinterval of the symbol that actually occurred. No bits
are emitted along the way; the interval is the state.

Concrete run: alphabet \{A, B\}, stream AAB, model
q(A) = 0.8 at the first position, q(A \mid A) = 0.8,
q(B \mid AA) = 0.2.

Step 1, A: [0, 1) \to [0, 0.8). Width 0.8.

Step 2, A: [0, 0.8) \to [0, 0.64). Width 0.8 \times 0.8.

Step 3, B: the top 0.2 fraction of [0, 0.64), which is
[0.512,\ 0.64). Width 0.128.

The final width is the product of the conditional probabilities,
0.8 \times 0.8 \times 0.2 = 0.128 = q(AAB), so its negative log is the
sum of the surprisals: -\log_2 0.128 \approx 2.97 bits. To transmit the
stream, the coder sends a binary fraction that pins down a dyadic
interval inside [0.512, 0.64): four bits, 1001, naming
[0.5625, 0.625), suffice.

Arithmetic coding of AAB: each symbol keeps a slice proportional to its conditional probability. Final width = q(AAB) = 0.128, so ≈ 2.97 bits, and 4 emitted bits cover it.

Step through the five frames and track the width: 1 \to 0.8 \to 0.64 \to
0.128, each step multiplying by the probability of the symbol taken.
Check the counter against the widths: -\log_2 0.64 = 0.64 and
-\log_2 0.128 \approx 2.97; the last symbol alone, at probability
0.2, contributes 2.32 of the 2.97 bits.

Decoding is the same walk run by the receiver: it holds the transmitted
number, runs the same model, subdivides [0,1) identically, and reads
off which subinterval contains the number: that is symbol 1, which fixes
the context for the model's next distribution, and so on. The model is
consulted, never transmitted; both ends must hold an identical copy.

The guarantee: two bits of overhead, total

Let q assign every symbol a positive conditional probability
q(x_t \mid x_{<t}), and let x_{1:n} be any stream. The arithmetic
coder driven by q emits a decodable binary string of length

\text{len}(x_{1:n}) \;\le\; -\log_2 q(x_{1:n}) + 2

The final interval has width w = \prod_t q(x_t \mid x_{<t}) =
q(x_{1:n}), since each step scales the width by one conditional
probability. Choose k = \lceil -\log_2 w \rceil + 1, so that
2^{-k} \le w/2. The dyadic cells [m2^{-k}, (m+1)2^{-k}) tile [0,1),
and an interval of width w \ge 2 \cdot 2^{-k} contains at least one
complete cell; transmit the k bits of that cell's left endpoint. Then
k < -\log_2 w + 2. Decodability: the cell lies inside the final
interval, hence inside every ancestor interval of the walk, so the
receiver's replayed subdivision identifies each symbol in turn.
Termination (knowing when n symbols have been read) is handled by
transmitting the length separately or reserving an end-of-stream symbol;
MacKay §6.2 uses the latter, and the cost stays O(1) plus one symbol's
surprisal.

The right-hand side is the model's log-loss on the stream: the sum of
the surprisals q assigns to each symbol in context, exactly the
quantity that Cross-entropy identified as the
training objective of a language model. The two extra bits are paid once
per stream, not per symbol; on a megabyte of text they are noise. This is
the repair of Huffman's flaw: the interval carries fractional bits across
symbols, so nothing is rounded until the very end.

A predictor plus an arithmetic coder is a lossless compressor whose file
size is the predictor's log-loss on the stream plus at most two bits:
cross-entropy is not analogous to a compressed size, it is one.

documents.title: From code to model: every compressor carries a probability model
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Compression as prediction › From code to model: every compressor carries a probability model
documents.text:
From code to model: every compressor carries a probability model

The reverse direction needs no new machinery.
The source coding theorem defined the implied
distribution of a code: lengths \ell(x) obeying the Kraft budget of
The Kraft inequality yield
q(x) = 2^{-\ell(x)} / c with c = \sum_x 2^{-\ell(x)} \le 1. The same
reading applies to a whole compressor. Fix an input length n; a lossless
compressor assigns each of the |\mathcal{X}|^n possible files a distinct
decodable output, so its lengths satisfy the budget (McMillan), and

q_C(x_{1:n}) \;\propto\; 2^{-\ell_C(x_{1:n})}

is a probability distribution over files. Files the compressor shrinks
well are exactly the files its implied model rates probable; picking the
shortest-encoding reconstruction is maximum-probability prediction.

The implied model even predicts next symbols. The extra bits the
compressor spends to append symbol a to a context x,
\Delta(a) = \ell_C(xa) - \ell_C(x), convert to conditional
probabilities:

q_C(a \mid x) \;\propto\; 2^{-\Delta(a)} :

continuations that compress well are continuations the compressor
expects. Delétang et al. run this
construction on gzip: querying \ell_{\text{gzip}}(xa) for every
candidate byte a turns gzip into a (weak) generative sequence model,
sampled from like any language model.

The equivalence, both ways: arithmetic coding maps a predictor to a compressor; the Kraft budget maps a compressor back to a predictor. One object, two interfaces.

Every lossless compressor is a probability model spending its Kraft
budget: q_C(x) \propto 2^{-\ell_C(x)}, with next-symbol predictions
q_C(a \mid x) \propto 2^{-[\ell_C(xa) - \ell_C(x)]}. There is no
model-free compression.

documents.title: The accounting: bits per symbol = entropy rate + divergence
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Compression as prediction › The accounting: bits per symbol = entropy rate + divergence
documents.text:
The accounting: bits per symbol = entropy rate + divergence

The two directions fix what a compressor is; the course's earlier
results fix what it costs. For an i.i.d. source p coded at the
model's surprisals, the expected bits per symbol are the cross-entropy,
and Cross-entropy decomposed it:

H(p, q) \;=\; H(p) \;+\; D(p \,\|\, q),

the entropy floor of The source coding theorem plus the
mismatch cost of KL divergence. For a stationary source
with memory, English being the standing example, the floor is the
entropy rate of Entropy of English text: the per-symbol
cost of a model with unlimited context. The per-symbol account of any
model-driven compressor is therefore

\underbrace{\text{bits per symbol}}_{\text{file size} / n}

Every term has an owner. The entropy rate belongs to the source; no
compressor moves it. The divergence belongs to the model, is zero only
for a perfect model, and is exactly what training on log-loss shrinks.
The overhead belongs to the coder and vanishes with stream length.

A 1.2-bits/char model on a ≈1.0-bit/char source: the file size per character is the floor plus the model's divergence. Only the divergence is improvable.

Concrete numbers, carried over from exercise 7 of
Cross-entropy: a character-level model at 1.2
bits/char compresses a 10^6-character text to 150{,}000 bytes against
10^6 bytes of ASCII, and with English's entropy rate near 1 bit/char,
about 0.2 bits of its rate is divergence: the model's own mismatch,
the only part a better model removes.

Compressed size per symbol = entropy rate + divergence rate + O(1/n):
the floor is the source's, the mismatch is the model's, and "better
predictor" and "better compressor" name the same reduction of the same
middle term.

documents.title: Better model, smaller file: three models on one string
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Compression as prediction › Better model, smaller file: three models on one string
documents.text:
Better model, smaller file: three models on one string

Code the 7-character string banana_ (_ marks a trailing space) over
the alphabet \{a, b, n, \_\}, charging each character
-\log_2 q(\cdot) under three models. Counts are taken from the string
itself; the cost of shipping those counts is deferred to the next
section.

Model 1, uniform: q = \tfrac14 per character, 2 bits each.
Total: 7 \times 2 = 14 bits.

Model 2, letter frequencies: counts (a{:}3,\ n{:}2,\ b{:}1,\
\_{:}1) give q = (\tfrac37, \tfrac27, \tfrac17, \tfrac17).
Per-character surprisals: \log_2 \tfrac73 \approx 1.222 for each a,
\log_2 \tfrac72 \approx 1.807 for each n, \log_2 7 \approx 2.807
for b and for \_. Total:
3(1.222) + 2(1.807) + 2(2.807) = 3.667 + 3.615 + 5.615 \approx 12.90
bits.

Model 3, bigram: first character from the frequency model, every
later character from counts of what follows its predecessor. In
banana_: b is always followed by a, n always by a,
and a by n twice and \_ once, so q(a \mid b) = 1,
q(a \mid n) = 1, q(n \mid a) = \tfrac23,
q(\_ \mid a) = \tfrac13. The seven charges:

Total: \approx 5.56 bits. The arithmetic coder realizes each total
within two bits: files of roughly 16, 15, and 8 bits for the same

Entropy of English text: after b or n the next character
is certain and costs nothing.

The same ladder holds for English at scale, with the canonical
per-character costs established earlier in the course: 8 bits for a raw
ASCII byte, 4.76 for a fixed-width 27-symbol code, about 4.0 under
letter frequencies, 3.3 with one letter of context, and an entropy rate
near 1 as the floor no model beats.

Bits per character of English under progressively better models, descending toward the ≈1-bit entropy rate. Each bar is a file size; the guide is the floor.

Type an English sentence and switch models: bits/char should fall from
8 to near 4 to near 3.5, and the total size with it. Then load the
repeated-character preset: the bigram model's bits/char collapses toward
0, since every symbol is predicted almost surely. Then mash the
keyboard: the three models nearly tie near 8, the signature of a
source with no structure for a model to bet on.

documents.title: Fine print: the model rides on both ends
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Compression as prediction › Fine print: the model rides on both ends
documents.text:
Fine print: the model rides on both ends

The model must be shared. Decoding replays the encoder's model
step by step, so the equivalence prices the coding cost given the
model. An honest total either fixes the same model on both ends in
advance (a pretrained language model both parties already hold, its cost
amortized over everything it will ever compress) or adds the bits to
describe the model itself: a two-part code, model bits plus data bits.
The banana example's model 3 quietly cheated on this account: its
bigram counts came from the string being coded. Making the two-part
accounting the object of study is
Minimum description length; exercise 6 runs the
break-even arithmetic for a shipped model.

Lossless only. The identity ties prediction to lossless coding.
JPEG and learned image codecs discard information and are governed by a
different trade-off, rate versus distortion, treated in
Rate-distortion theory; nothing in this lesson bounds them.

Units. Training frameworks report log-loss in nats. One nat is
1/\ln 2 \approx 1.443 bits (Surprisal): a model
at 0.8 nats/token is a compressor at 1.15 bits/token, the same
number in the coding unit.

Achievable, not automatic. The theorem bounds the coding cost of the
model's probabilities. A production compressor adds headers, containers,
and speed-motivated approximations, and a weak built-in model besides:
gzip's window-limited matching corresponds to a predictor with a few
kilobytes of memory. The claim "better predictor = better compressor" is
exact for the achievable size, and only approximate for any named tool.

The predict-then-code split is standard engineering, not a theoretical
curiosity. Video coding's CABAC (H.264/H.265) is a context-adaptive
binary arithmetic coder; zstd's entropy stage uses ANS, a
faster relative of arithmetic coding; the PAQ family and
Bellard's NNCP drive arithmetic coders with
context-mixing and neural sequence models and top the
Large Text Compression Benchmark.
The Hutter Prize pays for lossless
compression of a 1 GB Wikipedia extract on exactly the premise of this
lesson: better compression of text is better modeling of it.

documents.title: The measurement: a language model outcompresses PNG and FLAC
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Compression as prediction › The measurement: a language model outcompresses PNG and FLAC
documents.text:
The measurement: a language model outcompresses PNG and FLAC

Delétang et al., "Language Modeling Is Compression"
(ICLR 2024) executes the model-to-compressor direction literally:
Chinchilla 70B, a language model trained almost entirely on text, drives
an arithmetic coder over 2048-byte chunks of data it was never trained
on. Measured compressed sizes, as a fraction of raw size: 43.4% on
ImageNet image patches, against 58.5% for PNG; 16.4% on LibriSpeech
audio, against 30.3% for FLAC. A text model, used as a bettor on raw
bytes, beats the domain-specific compressors on their own data.

The same paper prices the fine print: those figures charge nothing for
the 70-billion-parameter model on both ends. Under an adjusted
compression rate that adds the model's own description length, the large
models stop winning on datasets of this size, exactly the two-part
accounting that Minimum description length develops.

Read as evaluation rather than engineering, the construction gives a
clean instrument: compression ratio on held-out bytes is a label-free,
task-free measure of predictive quality, the guessing game of
Entropy of English text with the human replaced by the model
and the score settled in bits. A lower loss is a smaller file; there is
nothing else in the number.

documents.title: The course in one line
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Compression as prediction › The course in one line
documents.text:
The course in one line
