The equivalence closes the arc the course has been building. Surprisal
prices one event (Surprisal); entropy averages it
and floors lossless description
(The source coding theorem); the Kraft budget makes
code lengths and probabilities interchangeable
(The Kraft inequality); KL divergence prices betting on the
wrong distribution (KL divergence); cross-entropy is
that price as a training loss (Cross-entropy); and
arithmetic coding cashes the loss out as a file. What no compressor can
do is beat the floor, and how far even the shortest-program ideal sits
out of reach is next, in Kolmogorov complexity.

The course to this point as one spine: entropy sets the floor, codes spend the Kraft budget, KL prices mismatch, cross-entropy trains against it, compression collects it as a file.

Entropy sets the floor, the Kraft budget makes lengths bets, KL prices
the mismatch, and cross-entropy is the coding cost: a predictive model's
loss on a stream is its achievable compressed size, so training a
language model is running a compression objective at scale.

documents.title: Exercises
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Compression as prediction › Exercises
documents.text:
Exercises

Code the 5-character string noon_ (_ marks a trailing space) over
\{n, o, \_\}, as in the worked example: compute the total bits
under (a) the uniform model, (b) the letter-frequency model with counts
taken from the string, and (c) the bigram model (first character from
letter frequencies, later characters from the string's bigram counts).
Use \log_2 3 \approx 1.585, \log_2 5 \approx 2.322,
\log_2 \tfrac52 \approx 1.322.

(a) Uniform: \log_2 3 \approx 1.585 bits per character;
5 \times 1.585 \approx 7.92 bits.

(b) Counts (n{:}2,\ o{:}2,\ \_{:}1), so
q = (\tfrac25, \tfrac25, \tfrac15). Total:
2 \log_2 \tfrac52 + 2\log_2 \tfrac52 + \log_2 5
= 4(1.322) + 2.322 \approx 7.61 bits.

(c) Bigrams in noon_: n is followed by o (position 1)
and \_ (position 4), so q(o \mid n) = q(\_ \mid n) =
\tfrac12; o is followed by o and n once each, so
q(o \mid o) = q(n \mid o) = \tfrac12. Charges: n from frequencies,
\log_2 \tfrac52 \approx 1.322; then o \mid n, o \mid o,
n \mid o, \_ \mid n at 1 bit each. Total:
1.322 + 4 \approx 5.32 bits.

The ladder 7.92 \to 7.61 \to 5.32 mirrors the worked example: the
frequency model gains little (the counts are nearly uniform), the
context model gains a third, and an arithmetic coder realizes each
total within 2 bits.

A memoryless model on \{H, T\} assigns q(H) = 0.9, q(T) = 0.1 at
every step. For the stream HHT: compute the arithmetic coder's
interval after each symbol (subintervals ordered H before T), verify
that the final width equals q(HHT), bound the codeword length with the
theorem, and exhibit an actual dyadic interval and codeword.

Intervals: H: [0, 0.9); H: [0, 0.81); T: the top 0.1
fraction of [0, 0.81), i.e. [0.729,\ 0.81). Width:
0.81 - 0.729 = 0.081 = 0.9 \times 0.9 \times 0.1 = q(HHT).

Length bound: -\log_2 0.081 \approx 3.63, so the coder needs at most
3.63 + 2 = 5.63, i.e. 5 bits.

Codeword: with k = \lceil 3.63 \rceil + 1 = 5, cells have width
2^{-5} = 0.03125. The cell [0.75, 0.78125) lies inside
[0.729, 0.81). Its left endpoint 0.75 = 0.11000_2, so the codeword
is 11000, 5 bits as bounded. (k = 4 fails: the width-0.0625
cells adjacent to [0.729, 0.81) are [0.6875, 0.75) and
[0.75, 0.8125), and neither is contained in it, which is why the
bound reserves the extra bit.)

A black-box lossless compressor C is queried on short files over
\{A, B, C, D\}. (a) On the four single-character files it outputs
1, 2, 3, 3 bits respectively; state the implied distribution
q_C over the next character and check it against the Kraft budget of
The Kraft inequality. (b) Appending to the file A, the
outputs are \ell_C(AA) = 2 and \ell_C(AB) = 3, with continuations
C, D costing 4 bits each. Compute the implied conditional
distribution q_C(\cdot \mid A).

(a) 2^{-\ell} gives (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18), which
sums to exactly 1: the budget is saturated, so no normalization is
needed and the code is complete. The implied model is
q_C = (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18); its
maximum-probability prediction is A.

(b) Length increments over \ell_C(A) = 1:
\Delta(A) = 1, \Delta(B) = 2, \Delta(C) = \Delta(D) = 3. Weights
2^{-\Delta} = (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18), summing to
1: q_C(\cdot \mid A) = (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18).
The compressor's spending pattern is a conditional model; here it
happens to match its unconditional one, i.e. the box treats the second
character as independent of the first.

A byte-level model reports a log-loss of 0.55 nats per byte on a
2-megabyte (2 \times 10^6-byte) log file. Convert to bits per byte,
compute the achievable compressed size in kilobytes (ignoring the
O(1) coder overhead), and the compression ratio against the raw file.

Bits per byte: 0.55 \times 1.443 \approx 0.794. Total:
2 \times 10^6 \times 0.794 \approx 1.587 \times 10^6 bits
= 1.587 \times 10^6 / 8 \approx 198{,}400 bytes \approx 198 kB.
Ratio: 2 \times 10^6 / 198{,}400 \approx 10.1{:}1, against 8 bits
per byte raw. The nats-to-bits factor is the whole conversion: the
loss already is the file size in the other unit.

A sensor emits H with probability 0.99 and T with probability
0.01, i.i.d. (a) Compute the entropy per flip. (b) State the best any
symbol code (one codeword per flip, per
Huffman coding) achieves, and its overhead. (c) Compute
the arithmetic coder's expected total for 10^4 flips under the true
model, and the resulting compression ratio against the symbol code. Use
\log_2 0.99 \approx -0.0145, \log_2 100 \approx 6.644.

(a) H = 0.99 \times 0.0145 + 0.01 \times 6.644 \approx 0.0144 + 0.0664
= 0.0808 bits per flip.

(b) A binary alphabet forces lengths (1, 1): L = 1 bit per flip,
an overhead of 1 - 0.0808 = 0.9192 bits, about 11 times the entropy
itself: the per-symbol rounding flaw at its worst.

(c) Expected log-loss of the true model is the entropy, so the coder
spends about 10^4 \times 0.0808 + 2 \approx 810 bits, against
10^4 bits for the symbol code: a ratio of 12.3{:}1. The two
overhead bits are paid once for the whole stream, which is exactly what
the block-coding table of The source coding theorem
approximated with ever-larger tables.

A pretrained model with 7 \times 10^9 parameters at 16 bits each
achieves 0.7 bits per character on a text collection; a self-contained
dictionary compressor achieves 2.7 bits per character with negligible
description length. Under two-part accounting (model bits + data bits),
find the collection size N in characters at which the model's total
first beats the compressor's, and the sizes at N = 10^{10}
characters.

Model description: 7 \times 10^9 \times 16 = 1.12 \times 10^{11}
bits. Totals: model 1.12 \times 10^{11} + 0.7N; compressor 2.7N.
Break-even: 1.12 \times 10^{11} = 2N, so
N = 5.6 \times 10^{10} characters, about 56 GB of text. Below
that, shipping the model costs more than it saves.

At N = 10^{10}: model total 1.12 \times 10^{11} + 7 \times 10^9
= 1.19 \times 10^{11} bits; compressor 2.7 \times 10^{10} bits. The
compressor wins by a factor of 4.4 although its per-character rate is
almost 4 times worse. This is the Delétang paper's adjusted-rate
finding in miniature, and the trade
Minimum description length turns into a model-selection
principle.

A character-level model scores 1.4 bits per character on held-out
English whose entropy rate is taken as 1.1 bits per character.
Identify the irreducible and improvable parts of its rate, compute both
as fractions, and give the achievable compressed size of a
500{,}000-character novel now and under a hypothetically perfect
model.

By the accounting identity, 1.4 = 1.1 + 0.3: the entropy rate 1.1
is the source's floor, and 0.3 bits per character is the model's
divergence rate, the only improvable part. Fractions: the mismatch is
0.3 / 1.4 \approx 21\% of every compressed file, and the model sits
0.3 / 1.1 \approx 27\% above the floor.

Sizes: now, 500{,}000 \times 1.4 = 700{,}000 bits = 87.5 kB.
Perfect model: 500{,}000 \times 1.1 = 550{,}000 bits \approx 69 kB.
No model, however trained, goes below the second number: that is the
source coding theorem of The source coding theorem
applied at the entropy rate.

G. Delétang, A. Ruoss, P.-A. Duquenne, E. Catt, T. Genewein, C. Mattern, J. Grau-Moya, L. K. Wenliang, M. Aitchison, L. Orseau, M. Hutter, J. Veness, "Language Modeling Is Compression," ICLR 2024 — §2 states the predictor–compressor equivalence via arithmetic coding; §3 measures Chinchilla 70B as a general-purpose compressor (ImageNet 43.4%, LibriSpeech 16.4%, vs PNG 58.5% and FLAC 30.3%) and defines the adjusted compression rate that charges model size. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.10668

D. J. C. MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms, Cambridge University Press, 2003 — ch. 6 "Stream Codes": why symbol codes fall short and how arithmetic coding reaches the entropy rate; §6.2 the encoder/decoder and the within-two-bits guarantee. Free online: https://www.inference.org.uk/mackay/itila/

T. M. Cover, J. A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006 — §5.4 the wrong-code cost H(p) + D(p\|q) behind the accounting section; §13.3 arithmetic coding.

I. H. Witten, R. M. Neal, J. G. Cleary, "Arithmetic Coding for Data Compression," Communications of the ACM, 30(6), 1987 — the classic practical treatment: incremental encoding/decoding and the separation of model from coder.

J. Rissanen, G. G. Langdon, "Arithmetic Coding," IBM Journal of Research and Development, 23(2), 1979 — the original general formulation of arithmetic coding.

documents.title: Kolmogorov complexity
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Kolmogorov complexity
documents.text:
The Kolmogorov complexity of a string is the length of the shortest program
that prints it: the single number under which no compressor, however clever,
can push the string. This lesson defines K(x) and establishes its
load-bearing properties: switching the programming language moves it by at
most an additive constant (invariance); almost every string sits within a
few bits of its own length (a counting argument); no algorithm computes it
(Berry's paradox); and for a computable source its per-symbol expectation
converges to the entropy. The result closes the module's thread at its
ceiling: the best compressor, and with it the best predictor, exists and
cannot be run.

documents.title: Three strings: regularity is a short program
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Kolmogorov complexity › Three strings: regularity is a short program
documents.text:
Three strings: regularity is a short program

Take three strings of n = 10^6 bits each:

x_1 = 000000…0: one million zeros.

x_2 = 010101…01: the pair 01 repeated 500{,}000 times.

x_3 = 110100…1: one million flips of a fair coin, recorded faithfully.

All three occupy the same megabit of storage. They differ in how short a
description suffices to regenerate them.

The programs

A program printing x_1 is a loop: emit 0, 10^6 times. Its text is a
fixed few dozen bytes of loop code — a constant c, independent of the
count — plus the number 10^6 itself, which takes
\lceil \log_2 (10^6 + 1) \rceil = 20 bits to state. Description length:
20 + c bits.

A program for x_2 is the same loop with the two-character body 01 and
the count 500{,}000, a \lceil \log_2 (5 \times 10^5 + 1) \rceil = 19-bit
numeral: 19 + c' bits, with c' exceeding c only by the cost of the
one extra body character.

For x_3 no pattern is available to exploit; the only general recipe is
print "1101000110…" with the million bits included verbatim, a program of
10^6 + c'' bits.

Per output bit: x_1 and x_2 cost on the order of 10^{-5} bits of
program per bit of output; x_3 costs 1. Three strings of identical
length, and the shortest known descriptions differ by five orders of
magnitude.

Three strings, three programs: the loops cost ≈ 30 bits, the coin flips cost the full million. Structure is what a short program exploits.

Write the two loop programs in a language of your choice and count their
bytes: both fit in under 40 characters, about 300 bits, against 10^6 bits
of output. Attempt the same for a string of coin flips; every honest attempt
ends with the data pasted into the source.

The gap is not about loops specifically. Any regularity (repetition,
symmetry, a formula, a grammar) is a handle some program can grip; a string
with no computable regularity leaves nothing to grip. Measuring the shortest
program therefore measures the total structure in the string.

Description length is the universal currency of structure: a string is
compressible exactly when some program shorter than the string can
regenerate it.

documents.title: The definition: the shortest program that prints x
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Kolmogorov complexity › The definition: the shortest program that prints x
documents.text:
The definition: the shortest program that prints x

Fix a programming language U that is universal: it can express an
interpreter for any other language. Python, C, and the universal Turing
machine all qualify. Programs are finite binary strings (source text at 8
bits per character); \ell(p) denotes the length of program p in bits.

The Kolmogorov complexity of a binary string x with respect to a
universal language U is

K_U(x) = \min \{\, \ell(p) : U(p) = x \,\},

the length in bits of the shortest program that outputs x and halts,
run on empty input.

The minimum is over a non-empty set: the literal program print "x" always
qualifies, so K_U(x) \le n + c for every n-bit string, where c is the
fixed cost of the quoting code. The loop programs above give the
complementary bound for structured strings: K_U(0^n) \le \log_2 n + c,
since the program need only contain the count n and a constant amount of
loop code.

K_U(x) is defined for an individual string. Every measure so far in
this course (entropy, mutual information, cross-entropy) required a
probability distribution before it could assign a number. K_U assigns a
number to 0101…01 itself, with no source, no ensemble, and no
probabilities in sight. This is the point of the algorithmic definition,
and the reason it can serve as the limit concept under all compression.

The first 10^6 bits of the binary expansion of \pi pass every standard
statistical test for randomness, yet a fixed spigot program plus the count
n prints them: K_U \le \log_2 n + c, about as small as for the
all-zeros string. High apparent disorder does not certify high K; only
the absence of any computable regularity does.

Every compressed file is a program

Compression as prediction treated a compressed file z and
its decoder as a pair. Bundle them: the program "run the following decoder
on the following bits", with the decoder's code and z inlined, prints x.
Its length is \ell_C(x) plus the fixed size of the decoder: a
self-extracting archive, and by construction an upper bound on K_U(x).

The self-extracting archive: decoder code plus compressed bits form one program printing x, so K(x) is at most ℓ_C(x) + c_C for every compressor C.

For every computable lossless compressor C there is a constant c_C,
independent of x, such that

K_U(x) \;\le\; \ell_C(x) + c_C \quad \text{for all strings } x,

where \ell_C(x) is the length of C's output on x.

Let D be C's decoder, a fixed program. For any x, the program
p_x = "run D on z", with z = C(x) included literally, outputs x
and halts. Its length is \ell_C(x) + c_C, where c_C covers D's code
and the glue that delimits z. The shortest program for x is no longer
than this particular one.

The theorem is the lesson's title claim: gzip, a block Huffman code, and a
language model driving an arithmetic coder are each one program family,
and K_U(x) sits at or below the output length of every one of them, up to
that family's fixed constant.

K_U(x) \le \ell_C(x) + c_C for every computable lossless compressor C:
the shortest program is the floor under all compression, reachable by none
of it by more than an additive constant.

documents.title: The invariance theorem: switching languages costs a constant
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Kolmogorov complexity › The invariance theorem: switching languages costs a constant
documents.text:
The invariance theorem: switching languages costs a constant

The subscript U looks like a defect: a "Python complexity" and a "C
complexity" could disagree, and a quantity that depends on a taste in
languages would not be a property of the string. The rescue is concrete. A
Python interpreter can be written in C, once, as a fixed file; call its
length c bits. Prepending that interpreter to any Python program p
yields a C program of length \ell(p) + c with identical output. Whatever
Python saves, C recovers at a one-time cost of c.

Let A and B be universal languages. There is a constant c_{AB},
depending on the pair of languages but not on x, with

K_A(x) \;\le\; K_B(x) + c_{AB} \quad \text{for all } x .

Applying the statement in both directions,
\lvert K_A(x) - K_B(x) \rvert \le \max(c_{AB}, c_{BA}) for all x.

A is universal, so some A-program I_B of fixed length c_{AB}
interprets B: given a B-program p appended to its own code (with a
fixed self-delimiting framing, absorbed into c_{AB}), it simulates B
running p. For the shortest B-program p^* printing x, the
A-program I_B\,p^* prints x and has length K_B(x) + c_{AB}; the
A-minimum is at most that.

Invariance: language A runs B's shortest program behind one fixed interpreter, so the two complexities differ by at most a constant that does not depend on x.

The constant is real, and can be large: the interpreter for a rich language
is megabytes of code, and for one specific short string the choice of
language can dominate the value. Invariance is an asymptotic guarantee:
as strings grow, a fixed \pm c becomes negligible against K(x), and
every statement in this lesson holds up to such a constant. No exact,
language-free value of K(x) exists; the honest notation for the rest of
the lesson is K(x) with a fixed universal U understood, and claims
carry +O(1).

Changing the universal language changes K by at most one interpreter's
length: K(x) is a property of the string, well-defined up to +O(1).

documents.title: Counting: almost every string is incompressible
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Kolmogorov complexity › Counting: almost every string is incompressible
documents.text:
Counting: almost every string is incompressible

The three-strings opener suggests compressibility is common; arithmetic
says the opposite. Count the descriptions available for 1000-bit strings.
Programs of length strictly below 980 bits number at most

1 + 2 + 4 + \cdots + 2^{979} = 2^{980} - 1 < 2^{980},

and each program prints at most one string. So fewer than 2^{980} of the
2^{1000} strings can be compressed by 20 or more bits: a fraction below
2^{-20}, under one in a million.

For every n and every c \ge 1, the fraction of n-bit strings with
K(x) < n - c is less than 2^{-c}. In particular, at least one n-bit
string satisfies K(x) \ge n for every n.

There are fewer than 2^{n-c} binary programs of length below n - c,
and each outputs at most one string, so fewer than 2^{n-c} of the 2^n
strings have such a program: a fraction below 2^{-c}. For the second
claim take c = 0: programs of length below n number 2^n - 1, one
short of the 2^n strings, so some string has no program shorter than
itself.

The census for n = 1000, c = 20: fewer than 2⁹⁸⁰ short programs exist for 2¹⁰⁰⁰ strings, so under one string in a million compresses by 20 bits.

Run the same census for c = 10: count the programs shorter than 990
bits and the resulting fraction. It should land below 2^{-10} \approx
10^{-3}: compressing by even 10 bits is already a one-in-a-thousand
property.

An n-bit string x is c-incompressible if K(x) \ge n - c, and
incompressible (algorithmically random) if K(x) \ge n.

The counting theorem gives the algorithmic reading of randomness developed
in Cover & Thomas §14.5: a fair-coin outcome is overwhelmingly likely to be
near-incompressible, and any compressible outcome (a run of a million
zeros, say) is an event of probability below 2^{-c}, not a typical draw.
Structure in data is always the exception that a counting argument prices.

Fewer than 2^{n-c} programs are shorter than n - c bits, so at most a
2^{-c} fraction of n-bit strings compresses by c bits:
incompressibility is the rule, and every compressible file is a rarity to
the exact extent it compresses.

documents.title: Uncomputability: the ideal compressor cannot be run
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Kolmogorov complexity › Uncomputability: the ideal compressor cannot be run
documents.text:
Uncomputability: the ideal compressor cannot be run

The natural next step is a program that computes K(x), turning the floor
into a tool. No such program exists, and the obstruction is a sentence.
Berry's paradox (reported by
Russell in 1908) asks for "the least integer not nameable in fewer than
nineteen syllables" — a phrase of eighteen syllables that names it.
Kolmogorov complexity makes the paradox precise, and precision turns it
from a curiosity into an impossibility proof.

Suppose a program Q, say 10^6 bits long, computed K(x) for every
x. Build the searcher R: "for each string x in order of length,
compute K(x) using Q; print the first x with K(x) > 10^9 and
halt." R contains Q, the threshold 10^9 (30 bits), and fixed loop
code: about 10^6 bits in total. The search terminates, because strings
with K(x) > 10^9 exist by the counting theorem. But then R is a
10^6-bit program printing a string whose complexity exceeds 10^9:
a contradiction three orders of magnitude wide.

No algorithm outputs K(x) on input x for all strings x.

Suppose Q computes K, with \ell(Q) = q. For a threshold L, let
R_L enumerate strings in length-lexicographic order, compute each
K(x) by running Q, and print the first x^* with K(x^*) > L. Such
a string exists (counting theorem), so R_L halts and prints x^*;
hence K(x^*) \le \ell(R_L) \le q + \log_2 L + c, the length of Q
plus the binary threshold plus fixed glue. But K(x^*) > L by the test
R_L applied. For L large enough that L > q + \log_2 L + c (true
for all sufficiently large L), the two conclusions contradict.
No Q exists.

Berry's paradox as a program: if K were computable, a ≈10⁶-bit searcher would print a string it proves needs 10⁹ bits. The contradiction rules out the searcher's only assumption: the subroutine Q.

K(x) is a perfectly definite integer for every x: the minimum of a
non-empty set of program lengths, bounded above by n + c. What fails is
the existence of an algorithm that returns it. K can even be approached
from above: run all programs up to the literal bound in parallel
(dovetailed), and record the shortest that has halted with output x so
far. The record converges to K(x), but certifying convergence would
mean certifying that no shorter program ever halts, which is the
halting problem. K is
upper-semicomputable, never computable.

The practical consequence organizes the whole compression stack: every
runnable compressor is a computable upper bound on an uncomputable floor.
gzip is one bound; a language model with an arithmetic coder is a tighter
one; nothing runnable is the floor itself. The same limitation, inherited
by Minimum description length, is why practical MDL
replaces shortest programs with restricted, computable model classes.

K is well-defined and uncomputable: an exact shortest-description finder
would contain Berry's paradox as a subroutine. The ideal compressor exists
as a mathematical object and cannot be run.

documents.title: Complexity meets entropy: E[K]/n converges to H
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Kolmogorov complexity › Complexity meets entropy: E[K]/n converges to H
documents.text:
Complexity meets entropy: E[K]/n converges to H

K was built with no distribution; entropy needs one. Put a distribution
back and the two meet.

Let the source be the course's 90/10 coin (H \approx 0.469 bits per
flip) and draw n = 10^4 flips. A typical draw x has about k = 1000
tails, and admits a two-part description:

State k: at most \lceil \log_2 (n+1) \rceil = 14 bits.

State which arrangement: an index into the
\binom{10^4}{1000} strings with exactly that many tails,
\log_2 \binom{10^4}{1000} \approx 4680 bits.

A fixed decoder turns the pair into the string, so
K(x) \le 14 + 4680 + c \approx 4700 bits: about 0.47 per flip, at the
entropy, for every string of typical composition, not on average but
individually. The general inequality behind step 2 is
\log_2 \binom{n}{k} \le n\,H(k/n); here
n\,H(1000/10^4) = 10^4 \times H(0.1) \approx 4690 bits, so the index
term sits within 10 bits of that ceiling.

Let X_1, X_2, \ldots be i.i.d. draws from a computable distribution p
on a finite alphabet \mathcal{X}. Then

\frac{1}{n}\, \mathbb{E}\left[ K(X_1 \ldots X_n) \right]

Sketch; the full statement is Theorem 14.3.1 of Cover & Thomas, and
chapter 7 of Shen–Uspensky–Vereshchagin. Upper bound: the two-part
description generalizes: state the count of each symbol
((|\mathcal{X}|-1)\lceil \log_2 (n+1) \rceil bits), then the index
within that type class (\le n H(\hat{p}) bits for empirical
distribution \hat{p}). Taking expectations,
\mathbb{E}[H(\hat{p})] \le H(p) by concavity of entropy, so
\mathbb{E}[K] \le nH + O(\log n). Lower bound: self-delimiting
programs form a prefix-free set, so their lengths obey the Kraft budget
of The Kraft inequality; shortest-program lengths are then
the lengths of a lossless description system, and the source coding
theorem of The source coding theorem floors their
expectation at nH minus a constant (plain, non-self-delimiting
programs shift the bound by O(\log n), which the division by n
kills).

E[K]/n for the 90/10 coin, squeezed between H and the two-part bound H + O(log n / n): the algorithmic and Shannon measures agree in the limit.

Both hypotheses earn their keep. Computable source: the decoder in the
upper bound must be able to work with p's structure; for sources with no
computable description the theorem's route fails. Expectation: the
agreement is on average over draws; an individual string can sit far below
(x_1, the all-zeros draw) or slightly above the entropy rate. Where no
distribution exists at all (one fixed file, one genome, one photograph),
entropy is silent and K is the measure that remains.

For a computable i.i.d. source, \mathbb{E}[K(X^n)]/n \to H(X): Shannon
entropy is the expected value of algorithmic information, and the two
theories certify the same per-symbol price wherever both apply.

documents.title: The ceiling: Solomonoff's predictor and the limit of learning
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Kolmogorov complexity › The ceiling: Solomonoff's predictor and the limit of learning
documents.text:
The ceiling: Solomonoff's predictor and the limit of learning

Compression as prediction established the dictionary:
predictors and compressors are one object in two interfaces. K is the
compression side's absolute floor; its prediction-side mirror is a mixture
over all programs. Work on a universal language whose valid programs are
self-delimiting (no program is a prefix of another; the machine knows
where the code ends). Program lengths then obey the Kraft budget of
The Kraft inequality, \sum_p 2^{-\ell(p)} \le 1, so weights
2^{-\ell(p)} can be read as a prior over programs.

For a binary string x, the universal mixture assigns

M(x) \;=\; \sum_{p\,:\; U(p) \text{ outputs a string starting with } x} 2^{-\ell(p)},

the total prior weight of all programs whose output begins with x.
Prediction is by conditioning:
M(\text{next bit} = 1 \mid x) = M(x1)/M(x).

Every program is a hypothesis about the data's law, weighted by
2^{-\ell}: short programs, the simple hypotheses, carry exponentially
more weight. The mixture's power is a one-line domination argument.

Let \mu be any computable distribution over binary streams, computed by
a program of length K(\mu). For every string x,

-\log_2 M(x) \;\le\; -\log_2 \mu(x) + K(\mu) + O(1) .

Read through Compression as prediction: coding with the
mixture costs at most K(\mu) more bits in total, not per symbol,
over coding with the true model, whatever the stream length.

The sum defining M(x) includes the programs that compute \mu and then
arithmetic-decode x's \mu-code; through that family
M(x) \ge 2^{-K(\mu) - O(1)}\, \mu(x), the true model's weight times its
probability. Taking -\log_2 of the domination gives the claim.

A predictor whose lifetime excess loss against every computable competitor
is a constant learns, in the limit, every regularity that any program can
express: this is Solomonoff's induction
(1964), the theoretical optimum of sequence prediction. It inherits K's
defect in full: M sums over all programs, including non-halting ones,
and is uncomputable. It is a ceiling to approximate, never an algorithm to
deploy; Delétang et al. (2023) (§2)
frame modern language-model training exactly so, as pushing a computable
predictor toward the Solomonoff limit, with the compression numbers of
Compression as prediction as the progress meter.

One text, one ladder: 8 Mbit raw, ≈2.6 Mbit gzip, ≈1 Mbit for a strong model. Every computable rung sits above the uncomputable floor K(x); better modeling descends toward it.

Fine print: what the ceiling does and does not govern

The whole construction is lossless: K prices exact regeneration of
x, and says nothing about coding within a distortion tolerance, which is
Rate-distortion theory's trade-off. And the mixture's two-part
skeleton (pay K(\mu) for a model, then -\log_2 \mu(x) for the data
under it) is the ideal MDL of Shen–Uspensky–Vereshchagin §14.3:
K(x) \le K(\mu) - \log_2 \mu(x) + O(1) for every computable model
\mu. Replacing "all programs" with a computable model class turns this
bound into a usable selection rule, the subject of
Minimum description length.

The Solomonoff mixture pays at most K(\mu) + O(1) total extra bits
against any computable source: compression, prediction, and learning share
one uncomputable ceiling, and a good learner is measured by how closely it
approximates it.

documents.title: Exercises
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information theory in machine learning › Kolmogorov complexity › Exercises
documents.text:
Exercises

Rank the following 10^6-bit strings by Kolmogorov complexity and justify
each rank with a program sketch and a length estimate: (a) one million
copies of the bit 1; (b) the first 10^6 bits of the binary expansion
of \sqrt{2}; (c) 10^6 bits produced by a fair coin.

(a) and (b) are both O(\log n); (c) is \approx n.

(a) "repeat 10^6 times: print 1": fixed loop code plus
\log_2 10^6 \approx 20 bits for the count: K \le 20 + c.

(b) \sqrt{2} is computable: a fixed digit-extraction routine (constant
size) plus the count n prints its first n bits: K \le 20 + c', the
same order as (a), despite the digits passing statistical randomness
tests.

(c) With probability at least 1 - 2^{-c}, a fair-coin string is not
compressible by c bits (counting theorem), so K \ge 10^6 - c except
with probability 2^{-c}; the literal program gives K \le 10^6 + c''.
Ranking: (a) \approx (b) \ll (c), with (a) and (b) not separable
beyond the \pm O(1) that invariance leaves undefined.

Prove the two general upper bounds from the definition: (a)
K(x) \le n + c for every n-bit string x; (b)
K(0^n) \le \log_2 n + c'. Then explain why, for small n, the bound
(a) can be the better of the two even for 0^n.

(a) The program print "x" with x inlined outputs x and halts; its
length is n bits of data plus a constant c of quoting code,
independent of x. The minimum over programs is at most this.

(b) The program "repeat n times: print 0" contains the loop code
(constant c') plus the binary numeral for n
(\lceil \log_2 (n+1) \rceil bits).

For small n the constants dominate: the loop machinery in c' (parsing
a numeral, maintaining a counter) can cost more than simply quoting a
handful of zeros under the smaller constant c. The crossover point is
language-dependent: exactly the \pm O(1) slack that the invariance
theorem says no statement about K may lean on.

(a) At most how many 1000-bit strings satisfy K(x) < 980, and what
fraction is that of all 1000-bit strings? (b) Show that for every n
some n-bit string has K(x) \ge n. (c) For X^n a uniform random
n-bit string, show \mathbb{E}[K(X^n)] > n - 2.

(a) Programs of length < 980 number 2^{980} - 1; one output each, so
at most 2^{980} - 1 < 2^{980} strings qualify: a fraction below
2^{980}/2^{1000} = 2^{-20} \approx 10^{-6}.

(b) Programs of length < n number 2^n - 1, but there are 2^n
strings of length n; by pigeonhole at least one string is the output of
no program shorter than itself, i.e. K(x) \ge n.

(c) For c \ge 1, \Pr[n - K \ge c] = \Pr[K \le n - c] < 2^{-(c-1)}
by the counting theorem (strings with K < n - c + 1 are fewer than
2^{n-c+1}). Summing the tail,

\mathbb{E}[\max(n - K, 0)] = \sum_{c \ge 1} \Pr[n - K \ge c]

and \mathbb{E}[n - K] \le \mathbb{E}[\max(n - K, 0)] < 2, so
\mathbb{E}[K] > n - 2: a uniform string is expected to be within two
bits of incompressible.

Languages A and B have interpreters for each other: an interpreter for
B written in A of 120{,}000 bits, and one for A written in B of
300{,}000 bits. (a) Bound \lvert K_A(x) - K_B(x) \rvert. (b) A
colleague reports "K of this 500-bit string is exactly 137 bits."
State precisely what is wrong with the claim.

(a) Prepending interpreters: K_A(x) \le K_B(x) + 120{,}000 and
K_B(x) \le K_A(x) + 300{,}000 for all x, hence
-120{,}000 \le K_B(x) - K_A(x) \le 300{,}000, and
\lvert K_A - K_B \rvert \le 300{,}000 bits.

(b) The number 137 is only meaningful relative to a named universal
language, and for a 500-bit string the interpreter constants between
reasonable languages (here up to 3 \times 10^5 bits) dwarf both the
string and the claimed value: another language can assign the same
string any value from O(1) up to \approx 500 + c. Exact
language-free values of K do not exist; only statements stable under
\pm O(1) (asymptotics, comparisons on long strings) are about the
string rather than the language.

Suppose a program Q of 2 \times 10^6 bits computes K(x) for all
x. Construct from it a program that yields a contradiction at the
threshold L = 10^{10}, verifying each step: the searcher's length, why
its search terminates, and the two incompatible conclusions.

Build R: "for each string x in length-lexicographic order, compute
K(x) by running Q; if K(x) > 10^{10}, print x and halt."
Length: Q's 2 \times 10^6 bits, the threshold
(\log_2 10^{10} \approx 34 bits), and constant loop code:
\ell(R) \approx 2 \times 10^6 + c.

Termination: by the counting theorem, strings with
K(x) \ge n exist at every length n, in particular strings with
K(x) > 10^{10}; the ordered search reaches the first one, x^*.

Conclusion 1: R prints x^*, so K(x^*) \le \ell(R) \approx
2 \times 10^6 + c. Conclusion 2: x^* passed the test, so
K(x^*) > 10^{10}. Since 2 \times 10^6 + c < 10^{10}, both cannot
hold. Every step used only Q's assumed existence, so no such Q
exists.

The bigram model of Compression as prediction achieves
3.3 bits per character on a 10^6-character English text x, its
count table costs 2^4 bits for each of 27 \times 27 context-symbol
pairs, and the arithmetic coder adds 2 bits. (a) Assemble the full
self-extracting program for x and compute the resulting upper bound on
K(x). (b) State which term the bound of the theorem "K undercuts every
compressor" absorbs into c_C and which it charges per file, and why a
70-billion-parameter model would change the accounting.

(a) The program must be self-contained: decoder and model code (a
constant c, thousands of bits), the count table
(27 \times 27 \times 16 = 11{,}664 bits), and the arithmetic-coded
data (3.3 \times 10^6 + 2 bits). Total:
K(x) \le 3.3 \times 10^6 + 11{,}664 + 2 + c \approx 3.31 \times 10^6
bits; the table is a 0.35\% surcharge.

(b) The decoder code is fixed across files and lands in c_C; the coded
data is per-file. The count table sits in between: fixed if the same
table is declared part of the compressor, per-file if fitted to x (as
in the worked example's model 3, which must then ship its counts). A
70B-parameter model at 16 bits per parameter puts
\approx 1.1 \times 10^{12} bits into the "constant": the bound on
K(x) still holds, but it is vacuous until the compressed data
outweighs the model: the adjusted-rate accounting of
Compression as prediction, and the trade-off
Minimum description length optimizes.

A run of n = 10^4 flips of the 90/10 coin comes back with k = 500
tails, half the expected count. (a) Compute the two-part description
length of this string (count, then index; use
\log_2 \binom{10^4}{500} \approx 2860). (b) Compute the length of its
codeword under the Shannon-optimal code for the true 90/10 model, i.e.
its surprisal (use -\log_2 0.9 \approx 0.152,
-\log_2 0.1 \approx 3.322). (c) Explain the direction of the gap using
the entropy concepts of Entropy and
The source coding theorem.

(a) Count: \lceil \log_2 (10^4 + 1) \rceil = 14 bits. Index:
\approx 2860 bits (consistent with the bound
\log_2 \binom{n}{k} \le n H(0.05) = 2864). Two-part total:
14 + 2860 + c \approx 2874 + c bits, so
K(x) \lesssim 2900 bits \approx 0.29 per flip.

(b) Surprisal under the true model:
9500 \times 0.152 + 500 \times 3.322 = 1444 + 1661 = 3105 bits: what
a code matched to the 90/10 distribution spends on this string.

(c) The string is atypical for the source: its empirical tail rate
0.05 differs from the source's 0.1, and the fixed code pays the
per-symbol mismatch (the cross-entropy reading: coding a
0.05-composition stream with the 0.1-model's code). The two-part
description instead adapts to the individual string, paying
nH(\hat{p}) + O(\log n) at the string's own empirical entropy
H(0.05) \approx 0.286 < H(0.1) \approx 0.469. K tracks the
structure the string actually has; distribution-based coding tracks the
structure the source was expected to have; expectation is where the two
reconcile (\mathbb{E}[K]/n \to H).

A. Shen, V. A. Uspensky, N. Vereshchagin, Kolmogorov Complexity and Algorithmic Randomness, AMS, 2017 — the opening survey "What is this book about?" and ch. 1: the definition, the Solomonoff–Kolmogorov invariance theorem, the counting argument, and non-computability via Berry's paradox; ch. 7: complexity and Shannon entropy; §14.3: the two-part code and the MDL reading. Free PDF: https://www.lirmm.fr/~ashen/kolmbook-eng-scan.pdf

T. M. Cover, J. A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006 — ch. 14: §14.2 definitions and the universality of K, §14.3 the \mathbb{E}[K]/n \to H theorem (Theorem 14.3.1), §14.5 incompressible and algorithmically random sequences, §14.6 universal probability.

G. Delétang, A. Ruoss, et al., "Language Modeling Is Compression," ICLR 2024 — §2 "Universal Coding": Solomonoff's mixture as the optimal predictor–compressor and the ceiling that trained models approximate. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.10668

D. J. C. MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms, Cambridge University Press, 2003 — ch. 28 §28.3: minimum description length and Occam's razor, the practical shadow of the ideal two-part code. Free online: https://www.inference.org.uk/mackay/itila/

documents.title: The maximum entropy principle
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The maximum entropy principle
documents.text:
Among all distributions consistent with known expectation constraints,
exactly one maximizes entropy, and it has exponential form; choosing any
other distribution assumes information you do not have. This lesson derives
that distribution. The route: an underdetermined inference problem (the
Brandeis dice), the exponential solution found numerically, the general
theorem proved with Gibbs' inequality from KL divergence,
and the two best-known instances of the solution, the Boltzmann
distribution of statistical mechanics and the softmax layer of machine
learning.

documents.title: One constraint, infinitely many distributions
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The maximum entropy principle › One constraint, infinitely many distributions
documents.text:
One constraint, infinitely many distributions

A six-sided die is tossed a great many times and the results average
4.5, not the 3.5 of a fair die. The task: assign probabilities
p_1, \dots, p_6 to the faces using this fact and nothing else. This is
the Brandeis dice problem, the running example of
Jaynes' 1962 Brandeis lectures.

The evidence supplies two equations for six unknowns:

\sum_{i=1}^{6} p_i = 1, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{6} i\, p_i = 4.5 .

Four degrees of freedom remain, so infinitely many pmfs fit the data.
Three of them, with their entropies from
Entropy:

candidate (p_1, \dots, p_6)

mean

H (bits)

(0, 0, .25, 0, .75, 0)

4.5

0.811

(0, 0, 0, .5, .5, 0)

4.5

1.000

(0, 0, .25, .25, .25, .25)

4.5

2.000

Every candidate satisfies the constraints; every candidate also asserts
more than the constraints contain. The first declares faces 1, 2, 4, and
6 impossible, an impossibility claim nowhere in the evidence. The second
rules out four faces on the strength of a single average. Even the third
zeroes two faces the data never excluded.

The principle: keep all the uncertainty the data does not remove

Entropy ranks the candidates by exactly the property at stake: H(p)
measures the uncertainty a distribution admits, so the candidate with
maximal H is the one that concedes the most ignorance while honoring the
data. Adopting any lower-entropy candidate narrows the possibilities
further than the constraints justify.

Given constraints on a distribution p (normalization plus known
expectation values), the maximum entropy principle adopts the
distribution

p^\ast = \argmax_{p\ \text{satisfying the constraints}} H(p),

the entropy maximizer over the feasible set of all distributions
consistent with the constraints.

Jaynes (1957),
§2: the maximum-entropy distribution "is the least biased estimate
possible on the given information; i.e., it is maximally noncommittal
with regard to missing information." The principle does not manufacture
knowledge; it refuses to pretend to knowledge that is absent.

Constraints select a set of distributions; entropy selects one point of it.

Expectation constraints select a set of distributions; entropy selects one
point of it: the unique member that assumes nothing beyond the
constraints.

documents.title: Solving the dice: tilt exponentially, then tune
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The maximum entropy principle › Solving the dice: tilt exponentially, then tune
documents.text:
Solving the dice: tilt exponentially, then tune

The maximization runs over a four-parameter set, but the search collapses
to one dimension. The theorem of the next section states that the
maximizer is exponential in the constrained quantity; the constrained
quantity here is the face value f(i) = i, so the solution has the form

p_i = \frac{e^{-\lambda i}}{Z(\lambda)}, \qquad

with a single unknown \lambda. Writing x = e^{-\lambda} gives
p_i \propto x^i: successive faces carry probabilities in a fixed ratio
x, a geometric ladder. One knob remains, and one constraint remains to
set it.

Tuning the knob

The mean \sum_i i\,p_i increases monotonically in x, so the equation
"mean = 4.5" has exactly one solution.

x = 1: the ladder is flat, p_i = \tfrac16, mean 3.5. Too low.

x = 1.2: Z = \sum_i 1.2^i = 11.916, giving
p = (.101, .121, .145, .174, .209, .251) and mean
\sum_i i\,p_i = 4.02. Still too low.

Solving numerically (bisection on x): the mean hits 4.5 at
x = 1.4493, i.e. \lambda = -\ln 1.4493 = -0.371. Then
Z(\lambda) = 26.66 and

p^\ast = (.054,\ .079,\ .114,\ .165,\ .240,\ .347).

Checks. Mean: \sum_i i\,p^\ast_i = 0.054 + 0.158 + 0.343 + 0.662 +
1.199 + 2.085 = 4.50. Entropy:
H(p^\ast) = -\sum_i p^\ast_i \log_2 p^\ast_i = 2.328 bits, below the
unconstrained maximum \log_2 6 = 2.585 but above every candidate in the
table: 0.811, 1.000, and 2.000 all fall short.

One step per frame: state the constraint, restrict to the exponential family, tune the one knob. Watch the mean marker close in on the 4.5 target.

No face is assigned zero probability: the exponential form is strictly
positive, so the solution never rules out an outcome the data left
possible. The tilt direction follows the sign of \lambda: a target mean
above 3.5 needs \lambda < 0 (ladder rising), below 3.5 needs
\lambda > 0 (ladder falling), and a target of exactly 3.5 gives
\lambda = 0, recovering the uniform distribution. A constraint the
uniform prior already satisfies costs no entropy at all.

The multiplier as a tilt dial: λ = 0 is the uniform maximum; tilting either way trades entropy for the constraint.

Set the target mean to 3.5 and check \lambda = 0, H = 2.585 bits:
the constraint is inert. Then load the Jaynes preset (4.5) and verify
\lambda \approx -0.371, H \approx 2.33 bits. Finish at mean 2: the
readouts should land near \lambda \approx 0.63 and H \approx 1.97
bits, a harder constraint buying less entropy.

One multiplier per constraint: restricting to the exponential family turns
a search over all feasible distributions into solving one equation for one
\lambda, and the constraint value determines \lambda uniquely.

documents.title: The general theorem: exponential in the constrained quantities
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The maximum entropy principle › The general theorem: exponential in the constrained quantities
documents.text:
The general theorem: exponential in the constrained quantities

The dice used one constraint function, f(i) = i. The general statement
allows any finite list. Throughout, exponentials are base e and
entropies are reported in bits; changing base rescales \lambda by
\ln 2 and nothing else.

Let \mathcal{X} be a finite alphabet, f_1, \dots, f_m real-valued
functions on \mathcal{X}, and \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_m real numbers.
The feasible set is the set of pmfs p on \mathcal{X} with

\sum_{x} p(x)\, f_r(x) = \alpha_r, \qquad r = 1, \dots, m .

The claimed maximizer generalizes the dice solution: one multiplier
\lambda_r per constraint, all sitting in one exponent.

The solution dissected: constrained quantities, their multipliers, and the partition function.

Suppose \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_m can be chosen so that

q(x) = \frac{e^{-\sum_{r} \lambda_r f_r(x)}}{Z(\lambda)},

lies in the feasible set. Then q uniquely maximizes H over the
feasible set: H(p) \le H(q) for every feasible p, with equality only
at p = q.

Let p be any feasible pmf. Insert q into the entropy and split the
logarithm:

H(p) = -\sum_x p(x) \log_2 p(x)

By the information inequality of KL divergence,
D(p\,\|\,q) \ge 0, so

H(p) \;\le\; -\sum_x p(x) \log_2 q(x).

The right side is where the exponential form pays: \log_2 q(x) =
\bigl(-\sum_r \lambda_r f_r(x) - \ln Z(\lambda)\bigr)/\ln 2 is a linear
combination of the constrained functions plus a constant, so

-\sum_x p(x) \log_2 q(x)

a number that depends on p only through the constrained expectations
\alpha_r, hence the same for every feasible p. In particular q is
itself feasible, so this number equals -\sum_x q(x) \log_2 q(x) = H(q).
Therefore H(p) \le H(q), with equality exactly when
D(p\,\|\,q) = 0, i.e. p = q.

The proof is Cover & Thomas'
Theorem 12.1.1, and it is Gibbs' inequality doing the work one more time:
the same D \ge 0 that priced wrong-code overhead and floored the coding
cost now certifies a maximizer, with no calculus required. The one
structural fact used is that \log_2 q is linear in the constraints,
which pins the bound -\sum p \log_2 q to a single value across the
whole feasible set.

Why nothing beats the exponential form, one step per frame. Watch the bound in frame 2 become an equality with H(q) in frame 3.

Step through the three frames, then verify frame 3's arithmetic by hand:
with -\log_2 q_i = 4.737 - 0.535\,i (that is, \log_2 Z = 4.737 and
\lambda/\ln 2 = -0.535), the bound evaluates to
4.737 - 0.535 \times 4.5 = 2.33 bits for every pmf with mean 4.5.

Tuning the multipliers: the partition function does the bookkeeping

For the dice, one bisection found \lambda. In general the partition
function Z(\lambda) organizes the tuning: differentiating \ln Z with
respect to \lambda_r brings down -f_r inside the sum, giving

\langle f_r \rangle

so the m constraint equations \langle f_r \rangle = \alpha_r are the
m equations -\partial \ln Z / \partial \lambda_r = \alpha_r in the
m multipliers (Jaynes 1957,
eqs. 2-6 to 2-9). Dice check: at \lambda = -0.371,
\ln Z = \ln 26.66 = 3.283, and the numerical derivative gives
-\partial \ln Z/\partial\lambda = 4.500, the constrained mean.

Higher derivatives of \ln Z generate higher moments:
\partial^2 \ln Z / \partial \lambda_r^2 = \operatorname{Var}(f_r),
which is Jaynes' variance formula and, in the statistical-mechanics
reading below, the heat capacity. The historical derivation of the
exponential form is also worth knowing: introduce Lagrange multipliers
\lambda_0, \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_m for the constraints and set the
gradient of -\sum p \ln p - \lambda_0 \sum p - \sum_r \lambda_r \sum p f_r
to zero; stationarity in each p(x) gives
\ln p(x) = -1 - \lambda_0 - \sum_r \lambda_r f_r(x), the exponential
form. The multiplier route finds the stationary point; the Gibbs route
above is what proves it is the global maximum, and it needs neither
calculus of variations nor second-order conditions.

The constraints must be mutually satisfiable over the alphabet: no pmf on
\{1, \dots, 6\} has mean 7, and an empty feasible set has no
maximizer. Separately, for some constraint sets on infinite alphabets the
supremum of H is not attained by any distribution (Cover & Thomas
§12.3 exhibit such anomalous cases); both situations are out of scope
here.

With no constraints at all (m = 0), the theorem's q is
e^{0}/Z = 1/|\mathcal{X}|, the uniform distribution: the range theorem
H \le \log_2 n of Entropy is the
constraint-free special case of maximum entropy.

The maximum-entropy distribution under expectation constraints is
exponential in the constrained quantities,
p^\ast(x) = e^{-\sum_r \lambda_r f_r(x)} / Z(\lambda), and Gibbs'
inequality proves no feasible distribution beats it: the entropy any
other choice loses is exactly D(p \,\|\, p^\ast).

documents.title: Boltzmann and softmax: one solution, two vocabularies
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The maximum entropy principle › Boltzmann and softmax: one solution, two vocabularies
documents.text:
Boltzmann and softmax: one solution, two vocabularies

The exponential solution predates its information-theoretic derivation by
some eighty years in physics, and postdates it by a few decades in
machine learning. Both are the theorem with one constraint list.

Physics: the energy constraint

Take \mathcal{X} to be the microstates i of a physical system, each
with energy E_i, and impose one constraint: the mean energy is a known
value U. The theorem returns

p_i = \frac{e^{-\beta E_i}}{Z(\beta)}, \qquad

with a single multiplier \beta tuned so
\langle E \rangle = -\partial \ln Z / \partial \beta = U. This is the
Boltzmann distribution, and physics names the multiplier: \beta = 1/kT,
inverse temperature. High temperature means a weak multiplier and a
near-uniform spread over microstates; low temperature concentrates the
distribution on the low-energy states.

Jaynes' 1957 paper
(§3) turns this observation into a program: equilibrium statistical
mechanics is maximum-entropy inference with an energy constraint, and
the standard machinery (partition function identities, thermodynamic
derivatives) follows from the inference, not from any dynamical
assumption such as ergodicity. Whether this founds statistical mechanics
is Jaynes' claim, and remains his to defend; what is theorem is that the
energy constraint alone forces the Boltzmann form. The physical price of
these bits is the subject of
Thermodynamics of information.

Machine learning: the softmax layer

A classifier head turns a vector of logits z_1, \dots, z_k into a
distribution by

p_i = \frac{e^{z_i / T}}{\sum_{j} e^{z_j / T}},

the softmax with temperature T (training uses T = 1). Matching
symbols against the theorem: the constraint function is the negative
logit, f(i) = -z_i, and the multiplier is 1/T. Softmax is the
maximum-entropy distribution whose expected logit is pinned; temperature
rescales the multiplier exactly as it does for Boltzmann. The
identification is standard in NLP, where
Berger, Della Pietra & Della Pietra (1996)
built classifiers by imposing feature-expectation constraints and derived
the exponential (log-linear) model as the unique maximum-entropy
solution; training the weights is tuning the multipliers so the model's
feature expectations match the data's, and the loss minimized is the
cross-entropy of Cross-entropy.

One maximum-entropy solution, two vocabularies: energies are negative logits, and temperature is the inverse multiplier in both.

Temperature in numbers

Logits z = (2.0,\ 1.0,\ 0.1).

T = 1: exponentials e^{2} = 7.389, e^{1} = 2.718,
e^{0.1} = 1.105; normalizer Z = 11.213; distribution
p = (0.659,\ 0.242,\ 0.099). Entropy: H = 1.222 bits.

T = 2: exponentials e^{1} = 2.718, e^{0.5} = 1.649,
e^{0.05} = 1.051; normalizer Z = 5.418; distribution
p = (0.502,\ 0.304,\ 0.194). Entropy: H = 1.481 bits.

Doubling T halves the multiplier: the constraint bites half as hard,
the distribution moves toward uniform, and the entropy climbs toward the
three-outcome ceiling \log_2 3 = 1.585 bits. As T \to \infty the
output is uniform regardless of the logits; as T \to 0 all mass
collapses onto the largest logit.

The Boltzmann distribution and the softmax layer are the same
maximum-entropy solution: an expectation constraint on energy in physics
vocabulary, on logits in ML vocabulary, with temperature as the inverse
multiplier in both.

documents.title: A method of reasoning, and its limits
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The maximum entropy principle › A method of reasoning, and its limits
documents.text:
A method of reasoning, and its limits

Jaynes' own assessment
(1957,
§6) is the right frame: maximum entropy is "a method of reasoning", not a
law of physics. It converts exactly the stated constraints into a
distribution, adding nothing; the output is a description of the state of
knowledge encoded in the constraints, not a claim about long-run
frequencies. Whether such subjective probabilities also match observed
frequencies is a further question Jaynes treats separately (§4) and this
course leaves aside.

Two operational consequences follow. First, the output is only as good as
the constraints fed in: a max-ent die built from the mean alone will be
revised, not patched, when a second moment arrives, by adding the
constraint and re-solving. Second, constraints are never free: adding one
shrinks the feasible set, so the achievable maximum entropy can only
decrease, exactly as the dice dropped from 2.585 to 2.328 bits when
the mean was pinned.

The continuous counterpart, with a caveat

Among probability densities on \mathbb{R} with fixed variance
\sigma^2, the Gaussian maximizes the differential entropy
h(f) = -\int f \ln f; the result is property 5 of
Shannon's 1948 paper,
§20. The solution is again exponential in the constrained quantity: the
constraint is on x^2, and e^{-\lambda x^2} normalized is the
Gaussian. The caveat: differential entropy is not the discrete entropy of
this course. It can be negative, and its value changes under a change of
coordinates (Shannon, §20), so the discrete statements proved above do
not transfer silently; the continuous theory is out of this course's
scope.

Maximum entropy turns exactly the stated constraints into a distribution,
and nothing else: its output is only as good as the constraints fed in,
and every added constraint can only lower the achievable entropy.

documents.title: Exercises
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The maximum entropy principle › Exercises
documents.text:
Exercises

Verify the candidate table of the first section: for
p = (0, 0, 0, .5, .5, 0) and p = (0, 0, .25, .25, .25, .25), compute
the mean and the entropy, and confirm both entropies fall below the
maximum-entropy value 2.328 bits.

First candidate: mean = 4 \cdot 0.5 + 5 \cdot 0.5 = 4.5. Entropy: two
equal outcomes, H = -2 \cdot 0.5 \log_2 0.5 = 1.000 bit.

Second candidate: mean
= 0.25(3 + 4 + 5 + 6) = 0.25 \cdot 18 = 4.5. Entropy: four equal
outcomes, H = \log_2 4 = 2.000 bits.

Both are feasible, and 1.000 < 2.328 and 2.000 < 2.328 as the theorem
requires: each zeroed face is an assumption the constraints do not
contain, and it costs entropy.

For the exponential form q_i = e^{-\lambda i}/Z, show that the ratio of
successive probabilities q_{i+1}/q_i is a constant, independent of i.
Then estimate that constant and \lambda from the printed Brandeis
solution p^\ast = (.054, .079, .114, .165, .240, .347) using the last
two entries.

Ratio: q_{i+1}/q_i = e^{-\lambda(i+1)}/e^{-\lambda i} = e^{-\lambda},
with no i dependence: exponential in i means geometric ratios.

Estimate: p^\ast_6 / p^\ast_5 = 0.347/0.240 = 1.446 (the rounded values
carry the last-digit error; the exact ratio is 1.449). Then
\lambda = -\ln 1.449 \approx -0.371, matching the tuned value. Any
neighboring pair gives the same estimate, e.g.
0.240/0.165 = 1.455 \approx 1.449: constancy of the ratio is a quick
test of exponential form.

Apply the theorem with no constraints (m = 0) to a distribution over
n outcomes, and state which earlier result this recovers.

With m = 0 the exponent is empty: q(x) = e^{0}/Z = 1/Z, and
normalization forces Z = n, so q is uniform. The theorem then says
H(p) \le H(q) = \log_2 n for every pmf p, with equality only at the
uniform distribution: the upper half of the range theorem of the entropy
lesson, re-derived. The proof specializes to
H(p) = \log_2 n - D(p\,\|\,\text{uniform}), so the entropy deficit from
the ceiling is exactly a KL divergence.

Find the maximum-entropy distribution on \{0, 1\} subject to
\mathbb{E}[X] = 0.3, and the multiplier \lambda that realizes it in
the form q(x) = e^{-\lambda x}/Z. State what is special about the
feasible set here.

On a two-point alphabet, normalization and the mean pin the distribution
completely: p(1) = 0.3, p(0) = 0.7. The feasible set is a single
point, so the maximization is trivial and maximum entropy adds nothing.

The exponential form still represents it:
q(1)/q(0) = e^{-\lambda} = 0.3/0.7 = 3/7, so
\lambda = \ln(7/3) \approx 0.847. Check:
q(1) = e^{-0.847}/(1 + e^{-0.847}) = 0.429/1.429 = 0.3. The principle
has content only when the constraints leave freedom; here every feasible
distribution is the solution.

Find the maximum-entropy distribution on the non-negative integers
\{0, 1, 2, \dots\} subject to mean 2, and compute its entropy in
bits.

The constrained quantity is f(k) = k, so the solution is
q_k \propto e^{-\lambda k} = \theta^k with \theta = e^{-\lambda} \in
(0,1): a geometric distribution q_k = (1-\theta)\theta^k.

Tune \theta to the mean: \sum_k k\,q_k = \theta/(1-\theta) = 2 gives
\theta = 2/3 (and \lambda = \ln \tfrac{3}{2} \approx 0.405), so
q_k = \tfrac13 \left(\tfrac23\right)^k.

Entropy: -\log_2 q_k = -\log_2 \tfrac13 - k \log_2 \tfrac23, so

H = \mathbb{E}[-\log_2 q_K]

No distribution on \{0, 1, \dots\} with mean 2 has larger entropy.
(This is Cover & Thomas' example 12.2.4; on a countable alphabet the
existence caveat applies, but here the geometric maximizer exists.)

A system has two states with energies E_0 = 0 and E_1 = \varepsilon,
at temperature T with \varepsilon = kT \ln 3. Compute the Boltzmann
distribution and its entropy, and give the limiting distributions as
T \to 0 and T \to \infty at fixed \varepsilon.

With \beta = 1/kT, the Boltzmann weights are e^{-\beta E_0} = 1 and
e^{-\beta E_1} = e^{-\varepsilon/kT} = e^{-\ln 3} = \tfrac13. So
Z = 1 + \tfrac13 = \tfrac43 and

p_0 = \frac{1}{4/3} = \frac34, \qquad p_1 = \frac{1/3}{4/3} = \frac14 .

Entropy: H = -\tfrac34 \log_2 \tfrac34 - \tfrac14 \log_2 \tfrac14 =
0.811 bits.

T \to 0: \beta \to \infty, e^{-\beta\varepsilon} \to 0, so
p \to (1, 0): all mass on the ground state, H \to 0. T \to \infty:
\beta \to 0, both weights tend to 1, so p \to (\tfrac12, \tfrac12)
and H \to 1 bit: an infinitely weak multiplier leaves the uniform
maximum-entropy distribution.

Logits z = (1.5,\ 0.5,\ -0.5). Compute the softmax distribution and its
entropy at T = 1, then show that adding a constant c to every logit
leaves the softmax unchanged, and connect that invariance to the
partition function.

T = 1: exponentials e^{1.5} = 4.482, e^{0.5} = 1.649,
e^{-0.5} = 0.607; Z = 6.737;
p = (0.665,\ 0.245,\ 0.090). Entropy:
H = -(0.665 \log_2 0.665 + 0.245 \log_2 0.245 + 0.090 \log_2 0.090)
= 0.391 + 0.497 + 0.313 = 1.201 bits.

Shift invariance: replacing z_i by z_i + c multiplies every
exponential by e^{c/T}, so

\frac{e^{(z_i + c)/T}}{\sum_j e^{(z_j + c)/T}}

The normalizer absorbs the shift: Z is multiplied by e^{c/T} and the
ratio is untouched. In multiplier language, c shifts the constraint
function by a constant, which changes only the bookkeeping term
\ln Z, never the distribution; only logit differences carry
information. (These logits are z = (2.0, 1.0, 0.0) shifted by -0.5;
the worked example's logits (2.0, 1.0, 0.1) differ in the third entry,
which is why its p = (0.659, 0.242, 0.099) is close but not equal.)

Show that for any pmf p on \{1, \dots, 6\},
H(p) = \log_2 6 - D(p \,\|\, u) where u is the uniform distribution,
and evaluate D(p^\ast \|\, u) for the Brandeis solution
(H(p^\ast) = 2.328 bits). Interpret the number.

Expand the divergence against the uniform u_i = \tfrac16:

D(p \,\|\, u) = \sum_i p_i \log_2 \frac{p_i}{1/6}

which rearranges to the claim. For the Brandeis solution:
D(p^\ast \|\, u) = 2.585 - 2.328 = 0.257 bits.

Interpretation: 0.257 bits is the entropy the mean-4.5 constraint
removed, measured as the coding overhead of the tilted die relative to a
code built for a fair one. The constraint's information content and the
KL divergence from the unconstrained maximizer are the same number, and
the identity also shows that maximizing H over a feasible set is
minimizing D(p \,\|\, u) over it: maximum entropy is minimum divergence
from uniform.

E. T. Jaynes, "Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics," Physical Review, 106(4), 1957 — §2 states the principle and derives the multiplier solution and partition-function identities (eqs. 2-1 to 2-15); §3 recovers the Boltzmann distribution from the energy constraint; §6 frames maximum entropy as a method of reasoning; Appendix A gives the axiomatic uniqueness of H. https://bayes.wustl.edu/etj/articles/theory.1.pdf

E. T. Jaynes, "Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics" (Brandeis Summer Institute lectures, 1962), in Statistical Physics 3, K. W. Ford (ed.), W. A. Benjamin, 1963 — the source of the Brandeis dice problem with the mean-4.5 constraint.

T. M. Cover, J. A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006 — ch. 12: Theorem 12.1.1 proves the exponential form via D(p\|q) \ge 0; §12.2 works the uniform, geometric, and Gaussian examples; §12.3 exhibits the anomalous cases with no maximizer.

C. E. Shannon, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication," Bell System Technical Journal, 27, 1948 — §20: differential entropy, its coordinate dependence, and the Gaussian as the fixed-variance maximizer (property 5).

A. L. Berger, S. A. Della Pietra, V. J. Della Pietra, "A Maximum Entropy Approach to Natural Language Processing," Computational Linguistics, 22(1), 1996 — maximum-entropy classifiers under feature-expectation constraints, deriving the exponential (log-linear, softmax) model form. https://aclanthology.org/J96-1002/

documents.title: Rate-distortion theory
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › Rate-distortion theory
documents.text:
Lossy compression trades bits for fidelity, and the rate-distortion function
R(D) = min I(X;X-hat) subject to expected distortion at most D is the fewest
bits per symbol that buy reconstruction within tolerance D. This lesson
prices two crude schemes on a fair-bit stream, defines distortion measures
and the rate-distortion function, pins down the function's endpoints and
shape, computes it exactly for a Bernoulli source under Hamming distortion,
states the Gaussian squared-error result, and closes where the theory runs
in practice today: neural codecs trained to minimize R + \lambda D.

documents.title: Two crude schemes: lossy coding priced on a fair-bit stream
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › Rate-distortion theory › Two crude schemes: lossy coding priced on a fair-bit stream
documents.text:
Two crude schemes: lossy coding priced on a fair-bit stream

A source emits fair, independent bits. The lossless price is settled:
H(X) = 1 bit per symbol, the floor of
The source coding theorem, met here by copying the stream.
Now fix a budget of half a bit per symbol. Perfect reconstruction is
impossible below the floor; the open quantity is how much error the budget
forces.

Two schemes bracket the problem:

Send nothing (rate 0). The decoder outputs all zeros. Each source bit
disagrees with its reconstruction with probability \tfrac12: half the
stream is wrong.

Send every other bit (rate \tfrac12). Odd positions arrive exactly;
even positions are guessed, each wrong with probability \tfrac12.
Average error fraction:
\tfrac12 \cdot 0 + \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac14.

Rate one-half buys a 25% error fraction this way. The theory of this lesson
puts the true optimum at rate one-half near 11% errors, and section 4
computes it; the schemes that approach it code long blocks jointly instead
of deciding bit by bit.

Distortion: the error metric is part of the problem statement

Counting "wrong bits" silently chose an error metric. The general theory
takes that choice as an explicit input.

A distortion measure on a source alphabet \mathcal{X} and a
reconstruction alphabet \hat{\mathcal{X}} is a function
d : \mathcal{X} \times \hat{\mathcal{X}} \to [0, \infty). For blocks,
distortion is averaged per symbol:
d(x^n, \hat x^n) = \tfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n d(x_i, \hat x_i). The two
standard instances:

Hamming distortion for discrete alphabets:
d(x, \hat x) = 1 if x \ne \hat x, else 0. Its average is the
fraction of misreconstructed symbols.

Squared error for real alphabets: d(x, \hat x) = (x - \hat x)^2.
Its average is the mean squared error of the reconstruction.

Both crude schemes above are points in a plane: coordinates
(D, R), distortion paid against rate spent. Send-nothing sits at
(\tfrac12, 0), send-every-other-bit at (\tfrac14, \tfrac12). The
subject of this lesson is the exact boundary between the (D, R) pairs
some code achieves and the pairs none does.

The frontier for fair bits: achievable (rate, distortion) pairs lie on or above the curve. The naive rate-½ scheme pays 25% errors; the frontier pays 11% at the same rate.

Lossy compression is a two-number problem: every scheme is a point
(D, R), and the rate-distortion function is the exact lower boundary of
the achievable region.

documents.title: The rate-distortion function: the least information compatible with the budget
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › Rate-distortion theory › The rate-distortion function: the least information compatible with the budget
documents.text:
The rate-distortion function: the least information compatible with the budget

Reconstruction is a channel from the source

Whatever machinery sits between source and reconstruction, encoder, bit
stream, decoder, its end-to-end effect on single symbols is a conditional
distribution p(\hat x \mid x): for each source symbol, the probabilities
of the reconstructions it may become. This conditional distribution is
called the test channel. The direction matters: \hat X is computed
from X, so X \to \hat X is a processing step, not a generative model
of the source, and the data-processing inequality of
The data-processing inequality applies to everything
downstream of X.

The rate this channel needs is measured by the mutual information
I(X; \hat X) of Mutual information: the compressed file
is a bottleneck between X and \hat X, and a file of R bits per
symbol cannot carry more than R bits of information about the source
into the reconstruction (the converse below makes this exact). Minimizing
rate therefore means choosing the test channel that satisfies the
distortion budget with the least mutual information.

For a source X \sim p(x) and a distortion measure d, the
rate-distortion function is

R(D) \;=\; \min_{p(\hat x \mid x)\,:\; \mathbb{E}[d(X, \hat X)] \le D}\; I(X; \hat X),

the minimum taken over all test channels whose expected distortion,
\mathbb{E}[d] = \sum_{x, \hat x} p(x)\, p(\hat x \mid x)\, d(x, \hat x),
stays within the budget D.

The objective dissected: search over test channels, pay rate in mutual information, obey the distortion budget.

The theorem: the minimum is achievable and tight

The definition is a formula about single-symbol distributions. Shannon's
theorem, 1948
(Part V, Theorem 21) with the discrete case completed in his 1959 paper,
gives it operational force.

For an i.i.d. source X \sim p(x) and a bounded distortion measure d,
R(D) is the boundary of achievability: for every \varepsilon > 0
there exist block codes of rate R(D) + \varepsilon whose expected
distortion is at most D + \varepsilon for all sufficiently large block
length, and no sequence of codes with rate below R(D) meets the budget
D.

Sketch; the full argument is Cover & Thomas §10.4 (converse) and §10.5
(achievability).

Converse. A rate-R code compresses X^n into an index
W \in \{1, \dots, 2^{nR}\} and reconstructs \hat X^n from W alone,
so X^n \to W \to \hat X^n is a Markov chain. The data-processing
inequality (The data-processing inequality) and the entropy
bound on W give
I(X^n; \hat X^n) \le I(X^n; W) \le H(W) \le nR. For an i.i.d. source
the block information single-letterizes,
I(X^n; \hat X^n) \ge \sum_{i=1}^n I(X_i; \hat X_i), each term is at
least R(\mathbb{E}[d(X_i, \hat X_i)]) by the definition of R as a
minimum, and convexity of R(D) (next section) pulls the average
through: nR \ge n\,R\bigl(\mathbb{E}[d(X^n, \hat X^n)]\bigr). A code
meeting budget D therefore spends at least R(D).

Achievability. Fix the minimizing test channel and draw a codebook of
2^{n(R(D) + \varepsilon)} reconstruction words i.i.d. from the induced
marginal p(\hat x). For a typical source block, with high probability
at least one codeword is jointly typical with it, and joint typicality
forces per-symbol distortion near \mathbb{E}[d] \le D. Encoding
transmits the index of that codeword. The calculation that
2^{nI(X;\hat X)} codewords suffice is the covering counterpart of the
random-coding argument sketched for
The noisy-channel coding theorem.

The theorem is a statement about limits, not about any particular
quantizer: R(D) is approached by coding long blocks jointly, and every
practical one-shot scheme sits strictly above the curve, as the
send-every-other-bit point did.

R(D) = \min I(X; \hat X) subject to \mathbb{E}[d] \le D is the exact
price of fidelity: achievable in the block-length limit, unbeatable by
any code.

Capacity's mirror image: the same quantity, the opposite extreme

Channel capacity defined
C = \max_{p(x)} I(X;Y): the channel is fixed and the input distribution
is tuned to push the most information through. Rate-distortion flips
every role: the source p(x) is fixed and the channel
p(\hat x \mid x) is tuned to let the least information through
while staying within the distortion budget. Communication maximizes
mutual information; compression minimizes it. The two problems are dual,
and one algorithm, Blahut–Arimoto, alternates the same two updates to
compute either function numerically
(Blahut 1972; treatment in
Polyanskiy & Wu).

One quantity, two extremes: communication tunes the input to maximize I; compression tunes the channel to minimize it.

documents.title: Endpoints and shape: from H(X) to zero, convex in between
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › Rate-distortion theory › Endpoints and shape: from H(X) to zero, convex in between
documents.text:
Endpoints and shape: from H(X) to zero, convex in between

Three structural facts hold for every source, before any specific curve
is computed.

For Hamming distortion (and any d with d(x, \hat x) = 0 exactly when
\hat x = x, on a common alphabet):

R(0) = H(X): the zero-tolerance corner is lossless source coding.

R(D) is non-increasing in D, and R(D) = 0 exactly when
D \ge D_{\max} = \min_{\hat x} \mathbb{E}[d(X, \hat x)], the
distortion of the best constant guess.

R(D) is convex on [0, D_{\max}].

(1) Budget D = 0 forces P(X \ne \hat X) = 0, so
I(X; \hat X) = I(X; X) = H(X)
(Mutual information, self-information).

(2) A larger D only enlarges the set of admissible test channels,
so the minimum cannot rise. If D \ge D_{\max}, the constant channel
\hat X \equiv \arg\min_{\hat x} \mathbb{E}[d(X, \hat x)] meets the
budget with I = 0. If D < D_{\max}, zero rate is out of reach:
I(X; \hat X) = 0 makes \hat X independent of X, and then
\mathbb{E}[d] = \sum_{\hat x} p(\hat x)\, \mathbb{E}[d(X, \hat x)] \ge
D_{\max} > D, violating the budget.

(3) Let channels q_1, q_2 attain R(D_1), R(D_2). The blended
channel q_\lambda = \lambda q_1 + (1 - \lambda) q_2 has expected
distortion exactly \lambda D_1 + (1-\lambda) D_2, since
\mathbb{E}[d] is linear in the channel, and mutual information is
convex in p(\hat x \mid x) for fixed p(x) (Cover & Thomas Theorem
2.7.4), so
I_{q_\lambda} \le \lambda R(D_1) + (1 - \lambda) R(D_2). The minimum
at the blended budget is no larger. This is Lemma 10.4.1 of Cover &
Thomas; exercise 5 reaches the same conclusion operationally, by
time-sharing two codes.

The curve therefore always runs from the lossless corner
(0, H(X)) down to (D_{\max}, 0), decreasing and convex, exactly the
shape shaded in the first figure. The next two sections fill in the only
two cases with standard closed forms.

R(D) interpolates between the two prices already known: the source
coding theorem at D = 0 and free majority-guessing at
D = D_{\max}, convexly in between.

documents.title: Bernoulli(p) under Hamming distortion: R(D) = H(p) − H(D)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › Rate-distortion theory › Bernoulli(p) under Hamming distortion: R(D) = H(p) − H(D)
documents.text:
Bernoulli(p) under Hamming distortion: R(D) = H(p) − H(D)

The closed form

For a biased-bit source the minimization has an exact solution, one of
the two classical closed forms
(Cover & Thomas
§10.3.1).

For X \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p) under Hamming distortion,

R(D) =

where H(\cdot) is the binary entropy function of
Entropy.

Take p \le \tfrac12 (relabel otherwise), so \min(p, 1-p) = p and
D \le p \le \tfrac12.

Converse: no admissible channel beats H(p) - H(D). Let
p(\hat x \mid x) satisfy P(X \ne \hat X) = \mathbb{E}[d] \le D.
Write the error indicator Z = X \oplus \hat X (XOR). Given \hat X,
knowing Z is knowing X, so
H(X \mid \hat X) = H(Z \mid \hat X) \le H(Z): conditioning cannot
raise entropy
(Joint and conditional entropy). Z is a binary
variable with P(Z = 1) \le D \le \tfrac12, and the binary entropy
function increases on [0, \tfrac12], so H(Z) \le H(D). Chaining:

I(X; \hat X) = H(X) - H(X \mid \hat X)

Achievability: one channel meets the bound. Build the joint
distribution backwards. Let \hat X \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi) with
\pi = \tfrac{p - D}{1 - 2D}, and let X = \hat X \oplus Z with
Z \sim \text{Bernoulli}(D) independent of \hat X: the
reconstruction passes through a binary symmetric channel with crossover
D to produce the source. The marginal checks out:
P(X = 1) = \pi(1 - D) + (1 - \pi) D = D + \pi(1 - 2D) = p. The
distortion is P(X \ne \hat X) = P(Z = 1) = D, on budget. The rate:

I(X; \hat X) = H(X) - H(X \mid \hat X) = H(p) - H(D),

since given \hat X the only remaining uncertainty in X is the
independent flip Z. For D \le p \le \tfrac12 the parameter \pi
lies in [0, 1], so the construction is a valid distribution, and the
converse bound is attained.

The formula reads as an information ledger: H(p) bits describe the
source exactly; a tolerated error pattern of rate D carries H(D)
bits; the encoder must pay only the difference. The sequence below
assembles the curve for p = 0.3.

R(D) = H(p) − H(D) built in three moves for p = 0.3: start at the lossless corner, subtract the bits the tolerated errors carry, land on zero at D = p.

Step through the three frames and check the arithmetic at D = 0.1:
frame 1 puts the corner at H(0.3) \approx 0.881 bits, frame 2 subtracts
H(0.1) \approx 0.469, and frame 3's curve accordingly passes through
R(0.1) \approx 0.412 before hitting zero at D = p = 0.3.

The flat tail is exact, not approximate. Once D \ge \min(p, 1-p), the
constant guess "always output the majority symbol" errs on a
\min(p, 1-p) fraction of symbols and costs zero bits; tolerating
that much error makes compression free.

Worked: the fair source, and the opener's gap closed

For p = \tfrac12: R(D) = 1 - H(D) on [0, \tfrac12].

Rate one-half. Solve 1 - H(D) = 0.5: H(D) = 0.5, so
D \approx 0.110, since
H(0.11) = 0.11 \cdot 3.184 + 0.89 \cdot 0.168 \approx 0.500. The
optimum at the crude scheme's rate misreconstructs 11% of bits, not
25%.

The crude scheme's distortion, priced. At D = 0.25 the curve gives
R = 1 - H(0.25) = 1 - 0.811 = 0.189 bits. The error fraction the naive
scheme bought with 0.5 bits is available for 0.189: the naive scheme
overspends by a factor of 2.6.

Bounds check. R(0) = 1 - H(0) = 1 = H(X), the lossless rate; and
R(0.5) = 1 - H(0.5) = 0, the free all-zeros guess.

For p = 0.25: H(0.25) = 0.811 bits, so R(D) = 0.811 - H(D) on
[0, 0.25].

At D = 0.1:
R = 0.811 - 0.469 = 0.342 bits per symbol, a 58\% saving over the
lossless 0.811 in exchange for errors on one symbol in ten.

The curve ends at D_{\max} = \min(0.25, 0.75) = 0.25: always guessing
0 errs exactly on the 25\% of symbols that are 1, at zero rate.
R(0.25) = 0.811 - H(0.25) = 0, consistent.

R(D) = H(p) - H(D) up to D = \min(p, 1-p), then exactly zero:
tolerated errors refund their own entropy, and once the budget covers the
minority symbol, the majority guess compresses for free.

documents.title: The Gaussian source under squared error: R(D) = ½ log₂(σ²/D)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › Rate-distortion theory › The Gaussian source under squared error: R(D) = ½ log₂(σ²/D)
documents.text:
The Gaussian source under squared error: R(D) = ½ log₂(σ²/D)
