The second classical closed form is continuous. It is stated here, not
derived: it is this course's one use of differential entropy beyond the
remark in The maximum entropy principle, and the derivation
(Cover & Thomas §10.3.2) runs the Bernoulli converse's pattern with
differential entropies in place of discrete ones.

For X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) under squared-error distortion,

R(D) =

Two flags on the statement. First, discrete intuitions do not transfer
silently: differential entropy can be negative and changes under a change
of coordinates, but R(D) is a difference of differential entropies,
and the coordinate-dependent terms cancel, so the rate is well-defined.
Second, the endpoints behave like the discrete case at one end only:
D_{\max} = \sigma^2 is the squared error of the best constant guess
\hat X = \mathbb{E}[X] = 0, but as D \to 0 the rate grows without
bound, because a continuous value needs infinitely many bits to
reconstruct exactly.

The Gaussian curve for σ² = 1: R = ½ log₂(1/D). Each extra bit divides the mean squared error by 4 — the 6 dB per bit rule.

Inverting the formula gives the working form D(R) = \sigma^2 \cdot
4^{-R}: each additional bit divides the mean squared error by 4,
halving the root-mean-square error, a drop of 6.02 dB. Audio engineers
know this as the 6 dB per bit rule for quantizer resolution. At
\sigma^2 = 1: one bit per sample leaves D = 0.25, two bits leave
0.0625, eight bits leave 1.5 \times 10^{-5}.

Load the fair source preset and drag D to 0.11: the rate readout
should land at 0.50 bits, the worked example's number. On the biased
source preset (p = 0.25), verify the endpoints R \to 0.811 as
D \to 0 and R = 0 from D = 0.25 on. Then toggle to the Gaussian
curve with \sigma^2 = 1 and read the rate at D = 0.25 and
D = 0.0625: the readouts should differ by exactly one bit.

The closed form has a geometric reading, the covering picture of
Polyanskiy & Wu's lecture notes. A typical length-n Gaussian block lies
near a sphere of radius \sqrt{n \sigma^2}; a reconstruction word covers,
within squared error D per symbol, a ball of radius \sqrt{nD}. A
codebook meeting budget D must cover the source sphere with such balls,
and volumes in n dimensions scale as radius^n, so the codebook needs
on the order of
\bigl(\sqrt{n\sigma^2} / \sqrt{nD}\bigr)^n = (\sigma^2 / D)^{n/2}
words: exactly 2^{n \cdot \frac12 \log_2(\sigma^2 / D)}, the theorem's
rate. Compression is sphere covering, where channel coding
(The noisy-channel coding theorem) was sphere packing.

R(D) = \tfrac12 \log_2(\sigma^2 / D) for the Gaussian source: rate buys
error on a log scale, one bit per halving of RMS error, with no finite
rate reaching D = 0.

documents.title: The trade-off made trainable: neural codecs minimize R + λD
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › Rate-distortion theory › The trade-off made trainable: neural codecs minimize R + λD
documents.text:
The trade-off made trainable: neural codecs minimize R + λD

The Lagrangian reading of the curve

Because R(D) is convex and decreasing, its constrained definition has
an unconstrained twin: every point of the curve minimizes

R + \lambda D

for some multiplier \lambda \ge 0, namely the negative slope of the
curve at that point, and sweeping \lambda from large to small walks the
solution from the low-distortion corner toward the zero-rate tail. This
is the same constraint-to-multiplier trade seen for
The maximum entropy principle: a hard budget becomes a price.

The objective, implemented with networks

Ballé, Laparra & Simoncelli (2017)
train image codecs on exactly this objective. An encoder network maps the
image x to a latent vector, which is quantized by rounding and
entropy-coded; a decoder network maps the quantized latent \hat y back
to a reconstruction \hat x. The loss is

\mathcal{L} \;=\;

where the rate term is the cross-entropy of the quantized latent under a
learned prior p(\hat y), which by
Compression as prediction is the achievable size of the
entropy-coded bitstream. One trained model realizes one point of the
codec's rate-distortion curve; retraining across a grid of \lambda
values sweeps it, exactly as the multiplier sweeps the theoretical curve.

A neural codec is the rate-distortion objective made trainable: networks as encoder and decoder, entropy-coded latent as the rate, λ selecting the point on the curve.

Rounding has zero gradient almost everywhere, so the objective as stated
cannot be trained directly. The paper's fix is a uniform-noise
relaxation: during training, rounding is replaced by adding noise drawn
uniformly from (-\tfrac12, \tfrac12), which matches the marginal
statistics of quantization error, makes both terms differentiable, and
is dropped at test time in favor of true rounding plus arithmetic coding.

Ballé et al. §3.1 push the correspondence further: the uniform-noise
relaxation of R + \lambda D coincides, term for term, with the negative
evidence lower bound of a variational autoencoder whose approximate
posterior is uniform, the rate term matching the KL term of the ELBO
(KL divergence) and the distortion term matching the
log-likelihood under a Gaussian observation model. Training a codec and
training a VAE at fixed \lambda are the same optimization; generative
modeling and lossy compression meet at this objective.

One assumption has run silently through the whole lesson: someone chose
d. Hamming and squared error are declarations about which differences
matter, and a codec optimized against squared error will spend bits on
imperceptible pixel deviations while discarding structure a human
notices. When no hand-picked distortion measure is defensible, the
constraint itself can be replaced: keep not "low d" but "information
about a target variable", trading I(X;T) against I(T;Y). That
objective is the information bottleneck of
Tishby, Pereira & Bialek, and
The information bottleneck develops it as rate-distortion
with the distortion measure derived rather than assumed.

\min R + \lambda D is rate-distortion theory as a loss function:
neural codecs train it end to end, \lambda picks the operating point,
and the one hand-picked ingredient left, the distortion measure, is what
the information bottleneck later removes.

documents.title: Exercises
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › Rate-distortion theory › Exercises
documents.text:
Exercises

For the fair-bit source, compute R(D) at D = 0.02, D = 0.05, and
D = 0.25, using
H(0.02) \approx 0.141 and H(0.05) \approx 0.286. State what fraction
of the lossless rate each tolerance saves, and where the savings grow
fastest.

R(D) = 1 - H(D) for the fair source.

R(0.02) = 1 - 0.141 = 0.859 bits: a 14.1\% saving.
R(0.05) = 1 - 0.286 = 0.714 bits: a 28.6\% saving.
R(0.25) = 1 - 0.811 = 0.189 bits: an 81.1\% saving.

The saving at tolerance D is exactly H(D), and the binary entropy
function is steepest near 0 (its slope \log_2 \tfrac{1-D}{D} grows
without bound as D \to 0): the first percent of tolerated error buys
more rate than any later percent. Raising the tolerance from 2\% to
5\% (hardly a visible change in fidelity) doubles the saving.

A sensor emits X \sim \text{Bernoulli}(0.1). Compute R(0),
D_{\max}, and R(0.05), using H(0.1) \approx 0.469 and
H(0.05) \approx 0.286. Name the zero-rate scheme that attains
D_{\max}.

R(0) = H(0.1) \approx 0.469 bits: the lossless rate of the 90/10
source.

D_{\max} = \min(0.1, 0.9) = 0.1: the constant guess \hat X \equiv 0
(the majority symbol) errs exactly when X = 1, a 10\% error
fraction, at zero rate. Hence R(D) = 0 for D \ge 0.1.

R(0.05) = H(0.1) - H(0.05) \approx 0.469 - 0.286 = 0.183 bits.
Tolerating errors on one symbol in twenty cuts the rate to 39\% of
lossless; the whole curve lives below half a bit.

A Gaussian source has \sigma^2 = 16. Compute the rate for budgets
D = 1 and D = 0.25, the budget reachable at 8 bits per sample, and
the number of additional bits needed to halve the RMS error from any
operating point.

R(1) = \tfrac12 \log_2 16 = 2 bits per sample.
R(0.25) = \tfrac12 \log_2 64 = 3 bits per sample.

At 8 bits: D = \sigma^2 \cdot 4^{-8} = 16 / 65536 \approx 2.4 \times
10^{-4}.

Halving RMS error quarters the squared error, and
R(D/4) - R(D) = \tfrac12 \log_2 4 = 1: exactly one extra bit,
from any starting point, the 6 dB per bit rule. Consistency check
between the first two answers: D fell by a factor 4 and the rate
rose by one bit.

Verify the achievability construction for the fair source. Let
\hat X \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\tfrac12), let
Z \sim \text{Bernoulli}(D) independent of \hat X with
D \le \tfrac12, and set X = \hat X \oplus Z. Show that X is a fair
bit, that the expected Hamming distortion is D, and that
I(X; \hat X) = 1 - H(D).

Marginal. P(X = 1) = P(\hat X = 1)P(Z = 0) + P(\hat X = 0)P(Z = 1)
= \tfrac12(1 - D) + \tfrac12 D = \tfrac12: fair, as required
(\pi = \tfrac{p - D}{1 - 2D} = \tfrac12 at p = \tfrac12).

Distortion. X \ne \hat X exactly when Z = 1:
\mathbb{E}[d] = P(Z = 1) = D, meeting the budget with equality.

Rate. I(X; \hat X) = H(X) - H(X \mid \hat X). The marginal gives
H(X) = 1. Given \hat X = \hat x, the source is
X = \hat x \oplus Z with Z independent of \hat X, so the
conditional distribution of X is a D-flip of a known value:
H(X \mid \hat X = \hat x) = H(D) for both values, hence
H(X \mid \hat X) = H(D) and I(X; \hat X) = 1 - H(D) = R(D). The
channel achieves the curve, matching the converse bound.

Prove that the achievable region is convex by time-sharing, without any
information quantities: given a code achieving (D_1, R_1) and a code
achieving (D_2, R_2), construct, for each \lambda \in [0, 1], a
scheme achieving \bigl(\lambda D_1 + (1-\lambda) D_2,\; \lambda R_1 +
(1-\lambda) R_2\bigr). Conclude that R(D), the region's lower
boundary, is convex.

Split the source stream into blocks and apply code 1 to a fraction
\lambda of them and code 2 to the rest (a fixed, position-based split,
so the decoder knows which code to apply where; no signaling bits are
needed in the limit).

Rate. Bits are spent at R_1 on a \lambda fraction of symbols and
R_2 on the rest: \lambda R_1 + (1 - \lambda) R_2 bits per symbol
overall.

Distortion. Per-symbol distortion averages the same way:
\lambda D_1 + (1 - \lambda) D_2.

Every convex combination of achievable points is therefore achievable.
A region closed under convex combinations has a convex lower boundary:
if R(D) ever bulged above a chord, time-sharing the chord's endpoint
codes would achieve points below the function, contradicting the
converse. Hence R\bigl(\lambda D_1 + (1-\lambda) D_2\bigr) \le
\lambda R(D_1) + (1 - \lambda) R(D_2).

The optimal fair-source test channel at D = 0.25 has the joint table
P(X{=}0, \hat X{=}0) = P(X{=}1, \hat X{=}1) = \tfrac38 and
P(X{=}0, \hat X{=}1) = P(X{=}1, \hat X{=}0) = \tfrac18. Using the
recipes of Mutual information (marginals from row and
column sums, conditional entropy as an average of column entropies),
compute \mathbb{E}[d] and I(X; \hat X) from the table, and check the
result against the Bernoulli formula.

Distortion. The off-diagonal mass is
\tfrac18 + \tfrac18 = \tfrac14: \mathbb{E}[d] = 0.25, on budget.

Marginals. Row and column sums all equal \tfrac12:
H(X) = H(\hat X) = 1 bit.

Conditional entropy. Given \hat X = 0 (probability \tfrac12),
the column (\tfrac38, \tfrac18) renormalizes to
(\tfrac34, \tfrac14), entropy H(0.25) \approx 0.811 bits; the
\hat X = 1 column gives the mirror image, the same entropy. So
H(X \mid \hat X) = 0.811 bits.

Mutual information.
I(X; \hat X) = H(X) - H(X \mid \hat X) = 1 - 0.811 = 0.189 bits.

Check. R(0.25) = 1 - H(0.25) = 0.189 bits: the table attains the
minimum, so it is an optimal test channel. (It is the exercise-4
construction at D = 0.25, written as a joint table.)

Prove in general that R(D) = 0 for D \ge D_{\max} =
\min_{\hat x} \mathbb{E}[d(X, \hat x)] and that R(D) > 0 for
D < D_{\max}, and evaluate D_{\max} for (a) X \sim
\text{Bernoulli}(p) under Hamming distortion and (b) X \sim
\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) under squared error.

Zero rate suffices for D \ge D_{\max}. Let \hat x^\ast attain
the minimum in D_{\max}. The constant channel
\hat X \equiv \hat x^\ast has I(X; \hat X) = 0 (a constant is
independent of everything) and expected distortion D_{\max} \le D: an
admissible channel with zero information, so the minimum is 0.

Zero rate fails for D < D_{\max}. I(X; \hat X) = 0 forces
independence (Mutual information, nonnegativity's
equality case). Under independence,
\mathbb{E}[d] = \sum_{\hat x} p(\hat x)\,\mathbb{E}[d(X, \hat x)], an
average of terms each at least D_{\max}, so
\mathbb{E}[d] \ge D_{\max} > D: no zero-information channel meets the
budget, hence R(D) > 0.

(a) The constant \hat x errs with probability p (choosing
\hat x = 0) or 1 - p (choosing \hat x = 1); the better choice is
the majority symbol: D_{\max} = \min(p, 1-p).

(b) For a constant c,
\mathbb{E}[(X - c)^2] = \sigma^2 + (\mu - c)^2, minimized at
c = \mu: D_{\max} = \sigma^2, attained by always outputting the
mean.

C. E. Shannon, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication," Bell System Technical Journal, 27, 1948 — Part V, §§27–29: fidelity criteria as averaged pairwise distortion, the rate R_1 = \min I under a fidelity bound (Theorem 21), and the Gaussian/RMS closed form.

C. E. Shannon, "Coding Theorems for a Discrete Source with a Fidelity Criterion," IRE National Convention Record, Part 4, 1959 — the complete discrete rate-distortion theorem, achievability and converse.

T. M. Cover, J. A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006 — ch. 10: §10.2 definitions, §10.3.1 the Bernoulli/Hamming form, §10.3.2 the Gaussian/squared-error form, Lemma 10.4.1 convexity, §10.4 converse, §10.5 achievability.

Y. Polyanskiy, Y. Wu, Lecture Notes on Information Theory (MIT 6.441 / UIUC ECE 563), 2016 — chs. 23–25: the rate-distortion definitions, the two closed forms (§25.1), the sphere-covering picture, and the Blahut–Arimoto algorithm. https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/itlectures_v5.pdf

R. E. Blahut, "Computation of Channel Capacity and Rate-Distortion Functions," IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 18(4), 1972 — the alternating-minimization algorithm computing C and R(D), the duality made computational.

J. Ballé, V. Laparra, E. P. Simoncelli, "End-to-end Optimized Image Compression," ICLR 2017 — learned image codecs trained on R + \lambda D, the uniform-noise relaxation of quantization, and (§3.1) the equivalence of the relaxed objective with a variational autoencoder loss. https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.01704

N. Tishby, F. C. Pereira, W. Bialek, "The Information Bottleneck Method," Proc. 37th Allerton Conference, 1999 — §1: the bottleneck objective introduced as rate-distortion with the hand-picked distortion measure replaced by relevant information. https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0004057

documents.title: Minimum description length
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › Minimum description length
documents.text:
Model selection is a compression problem: the best hypothesis for a dataset
minimizes the total description length L(H) + L(D|H) — the bits to state the
model plus the bits to state the data given the model. This lesson makes the
principle computable and runs it. The route: the retreat from shortest
programs to a fixed model class; fit measured as a code length; the two-part
principle and why the model term blocks overfitting; a complete selection
computed by hand on a 41-bit record; the (k/2)\log_2 n cost of parameters;
the asymmetric pricing of the two selection errors; and the same accounting
applied to trained neural networks.

documents.title: From the uncomputable floor to a computable rule
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › Minimum description length › From the uncomputable floor to a computable rule
documents.text:
From the uncomputable floor to a computable rule

Kolmogorov complexity established the ideal: the shortest
description of the data over all programs, well-defined and uncomputable,
with the two-part form K(\mu) - \log_2 \mu(D) as its model-selection
reading. The minimum description length (MDL) principle of
Rissanen (1978) is the
computable retreat: replace "all programs" by a fixed, searchable class
of candidate descriptions, and minimize length within the class.

Three 24-bit strings under one description scheme

The retreat is concrete. Fix one scheme for describing 24-bit strings:
first state the number of ones k, using
\lceil \log_2 25 \rceil = 5 bits; then state which arrangement, an index
into the \binom{24}{k} strings with that count, costing
\log_2 \binom{24}{k} bits. Apply it to three strings:

x_1 = 000000000000000000000000: k = 0, and only one such string
exists. Cost: 5 + 0 = 5 bits.

x_2 = 101101001110100001011010: k = 12, and
\log_2 \binom{24}{12} = \log_2 2{,}704{,}156 \approx 21.4 bits.
Cost: 26.4 bits, worse than the 24 literal bits. The scheme has
nothing to grip.

x_3 = 010000100001000010010001: k = 6, and
\log_2 \binom{24}{6} = \log_2 134{,}596 \approx 17.0 bits.
Cost: 5 + 17.0 = 22.0 bits, beating the literal string.

One scheme, three verdicts: 5 bits, 24 bits (literal wins), 22 bits. The count is the model part; the index is the data part.

The scheme is a miniature model class. The count k is a hypothesis
about the string's statistics; the index is the data described given that
hypothesis. x_1 has extreme structure and compresses to almost nothing;
x_2 has none, and the honest answer is the literal string; x_3 has
statistical structure only, no period and no formula, and still saves two
bits. That third case, structure visible only as a probability bias, is the
kind of regularity model selection deals in.

Within a fixed model class, description length is computable, and a string
is exactly as compressible as the statistical structure the class can
express: MDL is the two-part Kolmogorov idea with "all programs" cut down
to a menu that can be searched.

documents.title: Fit is a code length: L(D|H) = −log₂ P(D|H)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › Minimum description length › Fit is a code length: L(D|H) = −log₂ P(D|H)
documents.text:
Fit is a code length: L(D|H) = −log₂ P(D|H)

A hypothesis in this lesson is a probability model: H assigns the
observed data a probability P(D \mid H). The coding module priced exactly
this object. By the code–probability correspondence of
The source coding theorem, a code matched to H spends
-\log_2 P(D \mid H) bits on D, no code matched to anything else does
better on average, and an arithmetic coder realizes the number within two
bits (Compression as prediction). Define therefore

L(D \mid H) \;=\; -\log_2 P(D \mid H),

the fit term: the bits needed to state the data, given that both ends
hold the model H.

Take x_3 above (24 bits, 6 ones) and three Bernoulli hypotheses,
each claiming the bits are i.i.d. with P(1) = \theta:

\theta = \tfrac12: every bit costs 1 bit of code, so
L(x_3 \mid H) = 24.0 bits.

\theta = \tfrac14: each one costs -\log_2 \tfrac14 = 2 bits, each zero
-\log_2 \tfrac34 = 0.415 bits, so
L = 6 \times 2 + 18 \times 0.415 = 12 + 7.47 = 19.5 bits.

\theta = 0.9: each one costs 0.152 bits, but each zero costs
-\log_2 0.1 = 3.322 bits, so
L = 6 \times 0.152 + 18 \times 3.322 = 0.91 + 59.79 = 60.7 bits.

The hypothesis that rates the data most probable encodes it most cheaply;
a confident hypothesis pointed the wrong way is a catastrophe in bits.
Minimizing L(D \mid H) over \theta is precisely maximum likelihood,
and the minimizer here is the empirical rate \hat\theta = 6/24 = 1/4.

The fit term is also a familiar quantity from the machine-learning module:
-\log_2 P(D \mid H) is H's log-loss on D, the summed surprisal that
Cross-entropy identified as the cross-entropy training
objective. Fit measured in bits, fit measured by likelihood, and fit
measured by the loss curve are one number.

L(D \mid H) = -\log_2 P(D \mid H): assigning the data high probability
and encoding the data cheaply are the same property, so maximum likelihood
is minimum fit-bits.

documents.title: The two-part principle: charge the model its bits
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › Minimum description length › The two-part principle: charge the model its bits
documents.text:
The two-part principle: charge the model its bits

Fit alone cannot select a model. Enlarging the hypothesis class can only
raise the maximal P(D \mid H), and the limit is degenerate: the
memorizer H_D, the hypothesis "the source emits exactly D", achieves
P(D \mid H_D) = 1 and L(D \mid H_D) = 0 for any D whatsoever.
Selection by fit is maximum likelihood run over an unbounded menu, and it
always ends at a memorizer. This is overfitting stated in coding terms.

The repair is to price the hypothesis too. Stating H_D means stating
D: hypotheses live in a prefix-free code of their own, and the counting
argument of Kolmogorov complexity applies to it verbatim,
so fewer than 2^{n-c} of the 2^n strings' memorizers can be described
in under n - c bits. For all but a vanishing fraction of datasets,
L(H_D) + 0 is no better than the literal data. The bits pushed out of
the fit term reappear in the model term.

Let \mathcal{H} be a countable class of hypotheses, each assigning the
data a probability P(D \mid H), and fix a prefix-free code over
\mathcal{H} with lengths L(H), chosen before seeing the data. The
two-part description length of D under H is

L(H) \;+\; L(D \mid H) \;=\; L(H) - \log_2 P(D \mid H),

and the (crude) MDL principle selects

H^\ast \;=\; \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{H \in \mathcal{H}} \;\bigl[\, L(H) + L(D \mid H) \,\bigr].

For parametric hypotheses H = (k, \theta), the model term itself splits:
L(H) = L(k) + L(\theta \mid k), the structure plus its parameters.

The two-part message is literal: model bits, then data-given-model bits. Selection compares total lengths.

The definition is honest coding, not bookkeeping: the two parts
concatenate into one decodable message.

If the lengths L(H) belong to a prefix-free code over \mathcal{H} and,
for each H, the data lengths are L(D \mid H) = -\log_2 P(D \mid H),
then the concatenated descriptions are uniquely decodable and their total
lengths satisfy the Kraft budget:

\sum_{H} \sum_{D} 2^{-[L(H) + L(D \mid H)]} \;\le\; 1 .

Decoding is sequential: the hypothesis code is prefix-free, so the
receiver reads it to completion unambiguously, learns H, and then knows
which data code governs the remaining bits. For the budget,
\sum_H 2^{-L(H)} \le 1 by the Kraft inequality of
The Kraft inequality, and for each H,
\sum_D 2^{-L(D \mid H)} = \sum_D P(D \mid H) \le 1; the double sum
factors as \sum_H 2^{-L(H)} \sum_D P(D \mid H) \le 1. By the
achievability direction of the Kraft inequality, an actual prefix code
with these total lengths exists.

The clause "chosen before seeing the data" is load-bearing. A hypothesis
code tuned after looking at D can assign the best-fitting H a
one-bit codeword, driving L(H) to zero and collapsing the criterion
back to maximum likelihood; the smuggled bits are real but hidden in the
choice of code. Grünwald's tutorial (§2.4) makes the same point for
n-dependent parameter codes. A fixed code is what makes the total an
honest message length that a receiver could actually have decoded.

The Kraft budget gives the theorem a Bayesian reading, worked out in
MacKay's chapter 28: the
weights 2^{-L(H)} form a (sub-)prior over hypotheses, P(D \mid H) is
the likelihood, and
2^{-[L(H) + L(D\mid H)]} = 2^{-L(H)} P(D \mid H), so minimizing the
two-part length is maximizing prior times likelihood: MAP estimation in
coding units. MacKay's Occam factor, the probability mass of parameter
settings that remain consistent with the data, is the Bayesian face of
the parameter-precision argument two sections below: a model with more
adjustable parameters spreads its prior thinner, exactly as a longer
L(H) spends more bits. The two formalisms diverge in their fine print
(MDL's refined form optimizes worst-case regret, not posterior belief),
but at the level of this lesson they compute the same trade.

Fit bits alone always elect a memorizer; adding L(H) makes the election
honest, because bits removed from L(D \mid H) by enriching the
hypothesis reappear in L(H) unless the structure is genuinely in the
data.

documents.title: Curve fitting: the U-shape on one scatter
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › Minimum description length › Curve fitting: the U-shape on one scatter
documents.text:
Curve fitting: the U-shape on one scatter

The canonical picture, from §1.2 of
Grünwald's tutorial, is polynomial
regression. Take n = 10 points (x_i, y_i) measured to fixed precision.
A candidate hypothesis is a polynomial f of degree k plus Gaussian
noise; its two parts are L(H), the k + 1 coefficients stated to the
precision they need, and L(D \mid H) = \sum_i -\log_2 P(y_i \mid f(x_i)),
which up to a constant set by the recording precision behaves as
\tfrac{n}{2}\log_2 \hat\sigma^2: every halving of the mean squared
residual saves n/2 bits.

The two ends of the degree axis fail in opposite directions. Degree 0
states one coefficient and pays for every residual, in full, forever.
Degree n - 1 threads all ten points, drives every residual below the
recording precision, and owes essentially nothing in fit; its ten
finely-tuned coefficients dominate the total instead.

One scatter, three candidates: the constant underpays in model bits and overpays in fit; the interpolator does the reverse; the quadratic minimizes the sum.

Step through the four frames watching only the two bars: the blue fit bar
shrinks monotonically with degree, the amber model bar grows
monotonically, and the printed total falls from 78 to 50 before rising
back to 80. The minimum sits at degree 2, the trend actually present in
the points.

Drag k upward from 0 and find the degree where the total bottoms out;
it should match the sweet-spot preset. Then push k to the interpolating
preset and confirm the signature of overfitting in coding terms:
L(D \mid H) pinned near zero while the total climbs past the k = 0
underfit.

As the candidate grows richer, L(D \mid H) falls and L(H) climbs: the
total is U-shaped in model complexity, and its minimum, at neither end, is
the MDL choice.

documents.title: A selection by hand: Markov orders on a 41-bit record
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › Minimum description length › A selection by hand: Markov orders on a 41-bit record
documents.text:
A selection by hand: Markov orders on a 41-bit record

The polynomial picture is qualitative; this section is exact. The data is a
41-bit record from a sensor that alternates but occasionally repeats a
bit, printed in groups of ten:

0101011010 0101010101 0101010010 1010110101 0

Sufficient statistics, checkable by tallying the string: 20 ones and
21 zeros; among the 40 adjacent pairs, a 0 is followed by 1
eighteen times and by 0 twice, and a 1 is followed by 0 eighteen
times and by 1 twice.

The candidate class is the Markov chains of order k, written B(k): the
next bit's distribution depends on the previous k bits, giving 2^k
parameters \theta_{1 \mid \text{context}}. The hypothesis code, fixed in
advance: the order k in unary (k + 1 bits), then each parameter as one
of 64 evenly spaced values (6 bits per parameter). Initial symbols
without a full context are charged 1 bit each.

Order 0 (a Bernoulli coin, one parameter). Best fit at
\hat\theta = 20/41:

L(D \mid H) = -\bigl[\, 20\log_2\tfrac{20}{41} + 21\log_2\tfrac{21}{41} \,\bigr]

Model: 1 + 6 = 7 bits. Total: 48.0.

Order 1 (two parameters). From state 0 (20 transitions), the MLE
is \hat\theta_{1\mid 0} = 18/20 = 0.9, costing 20\,H(0.1) = 9.38
bits; from state 1, symmetrically, 9.38 bits; the first symbol costs
1 bit:

L(D \mid H) = 1 + 9.38 + 9.38 = 19.8 \text{ bits.}

Model: 2 + 2 \times 6 = 14 bits. Total: 33.8.

Order 2 (four parameters). The four contexts among the 39
transitions with two-bit history: context 01 occurs 18 times and is
followed by 1 twice (18\,H(1/9) = 9.06 bits); context 10 occurs
17 times, followed by 0 twice (17\,H(2/17) = 8.88 bits); contexts
00 and 11 occur twice each and are followed deterministically (0
bits). Two initial symbols cost 2 bits:

L(D \mid H) = 2 + 9.06 + 8.88 + 0 + 0 = 19.9 \text{ bits.}

Model: 3 + 4 \times 6 = 27 bits. Total: 46.9.

The doubling of parameters bought nothing: the new contexts 00 and
11 are perfectly predictive but occur twice each, so the fit term is
flat while the model term doubles.

Order 3 and beyond, without computing the fit. Even if an
order-3 chain fit all its in-context transitions perfectly, its fit term
could not drop below the 3 bits for the initial symbols, so its total
is at least 4 + 8 \times 6 + 3 = 55 bits. The parameter bill alone
eliminates it, and every higher order more so.
