MDL selects B(1): the record is best described as an alternator that
sticks with probability 0.1.

The worked example as a plot: after order 1 the fit term has nothing left to gain, the model term keeps growing, and the total turns over.

Verify the order-2 row from the printed record: tally the four context
counts (context 01: 18 with 2 exceptions; 10: 17 with 2; 00 and
11: 2 each, deterministic) and evaluate
2 + 18\,H(1/9) + 17\,H(2/17); it should land on 19.9 bits.

The table charges fit at the exact maximum-likelihood parameters, while
the code transmits them rounded to the 64-value grid. The rounding error
is at most 1/128 per parameter, and because the likelihood is
stationary at the MLE, it changes each fit entry by under 0.05 bits:
invisible at the table's precision. The next section turns this
observation into the general parameter price.

On the 41-bit record the totals read 48.0, 33.8, 46.9, \ge 55
bits for orders 0 through 3: the two-part sum rejects both the blind
coin and the over-parameterized orders by arithmetic alone.

documents.title: The parameter cost: (k/2) log₂ n
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › Minimum description length › The parameter cost: (k/2) log₂ n
documents.text:
The parameter cost: (k/2) log₂ n

The crude code above spent 6 bits per parameter by fiat. The right
spend is a trade the data itself sets, and it is where the celebrated
(k/2)\log_2 n penalty comes from.

Concrete first: how coarsely can θ = 0.9 be stated

Round a parameter by \varepsilon away from its MLE and the fit term
rises by the second-order Taylor amount

\Delta L \;\approx\; \frac{n\, I(\hat\theta)}{2\ln 2}\, \varepsilon^2

for n Bernoulli observations with Fisher information I; the
first-order term vanishes because the MLE is a maximum. For
\hat\theta_{1 \mid 0} = 0.9 estimated from its n = 20 transitions,
I = 11.1: a grid of spacing 1/8 (3 bits) misstates it by
\varepsilon = 0.025 and costs 0.10 bits of fit; the 6-bit grid costs
under 0.01 bits. Both grids overpay in description what they save in
fit — the trade has an interior optimum.

The trade in general

A grid of spacing d costs \log_2(1/d) bits per parameter and, at
worst-case rounding d/2, adds n I d^2 / (8 \ln 2) bits of fit.
Minimizing the sum over d gives

d^\ast = \frac{2}{\sqrt{n I}} \;\propto\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}},

parameters are worth stating to precision 1/\sqrt{n} and no finer,
because two parameter values closer than that produce codes for the data
whose lengths differ by a fraction of a bit. A k-parameter hypothesis
therefore costs

L(\theta \mid k) \;\approx\; \frac{k}{2}\log_2 n \;+\; O(k)

bits: the penalty grows with the data, but logarithmically, while fit
terms grow linearly. For the worked example's B(1) at n = 41, the
refined price is \log_2 41 \approx 5.4 bits instead of the crude 12;
the ranking of the table is unchanged (exercise 5).

The precision trade: coarser grids cost fit, finer grids cost description, and the optimum spacing 1/√n prices a parameter at (1/2) log₂ n bits.

Refined MDL: from a chosen code to a canonical one

The crude L(H) is arbitrary: unary versus binary for k, 64 versus 42
grid points, each choice shifts the totals. Refined MDL removes the
arbitrariness by replacing the two-part code for a parametric class
\mathcal{M} with a single one-part universal code, the normalized
maximum likelihood (NML) code, whose length is

-\log_2 P(D \mid \hat\theta(D)) \;+\; \mathrm{COMP}_n(\mathcal{M}),

the stochastic complexity of
Rissanen (1996). The leading term
recovers (k/2)\log_2 n; the integral term makes the price
parametrization-invariant. This lesson states the expansion without
deriving it; Grünwald's tutorial §2.6 gives the construction.

What NML normalizes. The maximum-likelihood "distribution"
P(D \mid \hat\theta(D)) sums over datasets to more than one, since every
D gets its own best parameters; dividing by the sum
\sum_{D'} P(D' \mid \hat\theta(D')) restores a genuine distribution,
and \mathrm{COMP}_n = \log_2 \sum_{D'} P(D' \mid \hat\theta(D')) is the
log of the excess: a direct measure of how many distinguishable datasets
the class can fit well. A class is complex exactly when it can fit many
things, which is why the same number is both a normalizer and a penalty.
The NML code is also minimax optimal: it minimizes the worst-case regret
against the best hindsight member of the class.

Dropping the O(1) terms of \mathrm{COMP}_n leaves
-\log_2 P(D \mid \hat\theta) + \tfrac{k}{2}\log_2 n, which is the
Bayesian information criterion
in base 2. The agreement holds only for fixed k as
n \to \infty: the Fisher-information term is O(1) in n but can be
large and can differ substantially between the classes being compared,
and for small samples or growing model families the two criteria part
ways (Grünwald §2.9.2). BIC is a truncation of refined MDL, not a synonym
for it.

Data of size n distinguishes a parameter only to precision
\sim 1/\sqrt{n}, so an honest code spends \tfrac12 \log_2 n bits per
parameter: L(H) \approx (k/2)\log_2 n, a penalty that grows with the
data but only logarithmically.

documents.title: The two errors are priced asymmetrically
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › Minimum description length › The two errors are priced asymmetrically
documents.text:
The two errors are priced asymmetrically

The U-curve's two arms rise at different rates, and the difference is the
practical content of the principle.

Underfitting is billed per symbol, forever. Insist on B(0) for the
sticky alternator and the fit overpayment is
41.0/41 - 18.76/40 \approx 0.53 bits per symbol: the divergence rate of
KL divergence between the true chain and the best i.i.d.
model. At n symbols the bill is \approx 0.53\,n bits, linear and
unbounded.

Overfitting is billed per parameter, logarithmically. Choosing B(2)
over B(1) costs the two superfluous parameters' description,
2 \times \tfrac12 \log_2 n bits: at n = 4{,}100 symbols, about 12
bits against roughly 2{,}200 for the underfit: a factor of about
180, two orders of magnitude, and the gap keeps widening because the
ratio 0.53\,n / \log_2 n is unbounded in n.

The two arms of the U-curve, priced over time: underfitting compounds at 0.53 bits per symbol, overfitting is a one-off log₂ n, and by n = 4,100 they are two orders of magnitude apart.

The asymmetry explains MDL's small-sample behavior, which Grünwald's
tutorial (§1.5–1.6) is careful to state as strategy rather than
metaphysics. At small n the criterion picks simple models even when the
true source is complex, and this is correct play: with too little data to
pin down a rich model's parameters to useful precision, the rich
hypothesis genuinely does not shorten the message, and the description
arithmetic prices that automatically. As n grows, a real regularity
eventually pays for its parameters and the selection upgrades. Preferring
the simple model is not the claim that the world is simple; it is the
worst-case-safe way to bet bits.

Two honesty clauses close the principle. MDL selects among the
candidates offered: if no hypothesis in \mathcal{H} is anywhere near
the source, the winner is merely the least bad description, and its
selection behavior can degrade (Grünwald §2.10 catalogs the failure modes
under misspecification). And the whole construction is lossless coding
of D given H: bits-for-fidelity trades belong to
Rate-distortion theory and are a different theory.

Underfitting costs \Theta(n) bits and overfitting costs
\Theta(\log n): preferring the simpler model at small sample size is a
bounded-loss strategy, not a claim about nature, and it self-corrects as
the data grows.

documents.title: Charging the network: the adjusted compression rate
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › Minimum description length › Charging the network: the adjusted compression rate
documents.text:
Charging the network: the adjusted compression rate

Compression as prediction ended on a caveat: a language
model's compression numbers charge nothing for the model, which must ride
on both ends of the channel. The two-part principle is exactly the missing
accounting, and
Delétang et al. (2023) (§3.3) run it
on real networks. Their adjusted compression rate for a model H
trained on and compressing a dataset D is

\frac{L(H) + L(D \mid H)}{\text{raw bits of } D},

with L(H) the encoded parameter bits and L(D \mid H) the arithmetic-
coding cost under the model: a two-part total, normalized.

The raw (unadjusted) rate improves monotonically with model scale: bigger
Transformers predict better, so L(D \mid H) only falls. The adjusted
rate does not. On a small corpus the parameter bits dominate and small
models win; on a larger corpus the same parameter bits amortize over more
data and the optimum moves to larger models. Each dataset size traces a
U-curve in model size, and the minimum migrates rightward as the dataset
grows — the same turnover as the Markov table, at nine orders of magnitude
the scale.

Charging the network its parameter bits: the raw rate falls forever, the adjusted rate is U-shaped, and the optimal model size grows with the dataset.

This is an MDL reading of scaling: "bigger is better" is a statement
about the fit term alone, and it survives the full accounting only when
the dataset is large enough to amortize the model. The break-even
arithmetic is elementary (exercise 6), and it reproduces in two lines the
paper's finding that a 70-billion-parameter model, unbeatable on raw
rate, loses the adjusted comparison on datasets far smaller than its own
description.

Charged its own parameter bits, a network's compression rate becomes
U-shaped in model size, and the optimal size grows with the dataset: the
two-part principle evaluated at modern scale.

documents.title: Exercises
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › Minimum description length › Exercises
documents.text:
Exercises

A 25-bit record reads 0000100100000010000010000 (four ones, at
positions 5, 8, 15, and 21; among the 24 adjacent pairs, 0 is followed
by 1 four times and by 0 sixteen times, and every 1 is followed by
0). Using the worked example's codes with
\lceil \log_2 26 \rceil = 5 bits per parameter (order in unary, 2^k
parameters for order k, 1 bit per initial symbol), compute the two-part
totals for B(0) and B(1) and state the MDL selection. Use
H(0.16) \approx 0.634, H(0.2) \approx 0.722.

B(0): \hat\theta = 4/25 = 0.16, so
L(D \mid H) = 25\,H(0.16) \approx 15.9 bits; model
1 + 5 = 6 bits; total \approx 21.9 bits.

B(1): first bit 1 bit. From state 0 (20 transitions,
\hat\theta_{1\mid 0} = 4/20 = 0.2): 20\,H(0.2) = 14.4 bits. From
state 1 (4 transitions, all to 0, \hat\theta_{1\mid 1} = 0): 0
bits. Fit = 1 + 14.4 + 0 = 15.4 bits; model 2 + 10 = 12 bits; total
\approx 27.4 bits.

MDL selects B(0): 21.9 < 27.4. Serial context improves the fit by
only half a bit (the ones are scattered, so knowing the previous bit
barely helps), while the second-order structure costs six extra model
bits. Same procedure as the worked example, opposite verdict — the
selection follows the data, not the richer candidate.

The 16-bit string 0010000101000010 has four ones. Compute the fit term
L(D \mid H) = -\log_2 P(D \mid H) under Bernoulli hypotheses
\theta = 0.5, \theta = 0.25, and \theta = 0.9, identify which is the
maximum-likelihood choice, and state the relation between the fit term and
the string's per-symbol cross-entropy under each hypothesis. Use
\log_2 3 \approx 1.585, \log_2 0.1 \approx -3.322,
\log_2 0.9 \approx -0.152.

\theta = 0.5: every bit costs 1 bit; L = 16.0 bits.

\theta = 0.25: ones cost 2 bits, zeros cost
\log_2 \tfrac43 = 2 - 1.585 = 0.415 bits;
L = 4 \times 2 + 12 \times 0.415 = 8 + 4.98 \approx 13.0 bits.

\theta = 0.9: ones cost 0.152 bits, zeros cost 3.322 bits;
L = 4 \times 0.152 + 12 \times 3.322 = 0.61 + 39.86 \approx 40.5 bits.

The empirical rate is 4/16 = 0.25, so \theta = 0.25 is the maximum-
likelihood hypothesis and, consistently, the smallest fit: 13.0 < 16.0
\ll 40.5. Each fit divided by 16 is the per-symbol cross-entropy of
the hypothesis on this string (0.81, 1.0, and 2.5 bits per symbol):
the fit term is the log-loss, i.e. the compressed size the hypothesis
achieves.

A model has k = 3 parameters and is fit to n = 10^4 observations.
(a) Compute the MDL parameter cost (k/2)\log_2 n and compare it with
shipping the parameters as three 32-bit floats. (b) State the parameter
precision the data supports. (c) By how many bits does the cost rise if
the dataset quadruples?

(a) (3/2)\log_2 10^4 = 1.5 \times 13.29 \approx 19.9 bits. Three
32-bit floats cost 96 bits: almost five times the information the data
can actually use; the extra 76 bits state digits of the parameters that
the sample cannot distinguish.

(b) Precision \sim 1/\sqrt{n} = 0.01 per parameter: about \log_2 100
\approx 6.6 bits each, which is (1/2)\log_2 n.

(c) At n = 4 \times 10^4:
(3/2)\log_2(4 \times 10^4) = (3/2)(13.29 + 2) \approx 22.9 bits, a
rise of (k/2)\log_2 4 = 3 bits. Quadrupling the data adds one bit of
usable precision per parameter.

Consider the "memorizer class": for every n-bit string s, a
hypothesis H_s with P(D \mid H_s) = 1 if D = s and 0 otherwise,
so L(D \mid H_{D}) = 0. Using the Kraft inequality of
The Kraft inequality, prove that in any prefix-free code for
this class, fewer than 2^{n-c} of the 2^n hypotheses can have
L(H_s) < n - c, and conclude that for all but a 2^{-c} fraction of
datasets the memorizer's two-part total is at least n - c bits.

The hypothesis code is prefix-free, so its lengths satisfy
\sum_s 2^{-L(H_s)} \le 1. If m hypotheses had lengths below n - c,
each would contribute more than 2^{-(n-c)} to the sum, forcing
m \cdot 2^{-(n-c)} < 1, i.e. m < 2^{n-c}. The class has 2^n
hypotheses, one per string, so at most a 2^{n-c}/2^n = 2^{-c} fraction
of strings D have L(H_D) < n - c. For every other D, the two-part
total is L(H_D) + 0 \ge n - c: within a couple of bits of sending D
literally. Memorization moves the bits from the data term to the model
term without shrinking the message — the same counting that made most
strings incompressible in Kolmogorov complexity, applied
to a hypothesis code.

Recompute the worked example's table with the refined parameter price of
(1/2)\log_2 41 \approx 2.68 bits per parameter in place of the crude
6, keeping the unary order code and the fit entries. Does the selection
change? What structural feature of the two-part totals does the
recomputation illustrate?

B(0): 1 + 1 \times 2.68 + 41.0 = 44.7 bits.
B(1): 2 + 2 \times 2.68 + 19.8 = 27.2 bits.
B(2): 3 + 4 \times 2.68 + 19.9 = 33.6 bits.
B(3): 4 + 8 \times 2.68 + (\ge 3) \ge 28.4 bits — now within reach
of B(1) numerically, but only by granting it an impossible perfect
fit; with any realistic fit near 20 bits it lands near 45.

The selection is unchanged: B(1) wins. The recomputation shows that
crude MDL's arbitrary constants (6 bits per parameter versus 2.68) shift
every total but tend to preserve comparisons whose gaps exceed a few
bits; the 14-bit and 6-bit margins here are robust. Refined MDL
exists precisely to remove the remaining arbitrariness when margins are
thin.

A small model (4 \times 10^6 parameters) achieves 1.9 bits/char; a
large model (4 \times 10^8 parameters) achieves 1.5 bits/char. Both
ship parameters at 16 bits each. Compute the adjusted compression
totals of both models on corpora of N = 10^9 and N = 10^{11}
characters, find the break-even N, and state the conclusion in the
terms of Compression as prediction.

Model bits: small 4 \times 10^6 \times 16 = 6.4 \times 10^7; large
4 \times 10^8 \times 16 = 6.4 \times 10^9.

N = 10^9: small total 6.4 \times 10^7 + 1.9 \times 10^9 =
1.96 \times 10^9 bits (1.96 bits/char); large total
6.4 \times 10^9 + 1.5 \times 10^9 = 7.9 \times 10^9 bits
(7.9 bits/char, worse than raw ASCII). The small model wins by
a factor of four.

N = 10^{11}: small total \approx 1.9 \times 10^{11} bits
(1.90 bits/char); large total 6.4 \times 10^9 + 1.5 \times 10^{11} =
1.56 \times 10^{11} bits (1.56 bits/char). The large model wins.

Break-even: 0.4\,N = 6.4 \times 10^9 - 6.4 \times 10^7, so
N \approx 1.6 \times 10^{10} characters. In the earlier lesson's
terms: the model rides on both ends, so its description is part of the
message; a better per-symbol predictor is a better compressor only once
the stream is long enough to amortize the model that achieves it.

The sticky alternator of the worked example has entropy rate
H(0.1) \approx 0.469 bits/symbol, while its best i.i.d. description
B(0) spends \approx 1.0 bits/symbol. (a) Identify the per-symbol
overpayment of B(0) as a quantity from KL divergence.
(b) Find the stream length n at which underfitting has cost 1{,}000
excess bits. (c) Compute the overfitting premium of B(2) over B(1)
at that n under the refined (1/2)\log_2 n price, and compare the two
errors.

(a) 1.0 - 0.469 = 0.53 bits/symbol is the divergence (KL) rate
between the true first-order chain and the best i.i.d. model: the
per-symbol price of coding with the wrong distribution, paid at every
symbol.

(b) n = 1{,}000 / 0.53 \approx 1{,}900 symbols.

(c) B(2) carries two superfluous parameters:
2 \times \tfrac12 \log_2 1900 = \log_2 1900 \approx 10.9 bits, paid
once. At n \approx 1{,}900 the underfit has cost 1{,}000 bits and
keeps growing linearly; the overfit has cost 11 bits and grows only
as \log_2 n. The errors are asymmetric by roughly a factor of a
hundred here and unboundedly for larger n, which is why a
description-length criterion can afford its bias toward simplicity.

P. Grünwald, "A Tutorial Introduction to the Minimum Description Length Principle," in Advances in Minimum Description Length, MIT Press, 2004 — the lesson's primary source: §1.2 regularity as compressibility and the polynomial example; §1.3 the crude two-part principle; §1.5–1.6 what MDL does and does not claim; §2.2 the codelength–probability correspondence; §2.4 crude MDL on Markov chains and the parameter-precision argument; §2.6 refined MDL, NML, and the complexity expansion; §2.9.2 and §2.10 the BIC comparison and misspecification. https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0406077

J. Rissanen, "Modeling by Shortest Data Description," Automatica, 14(5), 1978 — the original two-part MDL paper.

J. Rissanen, "Fisher Information and Stochastic Complexity," IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 42(1), 1996 — the NML stochastic complexity and its (k/2)\log(n/2\pi) + \log \int \sqrt{\det I} expansion.

D. J. C. MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms, Cambridge University Press, 2003 — ch. 28 "Model Comparison and Occam's Razor": the Bayesian dual of description-length selection and the Occam factor. Free online: https://www.inference.org.uk/mackay/itila/

G. Delétang, A. Ruoss, et al., "Language Modeling Is Compression," ICLR 2024 — §3.3: the adjusted compression rate and the optimal model–dataset size trade-off. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.10668

T. M. Cover, J. A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006 — §14.13: the minimum description length principle as the computable shadow of the Kolmogorov two-part code.

documents.title: The information bottleneck
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The information bottleneck
documents.text:
The information bottleneck makes relevant compression precise: choose a
stochastic encoder mapping X to T that minimizes I(X;T) - beta I(T;Y),
keeping the bits of X that inform the target Y and discarding the rest.
This lesson replaces rate-distortion's hand-picked distortion measure with
a second mutual information, computes the trade-off in full on a
four-symbol source with a binary label, maps every candidate encoder into
the information plane under two data-processing ceilings, states the
Gibbs-form optimal encoder whose distortion measure emerges as a KL
divergence, and derives the exchange rate \beta that prices a relevant
bit in bits of rate.

documents.title: Relevance replaces distortion: the flaw the bottleneck fixes
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The information bottleneck › Relevance replaces distortion: the flaw the bottleneck fixes
documents.text:
Relevance replaces distortion: the flaw the bottleneck fixes

Rate-distortion theory priced lossy compression as
R(D) = \min I(X;\hat X) subject to \mathbb{E}[d(x, \hat x)] \le D, and
its closing observation was that one ingredient is not derived: someone
must pick the distortion measure d, and that choice silently decides
which differences matter. A codec judged by squared error spends bits on
deviations no user of the data cares about.

Tishby, Pereira & Bialek (1999)
remove the hand-picked ingredient by changing what the constraint asks
for. Instead of "reconstruct X within tolerance d", the requirement
becomes "keep information about a target variable Y": predict a
label from an input, a disease from a scan, the next word from a context.
Which bits of X are relevant is then defined by the joint distribution
p(x, y) itself, not by a designer. The reconstruction term
\mathbb{E}[d(x, \hat x)] is replaced by a second mutual information,
I(T;Y), measured in the same currency as the rate.

One substitution: the hand-picked distortion budget becomes a second mutual information, and relevance is defined by the data.

The information bottleneck is rate-distortion with the distortion measure
removed from the designer's hands: the constraint "reconstruct X well"
becomes "inform about Y", and p(x,y) decides which bits are relevant.

documents.title: The objective: compress X, keep Y
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The information bottleneck › The objective: compress X, keep Y
documents.text:
The objective: compress X, keep Y

The pieces: a fixed joint, a chosen encoder

Two distributions play different roles. The joint p(x, y) is given:
it is the statistics of the data. The encoder is chosen: a
stochastic encoder is a conditional distribution p(t \mid x) mapping
each input x to a distribution over representation values t, with
deterministic maps T = f(X) as the special case of one-point
conditionals.

The encoder reads x only. T never sees Y, so the three variables
form the Markov chain Y \to X \to T of
The data-processing inequality: all of T's dependence on
Y routes through X. The arrow direction is a hypothesis, not a
decoration. T is a compressed code of X, not a hidden cause
generating Y; Tishby, Pereira & Bialek flag exactly this reading in a
footnote, and every figure in this lesson keeps the encoder arrow
pointing out of X.

Given a joint distribution p(x,y) and a trade-off parameter
\beta \ge 0, the information bottleneck problem is

\min_{p(t \mid x)} \; \mathcal{L}\bigl[p(t \mid x)\bigr]

the minimum over stochastic encoders p(t \mid x) with a fixed number
|\mathcal{T}| of representation values, where T obeys the Markov
chain Y \to X \to T.

The objective dissected: pay rate I(X;T), earn relevance I(T;Y), with β the price of a relevant bit. The encoder touches X only.

The two extremes of β

The parameter \beta prices relevant bits in units of rate, and its
extremes bracket the behavior:

\beta \to 0: relevance is worthless, and the objective reduces to
minimizing I(X;T) alone. The minimum is 0, attained by collapsing
every x to one constant value of T: maximal compression, zero
information about anything.

\beta \to \infty: rate is free, and the objective reduces to
maximizing I(T;Y). Copying, T = X, attains the maximum the next
section shows is I(X;Y): all the relevance X ever had, at full
rate H(X).

Every finite \beta buys a point between these extremes. The rest of
the lesson computes what the intermediate points look like, first by
brute force on a toy source, then in general.

\mathcal{L} = I(X;T) - \beta\, I(T;Y) trades bits kept about X
against bits kept about Y: \beta \to 0 collapses T to a constant,
\beta \to \infty makes T a copy of X, and finite \beta prices
every position in between.

documents.title: The trade-off computed: four symbols, one binary label
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The information bottleneck › The trade-off computed: four symbols, one binary label
documents.text:
The trade-off computed: four symbols, one binary label

The source: same rate, different relevance

Let X be uniform on \{a, b, c, d\}, p(x) = \tfrac14 each, with a
binary label Y attached through the conditionals

p(1 \mid a) = 0, \quad

writing p(1 \mid x) for p(Y{=}1 \mid X{=}x). The joint table:

p(x,y)

x = a

x = b

x = c

x = d

p(y)

y = 0

\tfrac14

\tfrac{3}{16}

\tfrac{1}{16}

0

\tfrac12

y = 1

0

\tfrac{1}{16}

\tfrac{3}{16}

\tfrac14

\tfrac12

p(x)

\tfrac14

\tfrac14

\tfrac14

\tfrac14

1

The label's marginal is fair, H(Y) = 1 bit. Given X, the label is
certain for a and d and a \tfrac14-coin for b and c
(H_2(\tfrac14) = H_2(\tfrac34) \approx 0.811):

H(Y \mid X) = \tfrac14\bigl(0 + 0.811 + 0.811 + 0\bigr) \approx 0.406

so by Mutual information,

I(X;Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) \approx 1 - 0.406 = 0.594 \text{ bits}.

X carries 0.594 bits about the label, out of H(X) = 2 bits of
description: less than a third of the input is relevant.

Three hard 2-cluster encoders, priced

Take the simplest nontrivial encoders: deterministic merges of the four
symbols into two clusters of two, T = f(X) with
|\mathcal{T}| = 2. There are three such pairings. For each,
I(X;T) = H(T) - H(T \mid X) = H(T) = 1 bit, since the clusters are
equiprobable and T is a function of X: all three cost the same
rate, so the comparison isolates relevance.

Cluster t_1 = \{a, b\}, t_2 = \{c, d\}, each with p(t) = \tfrac12.

Step 1: label given cluster. The mass with Y = 1 inside t_1 is
p(a)\, p(1 \mid a) + p(b)\, p(1 \mid b) = 0 + \tfrac14 \cdot \tfrac14 =
\tfrac{1}{16}, so
p(1 \mid t_1) = \tfrac{1/16}{1/2} = \tfrac18. Symmetrically
p(1 \mid t_2) = \tfrac78.

Step 2: conditional entropy. Both clusters are \tfrac18-coins:
H(Y \mid T) = H_2(\tfrac18) \approx 0.544 bits.

Step 3: subtract.

I(T;Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid T) \approx 1 - 0.544 = 0.456 \text{ bits}.

The merge keeps 0.456 of the 0.594 available bits; the loss is
0.138 bits.

The other two pairings, computed the same way (Exercise 1 works the
first in full):

\{a,c\} \mid \{b,d\}: cluster conditionals
p(1 \mid t) = \tfrac38 and \tfrac58, so
H(Y \mid T) = H_2(\tfrac38) \approx 0.954 and
I(T;Y) \approx 0.046 bits.

\{a,d\} \mid \{b,c\}: both cluster conditionals equal
\tfrac12, so H(Y \mid T) = 1 and I(T;Y) = 0 bits: one bit of
rate spent, nothing about the label kept.

Three merges, one price: each 2-cluster encoder costs I(X;T) = 1 bit, but relevance ranges from 0.456 bits to zero depending on which conditionals p(y|x) are fused.

Step through the four frames and track the dot strip: the merge that
pairs neighbors on the p(1 \mid x) axis (0 with \tfrac14,
\tfrac34 with 1) keeps 0.456 bits, and relevance falls to 0.046
and then 0 as the pairings fuse increasingly distant conditionals.

The ranking is decided entirely by which conditionals get fused.
Merging a with b works because p(y \mid a) and p(y \mid b) are
similar: inside the cluster, the label distribution barely blurs.
Merging a with d fuses opposite conditionals into a fair coin and
destroys everything. The Gibbs-form optimum below turns this observation
into the exact assignment rule.

One caveat scopes the enumeration: hard clusterings are a strict subset
of stochastic encoders. The definition optimizes over all
p(t \mid x), and the true optimum at a given rate can strictly beat
every hard partition; the hard points computed here are candidates, not
the frontier itself.

At equal rate I(X;T) = 1 bit, the three 2-cluster encoders keep
0.456, 0.046, and 0 bits about Y: relevance is decided by how
similar the fused conditionals p(y \mid x) are, not by how much of
X survives.

documents.title: The information plane: two ceilings cap every encoder
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The information bottleneck › The information plane: two ceilings cap every encoder
documents.text:
The information plane: two ceilings cap every encoder

Both bounds are the data-processing inequality

Plot every encoder as a point with coordinates
\bigl(I(X;T),\, I(T;Y)\bigr): rate spent against relevance kept. This
coordinate system is the information plane, and two lines cap it, both
inherited from The data-processing inequality.

The Markov chain Y \to X \to T reverses to T \to X \to Y (the
factorization is symmetric, as established there), and the DPI applied
to each reading direction gives one ceiling:

The relevance ceiling. From Y \to X \to T:
\;I(T;Y) \le I(X;Y). No encoder can know more about the target than
the input did; for the toy source, no point rises above 0.594 bits.

The rate diagonal. From T \to X \to Y:
\;I(T;Y) \le I(X;T). A representation cannot say more about Y
than it contains about anything: relevance never exceeds rate, so
every point lies on or below the 45° line.

Every encoder is a point under two DPI lines. The toy's hard encoders scatter below the β-swept frontier; the identity encoder ends the curve where it meets the ceiling.

The frontier: what β sweeps out

For each rate the interesting quantity is the largest relevance any
encoder achieves; the resulting upper boundary is the frontier, traced
by solving the bottleneck problem as \beta sweeps from 0 to
\infty. Three facts locate it:

It starts at (0, 0): zero rate forces T independent of X, hence
of Y (the \beta \to 0 collapse).

It ends on the ceiling: at rate H(X) = 2 bits the identity encoder
reaches I(T;Y) = I(X;Y) = 0.594, and more rate buys nothing.

It is concave, and there is one such curve per cardinality
|\mathcal{T}|: allowing more clusters relaxes the optimization, so
the curves nest, each approaching the |\mathcal{T}| = |\mathcal{X}|
master curve from below.

The toy's hard encoders sit under the frontier at their rates,
except where they happen to touch it; the stochastic optimum at rate
1 bit is at least the 0.456 bits of the aligned merge.

The feasible region of the bottleneck is bounded by two applications of
one theorem: I(T;Y) \le I(X;Y) and I(T;Y) \le I(X;T), the DPI read
along the chain in its two directions.

documents.title: The optimal encoder: the distortion measure emerges as a KL
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The information bottleneck › The optimal encoder: the distortion measure emerges as a KL
documents.text:
The optimal encoder: the distortion measure emerges as a KL

Exactly what a merge loses: an identity

The toy ranking suggested that the cost of assigning x to a cluster
t is the mismatch between p(y \mid x) and the cluster's aggregate
conditional p(y \mid t). That is an exact accounting, not a
heuristic.

For any encoder p(t \mid x) with Y \to X \to T,

I(X;Y) - I(T;Y)

the average, over inputs and their cluster assignments, of the KL
divergence of KL divergence between the input's label
conditional and its cluster's label conditional.

Expand the expectation:

\mathbb{E}\bigl[D\bigr]

The Markov chain gives p(y \mid x, t) = p(y \mid x), so
p(x,t)\,p(y \mid x) = p(x,t,y), and the sum splits into two full
expectations over the joint. The numerator term is
\sum_{x,y} p(x,y) \log_2 p(y \mid x) = -H(Y \mid X). The denominator
term is
-\sum_{x,t,y} p(x,t,y) \log_2 p(y \mid t)
= -\sum_{t,y} p(t,y) \log_2 p(y \mid t) = H(Y \mid T). Hence

\mathbb{E}\bigl[D\bigr] = H(Y \mid T) - H(Y \mid X)

and nonnegativity of each KL term makes the loss nonnegative, which is
the relevance ceiling again.

Numeric check on the aligned merge: the four assignment costs are
D\bigl((1,0) \,\|\, (\tfrac78, \tfrac18)\bigr) = \log_2 \tfrac87
\approx 0.193 bits for a, \approx 0.083 bits for b, and by
symmetry 0.083 and 0.193 for c and d. Their average,
\tfrac14(0.193 + 0.083 + 0.083 + 0.193) \approx 0.138 bits, is
exactly the loss 0.594 - 0.456 computed by brute force (Exercise 3
verifies the four divergences).

Theorem 4: the Gibbs form

The identity says the objective is rate plus \beta times an expected
KL "distortion". Minimizing it yields the central result of Tishby,
Pereira & Bialek, their Theorem 4, stated here without its Lagrange
derivation.

The stationary encoders of
\mathcal{L} = I(X;T) - \beta\, I(T;Y) satisfy

p(t \mid x) = \frac{p(t)}{Z(x, \beta)}

where Z(x, \beta) normalizes over t, and the cluster statistics are
determined self-consistently by the encoder:

p(t) = \sum_x p(x)\, p(t \mid x),

The exponent is the theorem's point: the quantity playing the role that
d(x, \hat x) played in rate-distortion is
D\bigl(p(y \mid x) \,\|\, p(y \mid t)\bigr), derived from the
objective rather than assumed. Relevance defines its own distortion
measure: the cost of putting x into cluster t is how differently
x and t predict the target.

Theorem 4 dissected: the optimal encoder is Gibbs in an emergent distortion — the KL divergence between how x and its cluster predict Y.

Three readings of the form:

It explains the toy ranking. The aligned merge won because its
assignment costs (0.193 and 0.083 bits) are the smallest any
2-cluster partition can offer; the \{a,d\} merge charges
D\bigl((1,0) \,\|\, (\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\bigr) = 1 bit per certain
symbol.

It is a soft assignment. At finite \beta the encoder is
genuinely stochastic, splitting borderline inputs between clusters
in proportion to e^{-\beta D}; hard partitions reappear only as
\beta \to \infty. This is how the frontier dominates the hard
points.

It is rate-distortion's own solution form. The Gibbs encoder is
the standard rate-distortion optimality condition with d(x, t)
replaced by the emergent KL, and the self-consistent equations are
solved by alternating updates exactly as
Blahut–Arimoto
(Cover & Thomas §10.8) solves R(D): Tishby, Pereira & Bialek's
Theorem 5 proves the iteration converges, though not to a unique
optimum; the algorithm itself is out of scope here.

The optimal encoder is
p(t \mid x) \propto p(t)\, e^{-\beta D(p(y \mid x) \| p(y \mid t))}:
the distortion measure rate-distortion required as an input is here an
output of the objective, and it is a KL divergence between label
conditionals.

documents.title: Along the frontier: one relevant bit costs β bits of rate
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The information bottleneck › Along the frontier: one relevant bit costs β bits of rate
documents.text:
Along the frontier: one relevant bit costs β bits of rate

The slope, derived from the Lagrangian

Write the frontier as a function: I_Y^\ast(R) is the largest
relevance any encoder achieves at rate I(X;T) = R. A \beta-optimal
encoder minimizes \mathcal{L} = R - \beta I_Y, so at its frontier
point a small move along the frontier cannot change the objective
to first order:

\delta \mathcal{L} = \delta R - \beta\, \delta I_Y = 0

Each additional bit of relevance costs exactly \beta bits of rate at
the operating point \beta selects; equivalently the frontier's slope
in the plane is 1/\beta. Conventions differ across write-ups (some
papers put \beta on the rate term, flipping the slope to \beta),
which is why the relation is derived here from the stated
\mathcal{L} rather than quoted.

Because the frontier is concave, its slope falls monotonically:
cheap relevant bits are bought first. Near the origin, one bit of
rate buys nearly one bit of relevance (small \beta suffices); near
the ceiling, each remaining sliver of relevance costs many bits of rate
(large \beta).

Compare three toy encoders by
\mathcal{L} = I(X;T) - \beta\, I(T;Y) as \beta varies:

\mathcal{L}_{\text{collapse}} = 0, \qquad

Collapse vs. merge. 1 - 0.456\,\beta < 0 exactly when
\beta > 1/0.456 \approx 2.19: below this price, relevance is too
cheap to bother paying a bit of rate for, and total collapse wins.

Merge vs. copy. 2 - 0.594\,\beta < 1 - 0.456\,\beta exactly when
0.138\,\beta > 1, i.e. \beta > 1/0.138 \approx 7.25: the extra bit
of rate from merge to copy buys only 0.138 bits of relevance, so it
pays only when a relevant bit is worth more than 7.25 rate bits.

Among these three candidates: collapse for \beta < 2.19, the aligned
merge for 2.19 < \beta < 7.25, the copy for \beta > 7.25. The
crossover values are exactly the inverse slopes
\Delta R / \Delta I_Y between consecutive points, the exchange-rate
relation read off discretely (Exercise 7 proves this in general).

β dials the operating point: collapse, the aligned merge, then the full copy, each optimal on its β range; the crossovers are the inverse slopes between the points.

Drag \beta from 0 upward and watch the point leave (0,0): it
should pass near the aligned merge's (1, 0.456) in the knee region
and flatten into the I(X;Y) = 0.594 ceiling as \beta grows. Check
the two crossover prices: below \beta \approx 2.19 the point stays
at the origin, and pushing past \beta \approx 7.25 buys the last
0.138 bits of relevance for a full bit of rate.

The β → ∞ limit: minimal sufficient statistics

At \beta \to \infty the objective keeps all the relevance,
I(T;Y) = I(X;Y), at the least possible rate. That is the equality
case of the DPI: T is a sufficient statistic for Y
(The data-processing inequality), and among sufficient
statistics the bottleneck selects a minimal one, the smallest I(X;T)
that still loses nothing
(Cover & Thomas
§2.9). The bottleneck at large \beta is therefore a variational
construction of minimal sufficiency; at finite \beta it relaxes
sufficiency into a continuum of lossy summaries. On the toy source the
four conditionals p(y \mid x) are pairwise distinct, so no merge is
sufficient and the minimal sufficient statistic is X itself: the
frontier reaches the ceiling only at full rate. Exercise 6 modifies
the source so a genuine 1-bit sufficient statistic exists.

What the objective does not give you

Everything above assumed the joint p(x, y) is known and small enough
to enumerate. Estimating the two mutual informations from samples of
high-dimensional data is its own hard problem, and it gates every
practical use of the objective: the trainable route, a variational
bound optimized with neural encoders, is
deep variational IB (Alemi et al.,
2017), and the general tool for bounding mutual information from
samples is the InfoNCE bound of the next lesson,
The InfoNCE bound.

Two adjacent literatures border the objective without being part of
it. First, the famous "information plane trajectories of deep
networks": Shwartz-Ziv & Tishby (2017)
plotted \bigl(I(X;T), I(T;Y)\bigr) for hidden layers T during SGD
training and reported a fitting phase followed by a compression phase;
Saxe et al. (2018) found
the compression phase absent for non-saturating activations and
sensitive to the mutual-information estimator. The 1999 paper contains
none of these claims (and zero figures); this lesson teaches the
objective, on which the dynamics debate has no bearing. Second, the
"keep few bits of the data" idea reappears in generalization theory:
Xu & Raginsky (2017) bound the
expected generalization gap of a learning algorithm by
\sqrt{2\sigma^2 I(S;W)/n}, where I(S;W) is the mutual information
between training set and learned weights, the quantity the aside of
The data-processing inequality introduced: an algorithm
that keeps few bits about its sample cannot overfit it, a sibling of
the bottleneck's compression term.

Moving along the frontier, one additional bit of I(T;Y) costs
\beta bits of I(X;T); \beta \to \infty recovers minimal
sufficient statistics, and finite \beta prices the lossy summaries
in between.

documents.title: Exercises
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The information bottleneck › Exercises
documents.text:
Exercises

Work the \{a,c\} \mid \{b,d\} merge of the toy source in full:
compute the cluster conditionals p(1 \mid t), the conditional entropy
H(Y \mid T), and I(T;Y), and state why this pairing loses almost
all relevance at the same rate as the aligned merge. Use
H_2(\tfrac38) \approx 0.954.

Clusters t_1 = \{a, c\} and t_2 = \{b, d\}, each with
p(t) = \tfrac12.

Cluster conditionals. Mass with Y = 1 in t_1:
p(a)\,p(1 \mid a) + p(c)\,p(1 \mid c) = 0 + \tfrac14 \cdot \tfrac34
= \tfrac{3}{16}, so p(1 \mid t_1) = \tfrac{3/16}{1/2} = \tfrac38.
In t_2: \tfrac14 \cdot \tfrac14 + \tfrac14 \cdot 1 = \tfrac{5}{16},
so p(1 \mid t_2) = \tfrac58.

Conditional entropy. Both clusters have entropy
H_2(\tfrac38) = H_2(\tfrac58) \approx 0.954 bits, so
H(Y \mid T) \approx 0.954 bits.

Relevance. I(T;Y) = 1 - 0.954 = 0.046 bits, against 0.456 for
the aligned merge at the identical rate I(X;T) = 1 bit.

The pairing fuses distant conditionals: 0 with \tfrac34, and
\tfrac14 with 1. Each cluster's aggregate conditional lands near
\tfrac12, blurring the label almost to a fair coin; relevance is
decided by the similarity of the fused p(y \mid x), not by the
cluster sizes.

Price the unequal split T with clusters \{a\} and \{b, c, d\}:
compute I(X;T) and I(T;Y), then verify both information-plane
ceilings from the data-processing inequality. Use
H_2(\tfrac14) \approx 0.811 and H_2(\tfrac13) \approx 0.918.

Rate. T is a function of X with
p(t_1) = \tfrac14, p(t_2) = \tfrac34:
I(X;T) = H(T) = H_2(\tfrac14) \approx 0.811 bits.

Relevance. Given t_1 = \{a\}: Y = 0 certain, entropy 0.
Given t_2: mass with Y = 1 is
\tfrac{1}{16} + \tfrac{3}{16} + \tfrac14 = \tfrac12, so
p(1 \mid t_2) = \tfrac{1/2}{3/4} = \tfrac23, entropy
H_2(\tfrac23) = H_2(\tfrac13) \approx 0.918 bits. Average:

H(Y \mid T) = \tfrac14 \cdot 0 + \tfrac34 \cdot 0.918 \approx 0.689

Ceilings. Relevance ceiling: 0.311 \le 0.594 = I(X;Y), the DPI
along Y \to X \to T. Rate diagonal: 0.311 \le 0.811 = I(X;T), the
DPI along the reversed chain T \to X \to Y. Both hold; the point
(0.811, 0.311) sits inside the feasible region, below the frontier.

Verify the relevance-loss identity on the aligned merge
\{a,b\} \mid \{c,d\}: compute the four assignment costs
D\bigl(p(y \mid x) \,\|\, p(y \mid t(x))\bigr) from the definition of
KL divergence, average them under p(x), and check the result against
I(X;Y) - I(T;Y) = 0.594 - 0.456. Use \log_2 \tfrac87 \approx 0.193
and \log_2 \tfrac67 \approx -0.222.

The cluster conditionals are
p(y \mid t_{ab}) = (\tfrac78, \tfrac18) and
p(y \mid t_{cd}) = (\tfrac18, \tfrac78), ordered (y{=}0, y{=}1).

Symbol a, p(y \mid a) = (1, 0):

D = 1 \cdot \log_2 \frac{1}{7/8} + 0 = \log_2 \tfrac87 \approx 0.193

(The y{=}1 term contributes 0 by the convention
0 \log \tfrac{0}{q} = 0.)

Symbol b, p(y \mid b) = (\tfrac34, \tfrac14):

D = \tfrac34 \log_2 \frac{3/4}{7/8} + \tfrac14 \log_2 \frac{1/4}{1/8}

Symbols c and d mirror b and a against t_{cd}:
0.083 and 0.193 bits.

Average. Under the uniform p(x):

\tfrac14 (0.193 + 0.083 + 0.083 + 0.193) \approx 0.138 \text{ bits},

which matches I(X;Y) - I(T;Y) = 0.594 - 0.456 = 0.138 bits: the
relevance the merge destroys is exactly the average KL divergence
between each symbol's label conditional and its cluster's.

At \beta = 3, rank the following toy encoders by the objective
\mathcal{L} = I(X;T) - \beta\, I(T;Y), using the coordinates computed
in this lesson: collapse (0, 0); the three 2-cluster merges
(1, 0.456), (1, 0.046), (1, 0); the split \{a\} \mid \{b,c,d\}
at (0.811, 0.311); the identity (2, 0.594). State the winner and
check it against the crossover prices of the worked example.

Evaluate \mathcal{L} = I(X;T) - 3\, I(T;Y):

collapse: 0 - 0 = 0

\{a,b\} \mid \{c,d\}: 1 - 3 \cdot 0.456 = -0.369

\{a,c\} \mid \{b,d\}: 1 - 3 \cdot 0.046 = 0.863

\{a,d\} \mid \{b,c\}: 1 - 0 = 1

\{a\} \mid \{b,c,d\}: 0.811 - 3 \cdot 0.311 = -0.122

identity: 2 - 3 \cdot 0.594 = 0.217

Ranking (best first): the aligned merge (-0.369), then
\{a\} \mid \{b,c,d\} (-0.122), collapse (0), identity (0.217),
\{a,c\} \mid \{b,d\} (0.863), \{a,d\} \mid \{b,c\} (1).

The winner is the aligned merge, consistent with the worked example's
regimes: \beta = 3 lies in the window 2.19 < \beta < 7.25 where the
merge beats both collapse and copy. The misaligned merges rank below
even the collapse: at any \beta, a bit of rate spent on clusters
that blur the label is a pure loss.

Prove from the data-processing inequality of
The data-processing inequality that every encoder
p(t \mid x) with Y \to X \to T satisfies both plane bounds,

I(T;Y) \le I(X;Y)

stating explicitly which Markov chain each application uses.

Relevance ceiling. The hypothesis is the chain Y \to X \to T
directly: T depends on Y only through X. The DPI (Cover & Thomas
Theorem 2.8.1, as proved in the prerequisite lesson) applied to this
chain gives I(T;Y) \le I(X;Y).

Rate diagonal. The Markov factorization
p(y, x, t) = p(x)\, p(y \mid x)\, p(t \mid x) is symmetric in y
and t, so Y \to X \to T holds exactly when T \to X \to Y does
(the chain-reversal fact of the prerequisite lesson). Apply the DPI to
T \to X \to Y, reading T as the source variable and Y as the
processed one: the information the endpoint carries about T is at
most what the middle carries, I(Y;T) \le I(X;T).

Both bounds are one theorem applied to one hypothesis read in its two
directions; no property of the bottleneck objective enters. Every
encoder, optimal or not, lives in the region under both lines.

Modify the toy source: keep X uniform on \{a,b,c,d\} but set
p(1 \mid a) = p(1 \mid b) = 0 and p(1 \mid c) = p(1 \mid d) = 1.
Compute I(X;Y), then show that the merge
T with clusters \{a,b\} and \{c,d\} is a sufficient statistic
for Y, and give the information-plane point at which the
\beta \to \infty solutions accumulate.

Budget. Y is now a deterministic function of X
(Y = 1 exactly on \{c,d\}), so H(Y \mid X) = 0; the marginal is
fair, H(Y) = 1, hence I(X;Y) = 1 bit.

Sufficiency of the merge. The clusters have
p(1 \mid t_1) = 0 and p(1 \mid t_2) = 1: given T, the label is
certain, H(Y \mid T) = 0, so

I(T;Y) = H(Y) - 0 = 1 = I(X;Y),

the equality case of the DPI, which is precisely the definition of a
sufficient statistic from the prerequisite lesson. Equivalently, every
assignment cost vanishes:
D\bigl(p(y \mid x) \,\|\, p(y \mid t(x))\bigr) = 0 for all four
symbols, so the relevance-loss identity gives loss zero.

The large-β point. The merge costs I(X;T) = H(T) = 1 bit, and no
cheaper encoder is sufficient: I(T;Y) = 1 requires
I(X;T) \ge I(T;Y) = 1 by the rate diagonal. So the minimal
sufficient statistic costs exactly 1 bit, and as
\beta \to \infty the optima accumulate at (1, 1), not at the
identity's (2, 1): the second bit of X (which symbol within the
cluster) is pure irrelevance, and the bottleneck discards it at any
price.

Two encoders occupy plane points (R_1, I_1) and (R_2, I_2) with
I_2 > I_1. Show that their objectives tie,
\mathcal{L}_1 = \mathcal{L}_2, at exactly

\beta^\ast = \frac{R_2 - R_1}{I_2 - I_1},

the inverse slope of the segment joining the points, and evaluate
\beta^\ast for the aligned merge (1, 0.456) against the identity
(2, 0.594). State how this connects to the frontier's slope
relation.

Set the objectives equal:

R_1 - \beta I_1 = R_2 - \beta I_2

For \beta < \beta^\ast the cheaper encoder wins (R dominates); for
\beta > \beta^\ast the more informative one wins (I dominates).

For the given pair:

\beta^\ast = \frac{2 - 1}{0.594 - 0.456} = \frac{1}{0.138} \approx

the merge-vs-copy crossover of the worked example.

Connection: on the smooth frontier, the optimum at price \beta sits
where dI_Y^\ast/dR = 1/\beta, i.e. \delta R / \delta I_Y = \beta.
The tie price \beta^\ast is the discrete version of the same
statement: it is the inverse slope \Delta R / \Delta I_Y between two
candidate points, the average price per relevant bit of upgrading from
one encoder to the other. As the candidates crowd the frontier, the
discrete exchange rate converges to the derivative relation.

N. Tishby, F. C. Pereira, W. Bialek, "The Information Bottleneck Method," Proc. 37th Allerton Conference on Communication, Control, and Computing, 1999 — §1 the relevance critique of rate-distortion; §3.1 the objective over stochastic encoders and the data-processing bound; §3.2 Theorem 4, the Gibbs-form encoder with the emergent KL distortion, and Theorem 5, convergence of the alternating iteration; §3.4 the information plane and the frontier. https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0004057

T. M. Cover, J. A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006 — §2.8 the data-processing inequality behind both plane ceilings; §2.9 sufficient statistics, the β → ∞ limit; §10.8 the Blahut–Arimoto algorithm the IB iteration generalizes.

A. A. Alemi, I. Fischer, J. V. Dillon, K. Murphy, "Deep Variational Information Bottleneck," ICLR 2017 — the variational bound making the objective trainable with neural encoders on high-dimensional data. https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.00410

R. Shwartz-Ziv, N. Tishby, "Opening the Black Box of Deep Neural Networks via Information," 2017 — the (contested) information-plane analysis of SGD training dynamics. https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.00810

A. M. Saxe, Y. Bansal, J. Dapello, M. Advani, A. Kolchinsky, B. D. Tracey, D. D. Cox, "On the Information Bottleneck Theory of Deep Learning," ICLR 2018 — the counter-evidence: the compression phase depends on activation choice and estimator. https://openreview.net/forum?id=ry_WPG-A-

A. Xu, M. Raginsky, "Information-theoretic analysis of generalization capability of learning algorithms," NeurIPS 30, 2017 — the generalization bound via I(S;W), the compression-controls-overfitting sibling of the bottleneck. https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.07809

documents.title: The InfoNCE bound
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The InfoNCE bound
documents.text:
A classifier trained to pick the true partner of a context out of N
candidates yields a mutual-information estimate: I(X;Y) >= log2 N - L_N,
where L_N is the contrastive cross-entropy loss. This lesson turns the
mutual information of Mutual information into a quantity
trainable from samples. The route: why joint-table estimation fails at
scale, the N-way contrastive task and its loss, the proof that the optimal
classifier scores candidates by the density ratio p(y \mid x)/p(y), the
derivation of the bound, exact numbers on a toy pair, the \log_2 N
ceiling that forces large candidate counts, and the loss's role in
contrastive representation learning.

documents.title: Joint tables do not scale: the estimation problem
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The InfoNCE bound › Joint tables do not scale: the estimation problem
documents.text:
Joint tables do not scale: the estimation problem

Every mutual information computed in this course came out of a complete
joint table: the 2\times 2 weather table of
Joint and conditional entropy, the 2\times 4 source of
The information bottleneck. The recipe reads p(x,y) off
every cell, takes marginals by summing and conditionals by renormalizing,
and evaluates I(X;Y) by the formulas of
Mutual information.

For the pairs modern learning cares about, the table does not exist. Let
X be a 32 \times 32 RGB image and Y a sentence describing it: X
alone ranges over 256^{3072} values, so the joint table has more cells
than there are atoms in the observable universe (about 10^{80}).
Estimating a cell probability by counting requires observing that cell
many times; no dataset visits more than a vanishing fraction of cells even
once. The counting recipe is not merely expensive at this scale: it is
undefined.

What a dataset does provide is samples. It provides draws from the
joint: the recorded pairs (x_i, y_i) \sim p(x,y). And it provides draws
from the marginal for free: shuffling the pairing detaches each y_i from
its context, giving samples of p(y) alone. The estimation problem is to
build, from these two kinds of samples, a computable quantity whose value
certifies something about I(X;Y).

The problem is exactly where the previous lesson stopped:
The information bottleneck defined the objective
I(X;T) - \beta\, I(T;Y) and noted that estimating its mutual
informations from high-dimensional samples gates every practical use.
Contrastive predictive coding
(van den Oord, Li & Vinyals, 2018) supplies the tool this lesson derives;
its motivating observation (§2.1 of the paper) is that mutual information
is the right training objective for representations, and that modeling
p(y \mid x) generatively (reconstructing every pixel of y) spends
model capacity on detail the shared information does not contain.

Every I(X;Y) so far came from a full joint table; for images, audio,
and text the table is unavailable. InfoNCE replaces it with a quantity
computable from two things every dataset has: paired samples and shuffled
samples.

documents.title: The contrastive setup: one true partner among N candidates
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The InfoNCE bound › The contrastive setup: one true partner among N candidates
documents.text:
The contrastive setup: one true partner among N candidates

The running toy pair

The toy joint for the whole lesson is the dependence-dial table of
Mutual information at agreement q = 0.75: binary X and
Y with uniform marginals, diagonal cells \tfrac38, off-diagonal cells
\tfrac18. Its conditionals are p(y{=}x \mid x) = 0.75, and its mutual
information is I(X;Y) = 1 - H_2(0.75) \approx 0.189 bits. Small enough
to enumerate exactly, so every claim below can be checked by hand.

The protocol: sample, shuffle, classify

One round of the contrastive task is built from the two available sample
types:

Draw the positive. One pair (x, y_{\text{pos}}) \sim p(x,y): the
context and its true partner.

Draw the negatives. N-1 candidates y_1, \ldots, y_{N-1},
independent draws from the marginal p(y).

Classify. Present x and the N candidates in random order; the
classifier must identify which candidate is the partner.

A classifier for this task is built from a critic: a function
f(x, y) > 0 scoring how well y fits x. The scores over the N
candidates are normalized by a softmax into a distribution over positions,
and the round bills the classifier the surprisal of the softmax weight it
placed on the true partner: a one-hot cross-entropy, the exact loss of
Cross-entropy with N classes.

One round: score every candidate against the context, softmax the scores, pay the surprisal of the weight placed on the true partner.

Given a joint distribution p(x,y), a candidate count N \ge 2, and a
critic f(x,y) > 0, the InfoNCE loss is

L_N[f] = \mathbb{E}\left[

the expectation running over the positive pair
(x, y_{\text{pos}}) \sim p(x,y) and the negatives
y_1, \ldots, y_{N-1} \sim p(y), drawn independently.

Chance baseline: a critic that has learned nothing, a constant
f, makes the softmax uniform, weight \tfrac1N on every candidate,
and pays L_N = \log_2 N bits. Any smaller loss is evidence that the
critic distinguishes true pairs from shuffled ones; the bound below turns
that evidence into a certified number of bits.

The negatives' distribution is not a free design choice: everything
derived below identifies ratios against p(y), so the negatives
must come from the marginal itself. In practice this is what a training
batch provides: for each context, the other pairs' partners are marginal
draws. This is the point of contrast with generic noise-contrastive
estimation (Gutmann & Hyvärinen, 2010),
which discriminates data from a designer-chosen noise distribution to fit
unnormalized models. Exercise 7 prices the mismatch when negatives come
from the wrong distribution.

The InfoNCE loss is an N-way cross-entropy: one candidate from
p(y \mid x), N-1 from p(y), and the classifier is billed
-\log_2 of the softmax weight it put on the true partner. Chance costs
\log_2 N bits.

documents.title: The optimal critic recovers the density ratio
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The InfoNCE bound › The optimal critic recovers the density ratio
documents.text:
The optimal critic recovers the density ratio

Bayes on one concrete round

Take the toy pair at N = 2, context x = 0, and suppose the two
candidates presented are y_1 = 0 and y_2 = 1. Bayes' rule identifies
the partner, over the two position hypotheses with a uniform prior:

p(\text{pos}{=}1 \mid \text{data})

Dividing numerator and denominator by p(y_1)\,p(y_2) = 0.25 rewrites
the same posterior in a more portable form:

p(\text{pos}{=}1 \mid \text{data})

The posterior depends on the candidates only through the ratios
p(y \mid x)/p(y): the per-cell departure from independence, which
Mutual information met as the pointwise mutual
information's argument. The general statement:

In one round with candidates y_1, \ldots, y_N (the positive at a
uniformly random position), the posterior probability that position i
holds the true partner is

p(\text{pos}{=}i \mid x, y_1, \ldots, y_N)

and L_N[f] is minimized exactly when the score softmax equals this
posterior. In particular every critic of the form
f(x,y) = h(x)\, r(x,y) with h > 0 is optimal, for every N
simultaneously.

The posterior. Given \text{pos} = i and the context x, the
candidate values have density
p(y_i \mid x) \prod_{j \ne i} p(y_j): the positive is drawn from the
conditional, the negatives from the marginal. The prior over i is
uniform, so Bayes' rule gives

p(\text{pos}{=}i \mid x, y_{1..N})

Divide numerator and denominator by \prod_{j=1}^{N} p(y_j), a positive
constant not depending on i: each term
p(y_k \mid x) \prod_{j \ne k} p(y_j) becomes
p(y_k \mid x)/p(y_k) = r(x, y_k), which is the stated softmax.

Minimality. Condition on x and the candidate values. The true
position is distributed by the posterior \pi, and the classifier's
softmax s_f is billed -\log_2 s_f(i) when the truth is i, so the
conditional expected loss is \sum_i \pi(i)(-\log_2 s_f(i)) =
H(\pi, s_f): a cross-entropy, minimized uniquely at s_f = \pi
(Gibbs' inequality, as in Cross-entropy). Averaging
over rounds preserves the minimizer. The softmax is unchanged by
rescaling f by any factor constant in the candidate, so
f = h(x)\, r attains it; r does not depend on N, so one critic is
optimal at every N.

The theorem is the mechanism's core. Training the classifier drives the
critic toward the ratio p(y \mid x)/p(y), and the ratio is obtained
without modeling either distribution. No density over images, no
density over sentences: only a scoring function whose softmax matches an
N-way posterior. That is what makes the construction usable exactly
where the joint table is not.

The loss-minimizing critic scores candidates by the density ratio
p(y \mid x)/p(y), the joint's cell-by-cell departure from independence,
learned without ever modeling p(y \mid x) or p(y) separately.

documents.title: The bound: log₂ N minus the loss never overstates I
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The InfoNCE bound › The bound: log₂ N minus the loss never overstates I
documents.text:
The bound: log₂ N minus the loss never overstates I

The last ingredient is the identity the whole derivation turns on.
Mutual information proved the divergence form
I(X;Y) = \sum_{x,y} p(x,y) \log_2 \tfrac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)}; since
\tfrac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)} = \tfrac{p(y \mid x)}{p(y)} = r(x,y), this
reads: mutual information is the expected log ratio at true pairs,

I(X;Y) = \mathbb{E}_{p(x,y)}\bigl[\log_2 r(x, y)\bigr]

(Cover & Thomas
§2.3). The critic has just learned r; the loss it pays is therefore an
expectation of the same logarithms, and comparing the two gives the
bound.

For every critic f and every N \ge 2, with L_N in bits,

I(X;Y) \;\ge\; \log_2 N - L_N[f].

Derivation at the level of rigor of
van den Oord et al., Appendix A.1;
two steps are approximations, flagged where they occur and discussed in
the remark below.

Step 1: reduce to the optimal critic. By the previous theorem,
L_N[f] \ge L_N[r] for every f: a lower bound established for the
optimal critic transfers to all critics.

Step 2: the optimal loss. With f = r, writing \rho = r(x,
y_{\text{pos}}) for the positive's ratio and
S = \sum_{j=1}^{N-1} r(x, y_j) for the negatives' total,

L_N[r] = \mathbb{E}\left[\log_2\!\left(1 + \frac{S}{\rho}\right)\right].

Step 3: the negatives sum to about N-1. Each negative is an
independent draw from p(y), and the ratio has unit mean under the
marginal:

\mathbb{E}_{y \sim p(y)}\bigl[r(x, y)\bigr]

(Exercise 3). So \mathbb{E}[S] = N - 1, and the first approximation
replaces S by its mean (the relative fluctuation of a sum of N-1
independent unit-mean terms shrinks as N grows):

L_N[r] \approx \mathbb{E}\left[\log_2\!\left(1 + \frac{N-1}{\rho}\right)\right].

Step 4: round N-1 up to N. Pointwise,
1 + (N-1)/\rho \ge N/\rho exactly when \rho \ge 1; the second
informal step applies it inside the expectation wholesale:

\mathbb{E}\left[\log_2\!\left(1 + \frac{N-1}{\rho}\right)\right]

Step 5: the divergence form finishes.

\mathbb{E}\left[\log_2 \frac{N}{\rho}\right]

since the positive pair is a draw from the joint. Chaining:
L_N[f] \ge L_N[r] \gtrsim \log_2 N - I(X;Y), which rearranges to the
statement.

Two steps were informal: replacing the negatives' sum by its mean
(step 3, accurate for large N), and applying the \rho \ge 1
inequality under the expectation (step 4; \rho < 1 occurs whenever the
positive pair is an anti-correlated cell). The conclusion survives both:
Poole et al. (2019) prove
I(X;Y) \ge \log_2 N - L_N[f] exactly, for every critic and every N,
placing InfoNCE in a family of variational mutual-information bounds.
The paper-level derivation is kept here because it shows where each term
comes from; the exact enumerations below use no approximation at all.

The derivation in four moves: Bayes over the candidates, marginals cancel, the ratio is the optimal critic, substitution gives the bound.

Step through the four frames and name the source of each move: frame 2
is division by \prod_j p(y_j), frame 4 uses the unit-mean identity
\mathbb{E}_{p(y)}[r] = 1 (Exercise 3) and the divergence form
I = \mathbb{E}_{p(x,y)}[\log_2 r] from
Mutual information.

Reading the inequality: a budget minus a bill

The three quantities in I(X;Y) \ge \log_2 N - L_N each have an
operational reading. \log_2 N is the bits needed to name one candidate
out of N, and it is exactly what the chance classifier pays: the
budget of the task. L_N is what the trained classifier actually pays.
The difference, the classifier's edge over chance, is a certified floor
under the mutual information: the partner can only be found faster than
chance if x and y share information, and every bit of edge is backed
by a shared bit.

Budget minus bill: the classifier's edge over the log₂ N chance loss is a certified floor under I(X;Y).

The inequality is a one-way certificate. A low loss proves high
mutual information: nothing but shared bits can produce an edge over
chance. A high loss proves nothing: it may mean the variables are nearly
independent, or only that the critic is bad. The direction matters in
practice: a trained InfoNCE loss reported as \log_2 N - L_N bits is a
floor under I, never a measurement of it.

The paper and every deep-learning framework compute L_N with natural
logarithms; the bound there reads I \ge \ln N - L_N in nats. The
conversion is the usual factor of Surprisal:
divide nats by \ln 2 \approx 0.693 to get bits. A reported InfoNCE
loss of 2.30 nats at N = 1024 certifies
10 - 2.30/0.693 \approx 6.7 bits (Exercise 6).

InfoNCE is one point in a family of sample-based mutual-information
estimators. MINE (Belghazi et al.,
2018) bounds I through the Donsker–Varadhan representation of the KL
divergence, training a single unnormalized critic without the N-way
softmax; its estimates can exceed \log_2 N but carry high variance.
Poole et al. (2019) unify both: the
trade is variance against bias, with InfoNCE the low-variance,
ceiling-limited end. The limits are not an artifact of these particular
estimators: McAllester & Stratos (2020)
prove that any distribution-free high-confidence lower bound on mutual
information computed from n samples cannot certify more than
O(\log n) bits. Certifying many bits is intrinsically expensive.

I(X;Y) \ge \log_2 N - L_N for every critic and every N: the
certificate can undershoot but never overstate. Low loss proves high
mutual information; high loss proves nothing.

Exact numbers: the bound on the toy pair

The toy pair is small enough to evaluate L_N exactly, with no sampling
and no approximation, using the optimal critic f = r. The ratio table has two
values: r = \tfrac{0.75}{0.5} = 1.5 on agreeing cells,
r = \tfrac{0.25}{0.5} = 0.5 on disagreeing cells.

One positive and one negative. The positive's ratio \rho is 1.5 with
probability 0.75 (the pair agrees) and 0.5 with probability 0.25.
The negative is a uniform marginal draw, independent of the pair: its
ratio r_2 is 1.5 or 0.5 with probability \tfrac12 each. Four
cases:

Certified: \log_2 2 - L_2 \approx 1 - 0.906 = 0.094 bits, against the
true I = 0.189. The bound holds and captures about half the
information.

The first row explains the slack. With probability \tfrac12 the
negative equals the positive's value: the two candidates are
identical, no classifier can beat the coin flip, and a full bit is paid.
Even the exact ratio critic pays for collisions between the marginal and
the conditional.

One positive, three negatives. Let k be the number of negatives whose
value agrees with x; each negative agrees independently with
probability \tfrac12, so k \sim \mathrm{Bin}(3, \tfrac12) with
weights \tfrac18, \tfrac38, \tfrac38, \tfrac18. The denominator is
\rho + 1.5k + 0.5(3-k).

Branch \rho = 1.5 (probability 0.75): denominator 3 + k,
losses -\log_2 \tfrac{1.5}{3+k} for k = 0..3: 1, 1.415, 1.737,

\tfrac18(1) + \tfrac38(1.415) + \tfrac38(1.737) + \tfrac18(2) = 1.557
bits.

Branch \rho = 0.5 (probability 0.25): denominator 2 + k,
losses 2, 2.585, 3, 3.322 bits. Weighted: 2.760 bits.

L_4 = 0.75 \cdot 1.557 + 0.25 \cdot 2.760 \approx 1.858 \text{ bits},

The same enumeration at N = 16 gives L_{16} \approx 3.823 bits and a
certificate of 0.177 bits. The loss itself rises with N, since the
task has more distractors, but the budget \log_2 N rises faster, and
the certified difference climbs toward the true 0.189:

Exact enumeration on the toy pair: the certificate 0.094 → 0.142 → 0.177 bits approaches the true 0.189 as N grows, never crossing it.

On the toy pair the certificate holds at every N and tightens with
more negatives: 0.094 bits at N{=}2, 0.142 at N{=}4, 0.177 at
N{=}16, against the true 0.189.

documents.title: Saturation: nothing above log₂ N is certifiable
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The InfoNCE bound › Saturation: nothing above log₂ N is certifiable
documents.text:
Saturation: nothing above log₂ N is certifiable

The softmax weight on the true partner is at most 1, so the loss is
never negative, and

\log_2 N - L_N \;\le\; \log_2 N

always. An N-way question can certify at most the bits it takes to
answer it. When the true mutual information exceeds \log_2 N, the
classification task is simply too easy to be informative: the classifier
answers nearly perfectly, the loss sits near its floor, and the
certificate pins at the ceiling whatever the surplus dependence.

Let X be uniform on four symbols and Y = X in lockstep:
I(X;Y) = H(X) = 2 bits. The ratio is r = 4 when y = x and 0
otherwise, so the optimal critic solves every round in which no negative
collides with the positive: the loss comes entirely from collisions.
With k colliding negatives the softmax weight on the positive is
\tfrac{4}{4(1+k)} = \tfrac{1}{1+k}, and
k \sim \mathrm{Bin}(N-1, \tfrac14):

L_N = \mathbb{E}\bigl[\log_2 (1 + k)\bigr].

At N = 2 the ceiling is \log_2 2 = 1 bit and the certificate cannot
even reach that: half the true information is invisible. Only at
N = 256 does the certificate approach the true 2 bits.

More negatives raise the ceiling, at the rate of one extra bit per
doubling of N. Certifying 8 bits requires N > 256; certifying the
\sim\!10 bits a rich image–caption pair might share requires
candidate counts in the thousands.

The certificate follows the true I until it clips at log₂ N: 1, 4, and 8 bits for N = 2, 16, 256. Doubling N raises the ceiling by one bit.

Load the strong dependence, small N preset: the plotted bound clips at
\log_2 N well below the true I. Raise N and watch the ceiling
lift by one bit per doubling; then lower the dependence and check the
regime where the bound tracks I closely: saturation only bites when
I approaches \log_2 N.

In practice L_N is itself estimated from a finite batch, so
\log_2 N - \hat L_N is a noisy estimate of a lower bound, not an
unbiased estimator of I, and on any given batch it can fluctuate above
the true value even though its target sits below. The two qualifications
compound: the quantity is (an estimate of) (a floor). Reporting it as
"the mutual information" overstates on both counts.

The ceiling is why contrastive training runs at extreme batch sizes.
In-batch negatives put N equal to the batch size, so the batch caps
the bits the loss can see:
SimCLR (Chen et al., 2020) trains
with batches up to 4096 (\log_2 4096 = 12 bits of ceiling), and
CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) uses
32{,}768 (15 bits). The gain per doubling is a single bit, which is
also why returns diminish: the jump from 256 to 32{,}768 negatives
buys 7 bits of ceiling, not a hundredfold improvement.

\log_2 N - L_N \le \log_2 N always: an N-way classification can
certify at most the bits needed to answer it, so dependence beyond the
ceiling stays invisible until N grows. This is why contrastive methods
use large batches.

documents.title: The payoff: one loss across audio, vision, text, and RL
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The InfoNCE bound › The payoff: one loss across audio, vision, text, and RL
documents.text:
The payoff: one loss across audio, vision, text, and RL

The bound was derived for representation learning, and the deriving
system shows where it sits in practice. Contrastive predictive coding
(CPC) processes a signal (raw speech, image patches read as a sequence,
text, an agent's observations) with an encoder producing latents z_t,
summarizes the past into a context c_t with an autoregressive network,
and scores future latents z_{t+k} against negatives from other
positions with a critic f_k(z_{t+k}, c_t). The InfoNCE loss on this
lineup is the system's only training signal: minimizing it maximizes
a certified floor under I(z_{t+k}; c_t), forcing the context to carry
the bits that predict the future, without reconstructing a single
sample of it.

CPC in one strip: encode, summarize, score the signal's own future against negatives. The InfoNCE lineup is the only loss in the system.

The same loss, unchanged, works across modalities: the paper's
experiments (§3) train the identical objective on four domains. On
LibriSpeech speech, a linear classifier on CPC representations reaches
64.6\% phone accuracy against 39.7\% for MFCC features and 74.6\%
for a fully supervised network: most of the supervised gap closed with
no labels. On ImageNet, a linear probe on CPC features reaches 48.7\%
top-1 accuracy; in reinforcement learning, adding the loss as an
auxiliary objective improves A2C agents on DeepMind Lab tasks. The
critic's density-ratio trick, with the pair (x, y) instantiated as
context–future, image–image view, or image–caption, is the shared core
of the contrastive representation learning that followed, SimCLR and
CLIP among it.

The lesson also closes the arc of this module.
The information bottleneck prescribed what a good
representation should optimize: keep I(T;Y), spend little I(X;T).
Both terms were uncomputable outside toy tables. InfoNCE makes the relevance
term trainable: \log_2 N - L_N is a differentiable floor under a
mutual information, maximized by gradient descent on the critic and
encoder jointly. A prescription became a loss function.

One InfoNCE loss trains representations in speech, vision, text, and RL;
the density-ratio critic is the common core of contrastive
representation learning, and the bound is the trainable surrogate for
the bottleneck's relevance term I(T;Y).

documents.title: Exercises
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Optimization principles in inference and learning › The InfoNCE bound › Exercises
documents.text:
Exercises

Repeat the N = 2 enumeration on the dependence-dial table at
q = 0.9 (diagonal cells 0.45, off-diagonal 0.05; the table of
Mutual information, Exercise 3, with
I(X;Y) \approx 0.531 bits). Write the ratio table, enumerate the four
cases for the optimal critic, compute L_2 and the certificate
\log_2 2 - L_2, and compare with the true I. Use
-\log_2 0.9 \approx 0.152 and \log_2 10 \approx 3.322.

Ratios. Diagonal: r = 0.9/0.5 = 1.8; off-diagonal:
r = 0.1/0.5 = 0.2.

Cases. The positive's ratio is 1.8 with probability 0.9, 0.2
with probability 0.1; the negative's is 1.8 or 0.2 with
probability \tfrac12 each, independently:

\rho

r_2

prob.

softmax

loss (bits)

1.8

1.8

0.45

0.5

1

1.8

0.2

0.45

0.9

0.152

0.2

1.8

0.05

0.1

3.322

0.2

0.2

0.05

0.5

1

L_2 = 0.45 + 0.45 \cdot 0.152 + 0.05 \cdot 3.322 + 0.05 \cdot 1

Certificate. 1 - 0.734 = 0.266 bits, against the true
I \approx 0.531: the bound holds and captures about half the
information. As in the lesson's toy, the dominant slack is the
collision row (\rho = r_2 = 1.8), where the candidates are identical
and a full bit is paid regardless of the critic.

Derive the optimal posterior for N = 2 directly. One candidate pair
(y_1, y_2) is presented for context x; with probability \tfrac12
the partner is y_1 (then y_2 \sim p(y)), otherwise y_2. Show from
Bayes' rule that

p(\text{pos}{=}1 \mid x, y_1, y_2)

and verify the formula on the lesson's concrete round (x = 0,
y_1 = 0, y_2 = 1, toy table at q = 0.75).

The two hypotheses have likelihoods
p(y_1 \mid x)\, p(y_2) and p(y_2 \mid x)\, p(y_1), each with prior
\tfrac12. Bayes' rule:

p(\text{pos}{=}1 \mid x, y_1, y_2)

Divide numerator and denominator by p(y_1)\, p(y_2) > 0:

= \frac{p(y_1 \mid x)/p(y_1)}

On the concrete round: r(0,0) = 1.5, r(0,1) = 0.5, so the posterior
is \tfrac{1.5}{1.5 + 0.5} = 0.75, matching the direct Bayes
computation in the lesson: \tfrac{0.75 \cdot 0.5}{0.75 \cdot 0.5 +
0.25 \cdot 0.5} = 0.75.

Prove the unit-mean identity used in step 3 of the bound's derivation:
for every x,

\mathbb{E}_{y \sim p(y)}\left[\frac{p(y \mid x)}{p(y)}\right] = 1,

and state in one sentence why it makes the negatives' score sum
concentrate near N - 1.

Expand the expectation over the marginal:

\mathbb{E}_{y \sim p(y)}\left[\frac{p(y \mid x)}{p(y)}\right]

since p(y \mid x) is a probability distribution over y for each
fixed x (terms with p(y) = 0 contribute nothing: such y is never
drawn). The negatives' total S = \sum_{j=1}^{N-1} r(x, y_j) is a sum
of N-1 independent terms each with mean 1, so
\mathbb{E}[S] = N-1 and the relative fluctuation of S around N-1
shrinks as N grows: the justification for replacing S by N-1 in
the derivation.

Prove that the certificate never exceeds the budget:
\log_2 N - L_N[f] \le \log_2 N for every critic f. Then compute the
saturation exactly for a binary lockstep pair (X uniform on
\{0,1\}, Y = X, so I(X;Y) = 1 bit) at N = 2 with the optimal
critic, and state what fraction of the true information is certified.

Ceiling. The softmax weight on the true partner is a term of a
distribution, hence at most 1, so every round's bill
-\log_2(\text{weight}) \ge 0 and L_N[f] \ge 0. Subtracting,
\log_2 N - L_N \le \log_2 N.

Binary lockstep at N = 2. The ratio is r = \tfrac{1}{1/2} = 2
when y = x and 0 otherwise; the positive always has \rho = 2. The
single negative is a fair marginal draw: with probability \tfrac12 it
collides (y = x), making the candidates identical: softmax
\tfrac{2}{2+2} = \tfrac12, loss 1 bit. With probability \tfrac12
it differs: softmax \tfrac{2}{2+0} = 1, loss 0.

L_2 = \tfrac12 \cdot 1 + \tfrac12 \cdot 0 = 0.5 \text{ bits},

The certificate is 0.5 of the true 1 bit: exactly half. Even a
perfect critic loses a full bit whenever the marginal draw duplicates
the positive, and at N = 2 that happens half the time. (Raising N
recovers the rest: the ceiling \log_2 N grows while collisions cost
only \log_2(1+k).)

Review of Mutual information: for the weather table
(p(\text{clear},\text{dry}) = \tfrac12,
p(\text{clear},\text{wet}) = 0,
p(\text{overcast},\text{dry}) = p(\text{overcast},\text{wet}) =
\tfrac14, with X the sky and Y the ground), compute the ratio
r(x,y) = p(y \mid x)/p(y) for each nonzero cell and verify the
identity the bound's derivation turns on:
\mathbb{E}_{p(x,y)}[\log_2 r] = I(X;Y) \approx 0.311 bits. Use
\log_2 3 \approx 1.585.

Marginals: p(\text{dry}) = \tfrac34, p(\text{wet}) = \tfrac14.
Conditionals given the sky: clear \Rightarrow dry certain
(p(\text{dry} \mid \text{clear}) = 1); overcast \Rightarrow each
with probability \tfrac12.

Ratios:
r(\text{clear}, \text{dry}) = \tfrac{1}{3/4} = \tfrac43;
r(\text{overcast}, \text{dry}) = \tfrac{1/2}{3/4} = \tfrac23;
r(\text{overcast}, \text{wet}) = \tfrac{1/2}{1/4} = 2. The
zero-probability cell (clear, wet) never occurs and is skipped.

Expected log ratio, weighted by the joint:

\tfrac12 \log_2 \tfrac43 + \tfrac14 \log_2 \tfrac23 + \tfrac14 \log_2 2

matching I(X;Y) \approx 0.311 from the mutual-information lesson: the
log ratios are the pointwise mutual informations, and their
joint-weighted average is I. An optimal contrastive critic on this
table would score (overcast, wet) highest (r = 2) and
(overcast, dry) below 1: the cell that occurs less often than
independence predicts.

A contrastive model trained with N = 1024 candidates reports an
InfoNCE loss of 2.30 nats. Convert the certificate to bits. Then state
what a reported loss of \ln 1024 \approx 6.93 nats would certify, and
why.

In nats the bound reads I \ge \ln N - L_N. Converting via
1 \text{ bit} = \ln 2 \approx 0.693 nats
(Surprisal): the loss is
2.30 / 0.693 \approx 3.32 bits, the budget is
\log_2 1024 = 10 bits, so

I(X;Y) \ge 10 - 3.32 \approx 6.7 \text{ bits}.

(Equivalently in nats: 6.93 - 2.30 = 4.63 nats = 6.7 bits.)

A loss of \ln 1024 nats is exactly the chance loss \log_2 1024 bits:
the certificate is 10 - 10 = 0 bits. It certifies nothing, consistent
both with independent variables and with a critic that has learned
nothing, which is the one-way direction of the bound.

Suppose the negatives are drawn not from the marginal p(y) but from
some other distribution q(y) with full support. Show that the
Bayes-optimal critic becomes f(x,y) \propto p(y \mid x)/q(y), and
that the expected log of this ratio at true pairs is

\mathbb{E}_{p(x,y)}\left[\log_2 \frac{p(y \mid x)}{q(y)}\right]

where p_Y is the true marginal and D is the KL divergence of
KL divergence. Conclude what goes wrong with the
certificate.

The critic. Rerun the posterior derivation with negatives from q:
given \text{pos} = i, the candidates have density
p(y_i \mid x) \prod_{j \ne i} q(y_j). Dividing numerator and
denominator of Bayes' rule by \prod_j q(y_j) leaves

p(\text{pos}{=}i \mid x, y_{1..N})

so the optimal critic is the ratio against the wrong reference,
r'(x,y) = p(y \mid x)/q(y).

The expectation. Split the logarithm:
