\mathbb{E}_{p(x,y)}\left[\log_2 \frac{p(y \mid x)}{q(y)}\right]

The first term is I(X;Y) (divergence form). In the second, the
integrand depends only on y, so the expectation collapses to the
marginal: \sum_y p(y) \log_2 \tfrac{p(y)}{q(y)} = D(p_Y \| q).

Conclusion. The role that I played in the derivation is now
played by I(X;Y) + D(p_Y \| q) \ge I(X;Y): for large N the quantity
\log_2 N - L_N approaches the inflated value, exceeding the true
mutual information by exactly the marginal mismatch. The one-way
certificate is broken: the reported number can overstate I. This is
why implementations build negatives by shuffling real partners (exact
marginal draws) rather than sampling from a convenient noise model.

A. van den Oord, Y. Li, O. Vinyals, "Representation Learning with Contrastive Predictive Coding," 2018 — §2.1 mutual information as the representation-learning objective and the case against generative reconstruction; §2.3 the InfoNCE loss and the optimal critic as a density ratio; Appendix A.1 (eqs. 6–11) the derivation of I \ge \log N - L_N; §3 the audio, vision, language, and RL experiments quoted here. https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.03748

T. M. Cover, J. A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006 — §2.3: mutual information as the expected log density ratio, the identity the derivation turns on.

B. Poole, S. Ozair, A. van den Oord, A. A. Alemi, G. Tucker, "On Variational Bounds of Mutual Information," ICML 2019 — the exact proof that InfoNCE lower-bounds I for every critic, and the bias–variance map of the estimator family. https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.06922

M. I. Belghazi, A. Baratin, S. Rajeswar, S. Ozair, Y. Bengio, A. Courville, R. D. Hjelm, "MINE: Mutual Information Neural Estimation," ICML 2018 — the Donsker–Varadhan alternative estimator discussed in the aside. https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.04062

M. Gutmann, A. Hyvärinen, "Noise-contrastive estimation: A new estimation principle for unnormalized statistical models," AISTATS 2010 — generic NCE with designer noise, the contrast for the marginal-negatives requirement. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v9/gutmann10a.html

D. McAllester, K. Stratos, "Formal Limitations on the Measurement of Mutual Information," AISTATS 2020 — distribution-free lower bounds from n samples cannot certify more than O(\log n) bits. https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.04251

N. Tishby, F. C. Pereira, W. Bialek, "The Information Bottleneck Method," 1999 — the objective whose relevance term I(T;Y) InfoNCE makes trainable. https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0004057

documents.title: Mutual information of a neural code
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information in the natural sciences › Mutual information of a neural code
documents.text:
A neuron is a noisy channel from stimulus to spike train, and the mutual
information I(S;R) = H(R) - H(R|S) measures, in bits, how much its
response reveals about what it saw. This lesson builds a small
stimulus-response table, computes I(S;R) by the direct method as a total
response entropy minus a noise entropy, divides the result by the mean spike
count to read off bits per spike, measures the code against the channel's
capacity as coding efficiency, and states honestly what a finite sample of
spikes can and cannot certify.

documents.title: A neuron is a noisy channel
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information in the natural sciences › Mutual information of a neural code › A neuron is a noisy channel
documents.text:
A neuron is a noisy channel

Present a stimulus to a sensory neuron and record its spikes; present the
same stimulus again and the spike pattern differs. The variability is the
channel's noise. Fix a short time bin and record whether the neuron fired at
least once (a spike, R = 1) or stayed silent (R = 0). Two stimuli, a
weak drive s_0 and a strong drive s_1, presented with equal frequency,
produce a two-row transition table:

p(r \mid s):\qquad

Each row is the response distribution for one stimulus: given s_0 the
neuron is usually silent, given s_1 it usually fires. Nothing about the
biophysics enters beyond this table: membrane currents, synapses, and ion
channels matter only through the numbers p(r \mid s). This is exactly the
discrete memoryless channel of the
channel lessons, relabelled: the stimulus is the input, the binned spike
count is the output.

The neuron as a transition table: stimulus in, binned spike response out, with the 1/8 crossings as noise.

The table is symmetric (the neural reading of \mathrm{BSC}(1/8)), but
nothing in what follows needs the symmetry; an asymmetric neuron gives
asymmetric rows and the same computation.

A neuron is specified, for information purposes, by its transition table
p(r \mid s): one response distribution per stimulus. The trial-to-trial
variability within a row is the channel's noise.

documents.title: The direct method: I(S;R) = H(R) − H(R|S)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information in the natural sciences › Mutual information of a neural code › The direct method: I(S;R) = H(R) − H(R|S)
documents.text:
The direct method: I(S;R) = H(R) − H(R|S)

The tuning curve of classical neurophysiology records only the mean response
per stimulus: here \mathbb{E}[R \mid s_0] = 1/8 and
\mathbb{E}[R \mid s_1] = 7/8. Two means do not say how reliably a downstream
neuron, seeing one spike count, can tell the stimuli apart. Mutual
information does, and it is computed from the same table by the direct
method: estimate the total response entropy H(R) and the average
per-stimulus noise entropy H(R \mid S), then subtract.

Total response entropy H(R). Marginalize the table over the two equally
likely stimuli:

p(R = 1) = \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{8} + \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{7}{8}

so the pooled response is a fair coin and H(R) = 1 bit. This is the full
variety the output could carry.

Noise entropy H(R \mid S). Each row is a (7/8, 1/8) split, whose
binary entropy is

H(\tfrac{1}{8}) = -\tfrac{1}{8}\log_2\tfrac{1}{8}

Both rows give the same value, so the weighted average is
H(R \mid S) = 0.544 bits: the response entropy that survives even when the
stimulus is known, which is noise by definition.

Subtract.

I(S;R) = H(R) - H(R \mid S) = 1 - 0.544 = 0.456 \text{ bits per bin}.

The direct method in three moves: pool for H(R), average the rows for H(R|S), subtract for I(S;R).

Step through the three frames and check the arithmetic at each stop: the
pooled response is (\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}) so H(R) = 1; each row
carries H(\tfrac{1}{8}) = 0.544 so H(R \mid S) = 0.544; the difference
1 - 0.544 = 0.456 bits is what one binned response reveals about the
stimulus.

The recipe is the entropy and mutual-information
machinery applied verbatim, with S and R in place of the weather
variables. Its neural name, the direct method, is due to
Strong et al. (1998),
who estimated both entropies straight from binned spike trains of the fly
motion-sensitive neuron H1 rather than from any model of the neuron.

Mutual information is symmetric, so the same 0.456 bits must come out of
I(S;R) = H(S) - H(S \mid R). The stimulus prior is uniform, H(S) = 1 bit.
Condition on the response instead. Since p(R = 0) = p(R = 1) = \tfrac{1}{2},
Bayes' rule gives, for R = 0,

p(s_0 \mid R = 0) = \frac{\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{7}{8}}{\tfrac{1}{2}}

so the posterior over stimuli is (7/8, 1/8) with entropy 0.544 bits;
R = 1 is the mirror image, also 0.544 bits. Averaging,
H(S \mid R) = 0.544, and

I(S;R) = 1 - 0.544 = 0.456 \text{ bits},

matching the response-side computation. A downstream neuron that sees one
spike bin resolves 0.456 of the 1 bit of stimulus uncertainty.

The direct method computes I(S;R) = H(R) - H(R \mid S) straight from the
response table: total response entropy minus the average within-stimulus
(noise) entropy — no model of the neuron required.

documents.title: Mutual information beats the tuning curve
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information in the natural sciences › Mutual information of a neural code › Mutual information beats the tuning curve
documents.text:
Mutual information beats the tuning curve

The tuning curve reports a mean and, at best, an error bar per stimulus. Two
neurons with identical tuning curves can carry very different information: if
the trial-to-trial response distributions overlap heavily, a single response
barely distinguishes the stimuli even when the means are far apart; if they
are tight and separated, one response nearly settles the question. The mean
cannot see this; the full distributions p(r \mid s) can, and I(S;R) reads
it off directly.

Same neuron, two summaries: the tuning curve hides the response overlap that mutual information prices exactly.

Mutual information also needs no assumption that the code is a firing rate. A
neuron that signals with precise spike timing rather than average rate has
a response distribution over timing patterns, and the direct method applies
unchanged once those patterns are binned — which is why
Strong et al. could
measure the information in H1's spike timing at millisecond resolution
without committing to any rate code.

The tuning curve keeps means; mutual information keeps whole response
distributions, and so measures discriminability the mean cannot — including
information carried by spike timing rather than rate.

documents.title: Bits per spike
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information in the natural sciences › Mutual information of a neural code › Bits per spike
documents.text:
Bits per spike

An absolute figure of 0.456 bits per bin is hard to compare across neurons
and experiments, because bins and firing rates differ. Dividing by the mean
number of spikes normalizes it. In the running example the mean count per bin
is

\mathbb{E}[R] = p(R = 1) = 0.5 \text{ spikes},

so the code delivers

\frac{I(S;R)}{\mathbb{E}[R]} = \frac{0.456}{0.5} \approx 0.91 \text{ bits per spike}.

Each spike, in this idealized neuron, is worth close to one bit: an
information-bearing symbol, not merely a tick contributing to an average
rate.

Information accumulates spike by spike: each spike adds close to one bit, empty bins add nothing.

The value 0.91 is a property of this constructed table. What makes it worth
computing is that real recordings land in the same neighbourhood.
Borst & Theunissen (1999)
collect measurements across species in their Table 2: bits per spike
clustered near 1, with a reported range of roughly 0.6 to 3.2 across
preparations. The number is an empirical regularity of recorded neurons, not
a theorem: it depends on the stimulus ensemble, the bin width, and the
species. Its order of magnitude is nonetheless robust, and it is the reason
spike trains are read as information-bearing codes rather than as smoothed
rates.

Not every neuron approaches a bit per spike. Take a neuron whose two
stimulus rows are p(r \mid s_0) = (\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{4}, \tfrac{1}{4})
and p(r \mid s_1) = (\tfrac{1}{4}, \tfrac{1}{4}, \tfrac{1}{2}) over spike
counts r \in \{0, 1, 2\}, with uniform stimuli. Pooling gives
p(R) = (\tfrac{3}{8}, \tfrac{1}{4}, \tfrac{3}{8}), so

H(R) = 2\cdot\tfrac{3}{8}\log_2\tfrac{8}{3} + \tfrac{1}{4}\cdot 2

Each row is a permutation of (\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{4}, \tfrac{1}{4})
with entropy 1.5 bits, so H(R \mid S) = 1.5 and
I(S;R) \approx 0.06 bits. The mean count is
\tfrac{1}{2}(0.75 + 1.25) = 1 spike, so this neuron spends a full spike per
bin to transmit 0.06 bits: about 0.06 bits per spike. High firing, almost
no information: the metric exposes a code that a tuning curve, showing a
clean difference in means, would flatter.

Dividing I(S;R) by the mean spike count gives bits per spike; recorded
single neurons cluster near one bit per spike (Borst & Theunissen, Table 2),
an empirical range across preparations, not a universal constant.

documents.title: Coding efficiency: I(S;R) / C
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information in the natural sciences › Mutual information of a neural code › Coding efficiency: I(S;R) / C
documents.text:
Coding efficiency: I(S;R) / C

The neuron's channel has a ceiling. Its
capacity is the largest mutual
information any stimulus ensemble could push through the fixed table,
C = \max_{p(s)} I(S;R), and coding efficiency is the fraction of that
ceiling a given code actually uses.

For a neuron with capacity C driven by a stimulus ensemble that transmits
I(S;R) bits, the coding efficiency is

\eta = \frac{I(S;R)}{C},

the fraction of the channel's capacity the code realizes, 0 \le \eta \le 1.

For the symmetric running table, \mathrm{BSC}(1/8), the capacity is
C = 1 - H(\tfrac{1}{8}) = 1 - 0.544 = 0.456 bits per bin, attained by the
uniform stimulus prior (Channel capacity). The running
example uses exactly that prior, so it sits at the ceiling by construction:
\eta = 0.456 / 0.456 = 1. This is an artifact of a symmetric toy driven by
its capacity-achieving input, not a claim that neurons choose optimal codes.

Change the ensemble and efficiency drops. Suppose the strong stimulus s_1
is presented nine times as often, p(s_1) = 0.9. The noise term is
unchanged, H(R \mid S) = 0.544, but the pooled response is now
p(R = 1) = 0.9\cdot\tfrac{7}{8} + 0.1\cdot\tfrac{1}{8} = 0.8, so
H(R) = H(0.8) = 0.722 and

I(S;R) = 0.722 - 0.544 = 0.178 \text{ bits}, \qquad

The same neuron now uses under 40\% of its channel: a stimulus set that
rarely exercises the silent response wastes the capacity.

Efficiency is stimulus-dependent: a naturalistic ensemble fills the channel; a noise ensemble leaves most of it empty.

Real measurements show the same stimulus dependence far more sharply.
Borst & Theunissen review cases
in which a neuron encodes a naturalistic stimulus with efficiency approaching
90\% while encoding a white-noise stimulus of matched power at a fraction of
that — on the order of 20\% in bullfrog auditory afferents. Sensory neurons
appear tuned to the statistics of their natural inputs, and efficiency, unlike
an absolute bit count, is comparable across those conditions.

Capacity for a continuous response. Real spike trains are not binary, and
their capacity is usually estimated through the Gaussian-channel bound rather
than a discrete maximization. Treating the response as a signal plus
independent Gaussian noise across frequency bands gives

C = \int \log_2\!\bigl(1 + \mathrm{SNR}(f)\bigr)\, df,

the continuous-channel formula whose single-band form
C = \tfrac{1}{2}\log_2(1 + P/N) was cited in
Channel capacity. Borst & Theunissen's Box 3 develops the
coherence-based upper and lower bounds built on it. The continuous derivation
is out of scope here; this course stays with the discrete table, where the
capacity is the same maximization the channel lessons already ran.

Coding efficiency \eta = I(S;R) / C is the fraction of channel capacity a
code uses. It is a property of the stimulus ensemble, not of the neuron
alone: naturalistic stimuli raise it, and mutual information is only
meaningful relative to a stated ensemble.

documents.title: What the estimate can and cannot claim
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information in the natural sciences › Mutual information of a neural code › What the estimate can and cannot claim
documents.text:
What the estimate can and cannot claim

Every number above assumed the true probabilities p(r \mid s). In an
experiment they are estimated from finitely many trials, and that introduces
a bias with a definite sign.

Finite samples overestimate. Entropy estimated by plugging empirical
frequencies into -\sum \hat{p}\log_2\hat{p} is biased, and for mutual
information the biases combine so that the plug-in estimate sits above the
true value. The clean diagnostic is a shuffled control: randomly repair
each response with a stimulus drawn independently, destroying any real
dependence, and re-estimate. The true mutual information of shuffled data is
zero, so whatever the estimator returns, often a visibly nonzero number, is
pure bias at that sample size. Corrections that extrapolate the bias away
(for instance a jackknife over subsets of the data) exist; the point here is
that a raw positive estimate is not, by itself, evidence of a code.

Finite samples fake information: the plug-in estimate decays onto the truth from above, and the shuffled control shows the bias sitting above zero.

A decoder only lower-bounds the information. A common alternative to the
direct method fits a model that reconstructs the stimulus from the response
and reports the information in the reconstruction. Because the reconstruction
\hat{S} is computed from R alone, the chain S \to R \to \hat{S} is
Markov, and the data-processing
inequality gives

I(S; \hat{S}) \le I(S; R).

Any decoding-based estimate is therefore a lower bound on the true mutual
information: a better decoder can only raise it toward I(S;R), never past
it. Borst & Theunissen (p. 949) make exactly this point in separating the
direct method from reconstruction methods.

The number is relative to the ensemble. Because I(S;R) averages over
p(s), it is defined only once the stimulus ensemble is fixed. Absolute bit
counts do not transfer between experiments with different stimuli; efficiency
and bits per spike, which normalize against capacity and spike count, are the
quantities that compare. The finite-sample MI-estimation problem is the same
obstacle that InfoNCE sidesteps for
high-dimensional data by replacing a plug-in entropy estimate with a
sample-based bound that stays valid without ever filling in a joint table.

Finite-sample mutual information is biased upward (a nonzero shuffled control
is bias, not signal); decoding-based estimates only lower-bound the truth by
the data-processing inequality; and every value is relative to the stimulus
ensemble it was averaged over.

documents.title: Exercises
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information in the natural sciences › Mutual information of a neural code › Exercises
documents.text:
Exercises

A neuron has the binned response table p(r \mid s_0) = (\tfrac{3}{4},
\tfrac{1}{4}) and p(r \mid s_1) = (\tfrac{1}{4}, \tfrac{3}{4}) over
r \in \{0, 1\}, with equally likely stimuli. Compute I(S;R) by the direct
method and the bits per spike. Use H(\tfrac{1}{4}) \approx 0.811 bits.

Pool. p(R = 1) = \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{4} + \tfrac{1}{2}
\cdot\tfrac{3}{4} = \tfrac{1}{2}, so H(R) = 1 bit.

Noise. Each row is a (\tfrac{3}{4}, \tfrac{1}{4}) split, entropy
H(\tfrac{1}{4}) \approx 0.811; averaging, H(R \mid S) = 0.811.

Subtract. I(S;R) = 1 - 0.811 = 0.189 bits per bin.

Bits per spike. \mathbb{E}[R] = p(R = 1) = 0.5 spikes, so
0.189 / 0.5 = 0.377 bits per spike. This noisier neuron (crossover
\tfrac{1}{4} against the lesson's \tfrac{1}{8}) carries less than half the
information per spike of the running example.

A different neuron behaves as \mathrm{BSC}(1/5) (crossover \tfrac{1}{5})
with equally likely stimuli. Compute I(S;R) from the stimulus side, as
H(S) - H(S \mid R) using the posterior over stimuli, and confirm it equals
the response-side value H(R) - H(R \mid S). Use H(\tfrac{1}{5}) \approx
0.722 bits. This is the symmetry of mutual information from
Mutual information.

Stimulus side. H(S) = 1 bit (uniform prior). The pooled response is
uniform, p(R = 0) = p(R = 1) = \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{4}{5} +
\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{5} = \tfrac{1}{2}. By Bayes, for R = 0,
p(s_0 \mid R = 0) = (\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{4}{5}) / \tfrac{1}{2} =
\tfrac{4}{5}, so the posterior is (\tfrac{4}{5}, \tfrac{1}{5}) with entropy
H(\tfrac{1}{5}) = 0.722 bits; R = 1 is the mirror image, also 0.722.
Averaging, H(S \mid R) = 0.722, hence I(S;R) = 1 - 0.722 = 0.278 bits.

Response side. H(R) = 1 bit (pooled response uniform); each row is a
(\tfrac{4}{5}, \tfrac{1}{5}) split, so H(R \mid S) = H(\tfrac{1}{5}) =
0.722, and H(R) - H(R \mid S) = 1 - 0.722 = 0.278 bits. The two routes
agree, as the symmetry of mutual information guarantees.

Treat a neuron as \mathrm{BSC}(1/4) (crossover \tfrac{1}{4}). (a) Compute
its capacity C. (b) Under the biased ensemble p(s_1) = 0.8, compute
I(S;R) and the coding efficiency \eta = I(S;R)/C. Use
H(\tfrac{1}{4}) \approx 0.811 and H(0.35) \approx 0.934 bits. This uses
the capacity recipe of Channel capacity.

(a) For a symmetric channel the noise term is H(\tfrac{1}{4}) = 0.811
regardless of input, and the uniform stimulus maximizes H(R) at 1 bit, so
C = 1 - 0.811 = 0.189 bits per bin.

(b) Noise term unchanged: H(R \mid S) = 0.811. Pooled response:
p(R = 1) = 0.8\cdot\tfrac{3}{4} + 0.2\cdot\tfrac{1}{4} = 0.6 + 0.05 = 0.65,
so H(R) = H(0.35) \approx 0.934. Then I(S;R) = 0.934 - 0.811 = 0.123
bits, and \eta = 0.123 / 0.189 \approx 0.65. The biased ensemble uses about
65\% of the channel; the uniform ensemble would reach \eta = 1 because it
is the capacity-achieving input for this symmetric neuron.

A decoder observes the binned response R of the running example and outputs
a stimulus guess \hat{S}. (a) For the identity decoder \hat{S} = s_1 if
R = 1 else s_0, compute I(S; \hat{S}). (b) For the constant decoder
\hat{S} = s_1 always, compute I(S; \hat{S}). (c) State which theorem
guarantees neither exceeds I(S;R) = 0.456 bits.

(a) With \hat{S} a relabelling of the binary R, the joint table of
(S, \hat{S}) is the table of (S, R) with r = 1 \mapsto s_1,
r = 0 \mapsto s_0. So I(S; \hat{S}) = I(S;R) = 0.456 bits: for a binary
response, the identity decoder loses nothing, because R is already a
sufficient statistic.

(b) A constant \hat{S} is independent of S, so
I(S; \hat{S}) = 0 bits.

(c) The chain S \to R \to \hat{S} is Markov (\hat{S} depends on S
only through R), so the data-processing inequality gives
I(S; \hat{S}) \le I(S;R) = 0.456. Both decoders respect it: 0.456 \le
0.456 and 0 \le 0.456. A decoding-based estimate is a lower bound on the
true information.

An experimenter estimates \hat{I}(S;R) = 0.30 bits from a small number of
trials, then repeats the estimate after randomly shuffling which response
goes with which stimulus and obtains \hat{I}_{\text{shuffled}} = 0.08 bits.
Interpret the shuffled value, and give a corrected estimate of the true
mutual information.

Shuffling destroys any real stimulus-response dependence, so the true mutual
information of the shuffled data is exactly 0. The estimate
\hat{I}_{\text{shuffled}} = 0.08 bits is therefore entirely the positive
bias of the plug-in estimator at that sample size. A first-order correction
subtracts it: \hat{I}_{\text{corrected}} \approx 0.30 - 0.08 = 0.22 bits.
The raw 0.30 overstated the code by roughly a third; only the excess of the
estimate over its shuffled control is defensible as signal, and even that is
best confirmed with more data or a jackknife extrapolation.

A neuron fires up to two spikes per bin, with
p(r \mid s_0) = (\tfrac{3}{4}, \tfrac{1}{8}, \tfrac{1}{8}) and
p(r \mid s_1) = (\tfrac{1}{8}, \tfrac{1}{8}, \tfrac{3}{4}) over
r \in \{0, 1, 2\}, with uniform stimuli. Compute H(R), H(R \mid S),
I(S;R), and the bits per spike. Use \log_2 3 \approx 1.585 and
\log_2 7 \approx 2.807.

Pool. p(R) = (\tfrac{7}{16}, \tfrac{1}{8}, \tfrac{7}{16}). With
\log_2\tfrac{16}{7} = 4 - 2.807 = 1.193:
H(R) = 2\cdot\tfrac{7}{16}\log_2\tfrac{16}{7} + \tfrac{1}{8}\log_2 8
= 2\cdot 0.4375\cdot 1.193 + 0.125\cdot 3 = 1.044 + 0.375 = 1.419 bits.

Noise. Each row is a permutation of (\tfrac{3}{4}, \tfrac{1}{8},
\tfrac{1}{8}) with entropy
\tfrac{3}{4}\log_2\tfrac{4}{3} + 2\cdot\tfrac{1}{8}\log_2 8
= 0.75\,(2 - 1.585) + 2\cdot 0.125\cdot 3 = 0.311 + 0.75 = 1.061 bits, so
H(R \mid S) = 1.061.

Subtract. I(S;R) = 1.419 - 1.061 = 0.358 bits per bin.

Bits per spike. \mathbb{E}[R \mid s_0] = \tfrac{1}{8} + 2\cdot\tfrac{1}{8}
= 0.375, \mathbb{E}[R \mid s_1] = \tfrac{1}{8} + 2\cdot\tfrac{3}{4} = 1.625,
mean 1.0 spike. So 0.358 / 1.0 = 0.358 bits per spike: by placing its
spikes to distinguish the two stimuli, this neuron gets about a third of a bit
from each spike, far above the wasteful neuron of the earlier example.

Explain, in two or three sentences, why "this neuron carries 2.4 bits" is an
incomplete claim, and what two normalized quantities make information measures
comparable across experiments.

Mutual information averages over the stimulus prior p(s), so a raw bit count
is defined only relative to the stimulus ensemble used; the same neuron
reports different I(S;R) under different ensembles, and the number does not
transfer to another experiment's stimuli. The comparable quantities are bits
per spike (I / \mathbb{E}[R]), which normalizes against firing, and coding
efficiency (I / C), which normalizes against the neuron's own channel
capacity.

A. Borst, F. E. Theunissen, "Information Theory and Neural Coding," Nature Neuroscience, 2, 1999, pp. 947–957 — the primary source: general framework and Boxes 1–2 (the three decompositions of I(R,S) and the direct method), the direct-versus-reconstruction distinction and data-processing argument (p. 949), Box 3 (Gaussian/coherence capacity bounds), and Table 2 (bits/second, bits/spike, and efficiency across species).

S. P. Strong, R. Koberle, R. R. de Ruyter van Steveninck, W. Bialek, "Entropy and Information in Neural Spike Trains," Physical Review Letters, 80, 1998, pp. 197–200 — introduces the direct method of estimating H(R) and H(R \mid S) from binned spike trains, applied to the fly motion-sensitive neuron H1.

F. Rieke, D. Warland, R. de Ruyter van Steveninck, W. Bialek, Spikes: Exploring the Neural Code, MIT Press, 1997 — book-length treatment of spike-train information, bits per spike, and the efficiency of naturalistic versus artificial stimuli.

T. M. Cover, J. A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006 — §§2.2–2.4 for the entropy, conditional-entropy, and mutual-information identities used by the direct method; §7 for channel capacity, reused here as the denominator of coding efficiency.

documents.title: Thermodynamics of information
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information in the natural sciences › Thermodynamics of information
documents.text:
Information has a physical price: Landauer's principle sets the minimum
heat dissipated when one bit is erased at kT ln 2, and Szilard's engine
shows one bit of information is worth exactly that much extractable work.
This lesson establishes both statements and balances the books between
them. The route: the unit bridge identifying Shannon's H with
thermodynamic entropy, Landauer's bound derived from second-law
bookkeeping, the Szilard engine's kT \ln 2 computed as an integral,
Bennett's resolution of Maxwell's demon, and the feedback second law
W \ge \Delta F - kT(\ln 2)\, I(X;M), which prices measured information
in the mutual-information currency of Mutual information.

documents.title: One entropy, two units: k ln 2 per bit
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information in the natural sciences › Thermodynamics of information › One entropy, two units: k ln 2 per bit
documents.text:
One entropy, two units: k ln 2 per bit

A fair coin flip carries H = 1 bit
(Entropy). A microscopic particle
resting in one of two wells of a symmetric trap, each side equally likely,
is described by the same half/half distribution, but a physicist reports
its entropy as

S = k \ln 2 \approx 9.57 \times 10^{-24} \text{ J/K},

where k = 1.380649 \times 10^{-23} J/K is Boltzmann's constant (also
written k_{\mathrm{B}}). Same count of possibilities, different unit.

The identification is general. Boltzmann's formula assigns a system with
W equally likely microstates the entropy S = k \ln W; the range
theorem of Entropy assigns the uniform
distribution over W outcomes the Shannon entropy H = \log_2 W bits.
Dividing, S = (k \ln 2)\, H. For non-uniform distributions the match
persists: Gibbs' entropy S = -k \sum_i p_i \ln p_i is term-for-term the
Shannon sum H = -\sum_i p_i \log_2 p_i, with \ln in place of
\log_2. By the units discussion of Surprisal,
that substitution is the bits-to-nats conversion:

S \;=\; k \cdot H_{\text{nats}} \;=\; (k \ln 2) \cdot H_{\text{bits}}.

One quantity, two units: a bit of Shannon entropy is k ln 2 ≈ 9.57 × 10⁻²⁴ J/K of thermodynamic entropy.

Thermodynamic entropy is Shannon entropy measured in nats and multiplied
by Boltzmann's constant, S = (k \ln 2) H_{\text{bits}}: one bit
corresponds to 9.57 \times 10^{-24} J/K.

The identity of the two functionals is the starting point of
Jaynes' 1957 paper,
already met in The maximum entropy principle: Boltzmann's H and
Shannon's H are the same expression, so equilibrium statistical
mechanics can be read as maximum-entropy inference under an energy
constraint. That lesson used the reading to derive the Boltzmann
distribution; this lesson runs the bridge in the other direction, from
bits to joules.

The conversion factor explains why the thermodynamic weight of
information went unnoticed for a century. The shuffled 52-card deck of
Entropy carries \log_2 52! \approx
225.6 bits, which converts to 225.6 \times 9.57 \times 10^{-24} \approx
2.2 \times 10^{-21} J/K. The thermal entropy of the cardboard itself is
of order 10^2 J/K: the information-bearing degrees of freedom are some
10^{23} times lighter than the thermal ones. Only when experiments
reached single-molecule and single-colloid scales (below) did the
information term become measurable.

documents.title: Landauer's principle: erasure has a heat floor
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information in the natural sciences › Thermodynamics of information › Landauer's principle: erasure has a heat floor
documents.text:
Landauer's principle: erasure has a heat floor

Take a one-bit memory: a physical system with two stable states, holding
0 or 1 with probability \tfrac{1}{2} each. The reset operation
returns it to a fixed state, say 0, regardless of its contents. Before
the reset the memory's entropy is 1 bit, i.e. k \ln 2; after, the
state is known and the entropy is 0. The reset removes k \ln 2 of
entropy from the memory, and the second law forbids destroying it: the
entropy must move into the environment, as heat.

Resetting a one-bit memory holding either state with probability
\tfrac{1}{2}, in contact with a heat bath at temperature T,
dissipates at least

Q \;\ge\; kT \ln 2

of heat into the bath. At T = 300 K,
kT \ln 2 \approx 2.87 \times 10^{-21} J (about 18 meV). More
generally, resetting a memory whose contents have distribution p
dissipates at least kT \ln 2 \cdot H(p).

The memory plus the bath form a closed system, so the second law gives
\Delta S_{\text{mem}} + \Delta S_{\text{bath}} \ge 0. The reset takes
the memory from entropy k \ln 2 (one bit, by the unit bridge) to 0:
\Delta S_{\text{mem}} = -k \ln 2. Hence
\Delta S_{\text{bath}} \ge k \ln 2. A bath at fixed temperature T
absorbing heat Q gains entropy \Delta S_{\text{bath}} = Q/T
(Clausius), so Q \ge kT \ln 2. For contents distributed as p the
memory's initial entropy is (k \ln 2) H(p) and the same bookkeeping
gives Q \ge kT \ln 2 \cdot H(p). When the two memory states have equal
energy, the dissipated heat is supplied as work: erasure costs at least
kT \ln 2 of work per uniformly random bit.

Erasure: the memory's k ln 2 of entropy leaves as heat, at least kT ln 2 ≈ 2.9 × 10⁻²¹ J at room temperature.

Many-to-one is what costs: erasing, writing, copying

The charge attaches to logical irreversibility: reset maps both inputs
\{0, 1\} to the single output 0, so the output does not determine the
input, and the lost distinction must be exported to the bath. Operations
that lose no distinction have no such floor:

NOT maps 0 \mapsto 1, 1 \mapsto 0: a permutation, invertible,
no minimum dissipation.

Copying onto a blank: (b, 0) \mapsto (b, b) is invertible (the
inverse blanks the copy against the intact original), so making a copy
of a bit into a known-blank register can in principle be free.

Overwriting an unknown register is erase-then-write: the old
contents are lost, and Landauer's price applies.

Bennett's 1973 result sharpens the
scope: any computation can be embedded in a logically reversible one that
keeps its intermediate results, so computation as such has no minimum
energy cost. The unavoidable charge falls only on discarding information.

A floor, not an operating point

The bound is a lower limit on dissipation approached only by slow,
carefully designed protocols.
Bérut et al. (2012) realized the
double-well memory with a colloidal particle in an optical trap and
measured the mean heat of erasure approaching kT \ln 2 as the protocol
slowed, confirming the principle experimentally. Production hardware sits
far above the floor: no current chip operates anywhere near
3 \times 10^{-21} J per erased bit, and the bound constrains only
logically irreversible operations in the quasi-static limit.

Erasing one bit at temperature T dissipates at least kT \ln 2 of
heat, 2.87 \times 10^{-21} J at 300 K; the charge is for logical
irreversibility (many-to-one maps), not for computation itself.

documents.title: The Szilard engine: one bit buys kT ln 2 of work
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information in the natural sciences › Thermodynamics of information › The Szilard engine: one bit buys kT ln 2 of work
documents.text:
The Szilard engine: one bit buys kT ln 2 of work

Landauer's principle has an exact converse, published thirty-two years
earlier. Szilard's 1929 engine
converts one bit of acquired information into kT \ln 2 of work,
using a gas of exactly one molecule.

The device: a box of volume V in contact with a heat bath at
temperature T, containing a single molecule. A thin partition drops
into the middle, trapping the molecule in one half. A measurement records
which half — one bit, since both sides are equally likely. The partition
now becomes a piston: knowing the molecule's side, the demon lets the
molecule push the partition toward the empty half, extracting work
through a reversible isothermal expansion from V/2 back to V. Then
the piston is removed and the cycle restarts.

The Szilard cycle, one step per frame: trap, measure one bit, expand. The measured bit selects which way the piston is released.

Step through the four frames and tally what has changed by the end of
frame 4: the weight is up by kT \ln 2, the bath is down kT \ln 2 of
heat, the gas is back to volume V — and the memory still holds one
bit. Every entry but the last is paid for; the next section charges it.

The work integral

A single molecule in volume V' at temperature T exerts the
time-averaged pressure of an ideal gas with N = 1: p = kT / V'. The
reversible isothermal expansion from V/2 to V delivers

W = \int_{V/2}^{V} p \, dV'

At T = 300 K: W = 2.87 \times 10^{-21} J. The expansion is
isothermal, so the molecule's internal energy is unchanged and the energy
delivered as work is drawn from the bath as heat: Q_{\text{in}} = W =
kT \ln 2. The gas ends where it started, in volume V at temperature
T.

The measured bit is what makes the extraction possible: without knowing
the side, the demon does not know which way to release the piston, and
releasing it blindly extracts nothing on average. One measured bit is
worth exactly kT \ln 2 — the engine's exchange rate equals Landauer's
price.

The apparent violation

The cycle looks like a perpetual motion machine of the second kind. The
Kelvin-Planck form of the second law forbids any cyclic process whose
only effect is converting heat from a single bath entirely into work, and
each Szilard cycle appears to do exactly that: bath heat in, lifted
weight out, gas restored. The resolution is that the cycle shown is
not closed — one system in the picture did not return to its initial
state.

One measured bit converts to exactly kT \ln 2 of isothermal work:
Szilard's engine and Landauer's erasure price the bit identically, from
opposite directions.

documents.title: Maxwell's demon: the reset balances the books
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information in the natural sciences › Thermodynamics of information › Maxwell's demon: the reset balances the books
documents.text:
Maxwell's demon: the reset balances the books

Maxwell states the puzzle in 1871 — a being, not a machine.

The Szilard engine is the minimal version of a much older puzzle. In his
1871 Theory of Heat, Maxwell imagined a molecule-sighted being
operating a frictionless trapdoor between two gas chambers,
letting fast molecules pass one way and slow ones the other. The demon
sorts the gas into hot and cold halves without doing work, creating a
temperature difference that can drive an engine: heat flows uphill, and
the second law appears to fail. Szilard distilled the puzzle to its core:
the demon's power comes entirely from information about individual
molecules, one bit per decision.

Bennett's 1982 analysis closed the
loophole. To run another cycle, the demon must return its memory to the
blank state — and by Landauer's principle that reset dissipates at least
kT \ln 2 per stored bit, exactly the work each bit yielded. Over the
full cycle, engine plus memory, the books balance:

W_{\text{total}} \;=\; \underbrace{kT \ln 2}_{\text{extracted}}

The demon's balance sheet, one entry per frame: extraction, the unpaid bit, the Landauer charge that closes the books.

Step through the three frames and watch the net line: +kT \ln 2 while
the bit sits in memory, 0 once the reset posts. Check the charge
against the erasure theorem: the stored bit is 0 or 1 with
probability \tfrac{1}{2} each, so blanking it dissipates at least
kT \ln 2 \cdot H(\tfrac{1}{2}) = kT \ln 2.

The cost's location was misassigned for fifty years. Szilard, and later
Brillouin, charged the measurement; Bennett showed that measurement can
be performed reversibly — recording which-side is a copy onto a blank
register, one of the free operations above — and that the unavoidable
charge is the reset of that register. The demon is not an open problem:
its apparent violation is an accounting error, an entropy entry
(the stored bit, worth k \ln 2) left off the books.

Maxwell's demon does not break the second law: it converts bits to work
at kT \ln 2 per bit and must pay the same rate to blank them, so the
closed cycle nets W_{\text{total}} \ge 0.

documents.title: The feedback second law: I(X;M) is a work voucher
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information in the natural sciences › Thermodynamics of information › The feedback second law: I(X;M) is a work voucher
documents.text:
The feedback second law: I(X;M) is a work voucher

The Szilard analysis generalizes from one perfect bit to any measurement
of any system, and the general bound is stated in the course's own
currency. The baseline: for a system in contact with a bath at
temperature T, define the Helmholtz free energy F = U - TS
(internal energy minus temperature times entropy). The second law in work
form says the average work W done on the system during an
isothermal process obeys W \ge \Delta F; equivalently, the extractable
work -W is at most -\Delta F. Measurement plus feedback relaxes this
bound.

Let a measurement of the system state X produce outcome M, and let
the subsequent protocol depend on M (feedback control). Then the
average work satisfies

W \;\ge\; \Delta F \;-\; kT \ln 2 \cdot I(X;M),

with I(X;M) the mutual information between system state and
measurement outcome, in bits.

Sketch; the full proof belongs to stochastic thermodynamics
(Sagawa & Ueda 2010;
Parrondo, Horowitz & Sagawa 2015
review it).

The bookkeeping that produces the I term is the chain rule of
Joint and conditional entropy: after the measurement,
H(X, M) = H(X) + H(M) - I(X;M), so the correlated pair (system,
memory) carries I(X;M) fewer bits of joint entropy than its parts
counted separately — by the unit bridge, a thermodynamic entropy deficit
of k \ln 2 \cdot I(X;M). Apply the ordinary second law to the joint
supersystem, for which the feedback is just an internal dependence:
its work bound is the joint free-energy change, which sits
kT \ln 2 \cdot I(X;M) below the sum of the parts because of the
deficit. Feedback is the mechanism that cashes the correlation: acting
on M steers the system through states of low conditional entropy
H(X \mid M), converting the deficit into extractable work before the
correlation decays. The W in the statement is an average over
measurement outcomes; individual runs fluctuate around it.

The feedback second law: each bit of mutual information between system and memory relaxes the work bound by kT ln 2.

The bound, checked on Szilard

Over one engine cycle the gas returns to its initial state, so
\Delta F = 0. The measurement is perfect: M determines the side X,
so I(X;M) = H(X) = 1 bit
(Mutual information, the upper bound at determinism).
The theorem gives W \ge -kT \ln 2: at most kT \ln 2 of work out,
and the reversible expansion attains the bound with equality.

The demon's detector misreads the side with probability
\varepsilon = 0.1: the memory records the true side with probability
0.9. System and memory are then coupled exactly like the
agreement-probability tables of Mutual information at
q = 0.9:

I(X;M) = 1 - H_2(0.9) \approx 1 - 0.469 = 0.531 \text{ bits},

using H_2(0.9) \approx 0.469 from
Entropy. With \Delta F = 0, the
extractable work per cycle is at most

-W \;\le\; kT \ln 2 \times 0.531

at 300 K. A noisy bit is worth its mutual information, not its raw
length: the 47\% of the bit lost to detector noise buys nothing.
Attaining the bound requires a protocol tuned to the noise (a full
expansion trusting a wrong reading compresses against the molecule and
loses work); the review discusses optimal feedback protocols that
approach it.

The demon's side of the ledger generalizes too: Sagawa and Ueda also
showed that measurement plus memory reset together cost at least
kT \ln 2 \cdot I(X;M) of work, so the voucher is never printed for
free — whatever the feedback gains, the measuring device pays.
Feedback engines have run in the lab:
Toyabe et al. (2010) steered a
colloidal particle up a staircase potential by feedback on its measured
position, demonstrating information-to-energy conversion at about
28\% of the kT \ln 2 \cdot I limit.

Measured information is a thermodynamic resource priced at kT \ln 2
per bit: W \ge \Delta F - kT \ln 2 \cdot I(X;M). The mutual
information built in this course, applied to a physical measurement,
buys joules.

documents.title: The physical price of computation
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information in the natural sciences › Thermodynamics of information › The physical price of computation
documents.text:
The physical price of computation

The course's entropy has now met physics twice, from opposite
directions. The maximum entropy principle ran inference toward
physics: maximizing H under an energy constraint produces the
Boltzmann distribution, so the physicist's equilibrium ensembles are
Shannon-entropy maximizers. This lesson ran physics toward information:
the second law charges kT \ln 2 per bit erased and credits the same
per bit measured, so Shannon's H carries joules. Both directions work
because the two entropies are one functional in two units.

Two physics faces of one entropy: an inference principle (Boltzmann via max-entropy) and an energy price (Landauer's bound).

For computing, the consequence is a hard floor with a precise scope.
Every logically irreversible step — every erased or overwritten bit — has
a thermodynamic minimum cost of kT \ln 2, unavoidable by any device at
temperature T; reversible logic is the only exemption the physics
grants. The floor is real but distant: it has been approached only in
single-bit laboratory erasures, and no production hardware operates near
it.

Landauer's bound is a floor on irreversible computation, not the
operating point of any current chip: kT \ln 2 per erased bit, escapable
only by computing reversibly.

documents.title: Exercises
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Information in the natural sciences › Thermodynamics of information › Exercises
documents.text:
Exercises

A storage device erases one gigabyte (8 \times 10^9 bits) of uniformly
random data at T = 300 K. Compute the Landauer minimum heat, and
compare it with the roughly 1 J a real drive dissipates for the same
operation.

Per bit: kT \ln 2 = 2.87 \times 10^{-21} J. Total:

Q \ge 8 \times 10^9 \times 2.87 \times 10^{-21}

about 23 picojoules. A real drive dissipating \sim 1 J sits roughly
10^{10} to 10^{11} times above the floor: Landauer's bound is a hard
limit, not a description of current hardware.

Compute the Landauer bound per bit at T = 77 K (liquid nitrogen) and
T = 4 K (liquid helium). Then show that running the erasure cold buys
nothing once the heat must be pumped into a 300 K room: compute the
total heat delivered to the room when erasure at T_c = 4 K is followed
by an ideal (Carnot) refrigerator moving the dissipated heat to
T_h = 300 K.

Per bit, Q = kT \ln 2: at 77 K,
Q \ge 1.381 \times 10^{-23} \times 77 \times 0.693 \approx 7.4 \times
10^{-22} J; at 4 K, Q \ge 3.8 \times 10^{-23} J. The floor scales
linearly in T.

Pumping: to move heat Q_c = kT_c \ln 2 out of the cold box, an ideal
refrigerator does work W \ge Q_c (T_h/T_c - 1), and the room receives
Q_c + W \ge Q_c \, T_h / T_c = k T_h \ln 2. The room-temperature
Landauer cost reappears exactly: cooling relocates the charge, it does
not reduce it. (Cold erasure still helps devices whose other losses
drop with temperature; the Landauer term itself is conserved.)

A one-bit memory holds 0 with probability 0.9 and 1 with
probability 0.1. Compute the minimum heat dissipated by resetting it
to 0 at T = 300 K, and state what the reset of an already-known bit
costs.

The memory's entropy is H_2(0.9) \approx 0.469 bits
(Entropy). The generalized bound
gives

Q \ge kT \ln 2 \cdot H_2(0.9)

A known bit has H = 0: resetting it can in principle dissipate nothing
(the map is one-to-one on the actually occupied state). The erasure cost
is the entropy of what is forgotten, not the number of physical bits
touched.

An asymmetric Szilard engine inserts the partition at one third of the
box: the molecule is trapped on the left (volume V/3) with probability
\tfrac{1}{3}, on the right (volume 2V/3) with probability
\tfrac{2}{3}. A perfect measurement records the side and the trapped
volume expands reversibly and isothermally back to V. Compute the work
in each branch, the expected work per cycle, and verify that it equals
kT \ln 2 \cdot H_2(\tfrac{1}{3}), the measured information priced at
kT \ln 2 per bit.

Left branch: W_L = \int_{V/3}^{V} kT/V' \, dV' = kT \ln 3 \approx
1.099 \, kT. Right branch: W_R = kT \ln \tfrac{3}{2} \approx 0.405 \,
kT.

Expected work:

\bar W = \tfrac{1}{3} kT \ln 3 + \tfrac{2}{3} kT \ln \tfrac{3}{2}

Measured information: the measurement resolves a (\tfrac{1}{3},
\tfrac{2}{3}) binary outcome, H_2(\tfrac{1}{3}) = \log_2 3 -
\tfrac{2}{3} \approx 0.918 bits. Price it:
kT \ln 2 \times 0.918 = kT \times 0.693 \times 0.918 \approx 0.6365\,
kT = \bar W. The match is exact:
\ln 3 - \tfrac{2}{3}\ln 2 = \ln 2 \,(\log_2 3 - \tfrac{2}{3}). The
engine converts every measured bit — here a fractional 0.918 of one —
into work at the full kT \ln 2 rate, saturating the feedback second
law with \Delta F = 0.

A Szilard engine's detector reports the wrong side with probability
\varepsilon = 0.2. Compute the mutual information between the
molecule's side X and the record M, and the maximum average work
extractable per cycle at 300 K.

X is a fair bit and M agrees with it with probability 0.8: the
agreement table of Mutual information with q = 0.8,
so

I(X;M) = 1 - H_2(0.8) = 1 - 0.722 = 0.278 \text{ bits},

using H_2(0.8) = -0.8 \log_2 0.8 - 0.2 \log_2 0.2 \approx 0.722.
With \Delta F = 0, the feedback second law bounds the extraction:

-W \le kT \ln 2 \times 0.278 \approx 2.87 \times 10^{-21} \times 0.278

Doubling the error rate from 0.1 to 0.2 nearly halved the voucher
(0.531 \to 0.278 bits): work tracks mutual information, and H_2 is
steep in this range.

Explain, by counting preimages, why copying a bit b into a register
known to hold 0 has no Landauer cost, while writing b into a
register holding an unknown bit a costs at least kT \ln 2 when a
is uniformly random. Give the map each operation implements on the pair
(source, register).

Copy onto blank: (b, 0) \mapsto (b, b). The possible inputs are
(0,0) and (1,0); the outputs (0,0) and (1,1) are distinct, so
the map is one-to-one on its domain and invertible — no distinction is
lost, no entropy must be exported, no heat floor.

Overwrite: (b, a) \mapsto (b, b). Inputs (b, 0) and (b, 1) both
map to (b, b): two-to-one. The register's bit a, worth H(a) = 1
bit = k \ln 2 of entropy when uniform, is destroyed; by Landauer's
bookkeeping the bath must absorb Q \ge kT \ln 2. Overwriting is
erasure of a followed by a free copy, and the erasure carries the
entire charge.

A demon is issued a tape of N pre-blanked bits and runs N Szilard
cycles, filling the tape and extracting N kT \ln 2 of work from a
single bath without ever paying an erasure cost. State why this does not
violate the second law, and account for the total entropy change of
bath plus tape.

The blank tape is a low-entropy resource, and the demon consumes it like
fuel. Entropy audit per cycle: the bath loses heat kT \ln 2, so
\Delta S_{\text{bath}} = -k \ln 2; the tape gains one uniformly random
bit (the molecule's side), so \Delta S_{\text{tape}} = +k \ln 2. Total
change: 0 \ge 0 — the second law holds with equality for the
reversible protocol. Over N cycles the demon has not created work from
nothing; it has traded N k \ln 2 of pre-paid entropy capacity for
N kT \ln 2 of work, exactly the rate Landauer's principle sets. When
the tape is full, continuing requires erasing it, which returns
N kT \ln 2 to the bath and closes Bennett's ledger. Blank memory is as
much a thermodynamic resource as a charged battery.

J. M. R. Parrondo, J. M. Horowitz, T. Sagawa, "Thermodynamics of Information," Nature Physics, 11, 131–139, 2015 — the primary review: the Szilard engine and Maxwell's demon, Landauer's principle, the feedback second law, and the experimental confirmations discussed here. https://doi.org/10.1038/nphys3230

R. Landauer, "Irreversibility and Heat Generation in the Computing Process," IBM Journal of Research and Development, 5(3), 183–191, 1961 — the original statement of the erasure bound and of logical irreversibility as its source. https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.53.0183

C. H. Bennett, "The Thermodynamics of Computation — a Review," International Journal of Theoretical Physics, 21, 905–940, 1982 — the resolution of Maxwell's demon via memory reset, and reversible computation as the exemption. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02084158

L. Szilard, "Über die Entropieverminderung in einem thermodynamischen System bei Eingriffen intelligenter Wesen," Zeitschrift für Physik, 53, 840–856, 1929 — the one-molecule engine and the first quantitative link between a bit of measurement and kT \ln 2.

T. Sagawa, M. Ueda, "Generalized Jarzynski Equality under Nonequilibrium Feedback Control," Physical Review Letters, 104, 090602, 2010 — the feedback second law W \ge \Delta F - kT\, I in its fluctuation-theorem form. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.104.090602

A. Bérut, A. Arakelyan, A. Petrosyan, S. Ciliberto, R. Dillenschneider, E. Lutz, "Experimental verification of Landauer's principle linking information and thermodynamics," Nature, 483, 187–189, 2012 — single-colloid double-well erasure approaching kT \ln 2. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10872

E. T. Jaynes, "Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics," Physical Review, 106(4), 620–630, 1957 — Boltzmann's and Shannon's H as one functional; statistical mechanics as maximum-entropy inference (see the max-entropy lesson). https://bayes.wustl.edu/etj/articles/theory.1.pdf

documents.title: Research brief: channel-capacity (Channel capacity)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: channel-capacity (Channel capacity)
documents.text:
Research brief: channel-capacity (Channel capacity)

status: planned
module: channels
type: core
goal: Compute the capacity of a discrete memoryless channel.

New lesson opening the scope expansion into the second half of Shannon's theory.
Entropy gave the source-coding limit; capacity gives mutual information its own
operational limit. Cover & Thomas fig. 1.2's "two extreme points" (min I =
compression, max I = capacity) is the framing. This lesson is computational:
define the channel, then compute C for the two canonical channels by hand.

Sources to consult

Shannon 1948, Part II, §11-12 — the noisy channel, equivocation
H_y(x), rate R = H(x) - H_y(x), and capacity C = max[H(x) - H_y(x)];
§15-16 work explicit capacity calculations (symmetric channels
C = log m + Σ p_i log p_i).

Cover & Thomas, §7.1 "Examples of Channels" (noiseless binary, noisy
typewriter, BSC §7.1.4, BEC §7.1.5), §7.2 "Symmetric Channels", §7.3
"Properties of Channel Capacity" — capacity C = max_{p(x)} I(X;Y),
0 ≤ C ≤ log|X|, concavity of I in the input.

MacKay, ch. 9, §9.5-9.6 — mutual information of a channel, capacity, worked
BSC / Z-channel / binary-erasure examples with the maximizing input.

Polyanskiy & Wu, ch. 4 (capacity as an information radius / saddle point)
and §16.4 (BSC/BEC capacities) — cross-check.

Key points the lesson must cover

A discrete channel is a transition table p(y|x): input alphabet X,
output alphabet Y, one conditional distribution per input. Memoryless = each
use independent. Concrete opener: the BSC, a bit flipped with probability p.

The channel's noise is H(Y|X); what the output tells you about the input
is I(X;Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X). I depends on both the channel and the chosen
input distribution p(x).

Capacity C = max_{p(x)} I(X;Y), in bits per channel use — the most
information any input can push through. Bound 0 ≤ C ≤ log|X|.

Binary symmetric channel: with a uniform input, I = 1 - H(p), and
uniform is the maximizer (symmetry), so C_BSC = 1 - H(p). Compute at
p = 0 (C = 1), p = 0.1 (C ≈ 0.53), p = 0.5 (C = 0, useless channel). Show the
full derivation: H(Y|X) = H(p) for any input, H(Y) ≤ 1 maximized at
uniform.

Binary erasure channel: fraction e of symbols erased; C_BEC = 1 - e.
Derive: a received non-erasure is the input exactly; the receiver learns
(1-e) bits per use on average. Contrast the two channels — erasure is
"easier" than flipping at the same noise level.

The maximizing input is not always uniform: state that in general C is a
concave maximization (Blahut-Arimoto computes it) but our two channels are
symmetric, so uniform wins; the neural-coding lesson uses this again.

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

Capacity maximizes over the input distribution, a design choice; it is not
a property of the channel's noise alone the way H(Y|X) is.

I(X;Y) here uses the same MI the course built; capacity is just its maximum
over inputs. Do not introduce a new information quantity.

BSC at p = 0.5 has zero capacity even though bits still arrive — the output
is independent of the input. Good <KeyFact>: a noisy channel and a useless
channel are different, and the boundary is C = 0.

BSC capacity 1 - H(p) is symmetric in p and 1-p (a channel that flips with
prob 0.9 is as good as 0.1: just invert the output). Note it.

Units: bits per channel use (log base 2). The Gaussian channel
C = ½ log(1 + P/N) is out of scope here — one-sentence forward pointer to
neural-coding, where it is cited not derived.

Capacity is an achievable limit; that it can actually be reached is the next
lesson's theorem, not assumed here.

FIGURE PLAN

single <Figure> (component) — the BSC as a two-node transition diagram:
inputs 0/1 on the left, outputs 0/1 on the right, straight-through arrows
labeled 1-p and crossing arrows labeled p. One idea: a channel is a
transition table. Inspiration: Cover & Thomas §7.1.4 / MacKay ch. 9.

single <Figure> (component) — the BEC transition diagram: 0/1 in, 0/?/1
out, erasure arrows to ? labeled e. One idea: erasure flags its own
failures. Inspiration: Cover & Thomas §7.1.5.

single <Figure> (component) — capacity of the BSC as 1 - H(p): the
binary-entropy curve subtracted from 1, plotted over p, with p = 0, 0.1, 0.5
marked (C = 1, 0.53, 0). One idea: capacity collapses to 0 at p = 1/2. Reuses
the binary entropy curve from entropy-as-average-surprise.

single <Figure> (component) — I(X;Y) vs input bias for a fixed BSC: an
inverted-U over p(x=1), peaking at the uniform input where I = C. Static
twin of the ChannelCapacityDial demo. One idea: capacity is a maximum over
inputs.

<FigureSequence> (3 frames) — the BSC derivation: frame 1 H(Y|X) = H(p)
(same for any input); frame 2 H(Y) ≤ 1, maximized at the uniform input;
frame 3 subtract to C = 1 - H(p). Delta = one line of the derivation per
frame.

single <Figure> (component) — BSC vs BEC at matched noise: two capacity
bars for p = e = 0.2 (C_BSC = 1 - H(0.2) ≈ 0.28 vs C_BEC = 0.8), payoff
"knowing which symbols failed is worth a lot". One idea: erasure beats
flipping. Inspiration: playbook two-panel comparison.

single <Figure> (component) — the two limits map: a spine
min I(X;X̂) = source coding … max I(X;Y) = channel capacity, entropy and
capacity as the two extreme points of the same quantity. One idea: capacity
is entropy's mirror. Inspiration: Cover & Thomas fig. 1.2 (recreate).

documents.title: Research brief: compression-is-prediction (Compression as prediction)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: compression-is-prediction (Compression as prediction)
documents.text:
Research brief: compression-is-prediction (Compression as prediction)

status: planned
module: information-in-ml
type: synthesis
goal: Explain why a better predictive model is exactly a better compressor, and vice versa.

Sources to consult

Deletang et al. 2023, "Language Modeling Is Compression" (arXiv:2309.10668)
— the primary ML-tail source. §2 states the predictor <-> lossless-compressor
equivalence (via arithmetic coding), and the experiments measure a large
language model as a general-purpose compressor (Chinchilla-70B compressing
ImageNet to 43.4%, LibriSpeech to 16.4% of raw). Use for the modern statement
and the empirical payoff.

MacKay, ch. 6 "Stream Codes" — arithmetic coding as the mechanism that
turns a probabilistic predictor into a near-optimal compressor (coding cost
≈ -log2 q(sequence), within O(1) bits total). This is the how behind the
equivalence. Also §6 intro on why symbol codes (Huffman) fall short and
stream codes reach the entropy rate.

Cover & Thomas, §5.10 "Arithmetic Coding" and §5.4 (wrong-code /
H(p)+D(p||q)) — the coding-cost accounting.

Reuse: source-coding-theorem-lite (entropy floor), cross-entropy-loss
(log-loss = coding cost), entropy-of-english (entropy rate), prefix-codes
(Kraft budget), kl-divergence (mismatch cost).

Key points the lesson must cover

A predictor defines a compressor: feed the model's next-symbol
probabilities q(x_t | x_{<t}) to an arithmetic coder; the coded length of a
stream is ≈ -Σ_t log2 q(x_t | x_{<t}) bits = the model's cross-entropy on
the stream. Better predictions (lower cross-entropy) = shorter files.

A compressor defines a predictor: any lossless coder implicitly assigns
q(x) = 2^{-length(x)} (Kraft budget), so the code is a probability model;
decompressing shortest-first is a maximum-probability prediction.

The entropy floor: no compressor beats the source's entropy rate
(source-coding-theorem-lite); a perfect predictor hits it, and the shortfall
of any model is D(p||q) extra bits per symbol (kl-divergence) — the exact
mismatch cost.

The whole course in one line: entropy sets the floor, model mismatch costs
KL, and prediction is paid for in bits. State it as the synthesis.

Empirical reality (Deletang): modern language models are strong
general-purpose compressors, and compression ratio is a clean, label-free
measure of predictive quality — "compression as an evaluation of intelligence".

Worked with the PredictiveCompressor sandbox: same text, three models (uniform
bytes -> letter frequencies -> bigram), watch bits/char and total size drop as
the model improves.

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

The model must be shared or transmitted: the equivalence is about coding
cost given the model. A fair accounting either fixes the model on both ends or
includes the model's description length (two-part / MDL code). For a fixed
pretrained model this is amortized; say so to avoid the "but you cheated by
shipping a 70B model" objection. Forward-ref minimum-description-length,
which makes exactly this accounting the object of study.

Arithmetic coding overhead is O(1) total, not per symbol — this is why
stream codes reach the entropy rate where Huffman's per-symbol 1-bit gap does
not (callback to huffman-by-hand's motivating flaw).

Lossless only: this equivalence is exact for lossless compression;
lossy compression (JPEG, VAEs as rate-distortion) is a different, related story
— mention as beyond scope, do not conflate.

Cross-entropy in nats (ML default) vs. bits (file size): convert by
1 nat = 1.443 bits. A model's nats/token is its bits/token up to that factor.

"Better predictor = better compressor" holds for the achievable size; a real
compressor also has implementation overhead. Keep the claim about the coding
cost, not a specific gzip number.

FIGURE PLAN

<FigureSequence> (4-5 frames) — the predict-then-code pipeline on a short
string: frame per symbol, the model emits q(next | context), the arithmetic
coder narrows its interval, the running bit-count ticks up by -log2 q. Delta
= one symbol per frame. The house-signature process sequence. Inspiration:
MacKay ch. 6 arithmetic-coding interval diagram (recreate).

single <Figure> (component) — the two-way equivalence: left "predictor ->
probabilities -> arithmetic coder -> bits", right "bits -> code lengths ->
q = 2^{-len} -> predictor", a bidirectional arrow labeled "same object". One
idea: prediction and compression are one map. Inspiration: Deletang §2.

single <Figure> (component) — bits/char across three models on the same
sentence: uniform bytes (8), letter frequencies (~4.1), bigram (~3.x),
descending toward the English entropy rate line (~1). Static twin of the
PredictiveCompressor demo. One idea: better model, smaller file.

single <Figure> (component) — coding cost = H(rate) + D(p||q) on a
stream: the entropy-rate floor plus the model's KL excess, as a stacked bar,
tying the file size to the two quantities the course built. One idea: file
size = floor + mismatch.

single <Figure> (component) — course capstone map: entropy (floor) ->
codes/Kraft (spend the budget) -> KL (mismatch cost) -> cross-entropy
(training) -> compression (prediction), a single left-to-right spine with each
node labeled by its lesson. One idea: the whole course in one picture. This is
the synthesis figure.

documents.title: Research brief: cross-entropy-loss (Cross-entropy)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: cross-entropy-loss (Cross-entropy)
documents.text:
Research brief: cross-entropy-loss (Cross-entropy)

status: planned
module: information-in-ml
type: core
goal: >
Explain why minimizing cross-entropy loss drives a model's predictions toward
the true label distribution.

Sources to consult

Cover & Thomas, §5.4 "Bounds on the Optimal Codelength" — the identity
Σ p(x)(-log q(x)) = H(p) + D(p||q), i.e. cross-entropy = entropy + KL. This
is the mathematical core; no separate "cross-entropy" section exists in Cover &
Thomas, so §5.4 is the anchor. Reuse D ≥ 0 from §2.6.

MacKay, ch. 2 / ch. 6 — the log-loss / predictive-coding reading; MacKay
frames prediction cost as bits, which is the bridge to the loss.

Deletang et al. 2023, "Language Modeling Is Compression", §2 (background) — the
explicit statement that a model's expected -log q on data = its coding cost,
used to frame log-loss training as compression. For the ML framing only.

Key points the lesson must cover

Log-loss on one example = model's surprisal at the truth: for observed
outcome x, the loss -log2 q(x) is exactly how surprised the model is that
x happened (reuse surprisal from what-is-surprise). A confident-correct
prediction costs ~0; a confident-wrong one costs a lot.

Cross-entropy H(p,q) = -Σ p(x) log2 q(x) = expected bits to code
p-data with q's code = average log-loss over the true distribution.

The decomposition H(p,q) = H(p) + D(p||q) — the lesson's headline
identity. H(p) is the irreducible data entropy; D(p||q) ≥ 0 is the
model's excess.

Why minimizing cross-entropy minimizes KL: H(p) does not depend on the
model q, so argmin_q H(p,q) = argmin_q D(p||q), achieved at q = p.
Training on cross-entropy is training on model-data divergence.

The classification case: labels are one-hot, so p is a point mass and
H(p,q) = -log2 q(true class) — plain negative log-likelihood; H(p) = 0, so
cross-entropy equals the KL there.

The confident-wrong blowup (worked example): q(true) small drives
-log q large; the same reason a rare event carries large surprisal. Motivates
why overconfidence is punished.

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

Cross-entropy is not symmetric: H(p,q) ≠ H(q,p); the loss uses
H(data, model). Keep the direction consistent with kl-divergence.

The H(p) term is out of the model's hands but is not zero in general
(only for one-hot labels). With soft/noisy labels the achievable loss floor is
H(p) > 0; a loss above zero is not necessarily a bad model. State this — a
common misreading of the loss value.

Minimizing cross-entropy = maximizing likelihood: -Σ log q(x_i) over data is
the empirical cross-entropy; make the equivalence explicit for the ML audience.

Softmax + cross-entropy: the gradient is the clean q - p (prediction minus
target); worth a one-line remark but the derivation is beyond scope.

Do not conflate cross-entropy (a loss/coding cost, ≥ H(p)) with entropy (a
property of one distribution).

FIGURE PLAN

single <Figure> (component) — the decomposition dissected:
H(p,q) = H(p) + D(p||q) as a stacked bar, H(p) (irreducible floor, one
color) plus D(p||q) (model's excess, accent), with labels-above-symbols
arrows onto each term. One idea: cross-entropy = floor + mismatch. This is the
lesson's centerpiece figure (course.yaml notes a figure carries the identity).
Inspiration: Cover & Thomas §5.4.

<FigureSequence> (4 frames) — training drives q -> p: a model
distribution q starting far from the true p, each frame a step closer, the
D(p||q) bar (and the cross-entropy) shrinking toward the fixed H(p) floor.
One delta per frame. Inspiration: gradient descent on log-loss.

single <Figure> (component) — one-hot collapse: a general p beside a
one-hot label; on the one-hot, H(p)=0 so H(p,q) = D(p||q) = -log2 q(true).
Two-panel comparison, the changed piece highlighted. One idea: for hard labels,
cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood.

single <Figure> (component) — the confident-wrong blowup: the -log2 q
curve with a dot sliding toward q(true) -> 0, the loss shooting up; annotate
"confident and wrong = large surprisal = large loss". Reuses the surprisal
curve from lesson 1. One idea: overconfidence is punished by the log.

single <Figure> (component) — log-loss = surprisal, side by side: the
surprisal definition -log2 p from lesson 1 next to the single-example loss
-log2 q(true), same curve, labels swapped. One idea: the loss is surprisal
under the model. Binds the module back to the foundations.

documents.title: Research brief: data-processing-inequality (The data-processing inequality)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: data-processing-inequality (The data-processing inequality)
documents.text:
Research brief: data-processing-inequality (The data-processing inequality)

status: planned
module: shared-information
type: core
goal: Apply the data-processing inequality to bound how much a representation reveals about a target.

New standalone lesson. In the previous pass the DPI was crammed into the
information-bottleneck lesson as a sub-result; with the cap removed it earns its
own chapter, placed right after mutual-information so that channel coding
(converse), rate-distortion, and the information bottleneck can all cite it. It
also carries the load-bearing ML reading: no learned feature of X can know more
about a target Y than X itself did.

Sources to consult

Cover & Thomas, §2.8 "Data-Processing Inequality" — Theorem 2.8.1 and its
chain-rule proof: expand I(X; Y,Z) two ways on the Markov chain X — Y — Z;
the Markov property zeroes one conditional MI, non-negativity of the other
finishes. (C&T state it as X—Y—Z ⇒ I(X;Y) ≥ I(X;Z); mirror to our
Y—X—T ⇒ I(Y;X) ≥ I(Y;T) and keep the naming consistent with the IB lesson.)

Cover & Thomas, §2.9 "Sufficient Statistics" — the equality case: a
sufficient statistic T(X) is exactly one for which I(θ;T) = I(θ;X); no
information about the parameter is lost.

Cover & Thomas, §2.10 "Fano's Inequality" — one-sentence forward pointer:
Fano (used in the channel converse) is the same DPI machinery turned into an
error bound.

MacKay, ch. 8 — mutual information identities reused; MacKay's "information
can only be destroyed" phrasing.

Xu & Raginsky 2017 (arXiv:1705.07809) — further-reading aside only:
gen ≤ sqrt(2σ² I(S;W)/n), generalization bounded by the mutual information
between training set and learned hypothesis — a DPI-flavoured ML payoff.

Key points the lesson must cover

The statement (this lesson's theorem): for a Markov chain Y → X → T
(T computed from X, possibly with added randomness, so T is conditionally
independent of Y given X), I(T;Y) ≤ I(X;Y). Concrete opener: a specific
lossy map T = f(X) on a small joint where you can watch I drop.

The proof, every step from quantities the course owns: chain rule for
mutual information gives I(Y; X,T) = I(Y;X) + I(Y;T|X) = I(Y;T) + I(Y;X|T);
the Markov property makes I(Y;T|X) = 0; I(Y;X|T) ≥ 0 closes it. Show both
expansions side by side.

Processing cannot create information: any deterministic or stochastic
function of X — a hash, a quantizer, a neural layer, a summary statistic —
has at most the information about Y that X had. Corollary I(f(X);Y) ≤ I(X;Y).

The equality case = sufficiency: I(T;Y) = I(X;Y) exactly when T retains
everything X said about Y, i.e. T is a sufficient statistic for Y. Worked with
a small example where a coarse T loses information and a well-chosen T does
not.

Worked computation: a 3- or 4-symbol X with a binary Y and an explicit
joint; a merge/quantization T; compute I(X;Y) and I(T;Y) and confirm the
inequality, then a lossless relabeling T' with equality.

Where it is used next (one sentence each, no content leak): channel
converse (Fano), rate-distortion (X̂ is processed from X), information
bottleneck (the whole objective lives under the DPI ceiling).

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

Arrow direction matters: the chain is Y → X → T; T must be conditionally
independent of Y given X. If T sees Y directly, the bound need not hold.

DPI bounds the average mutual information, not every pointwise term.

"Cannot create information" is about I with a fixed downstream target Y;
processing can still make information easier to use (that is representation
learning) without increasing I. State this — it prevents the "then why learn
features?" misreading.

Randomized processing is allowed (T need not be a function of X); the Markov
condition, not determinism, is what the proof needs.

Equality requires sufficiency for that Y; a statistic sufficient for one
target can be lossy for another.

FIGURE PLAN

single <Figure> (component) — the chain Y → X → T drawn as three nodes
with the processing arrow labeled p(t|x), and the DPI annotated across the
spans: I(T;Y) ≤ I(X;Y). One idea: processing sits between you and the
target. Inspiration: Cover & Thomas §2.8.

<FigureSequence> (3 frames) — the proof: frame 1 I(Y; X,T) expanded
via X first (I(Y;X) + I(Y;T|X)); frame 2 expanded via T first
(I(Y;T) + I(Y;X|T)); frame 3 the Markov term struck out and the inequality
read off. Delta = one expansion per frame. Inspiration: Cover & Thomas §2.8.

single <Figure> (component) — a worked drop: the joint table for X,Y,
a merge T shown as combining two X-columns, and the tally I(X;Y) = …,
I(T;Y) = … with the loss shaded. One idea: merging similar columns costs
little; merging dissimilar ones costs information.

single <Figure> (component) — the equality case: two T's on the same X,
one lossy (bars show I(T;Y) < I(X;Y)) and one a lossless relabeling
(I(T';Y) = I(X;Y)), labeled "sufficient statistic". One idea: equality means
nothing about Y was lost.

single <Figure> (component) — the ML reading: a stack data X → feature T → prediction, with a dashed ceiling line I(·;Y) ≤ I(X;Y) over
every downstream stage. One idea: no layer manufactures information about the
label. Inspiration: playbook bottom-up architecture stack.

documents.title: Research brief: entropy-as-average-surprise (Entropy)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: entropy-as-average-surprise (Entropy)
documents.text:
Research brief: entropy-as-average-surprise (Entropy)

status: retrofit
module: foundations
goal: Compute the entropy of a discrete distribution as expected surprisal.

Drafted before the dossier. This brief records what the draft covers and what a
density-upgrade revision should add.

Sources to consult

Shannon 1948, Part I, §6 — defines H = -Σ p_i log p_i, states the
extremal properties (max at uniform, min at certainty), and fig. 7 is the
binary entropy curve for two outcomes. Primary anchor for the range result.

Cover & Thomas, §2.1 (definition; the binary entropy function H(p),
their fig. 2.1) and Theorem 2.6.4 (H(X) ≤ log|X|, via Jensen). The draft
already cites Theorem 2.6.4 correctly.

MacKay, ch. 2, §2.4-2.5 — entropy of an ensemble, the binary entropy
function; ch. 2 (§2.1 monogram table) for the English single-letter
distribution giving H ≈ 4.11 bits/char over the 27-symbol alphabet. The
draft cites "MacKay, ch. 2" for this — keep; confirmed the monogram estimate
lives in ch. 2.

Key points the lesson must cover (already in the draft)

Entropy = probability-weighted average of surprisal, not the unweighted
average (weather example: 1.5 bits vs. the misleading 1.67).

Definition H(X) = -Σ p(x) log2 p(x) = E[-log2 p(X)], with the convention
0 log2 0 = 0 (justified by the limit).

Relabeling invariance: H depends only on the multiset of probabilities.

Range theorem: 0 ≤ H ≤ log2 n; zero iff a point mass, log2 n iff
uniform. Lower bound termwise; upper bound by Jensen on the concave log.

The binary entropy function H(p) = -p log2 p - (1-p) log2(1-p):
endpoints 0, max 1 bit at p=1/2, symmetry H(p)=H(1-p), vertical slope at
the endpoints (H'(p) = log2((1-p)/p)).

Entropies of common sources: fair die log2 6 ≈ 2.585, uniform byte 8 bits,
shuffled deck log2 52! ≈ 225.6 bits; English monograms ≈ 4.11 vs. the
uniform ceiling log2 27 ≈ 4.75.

Operational preview (Remark): H is the floor on expected bits / yes-no
questions per draw — sets up the coding module.

What a density-upgrade revision should add

The chapter is long (~2600 words) with 2 figures; add 4-6 small visuals
(FIGURE PLAN). This is the primary gap.

A <KeyFact> on the range result ("entropy is maximal exactly when you know
least — the uniform distribution").

The three-step worked-example pattern (surprisal -> weight -> sum) recurs four
times in prose; render it once as a small labeled figure so later instances
can point back rather than repeat.

A <Task> on the EntropyExplorer demo: the draft's demo caption already
states the task ("make H=0, then rebuild the 2-bit maximum") — promote it to a
green <Task> callout.

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

The upper-bound proof uses Jensen on E[log 1/p(X)] and equality forces
uniform-on-support; the draft states the strict-concavity equality condition
correctly — preserve it, QA checks equality conditions.

0 log2 0 = 0 is a convention with a limit justification, not a definition of
log 0.

The monogram 4.11 bits is context-free; the entropy rate of English is far
lower (~1 bit) — flag the distinction and forward-reference
entropy-of-english. Draft already does this.

Nats vs. bits is the same unit choice as surprisal; do not re-derive, link
back to what-is-surprise.

FIGURE PLAN

weighted-average.svg (exists, single <Figure>) — weather outcomes,
surprisal bars weighted by probability into H = 1.5. Keep.

binary-entropy.svg (exists, single <Figure>) — the H(p) inverted-U,
max 1 bit, 90/10 point marked. Keep; this is Shannon's fig. 7 recreated.

NEW, <FigureSequence> (3 frames) — the three-step entropy computation on
{1/2,1/4,1/8,1/8}: frame 1 the four probabilities, frame 2 each mapped to
its surprisal, frame 3 weighted and summed to 1.75. One delta per frame.
Inspiration: the draft's own step-numbered worked example.

NEW, <FigureSequence> (3-4 frames) — "concentrating mass lowers
entropy": start uniform over 4 (H=2), slide mass onto one outcome across
frames, H readout drops each frame; last frame is the point mass (H=0).
Binds the EntropyExplorer demo. Inspiration: Cover & Thomas's concavity
discussion.

NEW, single <Figure> (component) — endpoint-steepness of H(p): a
zoom-in near p=1 with the tangent going vertical, annotating
H(0.99) ≈ 0.081 — "one percent off certainty already buys 0.08 bits".
One idea: the derivative blows up at the ends.

NEW, single <Figure> (component) — the log2 n ceiling as a staircase:
coin (1), 4-outcome (2), byte (8), each uniform bar touching its ceiling, a
non-uniform bar sitting below. Inspiration: the "range of entropy" heading.

Revision round 2 — QA findings (2026-07-24, post-restructure)

Independent course-qa (opus): ready=false — light revision, not a
rewrite. 12 rubric PASS; the only WEAK is L6 visual density: FIGURE PLAN
items #4 and #5 remain unbuilt. Required, in priority order:

Build FIGURE PLAN #4 — <FigureSequence> "concentrating mass lowers
entropy": uniform-over-4 morphing to a point mass over 3-4 frames, H
readout dropping each frame (2.00 -> ... -> 0). Place it in "The
extremes: certainty and even spread" (also breaks that section's
3-paragraph prose run). Raw-SVG tier like the existing entropy-steps-N.

Build FIGURE PLAN #5 — single <Figure>: zoom of the binary-entropy
curve near p=1, tangent going vertical, annotated H(0.99) ~ 0.081 bits.
Anchors "Steep at the ends, flat in the middle" (currently prose-only).

Verify from the demo source that EntropyExplorer starts on a
non-degenerate distribution (D3) and the Task path (H=0 then rebuild
2.00 bits) is achievable; note the check in the report.

Nice-to-have (apply if cheap):

Operational <Remark>: replace generic "the coding lessons that follow"
with <Ref lesson="prefix-codes"> and <Ref lesson="source-coding-theorem-lite">.

One clause noting the operational claim is formalized via the typical set
in source-coding-theorem-lite (precise forward hook).

All round-1 pitfalls verified handled (Jensen equality condition, 0 log 0
convention, monogram-vs-rate distinction) — do not touch those passages.

documents.title: Research brief: entropy-of-english (Entropy of English text)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: entropy-of-english (Entropy of English text)
documents.text:
Research brief: entropy-of-english (Entropy of English text)

status: planned
module: shared-information
type: worked-practice
goal: Estimate the entropy of English text with Shannon's guessing game.

Sources to consult

Shannon 1951, "Prediction and Entropy of Printed English" — the primary
source. The whole paper: the guessing-game experiment, the derivation of upper
and lower bounds on the per-letter entropy from the distribution of guess
ranks, and the ~1 bit/letter and ~50-75% redundancy conclusions.

Cover & Thomas, §6.4 "The Entropy of English" (p. 168) and §6.6
"Gambling Estimate of the Entropy of English" (p. 173) — the modern
