treatment, entropy-rate framing, and the gambling reformulation of Shannon's
bounds. (Also relevant: ch. 4 "Entropy Rates of a Stochastic Process", §4.2
"Entropy Rate" for the formal definition of the per-symbol limit.)

Shannon 1948, Part I, §3 "The Series of Approximations to English" — the
zero-order / first-order / digram / trigram / word approximations and the
redundancy discussion; the ladder that motivates context reducing entropy.

MacKay, ch. 2, §2.1 (English monogram distribution, reused from the entropy
lesson) and ch. 6 "Stream Codes" (why a good English model = good
compressor, foreshadowing the ML module).

Key points the lesson must cover

Entropy rate = per-symbol entropy given unlimited preceding context,
H_rate = lim_n H(X_n | X_1...X_{n-1}). Context strictly lowers per-symbol
uncertainty from the monogram ~4.1 bits toward ~1-1.3 bits/letter.

The approximations ladder (Shannon 1948 §3): uniform 26+space
(log2 27 ≈ 4.75), monogram (~4.1), digram (~3.3), trigram (~3.1),
word-level lower still — each conditioning step buys bits.

Shannon's guessing game (1951): a human predicts the next letter given the
preceding text; the number of guesses until correct is recorded per position.
The distribution of guess-ranks bounds the entropy rate — because an ideal
predictor sharing the human's model could code each letter in
~ -log2 p(rank) bits.

Upper and lower bounds from the guess-rank frequencies q_i (fraction of
letters guessed right on the i-th try): Shannon's F_N bounds. The lesson can
state the bounds and compute a rough estimate from a tally, not re-derive them
fully.

Redundancy = 1 - H_rate / log2(alphabet) ≈ 50-75%: the gap between a raw
fixed-width encoding (ASCII's 8 bits, or log2 27 ≈ 4.75) and the entropy
rate. This is why English compresses.

Worked in prose (no demo, per course.yaml): play the game on a short sentence,
tally guess counts, convert to a bits-per-letter estimate; learner repeats.

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

Entropy rate vs. single-letter entropy: the ~4.1-bit monogram figure is
not the entropy of English; it ignores all inter-letter structure. The
headline number (~1 bit) is the rate. Keep the two distinct — this is the
lesson's central correction.

The guessing game gives bounds, not an exact value; the estimate is
model-dependent (depends on the predictor's skill) and corpus-dependent.
Shannon's own estimate is a range (~0.6-1.3 bits/letter).

Shannon's upper and lower bounds coincide only in the limit; a short tally
gives a crude estimate — be honest about sample size.

Alphabet choice matters (27 symbols vs. 26 vs. full ASCII with case and
punctuation changes every number). State the alphabet.

The game measures the entropy of the predictor's model of English, which
upper-bounds the true rate; a better predictor gives a tighter (lower) estimate
— directly foreshadowing compression-is-prediction.

FIGURE PLAN

single <Figure> (component) — the approximations ladder: descending bars
from log2 27 ≈ 4.75 (uniform) down through monogram, digram, trigram to the
~1-bit rate, each rung labeled with what it conditions on. One idea: context
buys bits. Inspiration: Shannon 1948 §3.

<FigureSequence> (4-5 frames) — the guessing game on one word
(e.g. "THE_QUICK"): each frame reveals the next letter and stacks the guess
count for that position; final frame shows the tally row. Delta = one letter
per frame. Inspiration: Shannon 1951's worked reveal.

single <Figure> (component) — guess-rank histogram: the fraction of
letters guessed correctly on try 1, 2, 3, ...; the mass concentrated on
"first try" is what makes the entropy low. One idea: a peaked guess
distribution means low entropy. Inspiration: Shannon 1951 rank statistics.

single <Figure> (component) — bits/letter vs. context length: a curve
dropping from ~4.1 (no context) toward the ~1-bit asymptote as the number of
preceding letters grows. One idea: the limit is the entropy rate.

single <Figure> (component) — the redundancy bar: an 8-bit (or 4.75-bit)
raw slot with the ~1-bit "actual information" shaded and the remaining ~75%
marked "redundancy — removable by compression". One idea: most of written
English is predictable. Foreshadows compression-is-prediction.

documents.title: Research brief: huffman-by-hand (Huffman coding)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: huffman-by-hand (Huffman coding)
documents.text:
Research brief: huffman-by-hand (Huffman coding)

status: planned
module: coding
type: worked-practice
goal: Build an optimal prefix code with the Huffman algorithm.

Sources to consult

Cover & Thomas, §5.6 "Huffman Codes", §5.7 "Some Comments on Huffman
Codes", §5.8 "Optimality of Huffman Codes" — the algorithm, worked
examples, and the exchange-argument optimality proof (their Lemma 5.8.1 and
Theorem 5.8.1). §5.4 "Bounds on the Optimal Codelength" gives
H(X) ≤ L* < H(X)+1.

MacKay, ch. 5, §5.4 "The Huffman coding algorithm" — the merge procedure,
a worked example, and MacKay's explicit critique of Huffman's shortcomings
("The disadvantages of the Huffman code", §5.5-ish) that motivates stream
codes in ch. 6. (Locate the exact subsection number for the critique.)

Key points the lesson must cover

The algorithm: repeatedly take the two lowest-probability symbols, merge
them into a node with summed probability, reinsert, repeat until one node
remains; read codewords off the tree (root-to-leaf, 0/1 per branch).

A fully worked example on {A:.5, B:.25, C:.15, D:.1} (course.yaml's
stated distribution) showing every merge, then the learner regenerates on a
fresh distribution.

Optimality: Huffman produces a minimum-expected-length prefix code. The
proof idea (exchange argument): an optimal code can be assumed to give the
two least-likely symbols the longest, equal-length, sibling codewords; merging
them reduces to a smaller optimal problem (induction).

The 1-bit guarantee: H(X) ≤ L_Huffman < H(X)+1. The overhead comes from
integer codeword lengths; connect to the ceiling ⌈-log2 p⌉ intuition.

Huffman is optimal among symbol codes but not perfect — the up-to-1-bit gap
per symbol motivates block coding (source-coding-theorem-lite) and stream /
arithmetic coding (compression-is-prediction).

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

Tie-breaking is free: when several symbols share the lowest probability the
choice is arbitrary and the tree is not unique, but every Huffman tree
achieves the same optimal expected length. State this to preempt "my tree
looks different".

The 1-bit overhead is per symbol, so it can dominate for low-entropy
sources (a 0.1-bit source still pays ~1 bit/symbol with a symbol code) — this
is the motivating flaw for the next lessons, name it explicitly.

Codeword lengths are what is optimal; the 0/1 labeling on branches is
arbitrary (swapping children relabels, same lengths).

Huffman needs the distribution in advance; adaptive/streaming variants exist
but are out of scope.

Do not claim Huffman achieves entropy — it achieves it only when all
probabilities are powers of 1/2 (dyadic).

FIGURE PLAN

<FigureSequence> (5-6 frames) — the merge process on
{A:.5, B:.25, C:.15, D:.1}: each frame merges the current two smallest into
a parent node (probabilities updating), forest shrinking by one, until the
root forms. The house-signature algorithm sequence; delta = one merge per
frame. Inspiration: MacKay §5.4 Huffman worked example.

single <Figure> (component) — the finished tree with codewords read off
each leaf and the expected-length tally L = 1.75 beside the source entropy,
showing the sub-1-bit gap. One idea: the output and its cost.

<FigureSequence> (3 frames) — the exchange argument, schematically: an
arbitrary optimal tree; swap a shallow rare leaf with a deep frequent one;
show expected length cannot increase — motivating "two rarest go deepest".
One idea per frame. Inspiration: Cover & Thomas §5.8 proof.

single <Figure> (component) — H ≤ L < H+1 on a number line for the
example, plus a low-entropy source (0.9/0.1 coin, H≈0.47) where L=1 shows the
overhead nearly doubling the cost. One idea: integer lengths cost up to a bit.

single <Figure> (component) — two valid Huffman trees for a tie-heavy
distribution side by side, different shapes, identical L. One idea:
non-unique tree, unique cost.

documents.title: Research brief: infonce (The InfoNCE bound)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: infonce (The InfoNCE bound)
documents.text:
Research brief: infonce (The InfoNCE bound)

status: planned
module: applications
type: core
goal: Derive the InfoNCE lower bound on mutual information from a contrastive classification loss.

Sources to consult

van den Oord, Li & Vinyals 2018, "Representation Learning with
Contrastive Predictive Coding" (arXiv:1807.03748) — the primary source.

§2.1 — why not model p(y|x) generatively: mutual information
I(x;c) = Σ p(x,c) log [p(x|c)/p(x)] as the objective; reconstruction
losses waste capacity on irrelevant detail.

§2.3 "InfoNCE Loss and Mutual Information Estimation" — the loss
L_N = -E[ log f(x_pos,c) / Σ_j f(x_j,c) ] (categorical cross-entropy
over 1 positive + N-1 negatives); proof that the optimal f is
proportional to the density ratio p(x|c)/p(x).

Appendix A.1 (eqs. 6-11) — the full derivation of
I(x;c) ≥ log N - L_N; also the MINE remark (alternative estimator,
stability comparison) for one sentence of context.

§3 — cross-modal experiments (audio, vision, text, RL): cite
precisely for the applications paragraph (LibriSpeech phone accuracy
64.6 vs 39.7 MFCC baseline; ImageNet linear-probe top-1 48.7).

Cover & Thomas, §2.3 — mutual information as the expected log
density-ratio E[log p(x,y)/(p(x)p(y))]: the identity the derivation
turns on; reuse from the mutual-information lesson.

Tishby et al. 1999 — one-sentence link back: IB says maximize I(T;Y); the
practical question this lesson answers is how to estimate/optimize such an
I from samples.

Key points the lesson must cover

The estimation problem (the flaw motivating the mechanism): the
course computed I(X;Y) from small joint tables; for images/audio/text the
joint is unavailable and counting fails. Needed: a quantity computable
from samples of pairs that certifies mutual information.

The contrastive setup: draw one true pair (x, y_pos) and N-1
"negatives" y_j from the marginal p(y); train a scoring function
f(x, y) and classify which candidate is the positive via softmax over
scores. The loss L_N is an N-way cross-entropy — reuse cross-entropy-loss
machinery directly.

The optimal classifier recovers a density ratio: the posterior that
candidate i is the positive is
p(y_i|x) Π_{j≠i} p(y_j) / Σ_k [p(y_k|x) Π_{j≠k} p(y_j)], which
simplifies to [p(y_i|x)/p(y_i)] / Σ_k [p(y_k|x)/p(y_k)] — so the loss
is minimized when f(x,y) ∝ p(y|x)/p(y). Full algebra shown; note the
ratio is learned without ever modeling p(y|x) or p(y) separately.

The bound: substituting the optimal f gives
L_N ≥ log2 N - I(X;Y) hence I(X;Y) ≥ log2 N - L_N (Appendix A.1
route: the expectation over negatives concentrates the denominator around
1 + (N-1)·E[ratio] -style terms; present the derivation at the paper's
level of rigor and flag the approximation step explicitly).

Worked toy example, exact numbers: a small discrete pair (e.g. 4×4
joint from the mutual-information lesson) where p(y|x)/p(y) is computable
by hand; evaluate L_N with the optimal critic for N = 2 and N = 4 and
compare log2 N - L_N to the true I(X;Y). Shows both the bound holding
and its looseness.

Saturation: the bound never exceeds log2 N — with I(X;Y) > log2 N even
a perfect critic saturates (the classification task becomes too easy to
certify more bits). More negatives raise the ceiling; this is why
contrastive methods use large batches.

The applications payoff (one section, precise): the same loss trains
representations across audio/vision/text/RL (CPC), and the density-ratio
trick is the common core of modern contrastive representation learning;
link back to IB — InfoNCE is a trainable surrogate for the I(T;Y) term.

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

It is a lower bound: low loss certifies high MI; high loss certifies
nothing (the critic may just be bad). Direction matters — state it as a
one-way certificate.

Negatives must come from the marginal p(y), not an arbitrary noise
distribution — otherwise the recovered ratio is against the wrong
reference. (Contrast with generic NCE in one sentence.)

Bits vs nats: the paper works in nats (log N); the course states the
bound in bits (log2 N). Convert consistently; ML implementations report
nats.

The optimal critic is independent of N, but the bound's tightness is not:
it degrades when true MI approaches or exceeds log N — the toy example
must exhibit this.

log2 N - L_N is an estimate derived from a bound, and finite-sample
estimates are biased; do not present it as an unbiased MI estimator.

Do not derive the full CPC architecture (encoder + autoregressive context);
a one-figure sketch suffices — the lesson's object is the bound, not the
network.

FIGURE PLAN

single <Figure> (component) — the contrastive setup: a context x on
the left, N candidate y's on the right (one highlighted as the true
partner, the rest marked "drawn from p(y)"), the scorer f(x,y) fanning
over candidates into a softmax. One idea: MI estimation as an N-way quiz.
Inspiration: CPC §2.2-2.3 setup (recreate schematically).

<FigureSequence> (4 frames) — the derivation: frame 1 the N-way
posterior over "which candidate is real"; frame 2 products of marginals
cancel, leaving density ratios; frame 3 optimal f ∝ p(y|x)/p(y)
boxed; frame 4 substitution yields I ≥ log2 N - L_N. Delta = one
algebraic move per frame. Inspiration: Appendix A.1 (eqs. 6-11).

single <Figure> (component) — the bound dissected:
I(X;Y) ≥ log2 N - L_N with labels-above-symbols — "budget: bits to name
1 of N", "what the classifier pays", "what is left is certified
information". One idea: certified bits = budget minus loss.

single <Figure> (component) — worked toy tally: the 4×4 joint, its
ratio table p(y|x)/p(y), and computed rows for N=2 and N=4: L_N, bound,
true I. One idea: the bound holds and tightens with N. Real numbers
plugged in (playbook rule 4).

single <Figure> (component) — saturation: bound value vs true MI
for N = 2, 16, 256 as three curves clipping at 1, 4, 8 bits. Static twin
of the InfoNCESaturation demo. One idea: you cannot certify more than
log2 N bits.

single <Figure> (component) — the CPC pipeline in one strip:
waveform/patches → encoder z_t → context c_t → score future z_{t+k}
against negatives; the InfoNCE box highlighted as "the only loss". One
idea: where the bound sits in a real system. Inspiration: CPC fig. 1
(recreate, simplify, never copy).

documents.title: Research brief: information-bottleneck (The information bottleneck)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: information-bottleneck (The information bottleneck)
documents.text:
Research brief: information-bottleneck (The information bottleneck)

status: planned
module: principles
type: core
goal: Analyze the information bottleneck objective as a trade-off between compression and preserved relevant information.

Updated for the restructure. Two dependencies that were crammed into this lesson
in the previous pass are now their own prerequisite chapters:
data-processing-inequality (the DPI is proved there, only used here) and
rate-distortion (the framework IB generalizes, taught in full there). This
lesson can therefore open cleanly with the framework-flaw-fix move: rate-
distortion needs a hand-picked distortion; the bottleneck replaces it with a
second mutual information. Do NOT re-derive the DPI or re-teach rate-distortion —
recap each in one sentence with a <Ref> and build.

Sources to consult

Tishby, Pereira & Bialek 1999, "The Information Bottleneck Method"
(arXiv:physics/0004057) — the primary source.

§1 + §2.1 — the motivation: Shannon's theory has no notion of
relevance; rate-distortion requires a hand-specified distortion function,
itself an arbitrary feature choice. (Recap territory now — the
rate-distortion lesson owns the framework.)

§3.1 — the objective L = I(X;T) - β I(T;Y) over stochastic encoders
p(t|x), and the data-processing bound I(T;Y) ≤ I(X;Y) (their eq. 14) —
cite the DPI from the prerequisite lesson.

§3.2, Theorem 4 — the optimal encoder
p(t|x) ∝ p(t) exp(-β D_KL[p(y|x) || p(y|t)]): the distortion measure
emerges as a KL divergence. State; do not reproduce the Lagrange proof.

§3.4 — the information plane (I(X;T), I(T;Y)) and the β-parameterized
frontier; one convex curve per cardinality |T|.

Cover & Thomas, §2.9 "Sufficient Statistics" — one remark: IB's β → ∞ limit
approximates a minimal sufficient statistic (the DPI equality case, from the
prerequisite lesson).

Cover & Thomas, §10.8 (Blahut–Arimoto) — pointer only: the IB iterative
algorithm generalizes it; out of scope.

Xu & Raginsky 2017 (arXiv:1705.07809) — further-reading aside: I(S;W) bounds
generalization, a sibling of the bottleneck's "keep only relevant bits" idea.

Key points the lesson must cover

The representation-learning problem: compress X (an input) into T (a
representation, fewer bits) while keeping what matters for a target Y. Recap in
one sentence that rate-distortion () would need
a hand-picked distortion d(x, x̂) — the flaw the bottleneck removes.

The objective: minimize I(X;T) - β I(T;Y) over stochastic encoders
p(t|x). Extremes: β → 0 collapses T to one value (maximal compression, zero
relevance); β → ∞ makes T a copy of X (all relevance, no compression). β
prices relevant bits in units of rate.

The DPI ceiling (recap, not re-proof): since Y → X → T,
I(T;Y) ≤ I(X;Y) () — the target
information T can preserve is capped by what X had. Also I(T;Y) ≤ I(X;T)
(T cannot say more about Y than it contains). These two bound the information
plane.

Worked toy example, computed in full: X ∈ {4 symbols} with a binary label
Y and an explicit joint table. Enumerate the hard 2-cluster encoders T,
compute I(X;T) and I(T;Y) for each, and exhibit the trade-off: the merge of
the two symbols with the most similar p(y|x) loses the least relevance. This
grounds Theorem 4's KL-form intuitively.

The information plane: plot the candidates from (4) as points in
(I(X;T), I(T;Y)); the DPI ceilings as the two boundary lines; the β-swept
frontier as the upper boundary. Static twin of the InformationPlane demo.

Theorem 4 stated: the optimal encoder is Gibbs-form with
D_KL[p(y|x) || p(y|t)] as the effective distortion — relevance defines its
own distortion measure, derived not hand-picked. Connect the exponent to the
toy example's merge rule and to the rate-distortion Lagrangian.

At the optimum, marginal exchange rate: moving along the frontier, one
additional bit of I(T;Y) costs β bits of I(X;T) (Tishby §3.4 states the slope
relation — derive it from the stated Lagrangian rather than quoting a
convention).

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

The Markov structure is T ← X ← Y (T is a code of X, not a generative
latent for Y); Tishby's own footnote warns against the generative reading —
keep the arrow direction explicit in every figure. (Same chain as the DPI
lesson; reuse its framing.)

The paper contains zero figures; the famous "information plane trajectories
of deep networks" plots come from later, contested literature. Do not import
claims about SGD dynamics or DNN compression phases; teach the 1999 objective.

Estimating I in high dimensions is its own hard problem — forward-ref
infonce as the modern trainable handle (and it is the next lesson).

Hard clusterings in the toy example are a strict subset of stochastic encoders;
the true frontier can dominate all hard points. Say so.

The slope-β relation's convention differs across write-ups (β vs 1/β); derive
it from the stated Lagrangian rather than quoting.

IB solutions are found by alternating minimization (generalized Blahut–Arimoto,
their Theorem 5) with convergence but no uniqueness — mention in one sentence,
algorithm out of scope.

FIGURE PLAN

single <Figure> (component) — rate-distortion vs IB comparison panel:
two near-identical objective boxes, ⟨d(x,x̂)⟩ (hand-picked, warning color)
replaced by -I(T;Y) (derived from data), payoff line "relevance without a
designed distortion". Playbook two-panel comparison. Inspiration: Tishby
§1-§3.1. (This is now the opener, since the DPI has its own lesson.)

single <Figure> (component) — the objective dissected:
L = I(X;T) - β I(T;Y) with labels-above-symbols — "bits kept about X (rate)",
"inverse temperature", "bits kept about the target Y (relevance)". One idea:
compress X, keep Y.

<FigureSequence> (4 frames) — the toy 4-symbol example: frame 1 the joint
table with p(y|x) per symbol; frames 2-4 candidate 2-cluster merges, each
frame tallying (I(X;T), I(T;Y)); the similar-conditional merge visibly keeps
more relevance. Delta = one candidate encoder per frame.

single <Figure> (component) — the information plane: axes I(X;T) and
I(T;Y), the DPI ceiling as a horizontal line at I(X;Y), the diagonal
I(T;Y) ≤ I(X;T), toy-example points plotted, frontier curve through the best
ones. Static twin of the InformationPlane demo. Inspiration: Tishby §3.4
(concept described but never drawn in the source — build from the math).

single <Figure> (component) — Theorem 4 dissected:
p(t|x) ∝ p(t) exp(-β D_KL[p(y|x)||p(y|t)]) with labels-above-symbols —
"prior for the cluster", "inverse temperature", "the emergent distortion: how
differently x and cluster t predict Y". One idea: the distortion is a KL,
derived not chosen. Reuses kl-divergence.

single <Figure> (component) — β extremes: three small encoder diagrams
(β ≈ 0: all x → one t; intermediate: the good 2-cluster; β large: identity),
each with its (I(X;T), I(T;Y)) pair. One idea: β dials where you sit on the
frontier.

documents.title: Research brief: joint-and-conditional-entropy (Joint and conditional entropy)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: joint-and-conditional-entropy (Joint and conditional entropy)
documents.text:
Research brief: joint-and-conditional-entropy (Joint and conditional entropy)

status: planned
module: shared-information
type: core
goal: Compute conditional entropy from a joint distribution table.

Sources to consult

Cover & Thomas, §2.2 "Joint Entropy and Conditional Entropy" — definitions
H(X,Y) = -Σ p(x,y) log p(x,y), H(Y|X) = Σ p(x) H(Y|X=x) = -Σ p(x,y) log p(y|x), and the chain rule Theorem 2.2.1 H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|X). Also
H(Y|X) ≤ H(Y) (conditioning reduces entropy) — their Theorem 2.6.5.

MacKay, ch. 8 "Dependent Random Variables", §8.1 — joint ensembles,
marginal / conditional entropy, the chain rule, and MacKay's diagram relating
H(X), H(Y), H(X,Y), H(X|Y), H(Y|X) (the additive area diagram,
MacKay fig. 8.1). Locate §8.1 precisely.

Key points the lesson must cover

A joint distribution table assigns one probability to each pair (x,y);
the row/column sums are the marginals p(x), p(y).

Joint entropy H(X,Y): the uncertainty in the pair, from the flattened
joint distribution — same entropy formula, over pairs.

Conditional entropy H(Y|X): the average over x of the entropy of the
conditional distribution p(y|x). Compute it two ways and show they agree:
Σ_x p(x) H(Y|X=x) and -Σ_{x,y} p(x,y) log p(y|x).

Chain rule H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|X) = H(Y) + H(X|Y): total uncertainty
splits into "learn X, then learn Y given X". Worked on a 2x2 (sky x rain)
table matching the JointEntropyGrid demo.

Conditioning reduces entropy on average: H(Y|X) ≤ H(Y), with equality
iff X and Y are independent. But pointwise H(Y|X=x) can exceed H(Y) for
a particular x — a specific observation can increase surprise.

Sets up mutual information as the drop H(Y) - H(Y|X).

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

H(Y|X) is an average, not H(Y|X=x) for some fixed x. The most common
error is confusing the averaged quantity with a single-conditional entropy.
The ≤ H(Y) bound holds for the average only.

Asymmetry of conditioning: H(Y|X) ≠ H(X|Y) in general (they differ by
H(Y) - H(X)); only the joint H(X,Y) is symmetric.

Independence gives H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y) and H(Y|X) = H(Y) — a checkable
special case; use the demo's "independent" preset.

Zero cells in the joint table contribute nothing (0 log 0 = 0), and
conditionals p(y|x) are undefined where p(x)=0 — skip those x (they carry
weight 0 anyway).

Deterministic dependence (Y = f(X)) gives H(Y|X) = 0 but H(X|Y) need not
be 0 — a good demo "perfectly linked" preset to probe.

FIGURE PLAN

single <Figure> (component) — the joint table as a 2x2 grid of masses
with marginals written along the margins; one cell highlighted with its
p(x,y) log 1/p(x,y) contribution. One idea: the joint table is the object.
Inspiration: MacKay's joint-ensemble grid (ch. 8).

<FigureSequence> (3 frames) — computing H(Y|X) as an average: frame 1
the two conditional rows p(y|X=sun), p(y|X=rain) with their separate
entropies; frame 2 weights each by p(x); frame 3 sums to H(Y|X). One delta
per frame. Inspiration: the two-way definition of conditional entropy.

single <Figure> (component) — the chain rule as a bar decomposition:
H(X,Y) bar split into H(X) + H(Y|X), and the same total split the
other way into H(Y) + H(X|Y). One idea: same whole, two orders.
Inspiration: Cover & Thomas Theorem 2.2.1.

single <Figure> (component) — the additive area diagram: two overlapping
regions for H(X) and H(Y), labeling the union H(X,Y), the crescents
H(X|Y), H(Y|X), and the overlap (foreshadowing I(X;Y), unlabeled here).
One idea: uncertainties tile an area. Inspiration: MacKay fig. 8.1 /
Cover & Thomas fig. 2.2 (recreate, do not copy).

<FigureSequence> (3 frames) — conditioning reduces entropy: independent
table (H(Y|X) = H(Y)), mildly linked (H(Y|X) < H(Y)), deterministic
(H(Y|X) = 0), the H(Y|X) bar shrinking each frame. One idea: information
about X eats uncertainty in Y. Binds the JointEntropyGrid demo.

documents.title: Research brief: kl-divergence (KL divergence)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: kl-divergence (KL divergence)
documents.text:
Research brief: kl-divergence (KL divergence)

status: planned
module: information-in-ml
type: core
goal: Compute the KL divergence between two distributions as expected extra bits.

Sources to consult

Cover & Thomas, §2.3 "Relative Entropy and Mutual Information" — definition
D(p||q) = Σ p(x) log[ p(x) / q(x) ], conventions (0 log 0/q = 0,
p log p/0 = ∞), and asymmetry. §2.6 "Jensen's Inequality and Its
Consequences" — the information inequality (Theorem 2.6.3): D(p||q) ≥ 0,
equality iff p = q (Gibbs' inequality, via Jensen on the convex -log).

Cover & Thomas, §5.4 "Bounds on the Optimal Codelength" — the operational
reading: coding p with a code built for q costs H(p) + D(p||q) bits, so
D(p||q) is exactly the expected extra bits (reuse from
source-coding-theorem-lite).

MacKay, ch. 2 — relative entropy is introduced with the entropy material;
MacKay's Gibbs'-inequality treatment. Locate the exact § (relative entropy
appears in the ch. 2 exercises / §2.6 region).

Key points the lesson must cover

Operational definition first (playbook: example before definition): a code
optimized for q gives symbol x length -log2 q(x); using it on data
distributed as p costs Σ p(x) (-log2 q(x)) on average, which exceeds the
optimal H(p) by exactly D(p||q).

Formula: D(p||q) = Σ p(x) log2[ p(x)/q(x) ], the expected log-ratio,
in bits.

Non-negativity (Gibbs): D(p||q) ≥ 0, zero iff p = q. Proof via
Jensen on the convex -log. This is why "coding with the wrong distribution
always costs".

Asymmetry: D(p||q) ≠ D(q||p) — it matters which distribution is real
(the data) and which is the code/model. Worked with a concrete asymmetric
example computing both directions.

Not a metric: asymmetric and violates the triangle inequality; it is a
divergence. Still the natural "distance" for coding cost and for ML.

The missing-outcome disaster: if q(x) = 0 but p(x) > 0, then
D(p||q) = ∞ — a model that rules out something the data produces pays
unbounded cost (matches the KLMismatch demo's "missing-outcome" preset).

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

Direction convention: D(p||q) with p = truth/data, q = model/code.
ML "forward" (D(p||q), mean-seeking) vs. "reverse" (D(q||p), mode-seeking)
KL differ in behavior; the coding story is always D(data||model). State the
convention up front and keep it consistent with cross-entropy-loss.

D is finite only when q is absolutely continuous w.r.t. p in the discrete
sense (q(x)=0 => p(x)=0); otherwise +∞.

Non-negativity is the workhorse theorem — it underlies the source coding
lower bound, I(X;Y) ≥ 0, and the cross-entropy story. Give it prominence.

KL is not symmetric even approximately for far-apart distributions; do not
average the two directions casually (that is a different quantity, JS
divergence — mention only as beyond scope).

Units: bits (log2) here; ML libraries usually report nats (natural log).

FIGURE PLAN

<FigureSequence> (3 frames) — extra bits per symbol: frame 1 the optimal
q-code lengths -log2 q(x); frame 2 overlay the ideal p-code lengths
-log2 p(x); frame 3 shade the per-symbol gaps, weighted by p(x), summing
to D(p||q). One delta per frame. Inspiration: Cover & Thomas §5.4.

single <Figure> (component) — the two draggable distributions p (true)
and q (model) as 4-bar charts with readouts H(p), cross-entropy H(p,q),
and the gap D(p||q). Static twin of the KLMismatch demo. One idea: the gap
is the divergence.

single <Figure> (component) — asymmetry, two panels: D(p||q) and
D(q||p) computed for the same pair, different values, arrow between them
crossed out to say "not equal". One idea: direction matters. Inspiration: the
forward/reverse-KL literature (recreate schematically).

single <Figure> (component) — the missing-outcome blowup: q puts zero
mass on an outcome p produces; the term p log p/0 shooting off to ∞,
annotated "a model that says 'impossible' about something real pays forever".
Warning-color. One idea: zeros in the model are catastrophic. Binds the demo's
"missing-outcome disaster" preset.

single <Figure> (component) — Gibbs schematic: the convex -log curve
with a Jensen chord, showing E[-log(q/p)] ≥ -log E[q/p] = 0. One idea: why
D ≥ 0. Inspiration: Cover & Thomas §2.6 Jensen figure (recreate).

documents.title: Research brief: kolmogorov-complexity (Kolmogorov complexity)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: kolmogorov-complexity (Kolmogorov complexity)
documents.text:
Research brief: kolmogorov-complexity (Kolmogorov complexity)

status: planned
module: information-in-ml
type: core
goal: Explain Kolmogorov complexity as the shortest-program limit under all compression.

New lesson closing the ML module. compression-is-prediction showed a good model
is a short code; this lesson pushes to the limit — the shortest possible code for
a string is the shortest program that outputs it, K(x). It ties the whole
"compression = prediction = learning" thread to its theoretical ceiling
(Solomonoff's universal predictor) and is the parent of MDL (ideal MDL = a
two-part Kolmogorov code), which follows in the principles module.

Sources to consult

Shen, Uspensky & Vereshchagin, Kolmogorov Complexity and Algorithmic
Randomness — the "What is this book about?" overview and ch. 1 for the
definition, the Solomonoff-Kolmogorov invariance theorem (K well-defined up to
+O(1)), and the counting argument for incompressibility; ch. 7 for
C(x)/N → H (complexity meets Shannon entropy); ch. 14.3 for the two-part
code = MDL principle and Occam's-razor framing. Overview + ch. 1/7/14 are
lesson-ready; the proof body is deep background.

Cover & Thomas, ch. 14 "Kolmogorov Complexity" — §14.2 definitions,
§14.3 K(x) ≈ H in expectation for i.i.d. computable sources, §14.5
incompressible/algorithmically-random sequences, §14.6 universal probability /
Solomonoff, §14.13 MDL. The compact textbook version.

MacKay, ch. 28 §28.3 — MDL/Occam as the practical, Bayesian shadow of the
ideal; the "shortest description" thesis.

Delétang et al. 2023, §2 "Universal Coding" — the modern statement that
optimal compression = optimal prediction, with Solomonoff/Hutter as the
ceiling; ties back to compression-is-prediction.

Key points the lesson must cover

Regularity = compressibility (concrete opener, reusing MDL's motivating
trio): three length-n strings — all-zeros, a fair-coin string, a
"0101…"-periodic string — and the length of the shortest program printing
each. Structure is exactly what a short program exploits.

Definition: K(x) = length in bits of the shortest program (for a fixed
universal machine) that outputs x and halts. Reuse the code↔program intuition
from compression-is-prediction: a program is a self-extracting archive.

The invariance theorem: choosing a different universal language changes
K(x) by at most an additive constant (the length of one interpreter), so K
is well-defined "up to +O(1)" and the choice of language does not matter
asymptotically. This is what makes K a real quantity.

Almost everything is incompressible (counting argument): there are 2^n
strings of length n but fewer than 2^{n-c} programs shorter than n-c
bits, so at most a 2^{-c} fraction can be compressed by c bits. Most data has
no short description — compressibility is the exception.

K is uncomputable (Berry's paradox / halting): no program computes K(x)
for all x; "the shortest incompressible string describable in under 100 bits"
is a contradiction. The ideal compressor exists but cannot be run — this is
why practical compression and MDL use computable approximations.

K meets entropy: for a computable source, E[K(X^n)]/n → H — the
algorithmic and probabilistic notions of information agree in the limit
(ch. 7 / Cover §14.3). And the ideal predictor (Solomonoff: mixture over all
programs weighted 2^{-length}) is the compression ceiling under
compression-is-prediction — a good learner approximates it.

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

Uncomputable ≠ undefined: K(x) is a perfectly well-defined number; it
simply cannot be computed by any algorithm. Keep the distinction sharp.

The +O(1) invariance constant is real and can be large for a specific string;
invariance is an asymptotic statement. Do not claim a language-free exact
value.

K(x) is for an individual string, unlike entropy, which needs a
distribution. This is the whole point of the algorithmic view — state it.

E[K]/n → H needs a computable source; for arbitrary strings K is the right
notion and entropy does not apply. Flag the hypothesis.

Do not present Solomonoff induction as a runnable algorithm — it is
uncomputable; it is the theoretical optimum practical learners approximate.

This is lossless/algorithmic; do not conflate with rate-distortion (lossy) —
one-sentence contrast, they live in different lessons.

FIGURE PLAN

single <Figure> (component) — three strings, three programs: all-zeros
("print 0 ×n", tiny), periodic ("print '01' ×n/2", small), fair-coin
(no short program, ≈ n bits), with description-length bars. One idea:
structure = short program. Inspiration: Shen et al. overview / Grünwald §1.2.

single <Figure> (component) — the invariance theorem: string x compiled
by machine A vs machine B, the two program lengths differing only by a fixed
"interpreter" block of length c, bracketed |K_A - K_B| ≤ c. One idea: the
language costs at most a constant. Inspiration: Shen et al. ch. 1 / Cover
§14.2.

single <Figure> (component) — the incompressibility count: a bin of all
2^n length-n strings, a much smaller sub-bin of the < 2^{n-c} short
programs, arrow "at most 2^{-c} compressible by c bits". One idea: most
strings cannot be shortened. Inspiration: Cover & Thomas §14.5.

single <Figure> (component) — Berry's paradox as a loop: a program
"output the shortest string with K > 100" that is itself under 100 bits,
flagged as a contradiction in warning color. One idea: K cannot be computed.
Inspiration: Shen et al. ch. 1 non-computability.

single <Figure> (component) — K meets H: a curve E[K(X^n)]/n
descending to the entropy line H as n grows, for a biased-coin source. One
idea: algorithmic and Shannon information agree in the limit. Inspiration:
Shen et al. ch. 7 / Cover §14.3.

single <Figure> (component) — the ceiling map: practical model →
Shannon-optimal code (H) → shortest program (K) → Solomonoff (ideal predictor), a left-to-right ladder of decreasing description length. One idea:
compression, prediction, and learning share one ceiling. Inspiration:
Delétang §2 "Universal Coding".

documents.title: Research brief: kraft-inequality (The Kraft inequality)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: kraft-inequality (The Kraft inequality)
documents.text:
Research brief: kraft-inequality (The Kraft inequality)

status: planned
module: coding
type: core
goal: Apply the Kraft inequality to decide whether a set of codeword lengths is achievable by a prefix code.

Second half of the re-split. prefix-codes established the tree/code
correspondence and expected length; this lesson answers the question that
raises: which sets of codeword lengths can a prefix code actually have? The
Kraft budget answers it, and McMillan shows the answer is the same for every
uniquely decodable code — the fact the source coding theorem leans on.

Sources to consult

Cover & Thomas, §5.2 "Kraft Inequality" — Theorem 5.2.1: a prefix code
with lengths l_i exists iff Σ 2^{-l_i} ≤ 1; both directions via the
code-tree / interval argument.

Cover & Thomas, §5.5 "Kraft Inequality for Uniquely Decodable Codes" —
McMillan's theorem: the same bound for the broader class, so prefix codes lose
nothing. State the result and the polynomial-of-lengths proof idea.

MacKay, ch. 5, §5.2 — the total-budget-of-1 framing of Kraft, which is the
CodewordBudget demo's model.

Key points the lesson must cover

A codeword of length L claims 2^{-L} of a budget of 1 — the fraction
of the infinite binary tree below it (all strings with that prefix). Concrete
opener: mark one length-2 codeword and shade its quarter of the tree.

Necessity: in a prefix code the codewords' subtrees are disjoint, so the
claimed fractions sum to Σ 2^{-l_i} ≤ 1. Prove by pushing every leaf down
to a common maximal depth and counting descendants.

Sufficiency: given lengths with Σ 2^{-l_i} ≤ 1, a prefix code with those
lengths exists — assign codewords in nondecreasing length order, each to the
next free node. Necessity and sufficiency are genuinely two different
arguments; show the construction on {1,2,3,3}.

Equality Σ 2^{-l_i} = 1 ⇔ a complete code, no wasted tree nodes; worked
with the demo presets: impossible {1,2,2,2} (sum 1.25), tight {1,2,3,3}
(sum 1).

McMillan: any uniquely decodable code obeys the same inequality (proof
sketch: raise (Σ 2^{-l_i})^k and bound the coefficient count by string
length). So nothing is lost by restricting to prefix codes — the hook the
source coding theorem uses.

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

Kraft is about the existence of lengths, not about a specific code or its
optimality; satisfying Kraft makes a code possible, not good. The best
assignment of lengths is the next lesson (Huffman).

Budget ≤ 1 does not bound the number of codewords; it bounds their
combined length-cost. Many short codewords overspend; many long ones do not.

The 2^{-L} fraction is the tree share, not a probability — though the
source coding theorem will read it as one (q(x) = 2^{-l(x)}). Flag, defer.

McMillan's theorem is stated at proof-sketch level; do not claim a full proof.

Sufficiency needs the lengths sorted; assigning out of order can strand a
short codeword above an already-used node.

FIGURE PLAN

single <Figure> (component) — the tree-subtree claim: a binary tree with
one length-2 codeword highlighted and its entire subtree shaded, labeled
"this codeword claims 1/4 of the tree — all strings starting 10". One idea:
a codeword owns its subtree. Inspiration: Cover & Thomas §5.2.

<FigureSequence> (4 frames) — the budget bar filling: add codewords
{1,2,3,3} one at a time, bar fills by 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8 to exactly full;
a fifth attempted codeword overflows red. Static twin of the CodewordBudget
demo. Delta = one codeword per frame. Inspiration: MacKay's budget picture
(§5.2).

single <Figure> (component) — impossible vs. tight: two small trees side
by side, {1,2,2,2} with colliding subtrees (sum 1.25, infeasible) and
{1,2,3,3} tiling the tree exactly (sum 1). One idea: overspending forces a
collision. Inspiration: playbook two-panel comparison.

<FigureSequence> (3 frames) — the sufficiency construction: sort lengths
{1,2,3,3}; each frame plants the next codeword at the shallowest free node
and greys out its subtree, ending with the finished prefix code. One idea:
shortest-first placement always fits when the budget holds.

<FigureSequence> (3 frames) — the trade-off: shorten one codeword from
length 3 to length 1 across frames; two other codewords forced longer to keep
the budget ≤ 1. One idea: short here means long there.

single <Figure> (component) — McMillan reach: a Venn of code classes
(uniquely decodable ⊃ prefix), with Σ 2^{-l_i} ≤ 1 written across both,
annotated "same length budget — prefix codes give up nothing". One idea: the
bound is not special to prefix codes. Inspiration: Cover & Thomas §5.1/§5.5.

documents.title: Research brief: max-entropy-principle (The maximum entropy principle)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: max-entropy-principle (The maximum entropy principle)
documents.text:
Research brief: max-entropy-principle (The maximum entropy principle)

status: planned
module: applications
type: core
goal: Derive the maximum-entropy distribution under expectation constraints.

Sources to consult

Jaynes 1957, "Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics" (Phys. Rev.
106, 620) — the primary source. §2 "Maximum-Entropy Estimates" (eqs.
2-1–2-15): the principle, the Lagrange-multiplier solution
p_i = exp{-[λ0 + Σ_r λ_r f_r(x_i)]}, the partition function
Z(λ) = Σ_i exp{-Σ_r λ_r f_r(x_i)}, ⟨f_r⟩ = -∂lnZ/∂λ_r, and the variance
formula. §3 (eqs. 3-1–3-8): energy constraint recovers the Boltzmann
distribution and all of equilibrium statistical mechanics. §6: max-ent
is "a method of reasoning", not a law of physics.

Cover & Thomas, ch. 12 "Maximum Entropy" — §12.1 (Theorem 12.1.1: the
max-ent distribution under moment constraints has exponential-family form,
proved via D(p||q) ≥ 0, no calculus of variations) and §12.2 (worked
examples: no constraints → uniform; mean constraint on positive support →
geometric/exponential). Use the C&T proof — it reuses Gibbs' inequality
from the kl-divergence lesson, which is the point of the prerequisite.

Shannon 1948, §20 property 5 — among fixed-variance distributions the
Gaussian maximizes differential entropy: mention as the continuous
counterpart (one paragraph, out of scope with a caveat on differential
entropy's coordinate dependence).

Jaynes 1957, Appendix A — the axiomatic uniqueness of H (link back to
what-is-surprise; do not re-derive).

Key points the lesson must cover

The inference problem: known expectations do not pin down a
distribution. Concrete opener — the Brandeis dice problem: a die averages
4.5 instead of 3.5; infinitely many pmfs on {1..6} have that mean. Which
to adopt?

The principle: adopt the distribution that maximizes entropy subject to
the constraints — the "maximally noncommittal" choice; any other assigns
structure the constraints do not contain (Jaynes §2 phrasing, quoted or
paraphrased precisely).

The solution's form: p(x) = exp(-λ0 - Σ_r λ_r f_r(x)), i.e.
p(x) = exp(-Σ_r λ_r f_r(x)) / Z(λ); the multipliers are tuned so the
constraints hold, ⟨f_r⟩ = -∂lnZ/∂λ_r.

The proof via Gibbs (C&T Theorem 12.1.1 route): for any p satisfying
the constraints and q of the exponential form,
H(p) = -Σ p log p ≤ -Σ p log q = H(q) where the middle equality uses
D(p||q) ≥ 0 and the last equality uses that log q is a linear
combination of the constrained f_r. Full derivation, every step visible.
This is the spiral payoff of kl-divergence.

Worked computation: solve the Brandeis dice numerically — the tilted
distribution p_i ∝ exp(-λ i) with λ chosen so the mean is 4.5 (give the
actual numbers; λ ≈ -0.371, p ranges ≈ .054 to ≈ .348 — recompute, do not
trust these from memory). Check the uniform special case (no constraints,
or mean 3.5 → λ = 0).

Two instances of the same solution: the Boltzmann distribution
p_i ∝ exp(-E_i/kT) (energy expectation constraint; Jaynes §3 — statistical
mechanics as inference, ergodicity not required) and the softmax layer /
exponential-family models in ML (logits as negative constraint functions,
temperature as 1/λ scaling). State both precisely.

What max-ent is and is not (Jaynes §6): a rule for turning partial
information into a distribution without inventing more; the output is only
as good as the constraints fed in.

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

The course assumes no calculus of variations: use the Gibbs-inequality proof
(C&T §12.1), and present the Lagrange route only as a remark for readers who
know multipliers. Jaynes' own derivation is the multiplier one.

Sign conventions differ across sources (λ vs -λ, base e vs base 2).
Fix one convention (natural log for the derivation, convert entropy to bits
at the end) and state it.

Constraints must be satisfiable and non-contradictory; and for some
constraint sets no maximizer exists (C&T §12.3 "anomalous" cases) — flag in
one sentence, out of scope.

The continuous case uses differential entropy, which is coordinate-dependent
and can be negative (Shannon §20 property 8) — do not silently extend the
discrete statements.

Max-ent gives a distribution, not a frequency claim; Jaynes' subjective vs
objective discussion (§4) is beyond scope — one remark at most.

Do not overclaim for physics: the lesson shows the Boltzmann form drops out
of the energy constraint; whether this "founds" statistical mechanics is
Jaynes' argument, attribute it as his.

FIGURE PLAN

<FigureSequence> (4 frames) — the Brandeis dice solved: frame 1 the
uniform die (mean 3.5); frame 2 the constraint stated (mean = 4.5) with
many candidate pmfs sketched; frame 3 the exponential tilt appears
p_i ∝ exp(-λ i); frame 4 λ tuned, final bars with values and H readout.
Delta = one step of the solution per frame. Inspiration: Jaynes §2 applied
to the classic Brandeis example.

single <Figure> (component) — the feasible set schematic: the simplex
of pmfs with the constraint plane cutting it and entropy level sets;
the max-ent point marked where the highest H contour touches the plane.
One idea: constraints leave a set, entropy picks a point.

single <Figure> (component) — the formula dissected:
p(x) = exp(-Σ λ_r f_r(x)) / Z(λ) with labels-above-symbols arrows —
"constrained quantity", "one multiplier per constraint", "normalization =
partition function". Playbook formula-dissection rule.

<FigureSequence> (3 frames) — the Gibbs proof: frame 1 the candidate
p and the exponential q with the same constrained expectations; frame 2
D(p||q) ≥ 0 unpacked into -Σ p log p ≤ -Σ p log q; frame 3 the
right-hand side collapses to H(q) because log q is linear in the
constraints. One idea per frame: why nothing beats the exponential form.

single <Figure> (component) — Boltzmann ≡ softmax: two panels, the
same formula labeled once with physics vocabulary (energy E_i,
temperature, partition function) and once with ML vocabulary (logit,
temperature, normalizer), the shared skeleton highlighted. One idea: one
solution, two fields.

single <Figure> (component) — λ as a tilt dial: three dice pmfs for
λ < 0, λ = 0, λ > 0 (means 4.5, 3.5, 2.5) side by side with H under each;
entropy is maximal at λ = 0 and drops as the constraint bites. Static twin
of the MaxEntDice demo. One idea: the multiplier trades entropy for the
constraint.

documents.title: Research brief: minimum-description-length (Minimum description length)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: minimum-description-length (Minimum description length)
documents.text:
Research brief: minimum-description-length (Minimum description length)

status: planned
module: applications
type: core
goal: Apply two-part code lengths to select a model that neither underfits nor overfits.

Restructure note: kolmogorov-complexity is now a prerequisite lesson. Practical
(computable) MDL is the approximation of the uncomputable ideal — a two-part
Kolmogorov code — so open by recalling that ceiling in one sentence with a
<Ref lesson="kolmogorov-complexity"/> rather than re-motivating it from
scratch.

Sources to consult

Grünwald 2004, "A Tutorial Introduction to the MDL Principle"
(arXiv:math/0406077) — the primary source.

Ch. 1, §1.2 — regularity = compressibility; the three bit-sequences
example (periodic / random / biased) and the polynomial curve-fitting
example (their fig. 1.1).

Ch. 1, §1.3-1.4 — the Crude Two-Part MDL Principle box: minimize
L(H) + L(D|H); why crude L(H) is arbitrary and refined MDL exists.

Ch. 2, §2.2 — the Kraft / codelength-probability correspondence
(L = -log P both ways) — recap territory, reuse from
source-coding-theorem-lite rather than re-teach.

Ch. 2, §2.4 — crude MDL worked on Markov chains / Bernoulli (Ex 2.8:
L(k,θ) + L(D|k,θ) = 2 log k + 1 + k log(n+1) - log P(D|k,θ)), and the
refinement to O(1/√n) parameter precision giving the (k/2) log n form.

Ch. 2, §2.6 — refined MDL / NML and the complexity expansion
COMP_n ≈ (k/2) log(n/2π) + log ∫√|I(θ)| dθ: STATE only, do not derive.

Ch. 2, §2.9.2 and §2.10 — MDL ≠ BIC; failure modes under
misspecification. For the honesty paragraph.

MacKay, ch. 28 "Model Comparison and Occam's Razor" — the Bayesian dual:
P(x) = 2^{-L(x)} makes MDL ≈ Bayesian model comparison; the Occam-factor
picture.

Delétang et al. 2023, §3.3 "Optimal Model-Dataset Size Tradeoff" — the
parameter-adjusted (two-part) compression rate of Transformers; U-shaped
adjusted-rate curves (their fig. 2): optimal model size grows with dataset
size. The modern payoff.

Cover & Thomas, §14.13 (MDL under Kolmogorov complexity) — one-line
pointer only.

Key points the lesson must cover

Regularity = compressibility (concrete opener): three 24-bit strings —
all zeros, a fair-coin string, a biased-coin string — and the length of the
shortest description of each. Structure is what a short description
exploits.

Fit measured in bits: L(D|H) = -log2 P(D|H) — the code-probability
correspondence from the coding module applied to a model: a hypothesis
that assigns the data high probability encodes it cheaply. Recap, not
re-proof (link source-coding-theorem-lite).

The two-part principle: pick H minimizing L(H) + L(D|H). The richest
model always wins on L(D|H) alone (overfitting = maximum likelihood run
amok); the L(H) term is the principled brake. Worked example with actual
numbers: Bernoulli vs higher-order Markov chains on a binary string
(Grünwald Ex 2.8 style), or polynomial degrees on a small dataset —
compute both terms per candidate and exhibit the U-shape.

The (k/2) log2 n parameter cost: a k-parameter model's parameters are
worth encoding only to precision 1/√n (finer precision buys no fit), so
L(H) ≈ (k/2) log2 n — the penalty grows with data size but slower than
the fit term. Derivation at the heuristic level Grünwald §2.4 gives; state
that refined MDL (NML) makes this exact and adds the Fisher-information
term.

Overfitting/underfitting asymmetry (Grünwald §1.6 box): underfit models
pay in L(D|H) forever; overfit models pay a bounded L(H) premium —
and preferring the simpler model at small n is a strategy that works
even when the true source is complex (the increasing-degree example).

The modern payoff (Delétang §3.3): charge a trained network its own
parameter bits and the "adjusted compression rate" becomes U-shaped in
model size — bigger is better only when the dataset amortizes the model;
an MDL correction the raw training loss omits. Connect to the
model-transmission caveat from compression-is-prediction.

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

Crude two-part L(H) is arbitrary — different hypothesis encodings give
different answers; refined MDL (one-part universal codes, NML) repairs this.
State the limitation honestly; this lesson teaches the crude version because
it is computable by hand.

MDL ≠ BIC: the (k/2) log n form matches BIC only for fixed k as
n → ∞ (Grünwald §2.9.2); do not present MDL as "BIC with extra steps".

The hypothesis code must be fixed before seeing the data — an
n-dependent or data-dependent code smuggles the data into L(H) and collapses
to maximum likelihood (Grünwald §2.4.2).

MDL selects among the candidates offered; under misspecification (no
candidate near the truth) it can behave badly (Grünwald §2.10.2) — one
honest sentence.

Two-part coding here is lossless coding of the data given the model —
distinct from lossy compression; do not conflate with rate-distortion.

MDL is not a metaphysical Occam claim ("the world is simple"); it is a
worst-case-regret coding strategy (Grünwald §1.5-1.6). Keep the register
factual.

FIGURE PLAN

single <Figure> (component) — three bit-strings with their shortest
descriptions and description lengths tallied ("repeat 0 ×24" ≪ 24 bits;
fair-coin string ≈ incompressible; biased string in between via its
-log2 P cost). One idea: structure = short description. Inspiration:
Grünwald §1.2.

<FigureSequence> (3-4 frames) — polynomial fits to one fixed scatter:
frame per candidate degree (0, 2, high/interpolating), each frame showing
the curve plus a two-bar tally L(H) / L(D|H); the interpolating frame's
L(H) bar dwarfs its zero fit cost. Delta = one candidate per frame.
Inspiration: Grünwald fig. 1.1 (recreate).

single <Figure> (component) — the U-curve: total L(H)+L(D|H) vs
model complexity k, its two components as thin lines, minimum marked "the
MDL choice". Static twin of the TwoPartCode demo. One idea: the sum turns
over.

single <Figure> (component) — the message diagram: a literal two-part
bitstream [ model bits | data-given-model bits ] for two candidate
models of the same data, total lengths compared. One idea: model selection
= shortest total message. Inspiration: two-part-code definition, Grünwald
§1.3 box.

single <Figure> (component) — the precision argument: a parameter
axis with coarse vs fine grids; finer grid costs log2 (grid size) bits
while the fit gain flattens below spacing 1/√n; annotate the resulting
(k/2) log2 n. One idea: encode parameters only as finely as the data can
see. Inspiration: Grünwald §2.4.2.

single <Figure> (component) — adjusted compression rate vs model size
for two dataset sizes: two U-curves whose minima sit at different model
sizes; raw (unadjusted) rate shown falling monotonically for contrast.
One idea: charging the model its bits moves the optimum with the dataset.
Inspiration: Delétang fig. 2 (recreate schematically, no copied data
points).

documents.title: Research brief: mutual-information (Mutual information)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: mutual-information (Mutual information)
documents.text:
Research brief: mutual-information (Mutual information)

status: planned
module: shared-information
type: core
goal: Compute the mutual information between two variables as the drop in uncertainty.

Sources to consult

Cover & Thomas, §2.3 "Relative Entropy and Mutual Information" (definition
I(X;Y) = Σ p(x,y) log[ p(x,y) / (p(x)p(y)) ] = D( p(x,y) || p(x)p(y) )) and
§2.4 "Relationship Between Entropy and Mutual Information" (Theorem 2.4.1:
I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y), and
I(X;X) = H(X), self-information). Non-negativity I ≥ 0 from §2.6 (Jensen /
information inequality).

MacKay, ch. 8, §8.2 "Mutual information" — the same identities and the area
diagram; MacKay is good on the "information conveyed about X by Y" reading.
Locate §8.2.

Key points the lesson must cover

Definition as a drop in uncertainty: I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y) — the bits
of uncertainty about X removed, on average, by observing Y. Compute directly
from the conditional entropies of the previous lesson.

Symmetry: I(X;Y) = I(Y;X) = H(Y) - H(Y|X) — Y tells you as much about X
as X does about Y. Non-obvious; show via the joint-entropy identity
I = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y).

Divergence form: I(X;Y) = D( p(x,y) || p(x)p(y) ) — mutual information is
the KL divergence between the true joint and the independent product; this is
why I ≥ 0, and why I = 0 exactly iff X and Y are independent
(forward-ref kl-divergence for D ≥ 0).

I(X;X) = H(X): a variable shares its full entropy with itself — hence
entropy is "self-information".

Correlation misses dependence, mutual information does not: an example of
a dependent pair with zero linear correlation (e.g. Y = X^2 on a symmetric X,
or a rotated joint) where corr = 0 but I > 0.

Worked on a 2x2 joint morphing from independent to lockstep (the
MutualInfoDial demo), splitting H(X) into H(X|Y) + I(X;Y) live.

Close with one forward-looking sentence: MI is the working currency of the
applications module (information-bottleneck optimizes it,
infonce bounds it from samples). No content from those lessons here.

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

I(X;Y) ≤ min(H(X), H(Y)) — you cannot learn more about X than X's total
uncertainty. State the bound; equality iff one variable determines the other.

Mutual information is not a distance (the "overlap" in the area diagram is a
helpful picture but for three or more variables the analogous "interaction
information" can go negative — flag as beyond scope).

Zero mutual information means statistical independence, a stronger and
cleaner condition than zero correlation. This is the lesson's headline
(<KeyFact>): "MI is zero only for genuine independence".

Units are bits (same log base as entropy); MI in nats if natural logs used.

Do not confuse I(X;Y) (a single non-negative number) with pointwise mutual
information log[p(x,y)/(p(x)p(y))], which can be negative for individual
pairs. MI is the average of PMI and is ≥ 0.

FIGURE PLAN

single <Figure> (component) — the area diagram completed from the
previous lesson: the H(X)/H(Y) overlap now labeled I(X;Y), with the
three identities (H(X)-H(X|Y), H(Y)-H(Y|X), H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y)) each shown
as a way to read the overlap off the picture. One idea: MI is the overlap.
Inspiration: Cover & Thomas fig. 2.2 (recreate).

single <Figure> (component) — the stacked-bar split: H(X) bar divided
into H(X|Y) (leftover) and I(X;Y) (removed by Y). One idea: observing Y
carves I bits out of H(X). Binds the MutualInfoDial demo.

<FigureSequence> (4 frames) — the dependence dial: joint distribution
morphing independent -> noisy -> coupled -> lockstep, with the I(X;Y) bar
growing from 0 to H(X) each frame while H(X|Y) shrinks to 0. One delta per
frame. Inspiration: the demo's dependence slider.

single <Figure> (component) — MI as divergence-from-independence: the
true joint grid beside the product p(x)p(y) grid, cell-by-cell differences
shaded, labeled I = D(joint || product). One idea: MI measures how far from
independent. Inspiration: Cover & Thomas §2.3.

single <Figure> (component) — correlation blind spot: a scatter/joint of
a dependent pair with corr ≈ 0 but visibly structured, tallying corr = 0
yet I > 0. One idea: correlation is a linear shadow; MI sees the whole
dependence. Warning-color the "corr = 0" to mark the trap.

documents.title: Research brief: neural-coding (Mutual information of a neural code)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: neural-coding (Mutual information of a neural code)
documents.text:
Research brief: neural-coding (Mutual information of a neural code)

status: planned
module: natural-sciences
type: worked-practice
goal: Estimate the information a neural spike code carries about a stimulus.

New worked-application lesson. The first of a two-lesson closing module applying
information measures outside engineering. A neuron is a noisy channel from
stimulus to spike train; mutual information measures what the spikes reveal, and
coding efficiency measures how much of the channel the code uses. Keep it
discrete and computable — the direct method on a small table — and cite the
continuous Gaussian-channel machinery without deriving it.

Sources to consult

Borst & Theunissen 1999, "Information Theory and Neural Coding" (Nat.
Neurosci. 2, 947-957) — the primary source.

General concepts + Box 1-2 — mutual information replacing the tuning
curve; the three decompositions I(R,S) = H(R) - H(R|S) = H(S) - H(S|R) = H(R) + H(S) - H(R,S).

"Calculating information transfer directly" — the direct method:
estimate H(R) and the noise entropy H(R|S) from repeated-trial
(binarized) spike counts, subtract.

Data-processing inequality (p. 949) — why a reconstruction/decoding model
can only lower-bound the true I(S;R) (reuse data-processing-inequality).

Table 2 — the cross-species numbers: bits/second, bits/spike (~1,
range 0.6-3.2), coding efficiency, spike-timing precision. Cite as the
source's measurements, not universal constants.

Box 3 + upper/lower-bound methods — the Gaussian-channel bound
C = ∫ log₂(1 + SNR(f)) df and coherence-based bounds: mention, do not
derive (continuous channel capacity is out of scope).

Cover & Thomas, §2.2-2.4 — the entropy/MI identities reused; §7 for
channel capacity, reused from channel-capacity to define efficiency.

Key points the lesson must cover

A neuron is a noisy channel S → R: stimulus in, spike response out.
Concrete opener: a small stimulus-response joint (e.g. 2 stimuli × a few
spike-count outcomes) with an explicit table.

The direct method: I(S;R) = H(R) - H(R|S), where H(R) is the total
response entropy and H(R|S) the average per-stimulus (noise) entropy.
Compute both from the table, subtract — this is the entropy/conditional-
entropy machinery applied verbatim. Also verify via H(S) - H(S|R).

Bits per spike: divide I(S;R) by the mean spike count; recorded single
neurons land near ~1 bit/spike (Table 2). Every spike is an
information-bearing unit, not just an average-rate carrier.

Coding efficiency = I(S;R) / C, the fraction of the neuron's channel
capacity the code actually uses. Efficiency is strongly stimulus-dependent —
naturalistic stimuli push it up (Table 2's frog-auditory example, ~20% for
noise vs ~90% for a natural call). Reuse channel-capacity for C.

Estimation caveats (honest, precise): finite samples overestimate MI
(entropy estimators are positively biased); MI is only meaningful relative
to a stimulus ensemble; decoding-based estimates only lower-bound the true
MI (data-processing inequality). One paragraph.

The bridge to the rest of the course: the same finite-sample MI-estimation
problem is what InfoNCE (already seen) sidesteps with a sampling bound — one
sentence back-reference.

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

MI estimates from finite data are biased upward; a nonzero MI on shuffled
controls is bias, not signal. State the correction exists (jackknife) without
deriving it.

Information is relative to the stimulus ensemble: absolute bit numbers do
not transfer across experiments; efficiency and bits/spike are the comparable
quantities.

The continuous Gaussian-channel formula is cited, not derived — this course is
discrete. Keep the worked computation on the discrete table.

Bits/spike ~1 is an empirical range across specific preparations (Table 2), not
a law; hedge it as the review does.

A decoder that reconstructs the stimulus gives a lower bound on I(S;R)
(data-processing) — do not present a decoding estimate as the true value.

Do not claim the neuron "chooses" a max-entropy or capacity-achieving code;
efficiency < 1 is the norm.

FIGURE PLAN

single <Figure> (component) — the neuron as a channel: stimulus S →
p(r|s) → spike train R, drawn like the BSC transition diagram from
channel-capacity. One idea: a neuron is a transition table. Inspiration:
Borst & Theunissen fig. 2 (recreate schematically).

<FigureSequence> (3 frames) — the direct method on a small table:
frame 1 the response distribution and H(R); frame 2 the two per-stimulus
rows and the weighted noise entropy H(R|S); frame 3 subtract to I(S;R).
Delta = one step. Inspiration: Box 2 decomposition.

single <Figure> (component) — MI beats the tuning curve: left, a mean±sd
tuning curve that hides overlap; right, the full response distributions per
stimulus with their MI. One idea: variance summaries lose what MI keeps.
Inspiration: Borst & Theunissen fig. 1 (recreate with a synthetic example).

single <Figure> (component) — bits per spike: a short spike train with
the running information tally ticking up ~1 bit per spike. One idea: every
spike carries information. Inspiration: Table 2 bits/spike column.

single <Figure> (component) — coding efficiency: a capacity bar C with
the transmitted I(S;R) shaded inside it, two versions (noise stimulus ~20%,
natural stimulus ~90%). One idea: efficiency depends on the stimulus.
Inspiration: Borst & Theunissen efficiency discussion / Table 2.

single <Figure> (component) — the estimation trap: MI vs sample size,
the raw estimate biased above the true value and decaying toward it, with a
shuffled-control line sitting above 0. One idea: small samples fake
information. Warning-color the bias gap. Inspiration: the review's
finite-sample-bias caveat.

documents.title: Research brief: noisy-channel-coding (The noisy-channel coding theorem)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: noisy-channel-coding (The noisy-channel coding theorem)
documents.text:
Research brief: noisy-channel-coding (The noisy-channel coding theorem)

status: planned
module: channels
type: core
goal: Explain why capacity is the exact threshold between reliable and unreliable communication.

New lesson. The headline theorem of the field: capacity is not a soft trade-off
but a sharp threshold. Below C, error can be driven to zero; above C, error is
bounded away from zero. This is the "explain-level" lesson — state the theorem,
sketch achievability (random coding + joint typicality) and the converse (Fano),
and ground it with the Hamming (7,4) code as a concrete finite construction.

Sources to consult

Shannon 1948, Part II, §13 "The Fundamental Theorem for a Discrete Channel
with Noise" (Theorem 11, the coding theorem and converse; random-coding
argument), §14 (redundancy already in the source helps), §17 (the
Hamming (7,4) single-error-correcting code reaching capacity blockwise).

Cover & Thomas, §7.5-7.7 — definitions of a code/rate, jointly typical
sequences, the channel coding theorem (Theorem 7.7.1) via random coding;
§7.9 "Fano's Inequality and the Converse"; §7.11 "Hamming Codes".

MacKay, ch. 9-10 — §9.6-9.7 statement and intuitive typical-set preview,
ch. 10 the full random-coding + joint-typicality proof and the converse; ch. 1
introduces the (7,4) Hamming code and repetition codes as a first taste.

Polyanskiy & Wu, ch. 14-16 (achievability bounds, Fano converse), ch. 20
§20.3 (dispersion — why the threshold is sharp at finite blocklength).

Arıkan 2009 (arXiv:0807.3917) — one-sentence modern payoff: explicit
capacity-achieving polar codes exist (the 5G lineage). Attribute the 5G
framing to later work, not to Arıkan's paper.

Key points the lesson must cover

Setup: a rate-R blocklength-n code maps 2^{nR} messages to length-n
inputs; decode the noisy output; error = wrong message. The question is which
rates R admit codes with error → 0 as n → ∞.

The theorem (statement): for a discrete memoryless channel of capacity C,
every rate R < C is achievable (codes exist with error → 0) and no rate
R > C is (error bounded away from 0). Capacity is the threshold.

Achievability, sketched (framework-first, then the trick): a single code
is hard to analyze; average over random codebooks. Encode 2^{nR}
messages as random length-n inputs; decode by joint typicality (pick the
message whose codeword is jointly typical with the output). The typical set
has ~2^{nH} members; a wrong codeword is jointly typical only with
probability ~2^{-nI(X;Y)}, and with 2^{nR} competitors the union bound
gives error → 0 when R < I(X;Y), maximized at C. State, do not fully prove.

Converse, via Fano: Fano's inequality H(W|Ŵ) ≤ 1 + Pe·log(2^{nR})
bounds how much the decoder can still not know when it errs; combined with
I(W;Ŵ) ≤ nC (data-processing along the code → channel → decoder chain) it
forces Pe bounded below once R > C. Introduce Fano here; lean on the
data-processing inequality from the prior lesson for I(W;Ŵ) ≤ nC.

A concrete code: the Hamming (7,4) code — 4 data bits, 3 parity bits,
corrects any single-bit error; rate 4/7 ≈ 0.571. Show the parity-check idea
and that it beats naive repetition at the same rate. Note it is one point, not
the theorem.

What the theorem does and does not give: it proves good codes exist
(non-constructively) but the random-coding proof yields no usable code; modern
explicit capacity-achieving codes (LDPC, turbo, polar/Arıkan) close that gap.
One paragraph, precise.

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

Sharp threshold, not a trade-off: below C error vanishes, above C it does
not. The <KeyFact>. Resist "higher rate = more error" gradualism.

The random-coding proof shows existence in expectation: if the average code
is good, some code is at least as good. It names no code.

Blocklength → ∞ is essential; at finite n there is a soft transition
(dispersion). Say the theorem is asymptotic; the demo shows the cliff
sharpening with n.

Fano bounds error from below in the converse; it is not a construction.

The Hamming code is a single finite code at a fixed rate, corrects one error
per block — it does not "achieve capacity" except in Shannon's specific
blockwise-channel sense (§17). Do not overclaim.

Capacity is per channel use; comparing to a source's entropy rate (source-
channel separation) is a further result — one-sentence pointer, out of scope.

FIGURE PLAN

single <Figure> (component) — the coding pipeline: message W →
encoder → length-n channel input → noisy channel → output → decoder → Ŵ, with
rate R = (log #messages)/n labeled. One idea: coding spreads a message over
many channel uses. Inspiration: MacKay ch. 9.1 big-picture diagram.

single <Figure> (component) — the threshold: achievable error vs rate,
a curve pinned near 0 for R < C and rising to a floor for R > C, the wall
at C marked. Static twin of the ChannelCodingThreshold demo. One idea: C is a
cliff. Inspiration: Cover & Thomas coding-theorem region / Polyanskiy §20.

<FigureSequence> (3-4 frames) — joint-typicality decoding: frame 1 the
received y; frame 2 the true codeword sitting in y's jointly-typical shell;
frames 3-4 random wrong codewords, almost all outside the shell, one rare
collision — union-bounded away as n grows. One idea: only the true codeword is
jointly typical. Inspiration: MacKay ch. 10 typicality picture (recreate).

single <Figure> (component) — the converse, schematic: the chain
W → X^n → Y^n → Ŵ with I(W;Ŵ) ≤ nC (data-processing) over it and Fano's
Pe bound underneath, meeting at "R > C ⇒ Pe cannot vanish". One idea:
capacity cannot be crossed. Inspiration: Cover & Thomas §7.9.

single <Figure> (component) — Hamming (7,4): the 4 data bits, 3 parity
bits, and the three overlapping parity circles (the classic Venn), with a
single flipped bit localized by which parities fail. One idea: three checks
pinpoint one error. Inspiration: MacKay ch. 1 / Cover & Thomas §7.11
(recreate the Venn, do not copy).

single <Figure> (component) — random-vs-repetition at rate 4/7: a tally
comparing repetition-code error to the Hamming code's on a BSC, payoff
"structure beats brute redundancy". One idea: how you add redundancy matters.
Inspiration: MacKay ch. 1 error-vs-rate curves.

<FigureSequence> (3 frames) — the cliff sharpening: error-vs-rate for
n = 10, 100, 1000, the transition around C steepening each frame toward a
step. One idea: the sharp threshold is the n → ∞ limit. Inspiration:
finite-blocklength/dispersion (Polyanskiy ch. 20).

documents.title: Research brief: prefix-codes (Prefix codes and code trees)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: prefix-codes (Prefix codes and code trees)
documents.text:
Research brief: prefix-codes (Prefix codes and code trees)

status: planned
module: coding
type: core
goal: Construct a prefix code from a decoding strategy and compute its expected length.

Re-split from the previous pass's merged prefix-codes lesson. That merge
folded the former guessing-games-and-codes and kraft-inequality chapters
into one. Under the removed 15-lesson cap the merge is undone: this lesson owns
the concrete object — a question strategy IS a prefix code, with an expected
length to minimize — and the next lesson (kraft-inequality) proves the
achievability theorem. L4: concrete object first, general theorem after.

Sources to consult

Cover & Thomas, §5.1 "Examples of Codes" — the singular / nonsingular /
uniquely-decodable / prefix (instantaneous) hierarchy and code trees.

MacKay, ch. 5 "Symbol Codes", §5.1 — codeword length as depth in a binary
tree (exactly the question-strategy picture).

MacKay, ch. 4, §4.1 — the "20 questions" / weighing-problem framing that
motivates expected-question-count = expected-codeword-length.

Olah, "Visual Information Theory" (figure inspiration only) — the codeword-
space-as-budget picture; recreate ideas, never the drawing.

Key points the lesson must cover

A yes/no question strategy over a finite outcome set is a binary decision
tree; each outcome sits at a leaf, and its depth = number of questions =
codeword length. Strategy and prefix code are the same object. Open by
building one concretely on {A:.5, B:.25, C:.15, D:.1}.

Prefix (instantaneous) code: no codeword is a prefix of another;
equivalently, outcomes sit only at leaves. This is what makes a
concatenated stream decodable without separators — show the broken tree
(outcome parked at an internal node) and the ambiguous stream it produces.

Expected codeword length L = Σ p(x) len(x), the quantity to minimize.
Compute it for two different codes on the same distribution and compare.

Good strategies split probability mass near in half at each question, so
likely outcomes get short paths — the intuition Huffman will make optimal.

Entropy is the floor H(X) ≤ L: state it here as orientation with a
worked side-by-side (H ≈ 1.74 vs L = 1.75 on the running distribution);
the proof is two lessons on (source-coding-theorem-lite). Do not leak it.

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

Prefix-free is sufficient but not necessary for unique decodability (comma
codes, reversed codes decode too). Kraft/McMillan (next lesson) is why
restricting to prefix codes costs nothing — forward-ref, do not cover here.

Expected length is an average over the distribution, not the number of
leaves; a balanced tree is optimal only for a uniform distribution.

Questions must be fixed before the draw (no adaptive cheating): the tree is
the strategy.

H ≤ L is stated, not proved, in this lesson. Keep the proof out.

Codeword lengths, not the specific 0/1 labels, are what matters; swapping a
node's children relabels codewords without changing lengths or L.

FIGURE PLAN

<FigureSequence> (4-5 frames) — build a question tree on
{A:.5, B:.25, C:.15, D:.1}: each frame adds one question node and routes
outcomes down; final frame labels each leaf with its codeword and depth.
Delta = one node per frame. Inspiration: MacKay's code-tree diagrams (ch. 5).

single <Figure> (component) — the correspondence panel: left, the
decision tree with yes/no questions; right, the same tree relabeled with
0/1 on each branch and codewords at leaves, bracket "depth = codeword
length". One idea: strategy ≡ code. Inspiration: Cover & Thomas §5.1.

single <Figure> (component) — a broken (non-prefix) tree: an outcome
parked on an internal node, its codeword 01 a prefix of leaf 011, the
ambiguous stream 011… annotated in warning color with its two parses. One
idea: leaves only.

single <Figure> (component) — two codes for the same distribution side
by side (a balanced code, lengths {2,2,2,2}, and the matched code
{1,2,3,3}); expected-length tally L = 2.0 vs L = 1.75 under the tally
rule. One idea: matching lengths to probabilities shortens L.
Inspiration: playbook two-panel comparison.

single <Figure> (component) — expected-length vs entropy: the matched
code's L = 1.75 bar beside the entropy H ≈ 1.74 floor, gap called out
"≈ 0.01 bits above the floor". One idea: L is the cost, H the floor
(proved later). Foreshadows source-coding-theorem-lite.

<FigureSequence> (3 frames) — split-near-half heuristic: frame 1 a bad
first question isolating the rarest outcome (unbalanced mass); frame 2 the
good first question splitting mass .5/.5; frame 3 the resulting shorter
L. One idea: balance the mass, not the count.

documents.title: Research brief: rate-distortion (Rate-distortion theory)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: rate-distortion (Rate-distortion theory)
documents.text:
Research brief: rate-distortion (Rate-distortion theory)

status: planned
module: principles
type: core
goal: Compute the rate-distortion function of a source under a fidelity constraint.

New lesson. The third of Shannon's coding theorems (lossless source coding,
channel capacity, lossy source coding) and the direct parent of the information
bottleneck, which generalizes it. It also carries a strong ML payoff: neural
image codecs (Ballé) minimize rate + λ·distortion directly. Placed after
max-entropy and before MDL/IB so the information-bottleneck lesson can open by
naming rate-distortion's flaw (a hand-picked distortion function) and fixing it.

Sources to consult

Shannon 1948, Part V, §27-29 — fidelity criteria reduce to an averaged
pairwise distortion ρ(x, x̂) (§27); the rate is
R_1 = min_{p(x̂|x)} I(x; x̂) subject to a fidelity bound (§28, Theorem 21);
the Gaussian/RMS closed form R = W log(Q/N) (§29). The origin of the field.

Cover & Thomas, ch. 10 "Rate Distortion Theory" — §10.2 definitions,
§10.3.1 the Bernoulli(p) / Hamming result R(D) = H(p) - H(D) for
D ≤ min(p,1-p), §10.3.2 the Gaussian / squared-error result
R(D) = ½ log(σ²/D), §10.4-10.5 converse and achievability. The primary
computational source.

Polyanskiy & Wu, ch. 23-25 — R(D) definition, the two closed forms
(§25.1), the "two nested spheres" packing picture, Blahut-Arimoto (pointer).

Ballé, Laparra & Simoncelli 2017 (arXiv:1611.01704) — the modern payoff:
end-to-end learned image compression as min R + λ·D, the differentiable-
quantization trick, and the exact R-D-objective ↔ VAE equivalence (§3.1).

Tishby et al. 1999, §1-2.1 — one-sentence forward pointer: IB generalizes
rate-distortion by replacing the distortion with a second mutual information.

Key points the lesson must cover

The problem (concrete opener): perfect reconstruction is unnecessary and
expensive. Fix a distortion measure d(x, x̂) (Hamming for bits, squared
error for reals) and a tolerance D; ask for the fewest bits per symbol that
reconstruct within average distortion D.

The rate-distortion function: R(D) = min over test channels p(x̂|x) of I(X;X̂) subject to E[d(X,X̂)] ≤ D. The reconstruction X̂ is a processed
version of X, so I(X;X̂) is the rate — mutual information is the currency
(reuse mutual-information; the DPI applies since X̂ is derived from X).

Endpoints and shape: R(0) = H(X) (lossless, recover source coding as
the D = 0 corner), R(D) decreasing and convex, hitting R = 0 when D is
large enough that a constant reconstruction suffices.

Bernoulli(p) source, Hamming distortion (worked, exact):
R(D) = H(p) - H(D) for 0 ≤ D ≤ min(p, 1-p), else 0. Compute at p = 0.5
(R(D) = 1 - H(D)) and a biased p; check R(0) = H(p) and the zero point. This
is the demo's curve.
