Gaussian source, squared error (worked, stated): R(D) = ½ log₂(σ²/D)
for D ≤ σ², else 0; note this uses differential entropy — flag it as the one
continuous result, stated, and that the difference of differential entropies
(the rate) is coordinate-safe even though differential entropy alone is not.

The modern payoff (Ballé, precise): a learned codec parametrizes the
encoder/decoder as networks and trains min R + λ·D, where R is the entropy
of the quantized latent and D the reconstruction error; λ sweeps the R-D
curve exactly as the Lagrangian here does. Uniform-noise relaxation makes
quantization differentiable; the objective coincides with a VAE loss.

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

X̂ is processed from X: the Markov chain is X → X̂ (a test channel),
not a generative model of X. The DPI applies and I(X;X̂) is the rate.

R(D) is the min of I over test channels satisfying the constraint — a
minimization, unlike capacity's maximization. Contrast the two explicitly (one
minimizes I to compress, the other maximizes I to communicate).

The Gaussian result uses differential entropy; do not silently carry
discrete-entropy intuitions over. It is stated, not derived, and flagged.

R(D) is an achievable limit (achievability + converse), not the performance
of any particular quantizer; real codecs sit above it.

Hamming-distortion R(D) is flat 0 past D = min(p,1-p): once you may err on a
min(p,1-p) fraction, guessing the majority symbol costs no rate. Show it.

Distortion is chosen by the designer — this is exactly the flaw the
information-bottleneck lesson removes. Plant the pointer, do not resolve it.

FIGURE PLAN

single <Figure> (component) — the R(D) plane: rate vs distortion, the
convex R(D) curve, R(0) = H(X) at the left axis and R = 0 where
distortion is free, the achievable region shaded above the curve. One idea:
fewer bits buy more error. Static twin of the RateDistortionCurve demo.
Inspiration: Ballé fig. 2 / Cover & Thomas ch. 10 (recreate).

single <Figure> (component) — the objective dissected:
R(D) = min_{p(x̂|x)} I(X;X̂) s.t. E[d] ≤ D with labels-above-symbols —
"test channel", "rate = mutual information", "fidelity constraint". One idea:
compress = minimize I under a distortion budget. Inspiration: Shannon §28.

<FigureSequence> (3 frames) — the Bernoulli curve built: frame 1 the
lossless corner R(0) = H(p); frame 2 subtract H(D) as D grows; frame 3 the
curve hitting 0 at D = min(p,1-p). Delta = one construction step. One idea:
R(D) = H(p) - H(D). Inspiration: Cover & Thomas §10.3.1.

single <Figure> (component) — capacity vs rate-distortion side by side:
two near-identical panels, C = max I(X;Y) (communicate) and
R(D) = min I(X;X̂) (compress), the changed word (max/min, Y/X̂)
highlighted. One idea: the two extreme points of mutual information.
Inspiration: Cover & Thomas fig. 1.2 / playbook two-panel comparison.

single <Figure> (component) — the neural codec loop: image →
encoder → quantize → entropy code (rate R) → decoder → reconstruction
(distortion D), trained on R + λ·D; the λ dial sweeping the R-D curve. One
idea: the trade-off made trainable. Inspiration: Ballé fig. 1 (recreate,
simplify).

single <Figure> (component) — the Gaussian curve R(D) = ½ log₂(σ²/D):
the log curve over D ∈ (0, σ²], with the "6 dB per bit" annotation (each extra
bit quarters the distortion). One idea: for a Gaussian source, one bit halves
the amplitude error. Inspiration: Cover & Thomas §10.3.2.

documents.title: Research brief: source-coding-theorem-lite (The source coding theorem)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: source-coding-theorem-lite (The source coding theorem)
documents.text:
Research brief: source-coding-theorem-lite (The source coding theorem)

status: planned
module: coding
type: core
goal: Explain why no lossless code can average fewer bits per symbol than the entropy.

Restructure note: prerequisites are now huffman-by-hand and
entropy-as-average-surprise (the Kraft achievability engine moved to its own
kraft-inequality lesson, upstream of Huffman). This lesson also formally
introduces the typical-set concept (the AEP/typical-set argument in point 4),
which the noisy-channel-coding lesson later reuses for joint typicality.

Sources to consult

Cover & Thomas, §5.3 "Optimal Codes" and §5.4 "Bounds on the Optimal
Codelength" — the derivation L ≥ H(X) via the Kraft budget and the
wrong-code / mismatch identity L = H(p) + D(p||q) + (Kraft slack), where
q(x) = 2^{-l(x)} / Σ 2^{-l}. Theorem 5.4.1 gives H(X) ≤ L* < H(X)+1. This
§5.4 identity is the conceptual spine reused in the ML module.

MacKay, ch. 4 "The Source Coding Theorem" — the block-coding version via
the typical set and the asymptotic-equipartition idea (raw vs. essential
bit content, H_delta), showing per-symbol cost -> H as block length grows.
Use MacKay for the "block coding closes the gap" half.

Shannon 1948, Part I, Theorem 9 (the noiseless coding theorem) — the
original statement that H is the achievable limit.

Key points the lesson must cover

Every prefix code implicitly bets on a distribution q(x) = 2^{-l(x)}
(normalized): assigning length l(x) is assigning probability 2^{-l(x)}.
The Kraft budget is why these q sum to ≤ 1.

Expected length decomposes: L = Σ p(x) l(x) = H(p) + D(p||q) + slack.
Since D(p||q) ≥ 0 (Gibbs, forward-ref to kl-divergence) and slack ≥ 0,
L ≥ H(p), with equality only when q = p and lengths are exactly
-log2 p(x) (dyadic case). This is the theorem's lower half.

Achievability: the Shannon code l(x) = ⌈-log2 p(x)⌉ satisfies Kraft and
gives L < H(p)+1 — the same 1-bit gap Huffman achieves.

Block coding closes the gap: coding blocks of n symbols at once spreads
the ≤1-bit overhead over n symbols, so per-symbol cost -> H as n -> ∞
(typical-set argument, stated not fully proved — this is the "lite" version).

Statement of the source coding theorem: the minimum achievable expected
bits per symbol equals the entropy H(X) (entropy rate for sources with
memory, forward-ref entropy-of-english).

Ties the module together: Kraft (achievability of lengths) + entropy (the
floor) = no lossless code beats H.

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

The "bet on q" framing is the load-bearing idea and the bridge to the ML
module — make it explicit, it is where cross-entropy and KL come from.

"Lite" = the block-coding limit is asserted via the typical set, not proven
with full AEP machinery. Say so; do not overclaim a proof.

The bound is on expected length over the true p; a particular message can
be shorter or longer. Lossless, symbol-by-symbol independence assumed for the
single-symbol version.

Distinguish the per-symbol 1-bit overhead of symbol codes from the
vanishing per-symbol overhead of block codes — this is exactly the flaw
Huffman-by-hand left open.

H here is the source's entropy; for sources with dependence the floor is the
entropy rate, lower than the single-symbol H. Flag, defer.

FIGURE PLAN

single <Figure> (component) — "a code is a bet": a codeword-length table
beside the implied q(x) = 2^{-l(x)} bars, next to the true p(x) bars, with
the mismatch highlighted. One idea: lengths are a probability model.
Inspiration: Cover & Thomas §5.4 framing.

single <Figure> (component) — the decomposition L = H(p) + D(p||q)
dissected: a stacked bar, the H(p) floor in one color and the wasted
D(p||q) extra on top, with the label "extra bits from betting wrong". One
idea: cost = floor + mismatch. Forward-binds to kl-divergence.

<FigureSequence> (5 frames) — the block-coding gap shrinking: block size
n = 1,2,4,6,8 on a 0.9/0.1 coin, each frame plots best-achievable
bits/symbol dropping toward the entropy line H ≈ 0.47. This is the
BlockCodingGap demo static; delta = block size per frame. Inspiration: MacKay
ch. 4 typical-set convergence.

single <Figure> (component) — the typical set, schematically: the space
of length-n sequences with a shaded "typical" region of size ~2^{nH} that
carries almost all probability; atypical sequences outside, nearly never seen.
One idea: only 2^{nH} sequences matter, so nH bits suffice. Inspiration:
MacKay's typical-set figure (ch. 4).

single <Figure> (component) — the Shannon code l(x) = ⌈-log2 p(x)⌉:
the real -log2 p values rounded up to integers, the rounding gap shaded, its
total bounded by 1 bit. One idea: rounding costs less than a bit.

single <Figure> (component) — module capstone: a number line with H
marked as a hard wall, Huffman/Shannon codes landing in [H, H+1), and block
codes converging onto H from the right. One idea: H is the floor nothing
crosses.

documents.title: Research brief: thermodynamics-of-information (Thermodynamics of information)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: thermodynamics-of-information (Thermodynamics of information)
documents.text:
Research brief: thermodynamics-of-information (Thermodynamics of information)

status: planned
module: natural-sciences
type: core
goal: Explain Landauer's principle and compute the work bound of a Szilard engine.

New lesson closing the course. It gives Shannon's entropy a physical price and
closes the entropy concept's spiral at its deepest level: a bit is not just a
coding unit but a thermodynamic quantity worth kT ln 2 of work. It pairs with
max-entropy-principle (the two physics faces of the theory) and pays off the
mutual-information machinery via the feedback second law, where measured
information enters as I(X;M).

Sources to consult

Parrondo, Horowitz & Sagawa 2015, "Thermodynamics of Information" (Nat. Phys.
11, 131-139) — the primary review.

Maxwell's demon — the apparent second-law violation and its setup.

Szilard engine — one molecule, a measured bit, reversible isothermal
expansion extracting W = kT ln 2.

Landauer's principle — erasing/overwriting one bit dissipates at least
kT ln 2; logical vs thermodynamic irreversibility.

Bennett's resolution — the demon's memory reset pays back exactly what
the engine extracted; the full cycle obeys W_total ≥ 0.

Feedback second law (Sagawa-Ueda) — W ≥ ΔF - kT (ln 2) I(X;M):
measured information is a thermodynamic resource priced in bits of mutual
information (reuse mutual-information).

Jaynes 1957 (already the max-entropy source) — one back-reference: Boltzmann's
H and Shannon's H are the same functional; statistical mechanics as inference.

Landauer 1961 and Bennett 1982 — the original results the review synthesizes;
cite as primaries in References.

Key points the lesson must cover

Shannon entropy is thermodynamic entropy in different units: physical
entropy S = k_B ln W and Shannon H = -Σ p log p are the same functional;
one bit of Shannon entropy is k_B ln 2 of thermodynamic entropy. Concrete
opener: the conversion, 1 bit ↔ k_B ln 2 ≈ 9.6 × 10⁻²⁴ J/K.

Landauer's principle: erasing one bit — resetting a two-state memory to a
known value regardless of its prior state — reduces the memory's entropy by
k_B ln 2, so at temperature T it dissipates at least kT ln 2 of heat
(≈ 2.8 × 10⁻²¹ J at room temperature). Computation, with the number.
Logical irreversibility (erasure) forces the cost; a reversible copy does not.

The Szilard engine (worked): one molecule in a box, a partition inserted,
a measurement of which side it is on (one bit), then reversible isothermal
expansion against the partition extracts W = kT ln 2 of work per cycle. One
measured bit is worth exactly kT ln 2.

Maxwell's demon and its resolution: the demon seems to extract work from
thermal noise forever, violating the second law. Bennett's resolution: the
demon's memory must be reset to measure again, and that erasure costs kT ln 2
by Landauer — exactly the extracted work. The full cycle obeys the second law;
W_total ≥ 0. Information is the missing bookkeeping entry.

The feedback second law (the mutual-information payoff): with measurement,
the work bound generalizes to W ≥ ΔF - kT (ln 2) I(X;M), where I(X;M) is
the mutual information between the system state X and the measurement outcome
M. Better measurements (more bits of I) license more extractable work. This
is the same mutual information the course built, now a physical resource.

Why it matters (precise, not hand-wavy): Landauer's bound is a hard floor
on the energy cost of irreversible computation — every erased bit in a chip
has a thermodynamic minimum cost, approached by recent experiments. Cite the
review's experimental confirmation (optical-trap bit erasure) in one sentence.

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

Landauer's cost is for erasure (logical irreversibility), not for
computation in general; reversible operations have no such floor. Keep the
distinction (erasing ≠ writing ≠ copying).

kT ln 2 uses natural log because it is k_B × (entropy in nats); the
"one bit" factor is the ln 2 converting bits to nats. State the unit bridge
carefully (ties back to the surprisal units discussion).

The demon does not violate the second law; the naive paradox omits the
memory-reset cost. Do not present it as an open puzzle.

The feedback second law's sign convention and the direction of I(X;M) follow
the review; derive the bound's meaning, do not just quote a formula.

This is a lower bound on dissipated heat / an upper bound on extractable
work — real devices sit well above the Landauer floor. Do not claim current
hardware runs at the limit.

Shannon ↔ thermodynamic entropy equality is a statement about the same
functional, made precise by Jaynes; attribute the "statistical mechanics as
inference" reading to him, one remark.

FIGURE PLAN

single <Figure> (component) — the units bridge: one bit shown as
H = 1 bit (Shannon) and ΔS = k_B ln 2 (thermodynamic), a labeled
conversion arrow × k_B ln 2. One idea: entropy is one quantity, two units.
Ties back to the surprisal units strip.

<FigureSequence> (4 frames) — the Szilard cycle: frame 1 one molecule in
a box; frame 2 partition inserted; frame 3 measurement records which side
(one bit); frame 4 reversible expansion extracts W = kT ln 2. Delta = one
step. One idea: a measured bit is worth kT ln 2. Inspiration: Parrondo et
al. Szilard figure (recreate — this is the field's canonical diagram).

single <Figure> (component) — Landauer erasure: a double-well potential
(two memory states) collapsed to a single well (reset), the freed entropy
k_B ln 2 leaving as heat Q ≥ kT ln 2, with the room-temperature number.
One idea: forgetting a bit costs heat. Inspiration: Parrondo et al. bistable-
potential figure (recreate).

<FigureSequence> (3 frames) — the demon's balance sheet: frame 1 demon
measures + extracts kT ln 2; frame 2 demon's memory fills (books unbalanced,
apparent violation); frame 3 memory reset pays kT ln 2 back, W_total = 0.
One idea: the reset closes the loophole. Inspiration: Bennett's resolution /
Parrondo feedback-cycle figure.

single <Figure> (component) — the feedback second law dissected:
W ≥ ΔF - kT (ln 2) I(X;M) with labels-above-symbols — "free-energy change",
"measured information", "the bits you gathered buy this much extra work". One
idea: mutual information is a physical resource. Inspiration: Sagawa-Ueda
result as stated in the review.

single <Figure> (component) — the two physics faces: a small panel
pairing max-entropy (Boltzmann p ∝ e^{-E/kT}) with Landauer (a bit costs
kT ln 2), both labeled "Shannon H = thermodynamic S". One idea: the course's
entropy is the physicist's entropy. Inspiration: Jaynes 1957 / course spiral.

documents.title: Research brief: what-is-surprise (Surprisal)
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Research › Research brief: what-is-surprise (Surprisal)
documents.text:
Research brief: what-is-surprise (Surprisal)

status: retrofit
module: foundations
goal: Compute the surprisal of an event from its probability.

This lesson was drafted before the dossier existed. This brief records what the
existing draft already covers, then what a density-upgrade revision should add.
It is not a rewrite spec — the argument and the numbers below are already
correct in the draft.

Sources to consult

Shannon 1948, Part I, §6 "Choice, Uncertainty and Entropy" — the
logarithmic measure of information and its motivation (additivity over
independent choices). This is the primary anchor.

MacKay, ch. 2, §2.4 — "Shannon information content" defined as
h(x) = log2 (1/p(x)); note MacKay's lowercase-h notation for the per-symbol
content versus H for the ensemble average.

Cover & Thomas, §2.1 — entropy is defined directly; surprisal appears as
the summand log 1/p(x). No standalone "surprisal" section, so use it only
for the definition and the E[log 1/p] framing.

Hartley 1928 — historical, for the units paragraph (the base-10 hartley).

Key points the lesson must cover (already in the draft)

Information content is a property of the reported event's probability,
not of message length or wording (sunrise vs. Cairo-snow contrast).

Two constraints on any candidate f(p): f(1)=0, and f strictly
decreasing. These alone underdetermine the form (draft shows 1-p and
1/p - 1 both pass and both fail additivity).

The additivity axiom over independent events, f(pq)=f(p)+f(q), reduces
to Cauchy's functional equation via g(t)=f(e^{-t}); continuity forces
f(p) = -c log p. This is the load-bearing derivation.

Definition: I(x) = -log2 p(x), in bits; I=0 at p=1,
I -> infinity as p -> 0.

Units: bits (base 2), nats (base e), hartleys (base 10) as a change of
measurement unit only; conversion factors 1 nat = log2 e ≈ 1.443 bits.

Composite events: additivity holds only for independent events; the
general case is the conditional decomposition
I(A∩B) = I(A) + I(B|A); disjoint events fail it the other way.

ML tie-in: surprisal = negative log-likelihood loss on one example; the
log-domain also fixes floating-point underflow.

What a density-upgrade revision should add

The draft has only 2 figures for a ~1900-word chapter; the norm is 6-12
per 1000 words. Add 3-5 small single-idea visuals (see FIGURE PLAN). This is
the main gap.

A <KeyFact> (rose) one-liner stating the punchline — "information is
-log2 p, and additivity is the only reason it is a log" — currently the
chapter has no rose callout.

A <Task> (green) tied to the SurprisalSlider demo naming what to watch
(drag p across a decade, watch surprisal rise by a fixed 3.32 bits per
factor-of-10). The demo is present but has no instruction callout.

Promote the units conversion into a small table figure rather than an inline
display equation.

Pitfalls / subtleties to flag

Surprisal is defined per event, not per random variable (the draft's
closing Remark — keep it; it sets up the entropy lesson).

The constant c is exactly the choice of log base; there is no further
freedom. Do not present base-2 as "natural" — it is a unit choice.

-log2 p is undefined at p=0; surprisal of an impossible event is not
"infinite information", it is undefined (the 0 log 0 convention is an
entropy-lesson concern, not here).

Corpus letter frequencies are estimates, not constants (draft already says
this — keep it, QA flags unhedged frequency claims).

FIGURE PLAN

rarity.svg (exists, single <Figure>) — three events ordered by

documents.title: Surprisal
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Surprisal
documents.text: Information content of one event: -log2 p, in bits

documents.title: Entropy
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Entropy
documents.text: Expected surprisal of a distribution

documents.title: Prefix code
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Prefix code
documents.text: A code where no codeword is a prefix of another, decodable without separators; equivalently, outcomes sit only at the leaves of a binary code tree

documents.title: Kraft inequality
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Kraft inequality
documents.text: Codeword lengths L_i are achievable by a prefix code iff sum of 2^-L_i <= 1; McMillan extends the bound to all uniquely decodable codes

documents.title: Huffman coding
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Huffman coding
documents.text: Greedy construction of an optimal prefix code by merging least likely symbols

documents.title: Source coding theorem
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Source coding theorem
documents.text: Lossless codes need at least H(X) bits per symbol on average, and block codes can get arbitrarily close

documents.title: Typical set
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Typical set
documents.text: The ~2^{nH} long sequences of near-average surprisal that together carry almost all the probability of a source

documents.title: Conditional entropy
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Conditional entropy
documents.text: Average uncertainty H(X|Y) left in X after observing Y

documents.title: Mutual information
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Mutual information
documents.text: Bits of uncertainty about one variable removed by knowing another: I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y)

documents.title: Data-processing inequality
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Data-processing inequality
documents.text: If T depends on Y only through X (Y -> X -> T), then I(T;Y) <= I(X;Y): processing cannot create information

documents.title: Entropy rate
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Entropy rate
documents.text: Per-symbol entropy of a source given unlimited context, in the long-sequence limit

documents.title: Channel capacity
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Channel capacity
documents.text: The largest mutual information a channel p(y|x) admits over input distributions: C = max_p(x) I(X;Y), in bits per channel use

documents.title: Noisy-channel coding theorem
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Noisy-channel coding theorem
documents.text: Reliable communication is achievable at every rate below capacity C and impossible above it

documents.title: Fano's inequality
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Fano's inequality
documents.text: A lower bound on error probability in terms of conditional entropy, H(X|Y) <= 1 + Pe log(|X|-1); the engine of the coding-theorem converse

documents.title: KL divergence
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › KL divergence
documents.text: Expected extra bits per symbol from coding true distribution p with a code built for q

documents.title: Cross-entropy
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Cross-entropy
documents.text: Expected bits per symbol when events from p are coded with q's code: H(p,q) = H(p) + KL(p||q)

documents.title: Kolmogorov complexity
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Kolmogorov complexity
documents.text: The length of the shortest program that prints a string; the ultimate, uncomputable compression limit, defined up to an additive constant

documents.title: Maximum entropy principle
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Maximum entropy principle
documents.text: Given expectation constraints, adopt the entropy-maximizing distribution; it is exponential in the constrained quantities

documents.title: Rate-distortion function
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Rate-distortion function
documents.text: The least rate for lossy coding within a fidelity bound: R(D) = min over p(x-hat|x) of I(X;X-hat) subject to expected distortion <= D

documents.title: Minimum description length
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Minimum description length
documents.text: Model selection by minimizing total code length L(H) + L(D|H): model bits plus data-given-model bits

documents.title: Information bottleneck
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Information bottleneck
documents.text: Encoder objective minimizing I(X;T) - beta I(T;Y): compress X while preserving information about a target Y

documents.title: InfoNCE bound
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › InfoNCE bound
documents.text: Contrastive N-way classification loss whose value bounds mutual information: I(X;Y) >= log2 N - L_N

documents.title: Coding efficiency
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Coding efficiency
documents.text: The fraction of a channel's capacity a code actually uses: information transmitted divided by capacity

documents.title: Landauer's principle
documents.breadcrumb: Information Theory › Concepts › Landauer's principle
documents.text: Erasing one bit of information dissipates at least kT ln 2 of heat, giving Shannon information a physical, thermodynamic price
